CHAIN GANG. The Con- 
sumer Product Safety Com- 
mission is going after bicycle 
retailers in southern Califor- 
nia because many of them al- 
legedly have removed chain 
guards from ‘‘motorcross”’ 
bikes prior to sale, a violation 
of the commission’s safety 
standards. Retailers are crim- 
inally liable for deliberate al- 
terations and will be responsi- 
ble for recalling. 


CLOSED. Jefferson has 
closed the former J. B. Hunt- 
er store in Rochester, N.Y., 
which it acquired as part of a 
package earlier this year from 
Allied Stores. Jefferson ex- 


ecutives said that a single 
store in the market was not 
cost effective and that the 
chain, involved with other ex- 
pansion projects, did not wish 
to tie up additional resources 
in Rochester.

Another result of the highly publicized buy 
may be atemporary tightening of the second- 
ary market in branded or designer apparel, 
making it more difficult for apparel discount- 
ers to get current merchandise. The confron- 
tation is the latest in a series of skirmishes 
between discounters and conventionals, 
which began several years ago when chains 
like Target and Two Guys began to promote 
Brittania and Levi jeans. 

Target boosted its image and built traffic 
when it advertised the $35 Klein, Vanderbilt 
and Sasson originals for $19.99. But the ad, 
which ran in Minneapolis, Dallas, Houston, 
St. Louis, Denver and Colorado Springs, 
broke one of the unwritten rules of apparel 
discounting. Most apparel discounters np 
low profile and advertise only “famous maker 
labels.” 

“These are the same jeans sold for $35 
elsewhere, not discontinued styles or close- 
outs,” the ad said. “We purchased 21,000 pairs 
and when they’re gone, there will be no 
more.” The jeans quickly sold out—report- 
edly within three to four hours in some stores 
and within a week chainwide. 

The three manufacturers contacted by Dis- 
count Store News pointed out, “We don’t sell 
to discount stores,” and suggested Target 
was selling stolen merchandise. (Sasson ac- 
knowledged the recent Supreme Court ruling 
that vendors may limit distribution for rea- 
sons other than price. Usually an upstairs 
supplier blames supply problems in order to 
avoid the discount market. )

firmed an “active investigation into a possible

Nationwide DSN Report 

Three major ammunition 
cost increases this year coupled 
with the rising cost of firearms 
are a growing concern among 
buyers who, nonetheless, re- 
main optimistic about sales to 
die-hard hunting enthusiasts 
for the upcoming season. 

A tourth ammunition cost in- 
crease, in July, was rescinded, 
but with three boosts of 4%-&% 
each, buyers are predicting 
that hunters will cut down on 
practice shots. 

“Instead of buying two or 
three boxes to allow for prac- 
tice, the customer will buy one 
or two. But he won’t stop hunt- 
ing because the price of shells 
goes up,” suggested a spokes- 
man for Murphy’s Mart. “How- 
ever, hunters might put off 
purchases of new guns.” 

But, in the words of one 
buyer, “hunting is still the 
Christmas of sporting goods.” 
The category is responsible for 
up to 80% of all winter sporting 
goods business and may ac- 
count for 40%-45% of all sport- 
ing goods volume for discount- 
ers. 

Seasons, types of hunting 
and regulations vary widely by 
state, even in the same region, 
and stores must be stocked ac- 
cordingly. But chains nation- 
wide depend on high-margin 
accessories such as shell belts 
and gun slings—preferably 
bought direct—to maintain 
overall hunting margins of 
about 30%. 

Many chains promote fire- 
arms, shells, bows and accesso- 
ries as early as the end of July, 
but the first big thrust is in- 
cluded in back-to-school promo- 
tions. Marlin Glenfield .22 rifles 
are the most widely promoted, 
with chains including Magic 
Mart, Meijer’s, Murphy’s Mart, 
S. E. Nichols and Ayr-Way ad- 
vertising price points at 
$45-$55. 

Black powder rifles have be- 
come a regional category after 
an upsurge stimulated by the 
Bicentennial. A spokesman for

States was having domes-

Europeans continue to talk 
about is the decline in produc- 
tivity in the United States. 

It was particularly shocking 
in April of 1979 to note, among 
major industrialized nations, 
that productivity gains in the 
United States were below 
those of Great Britain.

Throughout history, a stable

If today’s middle class is rel-

GOLDEN OLDIES. The current 
Housewares PMA is a collection 
of familiar products. In fact, only 
four items have broken onto the 
list and promotional products 
also showed weakness in mid- 
summer. Staples were the 
strongest performers with 48% 
of the 150 spots and stepped-up 
housewares also did well as 
consumers seemed willing to 
spend a little more for higher 
quality. (P. 14)

glectea, reordering is a key 
component of any merchandis- 
ing plan. Types of merchandise, 
replenishment factors and 
methods are discussed to help 
clarify reordering techniques. 
(P. 12) 


GREAT OUTDOORC. Camping 


and hunting dominate the 


Sporting Goods PMA for the 
mid-July to mid-August period. 
Half of the top 50 dollar pro- 
ducers are in the camping or 
BB/pellet gun categories while 
retailers filling the ammunition 
pipeline for the fall hunting sea- 
son put 11 related products onto 
the list. (P. 13) 


PRODUCTIVE SECURITY. 
Bob Curtis continues his seven- 
part series on increasing the 
productivity of store detectives, 
examining the process of hiring 
and screening prospective se- 
curity officers. Tips for choosing 
the right people for the job are 
part of this issue's installment. 
(P. 24) 


FALL BUILDUP. Retailers were 
stocking up for fall in August, the 
results of the Hardware PMA in- 
dicate. While cautious of being 
overstocked, due to economic 
fears, chains have increased 
the dollar volume of power tool 
orders significantly. (P. 22)

Dec. 31, 1978 and a book value of 
about $11 a share, was trading 
in the $17-$19 range at press- 
time. There are 6,475,665 
shares outstanding. 

A $20-$30 price for Heck’s 
stock would be within the pre- 
mium of other recent retail ac- 
quisitions. It would mean that 
the acquiring company would 
have to pay $130 million to $194 
million for Heck’s, which had 
$285,935,791 in sales and 
$10,049,465 in net income in fis- 
cal 1978. 

The $17-319 price for Heck’s 
stock is a high that reflects Wall 
Street's expectation that the 
discounter will be acquired. Be- 
fore Heck’s interest in being ac- 
quired was acknowledged by 
Haddad, the company’s stock 
was trading in the $11 range. 
Last vear Heck’s stock ranged 
from $8 to $14.50. 

Heck’s is among the most 
profitable discounters as mea- 
sured by net income as a per- 
centage of sales. DSN’s ranking 
in the 1979 80 Census issue had 
Hecks in second place with net 
income as 3.77 of sales. 

The other brokerage house 
looking for a buver for Heck’s is 
Merrill Lynch’s White Weld 
Capital Markets Group. 


Shifting Gears 


The decision of Heeks man- 
agement—and particularly of 
Haddad—to look fora carmNpusrty 
vo acquire or merge with the 


discounter is a major change in 
Heck’s growth thrust. In the 
past. the company has ag- 
gressively acquired other 
firms. Its business activities to- 
day include specialty store re- 
tailing, wholesaling and sale 
and lease of off-the-road vehi- 
cles and heavy construction 
equipment. 

Haddad, who has been the 
kev executive with Hecks since 
he helped found the company 1n 
1959, said that he would con- 
tinue with the chain after an 
acquisition, but that such a 
move would give him a chance 
to relax a little. 

Haddad’s direction of Heck’ 
has been marked by its aggres- 
sive acquisition program—the 
discounter has 10 subsidiary 
companies—and by a lean ad- 


| ministration with just a few 
| longstanding top executives. 


While Heck’s has 10 subsid- 
iarv companies, none of the of- 
ficers of these firms are listed 
as either directors or officers of 
the parent. 

The complete dominance of 


' executives associated with 


| Heck’s discount stores in the 
| company’s top management de- 
' notes both the overwhelming 
| impact that the discount stores 
_ have on the parent’s finances 

and Heck’s method of acquiring 
firms which is to mainly use 
cash and thereby limit the dilu- 
tion of the common stock. 

In the fiscal vear ended Dec. 
31, 1978, Heck’s discount stores 
generated $180.7 million in 
sales or 62.7% of total corporate 
revenues. In the previous fiscal 
vear the discounter stores pro- 
duced $147.7 million in sales. 

Discount stores sales went 
up 22.3% but accounted for a 
smaller portion of total reve- 
nues because of the infusion of 
$22.6 million in sales from the 
Kelsway Corp..

Home improvement and au- 


tomotive accessory de ‘part- 
ments were the most consistent 
sales producers for discount 


stores last year, according to 
79 Mass 


statistics in the 1978- 
Retailers’ Merchunciater Re-

Mass Retailing Institute. 

The report breaks out sales

sales accounting period, giving 
the percentage of department

periods (of four or five weeks 
duration). 

Sales in home improvement 
departments ranged from a low 
of 5.7% in the first period (Feb- 
ruary) to a high of 11.1% in the 
period that cor responds rough- 
ly with September, showing the 
least seasonality of all depart- 
ments measured. 

Auto accessory sales were al- 
most as consistent during the 
year, ranging netween 4.8% (in 


February) and 10.4% (in De- 
cember). 

Basie apparel items proved 
their year-long appeal, as bras 
and foundations; blouses, 
sweaters, and sports, leisure 
and beach wear, and infants’ 
clothing all showed sales per- 
centage ranges lower than 9.2 
percentage points (see chart).

within the infants’ wear cate- 
gory made the department's 
sales even more consistent. 


Nonseasonal sales of such items 
as high chairs, cribs, playpens 
and car beds flattened out the 
peaks and valleys, reducing the 
percentage variation to &.5 
points. 

Books recorded more than 
14% of their sales during the 
period that coincides (roughly) 
with December, reflecting the 
giftability of hardcover edi- 
tions. The lowest sales period 
for the book department was 
5.8%, in February, and the vari- 


ance of only &.6 percentage 
points makes books one of the 
most consistent sellers. 

Two other basic departments 
—housewares and paint—were 
also among the 10 most consis- 
tent departments, with no 
more than 9.5 percentage 
points variation between the 
best-selling period and the 
slowest. Paint peaked in the 
summer months, (when DIYers

1st Jefferson on Fla. W. Coast 
Gets Warm Sales Reception 


FORT MYERS, Fla. 
Jefferson has opened its first 
store on the west coast of Flor- 
ida, surprising even itself with 
the initial acceptance in the 
new market. 

“If we continue at this rate.” 
said store manager Bill Allen a 
week after the opening, “we'll 
do our first month’s sales pro- 
jections in the first two weeks.” 

While Allen and headquar- 
ters executives would not re- 
veal the first week’ sales, other 
sources at the chain reported 
that the Fort Mvers store ex- 
ceeded $500,000 in that period. 

The store, located on Colo- 
nial Read less than a mile from 
Route 41—the Tamiami Trail 
which is the major highway 
through the citv—is sur- 
rounded by major competitors 
within a mile radius. Other 
mass merchandisers nearby in- 
clude a Woolco, K mart and a 
Gibson’s and conventional de- 
partment store chains in a mall 
almost adjacent to the new 
store are Sears, Penney and 
Burdine’s. 

The new Jefferson, with 
135,000 sq. ft. of total area and 
approximately 95,000 sq. ft. of 
selling space includes several 
new wrinkles for the chain. One 
major change is a much larger 
stockroom than previous 
Jefferson stores. 

Located on the second floor 

the rear of the building adja- 
cent to the office area, the 
stockroom has almost 20,000 
sq. ft. of storage space, Allen 
sad. 

“Our previous stores were all 
clustered on the east coast near 
the distribution center in 
Miami,” Allen said. ‘We're a 
three-hour drive from Miami so 
it was decided to give us more 
storage area than stores closer 
to Miami would have.” 

The Fort Mvers store also 
has a department similar to 
that in other stores but which

Wine Cellar.” In other

known as the gourmet shop 
and, in addition to wine, carries 
steaks, fruit (main'y for tou

anges and grapefruits), bulk 
candy and snacks. 

“We have never really done 
too much in the way of ‘gourmet 
food’ so that name really wasn't 
appropriate for the depart- 
ment,” Allen said. “However, 
we doa great business In wine 
and all the stores will even- 
tually switch to that name.” 

Like other Jeffersons, all 
merehandise departments are 

company owned, as Is the 

taurant. The only leased de- 
partment is the optical center, 
which is located in the front of 
the store to the left of the main 
entrance across from the cus- 
tomer service desk in an alcove 
leading to the restaurant.

Begins Full-scale 
Wanding Program 


MIiAMI—Jetlerson has be- 
come the first major Mass Mer- 
chandiser to begin full-scale 
implementation of wanding— 
automated point of sale termi- 
nals. 

Accor ding to Fred Heard. 
Jefferson’s vice presideit of 
systems, all 12 Florida stores 
will have = ids installed at all 
terminals by the end of the fall 
and the chain’s stores in north- 
ern markets will have the hard- 
ware installed within two 
vears. 

The installation of wands— 
hand-held scanners—com- 
pletes Jefferson's modern elec- 
tronic inventory Management 
system. Prior to the conver- 
sion, Which has been completed 
in the Hialeah store and the 
new Fort Mvers unit, sales in- 
formation was fed daily from 
the store terminals to a central 
computer, but was f into the 
terminals manually by cash- 
ers.

so We Were gettine the inven- 
tory information. The benefit 
with wanding will be that the 
information will be more accu- 
rate,” Heard explained.

sibility of cashier error in ring- 
ing up the price, which will have 
a financial impact. But there is

Wanding Program 


(Continued from page 3) 
same time making a small re- 
duction in the number of cash- 
iers. If you can have 10 people 
using wands handle the flow 
that 20 could do manually, 
maybe vou cut back to 15,” he 
said. 

While Heard would not dis- 
close the cost of,converting the 
stores to wanding, he estimates 
that pavback will be achieved 
within two vears. Besides the 
wanding hardware itself, the 
terminals memory has to be 
upgraded by 50% to accommo- 
date the new tasks. Each store 
has about 30 terminals. 


No Added Cost 


Heard said, however, that 
there was virtually no addi- 
tional cost in preparing the spe- 
cially printed price tickets. 
“You have to put a ticket on any- 
way and the characters are legi- 
ble both to the optical character 
reader and to the human eve.” 

Jefferson is using a system 
made bv Recognition Products 
Inc., and a tvpe font known as 
OCR-A. Virtually all merchan- 
dise is ticketed with the OCR-A 
characters so that eashiers 
rarely must ring up sales man- 
ually. According to Heard, for 
wanding to be effective, at least 


| 75% of the merchandise must 


be tagged so that the scanner 
can automatically read the 
ticket. 


Major Difference 


The major difference be- 
tween this tvpe of wanding and 
the scanners used in supermar- 
kets is that supermarket-type 
scanners read Universal Prod- 
uct Code (UPC) markings, 
which are printed on the items 
by the manufacturers and 
which are not legible to custom- 
ers. With OCR-A wanding, the 
retailer typically puts on his 
own tags, which are clearly 
readable. While one pass over a 
(UPC) seanner records the 
product information, wands 
must be passed over each line of 
information on the ticket. 

In Jefferson’s case, three 
lines are printed on each ticket, 
department identification, sku 
number and price. Sale items 
have a red tag pasted over the 
price line on the bottom and 
while the first two lines can be 
read by the wand, sale prices 
must be rung manually. 

Since last December, ail 
stores have had tickets printed 
with OCR-A characters al- 
though the wands were in- 
stalled in Hialeah only in July, 
with Fort Myers opening last 
month.

In fishing equipment, retail- 

ers filling in their depleted 

stock of basic outfits pushed 
nine rod-and-reel combinations 
onto the top 50 list, including 
seven Zebco outfits and two 
Daiwa sets. 

Zebco’s 2490, 3790, 1245, 
1545, 3490, 1515 and 8040 com- 
binations appeared on the top 
50 list, in that order, and 
Daiwa’s 208RL/1330P spincast 
combination and MC1-38 
MC2-38 minicast combination 
also made the top 50. 

Crosman led the way among 
BB and pellet guns, placing 
nine different products on the 
list. Daisy had two lines in the 
top 50, and the Marksman 
MPR/1010 also made it. 

Crosman’s 760 rifle finished 
in eighth place among the top 
dollar movers, followed closely 
by the CO-2 powered 5073 ri- 
fle. Powerlets for the CO-2 rifle 
finished 13th, followed by the 
1377 nistol, the 766 rifle, the 
38T revolver, the 2200 pellet ri- 
fle and the pellet dispenser, 
which made the top 50 retail 
dollar movers in spite of its low 
(63¢) average ticket. 

Three Spalding basket- 
balls—the Dr. J, Rick Barry 
and Swisher models—finished 
in second, llth and 39th respec- 
tively. The Dr. J. model, with 
$19,437 in retail sales during 
the period, was the leader. 


Canister-Packed Soft 
Drinks Lap Up Sales 


Canister-packed non- 
carbonated soft drinks are 
one of the hottest consum- 
able categories. 

The national market at 
retail of more than $500 
million in such products as 
Kool-Aid, Country Time, 
Wyler’s and Hawaiian 
Punch powdered drink 
mixes lends itself ideally 

to high-profile, self-ser- 
vice merchandising. The 
nationally known brand 
names aid in promotions, 
pulling traffic into the 
stores when featured (as 
they are frequently) on the 
front of inserts and circu- 
lars. 

Canisters—in 8- and 
12-qt. sizes—have cap- 
tured more than 80% of 
the market, and the popu- 
lar soft drinks are becom- 
ing less of a summer 
seasonal line, although 
the April- September pe- 
riod still moves approx- 
imately 65% of the total. 

Most popular flavor? 
Lemonade, far and away, 
which gets 42% of the 
business. Other flavors, in 
order of their popularity, 
are punch, grape, cherry, 
strawberry, orange and 
raspberry.

cooky sheet with a nonstick 
finish at $2.69 (No. 49).

the glassware and cookware 
categories denotes the con- 
sumer demand for value and 
quality and shoppers’ readiness 
to buy this merchandise.

Alexander's Acquires 
Margo’s La Mode Chain 


NEW YORK—Alexander's 
has completed its acquisition of 
Margo's La Mode, a 72-unit ap- 
parel specialty chain in the 
South and Southwest, for 
$9,454,246. 

Margo’s La Mode will be a 
wholly owned subsidiary of 
Alexander's Holding Corp., 
which is wholly owned by Alex- 
ander'’s. 

In the fiscal vear ended Dee. 
31, 1978, Margo’s La Mode had 
income of $791,000 on sales of 
$38,036,000. 

The acquisition terms call for 
Margo’s La Mode’s stock- 
holders to receive $10.30 for 
each share of common stock.

PRODUCT MOVEMENT AUDIT 


Volume Reflects 


Fall Seasonals, 
Ath-Qtr. Buildup 


By STEVE HITTNER 
President, 
Hardware Distributors 
The August movement fig- 
ures reflect fall seasonality in 
hardware sales and the buildup 
to fourth-quar- 
ter stock posi- 
tions, which 
seem to be 
holding their 
own, despite 
fears about the 
economy. 
Retailers 
are cautious of 
overstocking, 
but overall vol- 
ume in categories such as power 
tools is up significently. Much of 
this may be attributed to the 
wariness of stock positions at 
retail, since customers are 
turning to distributors to fill in 
peak and valley differences. 
Turning to some of the cate- 
gories specifically, in hardware 
we see the effect of a rope pro- 
gram many of our customers 
have been running. Some 


Figures supplied by Hard- 
ware Distributors, Secaucus, 
N.J., cover 350 stores, includ- 
ing 141 discounters, in 20 states 
east of the Mississippi River. 
Suggested retail prices listed by 
the distributor reflect typical 
price points for discount cli- 
ents. 


stores have doubled rope space 
on the selling floor, and the vol- 
ume difference for us has been 
tremendous. 

Nails in bulk, which many of 
our customers have been using 
as low-ticket promotional 
items, slipped in volume off the 
hardware chart as the summer 
building boom slowed. They 
were replaced in volume pri- 
marily by fashion hardware fix- 
tures, such as antique hinges. 
Several ceramic. doorknobs did 
not show up on the chart, but 
were only slightly less in dollar 
volume. 

The strong movement in fix- 
tures indicates the hope at re- 
tail that gas prices and reces- 
sion will keep consumers at 
home, and they traditionally 
spend some of that time making 
improvements around the 
house. 

We see movement in basic 
hand tools holding steady with- 
out large volume increases; sets 
such as Stanley’s six-piece 
screwdriver set and Great 
Neck’s five-blade saw set have 
moved up in volume. 

Arrow’s staple gun/tacker, 
often ranked first in dollar vol- 
ume because of its popularity as 
a promotional item at retail, has 
been knocked off the top of the 
chart, but is still solid in move- 
ment. 

Just off the chart due to 
slightly less dollar volume in 
the hand tool category were 
woodchopping tools, an indica- 
tion of the viability of energy- 
related items.

In power tools, volume is = 
100% over last year, althoug 
position on the chart is de- 
pendent on product availability 
as well as demand. 

Black & Decker’s basic Jig- 
saw, single-height Workmate 
and 5¥-in. circular saw lead all 
other products in power tools, 
despite the popularity of the 
basic promotional drills, the 
variable speed drills, the 7-in. 
circular saw and the table-top 
Workmate model. 

We continue to move prod- 
ucts quickly in the power tools, 
but the individual positions in 
volume fluctuate with the sup- 
ply. 

In security hardware, we 
have the shift back to entrance 
locksets after the back-to- 
school rush in padlocks. A Mas- 
ter padlock tops the chart in 
both unit movement and dol- 
lars, but the other padlocks 
have slackened and entrance 
locksets have picked up in the 
traditional seasonal swing. 

Security hardware is doing 
well this season, up almost one- 
third over last year. We found 
our move to an abbreviated as- 
sortment in Yale, to include 
Weslock and Kwikset as com- 
plements, has worked out well. 


In the glues, lubricants and 
adhesives category, volume is 
up over the flat midsummer pe- 
riod with the traditional lead- 
ers repeating on the chart. 
These items do a tremendous 
unit movement for the mass 
merchants. Perhaps most inter- 
esting to note in this category is 
the top item, Woodhill’s 
Gluematic Pen. This is a new 
product that has jumped right 
to the top of the chart in dollar 
movement, due to higher re- 
tails than other products in the 
category. (Krazy Glue is still 
the top item in unit movement. ) 


Energy Savers Heat Up 


In seasonal items, we are 
seeing the fall buildup of door 
and window insulation, heating 
tapes and other insulation. 
With the skvrecketing price of 
heating oil and enc:zy for the 
home in general, retailers are 
looking for a strong season 
here. 

Storm window kits, felt and 
fiberglass insulation in several 
packaged forms were also just 
off the chart, with slightly less 
dollar volume. Fiberglass avail- 
ability is not a problem, as it 
was in the past. We expected a 
very cautious ordering pattern

Charleston, S.C., on which 
Nichols has bid. 

Sixteen other Fields remain 
to be sold and the auction of 
these stores is expected to take 
place sometime in November. If 
bids on any of these units are 
received in time for the Oct. ll 
auction, the stores will be in- 
cluded in that sale, a spokes-

originally bid $200,000 fcr the

only bidder for these three 
Fields. 

A representative of Stone 
East Associates, one of the two 
companies handling the sale of 
the Fields stores, objected to 
Nichois bids, asserting that the 
price was too low. 

Stone East’s asking price was 
$500,000 for the Greenville 
store and $1,000,000 for each of 
the Charleston units. 

Nichols then raised its bid for 
the Greenville store to $250,000 
and made a bulk bid of $900,000 


4-for the two in Charleston. 


The Stone East representa- 
tive again rejected the two bids 
and asked that the stores be re- 
moved from the auction. Bank- 
ruptcy Court Judge John Gal- 
gay turned down the request 
and said he would decide later if 
Nichols’ bids were to be ac- 
cepted. 


Bid Accepted 


In subsequent discussions, 
Nichols’ $250,000 bid for the 
Greenville store was accepted 
as was a $575,000 offer for one 
Charleston unit. 

If Nichols’ bid for the remain- 
ing Charleston Fields is ac- 
cepted, the discounter would 
remodel and open both stores 
simultaneously in 1980. 

Nichols’ remodeling of the 
Greenville store will follow the 
discounter’s standard mix of de- 
partments. 

The move into South Car- 
olina put Nichols into its fourth 
southern state. The discounter 
already has stores in Virginia 
West Virginia and North Car 
olina, including Gastonia and". 
Lumberton, N.C., close to the 
state line with South Carolina. — 

Nichols’ competition in 
Greenville, S.C., includes four 
Sky City stores, three units 
each operated by K mart and 
Big K, one Woolco and one Sam 
Solomon catalog showroom, 
while in Charleston there are 
eight Big K’s, three K marts 
and two Sam Solomons.

Discounters Tighten Inventory 
In Face of Uncertain Economy 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Concern about an uncertain 
economy—reinforced by a soft 
second quarter at some 
chains—has led discounters to 
tighten inventory for the fourth 
quarter a couple of points under 
last year's levels. 

The conservative planning 
could bring a problem if the 
quarter turns out strong. 
Manufacturers are themselves 
planning conservatively, not 
looking for every last sale, 
counting on some order can- 
cellations and producing mini- 
mal goods. This will lead to a 
scramble for product if early 
signs point to a very strong 
Christmas season. 

Spokesmen at Woolco, Kor- 
vettes, Zayre, Venture, James-

Stores Hook Onto Soft Craft Craze; 
Eye Enormous Profit Potential, Risks 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Discounters are capitalizing 
on the national enthusiasm for 
soft crafts such as latch hook, 
macrame and needlepoint—re- 
cognizing the enormous profit 
potential as well as the risk. 

The soft craft kits, usually 
merchandised near domestics 
departments, appear to be ex- 
periencing more spectacular 
growth in discount stores than 
the steady models and hobby 
kits which are usually included 
in toy sections. 

The craft and hobby market 
accounted for $2 billion in retail 
sales nationwide, and $1.3 bil- 
lion in billings by manufactur- 


ers and importers in 1978, 
according to a study by the 
Hobby Industry of America. 

Of the $1.3 billion, $437 mil- 
lion was in soft crafts, with nee- 
dlework, macrame and varn 
accounting for almost half of 
this business. Other major 
craft categories were number 
crafts and stencil art ($21 mil- 
lion) and poster art ($20 mil- 
lion). 

Models, including plastic 
kits, model railroads, slot and 
slotless sets, remote control ve- 
hicles and dollhouses, ac- 
counted for $655 million in 
billings. So-called common cat- 
egories such as tools, woods, 


provide themselves. 


K mart Tests Adjacent 
Box Supermarket 


TROY, Mich.—K mart will test a box supermarket next to its 
discount store in Pontiac, Mich. A company spokesman said 
the chain is leasing 10,000 sq. ft. in a closed supermarket 
adjacent to the discount store for the experiment. 

No time limit has been set and the chain has no present 
plans to expand the test, the spokesman added. The store, 
which will open by early next month, will be limited to non- 
perishable goods in what has evolved to be the typical no-frills 
food store layout. It will include cut-carton displays and shop- 
pers will bag their own purchases in boxes or bags which they 


The experiment, which K mart vice chairman B. M. Fauber 
Said the company undertook “out of curiosity,” is considered 
to be a test of the traffic-drawing power of box stores. In years 
past, K mart policy had been to open discount stores adja- 
cent to other chains supermarkets So that each would benefit 
from the other's traffic. However, while the discount stores 
prospered, many of the supermarkets were unsuccessful. In 
this case, however, the food store will be operated by K inart. 

In addition to the box store test, Fauber told stock analysts 
in Chicago, K mart is still giving a high priority to acquisitions 
in the “food-away-from-home’” industry despite the rejection 
of its bid for Morrison Inc. K mart had offered $228.8 million in 
stock and cash to buy the cafeteria and food-service chain.

Jamesway to Slow to 9-6 Yearly Bows After Spree 


HACKETTSTOWN, N.J.— 
Jamesway chairman Herbert 
Fisher told security analysts 
here the chain would slow down 
to five or six bows a year after 
opening 12 stores, including 
seven Westons units, this vear, 
and three stores early next 
vear—its biggest expansion 
drive. 

Fisher said Jamesway should 
benefit from strong fourth- 
quarter sales from the seven 
Westons stores in New York 
and Pennsylvania which were 
acquired in August. Two of the 
seven have been converted, he 
said, while the remaining five 
kept their old logo. 

“These stores don’t yet have 
the merchandise to back up our 
circulars,” he said. “We'll wait 
until the winter and then close 
them for remodeling.” 

Fisher said the new units 
should help boost Jamesway’s 
1979 volume by 20% to $245 mil- 
lion. The chain will be operat- 
ing 60 units at the end of the 
year. 

The Jamesway chairman said 
he planned to slow down to a 
pace of five or six openings a 
year after the current expan- 
sion is completed. He expects 
to “fill in” secondary markets in 
New York, New Jersey and 
Pennsylvania. 


“A few years ago we thought 
we had saturated the three- 
state area; that’s why we went 
to Ohio,” he said. “But it took us 
along time to get off the ground 
there. Meanwhile we dis- 
covered more locations avail- 


able in our other markets.” 
Fisher said the chain would 
continue to operate its three 
Ohio stores and single Virginia 
unit because they are profit- 
able.

Discounting Week 


GOING STRONG. Despite a 
softening sales pattern among 
other retailers, discounters 
again recorded strong growth 
in September. Wal-Mart led 
the way with a 36% increase 
over the previous September 
while Caldor recorded a 
healthy 22% boost. Dayton 
Hudson, to which Target is a 
major contributor, was up 
11.8%. K mart rose 13.6% and 
Woolworth climbed 11.2%. 
Sears, Ward and Penney fared 
far less well for the month, 
with Sears up 2.4%, Penney up 
2% and Ward up a miniscule 
0.7%.

hark back to when the company

sarily coincide with what com- 
pany officials felt was the fair 
value of a stockholder’s propor- 
tionate interest in the com- 
pany—especially in October of 
last year when stock prices 
were severely depressed. 

One important difference 
from the practice of the days of 
private ownership, Black 
noted, is that formerly the 
price—which was based on 
book value—that the company 
offered shareholders was the 
only offer that could be ac- 
cepted. Now, shareholders 
have the option of selling in the 
open market for more, should 
that be at a higher price than 
the base at which Glosser is 
willing to buy back the stock. 

Kopf said that while Glosser's 
plan may give its stock a slight 
competitive edge over that of 
other similar regional retailers, 
he does not anticipate it having 
any dramatic impact on the 
open market price.

some protection against a silly 
market—he’s protected against 
loss of capital—but the com- 
pany still has a relatively low 
yield. It won’t make it a glam- 
our stock. Investment yields 
are still what will attract most 
stockholders.”

It's Tith Hour For Korveties_ 


“We believe that Agache-Willot has backed us to 
the point where our operations will become profit- 
able.’"—Nicholas Palihnich, president, Korvettes. 


NEW YORK—Time is running out for 


Korvettes. 

As the troubled chain enters the crucial 
holiday sales period, industry observers are 
wondering why the new French management 
does not make its move. 

Extensive cost-cutting measures and strict 
controls have been put in place by chairman 
Alain Mathieu, but few merchandising or 
marketing changes have been seen. 

Korvettes’ lack of clear positioning in its 
markets, the poor in-stock condition in hard 
lines, and the lack of specific merchandising 
or marketing steps to effect the turnaround 
have many retailers wondering about the 
effectiveness of the new management’: pol- 
icies. 

President Nicholas Palihnich insists that 
the $19 million in cost cuts, financial support 
from parent Agache-Willot and slight mer- 


chandising efforts will make the chain profit- 
able next year. 

The merchandising effort focuses on posi- 
tioning Korvettes between a discounter and a 
conventional department store. “We’re a

Passage Doubtful, Interest Remains 
In Retail Antitrust, Polygraph Bills 


WASHINGTON—A bill that 
could extend antitrust suits to 
mass merchants, and another 
that would restrict the use of 
polygraphs appear unlikely to 
pass this Congress—but the is- 
sues may be alive next vear. 

The Illinois Brick antitrust 
legislation (S. 306), which 
would repeal a 1977 Supreme 
Court decision that allows anti- 
trust sults only from direct 
claimants and excludes indirect 
purchasers, did not have the 
necessary votes for passage at 
DSN presstime. 

This bill, “which would allow 
any customer who feels she had 
been mistreated by a store, to 
sue for antitrust violations,” in 
the words of S. E. Nichols pres- 
ident Manfred Brecker, was 
lobbied against heavily by mass 
merchants and by industry as- 


sociations. 

Other legislation, proposed 
to restrict use of polvgraphs (S. 
854 in the Senate and H. R. 
3255 in the House of Represen- 
tatives), was considered a dead 
issue earlier in the vear but re- 
cent developments indicate a 
growing interest. 

First, the House Judiciary 
Subcommittee on Civil and 
Constitutional Rights is draw- 
ing up its own polygraph bill, 
which will reportedly be even 
broader than current pro- 
posals. 

In a second development, the 
House Education and Labor 
Committee's Subcommittee on 
Labor-Management Relations 
recently held hearings on work- 


ers rights, including the use of 


polygraph, privacy issues and

Execs Skeptical of Figures 
Reported For Small Chains 


Chain executives contacted by DSN questioned the figures 
released in the NMRI/Cornell study, skeptical of such re- 
ported substantial gains in both the number and dollar 
amount of average transactions for small chains. 

‘A gain of 14% in the size of the average transaction, 
coupled with a 7% gain in the number of transactions (as 
reported in the study for chains with sales under $100 million) 
is a total compound gain of 22%,” pointed out Tom Banks, 
vice president of Roses. “I don't know of many small chains 
growing that rapidly.” 


in Doubt 


Some retailers feel that the combined effect of new stores, 
inflation and plus business could result in a 22% growth rate, 
and point to the less dramatic rate among larger chains— 
about 18% in medium-sized companies and 16% in the larg- 
est chains reporting. But the 14% reported gain in transaction 
value and 7% gain in the number of transactions got iittle cre- 
dence f.om retail executives. 

“| don't believe it,” was Dave Grundfest's reaction. The 
president of Magic Mart—which does just over $100 million in 
annual sales volume—added that the reported gain in the 
number of transactions was particularly Suspect, since that 
class of discount chains had also reported a substantial in- 
crease in gross margin as a percentage of sales. 

“It may have been true during the last part of 1978 and the 
first quarter this year,” said S. E. Nichols president Manfred 
Brecker, “but it certainly isn’t true now.” Brecker also added 
that the apparent loss of market share by smaller chains was 
not surprising, Given the greater resources of the bigger-

McKEESPORT, Pa.—G. C.

holders. 

The National Association of

A panel of financial experts

an dvertising News ) 


Catalog Showrooms 


What's happening on the dis- 
count advertising scene? The 
catalog showroom fourth-quar- 
ter push in advertising is due 
again; retail ads in newspapers 
are lagging behind total adver- 
tising gains for the year to date; 
a new licensing program ties 
together vendors, stores and 
newspapers in a coupon game. 


CATALOG AD ASSAULT. As 
discounters are beginning to re- 
alize, catalog showrooms are in- 
creasing advertising tremen- 
dously—47% on average last 

ear over 1977—but of particu- 
ar interest now is their focus on 
the fourth quarter. 

Catalogers averaged almost 
51% of their newspaper adver- 
tising in the fourth quarter last 
year. Discounters commonly 
run 30% to 40% of their ads in 
the last quarter. 

What this means is more 
fourth-quarter leverage from a 
smaller total advertising base 
for the catalogers. The largest 
newspaper advertiser among 
catalogers last year was Ser- 
vice Merchandise, which 
bunched almost 75% of its ads 
in the fourth quarter. 

Service, which is almost com- 
parable with Bradlees in vol- 
ume, ran 1.8 million lines of 
advertising in the fourth quar- 
ter last year compared to 
Bradlees’ 2.7 million lines. 

Bradlees thus ran 50% more 
advertising than Service in the 
fourth quarter, but over the en- 
tire year ran three times as 
much advertising as the cata- 
loger (7.1 million lines com- 
pared to 2.4 million), according 
to Media Records figures. 

Value House showrooms, 
now owned by Service, shared 
the extreme fourth-quarter ad- 
bunching philosophy, with al- 
most 60% of their advertising 
run then. Best, Century House 
and Basco also illustrate pro- 
nounced emphasis on advertis- 
ing for Christmas. 

A few catalogers, including 
Naum’s and McDonalds, spread 
their advertising more evenly 
through the year and budget 
percentages comparable to dis- 
counters in the last quarter. 

Catalogers are still minor ad- 
vertisers compared to discount- 
ers, of course, but the rate of 
advertising growth is impres- 
sive. Service increased adver- 
tising almost 87% last year 
from 1977, while Best and O. G. 
Wilson more than doubled 
theirs. 

Top advertising spot for this 
year may continue to be tightly 
contested among catalogers; 
members of the Modern Mer- 
chandising group also increased 
linage last year, and taken as a 
total represented 2.36 million 
lines in 1978, only slightly be- 
hind Service at 2.37 million, ac- 
cording to Media Records fig- 
ures. 


* * *

according to estimates made by 
the Newspaper Advertising 
Bureau. 

Retail ads in newspapers 
were up 12.6% in August, com- 
_- to total advertising 
inage gains of 14.3% for the

month in newspapers nation- 
wide.

1979. newspaper advertising 
was up 12.8% while retail ads

5-Wk. Sales Rise 
22% at Caldor 


NORWALK, Conn.—The 
opening of two stores and a 
strong back-to-school season 
enabled Caldor to record a 22% 
jump in sales in the five weeks 
ended Sept. 29. Volume was 
$51,604,000 compared with 
$42,312,000 for the same period 
last year. 

The eight-month period’s 
sales of $323,414,000 were up 


16% from $278,744,000. 

The two new stores give the 
northeast regional chain 52 
units with four more due to be 
opened.

Nathanson Is Named Sattlers’ Prez 


BUFFALO, N.Y.—Gerald 
Nathanson, former president of 
J. M. Fields, has succeeded 
Ralph Wilcove as president of 
Sattlers, a five-store conven- 
tional department store chain 
here. 

Two former Fields execu- 
tives have joined Nathanson at 
Sattlers. They are Tom Seifert, 
named senior vice president 
and general merchandise man- 
ager, hard lines and budget 
shop, and Jim VanGundy, se- 
nior vice president, operations 
and corporate facilities. 

Nathanson has bought an in- 
terest in Plapinger Associates 


which has purchased Sattlers. 
Plapinger had tried to buy 
Fields when its parent Food 
Fair decided to sell the then 79- 
store discounter as part of its 
Chapter XI reorganization. 

Sattlers wouldn’t be changed 
into a discount store operation, 
Nathanson asserted. 

The chain has one store in 
downtown Buffalo, and units in 
four malls in the upstate New 
York market. Its major com- 
petitors include five other con- 
ventional department store 
chains, one of which, Hens & 
Kelly, is owned by discounter 
Twin Fair.

Two Guys’ Sales 


Continue Flat 


GARFIELD, N.J.—Two 
Guys’ sales continued flat for 
both the four weeks and eight 
months ended Sept. 29. 

In the September period, 
company-owned volume was 
$49,213,000, up 1.1% from 
$48,657,000. Leased depart- 
ment sales of $2,337,000 in the 
month this year were up 5.7% 
from $2,207,000 and helped 
raise total chain volume to 
$51,550,000, a 1.3% increase 
irom $50,864,000. 

The 35-week volume was 
$416,593 ,000, a 3% increase 
from $404,365,000. Adding 
leased department sales of $17,- 
729,000 which were up 3% from 
$17,186,000, boosted total vol- 
ume to $434,322,000, a 3% in- 
crease from $421,551,000.

Paper Shortage 


Severe shortages of the paper usu- 
ally used by Discount Store News 
have forced us, like other major 
publications, to use lighter-weight, 
uncoated stock for some pages. As 
soon as our suppliers obtain the 
necessary stock, we will return to 
full use of the better-quality, coated 
paper you have come to associate 
with DSN. 


Advertising News 


(Continued from page &) 
pleted cards for weekly first 
prizes of $1,000, and runner-up 
prizes of free merchandise from 
participating retailers. 

Retailers that participate in 
the program must feature at 
least one item in their ad that 
matches an item on the bingo 
card, as well as run a 4-column- 
in. inset in their ad with the 
Coupon Bingo logo and mention 
of the $1,000 first prize. 

Thus far, manufacturers such 
as Procter & Gamble, Nestle 
and Coca-Cola have partici- 
pated, and the retailers lave 
been supermarkets. Small said 
the newspapers have concen- 
trated upon supermarkets in 
selling the program, but mass 
merchandisers may be ap- 
proached in the future. He an- 
ticipates vendor participation 
from H&BA and household 
consumables manufacturers, in 
merchandise categories ap- 
plicable to mass merchants. 

Newspapers sell the pro- 
gram to local retailers and ven- 
dors on the premise that since 
the coupon/ads are aids to the 
consumer in a chance to win 
$1,000 or free merchandise, 
they will have the highest 
awareness level. 

The newspaper pays for the 
prizes but has an adveriising 
package to sell; manufacturers 
hope to get better sell-through 
from increased coupon redemp- 
tions (Small estimates that only 
5% of the 80 billion cents-off 
coupons run annually are re- 
deemed); retailers—those who 
handle cents-off coupons, which 
discounters nave traditionally 
shied away from handling—get 
an additional discount to offer 
the customer without paying 
for it themselves.

the products on the report au- 
gurs well for the potential of

Dryers With Asbestos 
Release It: CPSC 


WASHINGTON—AI! of the 
hair dryers containing as- 
bestus, studied by the Con- 
sumer Product Safety Commis- 
sion, release asbestos, accord- 
ing to a commission spokes- 
man. 

Following reports earlier this 
year that many portable hair 
dryers pose a potential health 
hazard because of possible as- 
bestos emission, the commis- 
sion undertook its investiga- 
tion. The first phase of the 
investigation has been com- 

leted and the results have 

een sent to two doctors at 

Mount Sinai hospital in New 
York City to measure the po- 
tential health hazards. 


Final Results Expected 


The commission spokesman 
would not reveal the amounts of 
asbestos released: by the dryers 
or list brand or manufacturer 
names. According to a source 
close to the commission, how- 
ever, every dryer containing as- 
bestos was found to release a 
portion of the substance when 
the dryer was used. Final re- 
sults are expected in about a 
month from the commission.

year.

1980, even if no further pur-

CHICAGO—Fuel saving and 
do-it-yourself were the domi- 
nant themes of this year’s Auto- 
motive Parts and Accessories 
Association show. 

Few new products were (lis- 
played by manufacturers, and 
merchandisers for discount 
chains seemed to concentrate 
on new lines of polymer pol- 
ishes offered by several com- 
panies. 

“One thing we really want to 
look over while we’re here are 
the poly waxes,” said George 
Richardson, hard lines mer- 
chandise manager for Mr. 
Wiggs. 

Among the exhibitors offer- 
ing such products to retailers 
for the first time were Poly- 
glycoat, which previously 
worked only through new-car 


dealers, and Turtle Wax. 

Bernie Zirnheld, auto buyer 
for Ayr-Way, said he plans to 
introduce in his stores next 
spring both Turtle’s PolyShell 
and Blue Coral’s Blue Poly. 
While Ayr-Way will discount 
both products, its price points 
of almost $20 represent a tre- 
mendous jump from the $4-$5 
for most premium waxes. 

“With the kind of ad support 
Turtle Wax will give and with 
the Turtle name, you almost 
have to carry that product. Peo- 
ple will come in and ask for it, so 
vou better have it. I think it will 
sell, even with the relatively 
high price,” he said.

Heck’s, said he, too, will proba-

GREENVILLE, N.C.—Ina 
move that will boost store vol- 
umes 15% to 20%,S. E. Nichols 
will open three home improve- 
ment centers in the next six 
weeks, similar to the new unit 
here. 

New home improvement cen- 
ters will open in Greenville, 
S.C., where Nichols is set to 
open a former J. M. Fields 
store by the end of this month, 
and in Harrisonburg, Va., and 
Martinsburg, W. Va., by the 
end of the year. 

S. E. Nichols has taken over 
adjacent supermarkets in the 
Virginia and West Virginia sites 
to make room for the home im- 
prove ment centers. 

“We want to get every store 


on a chainwide program of 


home improvement centers,” 
said the chain’s hard lines mm 
Irwin Levine, “because more 
people are going the DIY route 
eo than pay a contractor for 

We’re firmly committed to 
the concept.” 

Nichols has already con- 
verted 24 of its 41 stores to in- 
clude home improvement cen- 
ters, ae from 18,000 to 
30,000 sq. The centers add 
15% to 20% ‘a each store's total 
volume, although Levine sug- 
gested that 15% is a conserva- 
tive figure. 

The Greenville, N.C., unit is 
typical of the home improve- 
ment centers. At 20,000 sq. ft., 
it is the average size and was 
installed at the end of July as an 
addition to the 100,000-sq.-ft. 
store. 


Space and stock were more 
than doubled; the old hardware 
department ran %,000 sq. ft. 
Categories adde d included 
storm doors and windows, hot 
water heaters, bedding and 
other furniture, sheetrock, 
paneling, moulding and lumber. 

Paint and electrical sections 
were expanded by 40 ft. each 
(electrical now has four 24-ft. 
runs). Hand tools were tripled 
from the former 24-ft. run, and 
mailboxes were given 16 ft. 
(they occupied 4 ft. prior to the 
addition). 

Plumbing, which had consist- 
ed of a small blister-pack pro- 
gram, Was given two 40-ft. runs 
and now includes open stock. 
Levine said the chain found 
that “customers like to feel the 
item in open stock, whether it’s 
a Y joint or any plumbing 
item.” 

Store manager Doug Lock- 

lear said his store is near the 
15% maik in increased volume 
after the addition, although 
“vou need greater momentum 
to get going because of shop- 
ping habits the customers had 
already developed.” 

Locklear is in an area loaded 
with competition. Home center 
Moore's, with roughly 30,000 
“4. ft. of lumbervard and 15,000 

ft. of store space, is adja- 
onal to the Nichols store. Home 
center chains Lowe's and 
Wickes are also represented, 
with Wickes only /s mile away.

survey, covering the period Aug. 
3 to Sept. 21, showed that retail- 
ers anticipate shoppers desire 
for more fashionable items for 
the holiday season. How does 
your chain’ performance com- 
pare with these findings?

SPECIALTY CHALLENGE. Off- 
price apparel stores, such as 
Marshalls and the new J. Bran- 
nam, have recently been gain- 
ing market share at the expense 
of the traditional discounter. By 
offering name brands at a cut 
price, these new merchandisers 
have created problems for many 
of their competitors, including 
upscale discounters. Learn how 
Bradlees and Target are reacting 
to the specialty threat. (P. 28) 


U-PAK. WE PACK. K mart has 
opened a new U-Pak box store 
in Pontiac, Mich., with prices 
10%-30% below normal super- 
markets. But Kroger. its chief 
competitor in the area,is not ex- 
actly giving up. DSN coverage 
also indicates possible weak 
points in the K mart concept. 
Compare the shelf and unit 
prices for yourself, then decide 
if the savings U-Pak offers out- 
weigh the limited assortment.

Nationwide DSN Report 

Discount store and catalog 
showroom housewares/elec- 
trics merchandisers in the first 
half of the year will concentrate 
on improving return on invest- 
ment. They will be buying less 
and relying more on distribu- 


tors to reduce their inventory 
investment and increase turn- 
over. 

The reasons behind this fi- 
nancial-oriented merchandis- 
ing are the high interest rates 
and the uncertain state of the 
economy, especially in the first

K mart Switches From Controlled Brand 
lo Hoover Derivative Vacuum Cleaners 


By Arthur Markowitz 

TROY, Mich.—K mart has 
phased in a line of four Hoover 
derivative vacuums as the re- 
placement for its controlled 
brand of Flor Genie floor care 
products. 

It's amove to offer shoppers a 
mix of national brand vacuums 
that can’t be price-compared 
with items carried by other dis- 
counters or catalog showrooms. 

The Hoover vacuums are 


positioned as the lead-in to the 
Eureka derivative models that 
were also K mart’s top-of-the- 
line when the discounter car- 
ried Flor Genie models. 

K mart’s use of Hoover deriv- 
ative vacuums reflects the 
growing interest among dis- 
counters to use such items to 
merchandise floor care appli- 
ances that can’t be price-shop- 
ped, and that have a stable 
continuity. Manufacturers in 


the past have changed models 
as often as twice a year, result- 
ing in discounters needing to 
mark down leftovers.

wasn’t the only housewares/ 
electrics change under way at 
K mart. Other moves included:

WORTHINGTON, Ohio— 
Federated has tapped James 
Guinan, a department store ex- 
ecutive with a strong opera- 
tions background, for the presi- 
— of discounter Gold Cir- 
cle. 

He succeeds Norman Mat- 
thews, who in turn replaces 
founder Hal W. Field as chair- 
man and ceo. Field retired at 
the end of 1979 after 17 years at 
Gold Circle and Federated’s 
Lazarus division. 

Guinan, 44 president of Mil- 
waukee's Boston Store, will try 
to apply his oparations skills to 
brighten Gold Circle’s lacklus- 
ter bottom line. His experience 
in personnel, finance, and dis- 
tribution should complement 
Matthews’ merchandising ori- 
entation” 

Matthews became president 
of the Ohio discounter in July 
1978, after a five-year stint at 
Korvettes, asua senior vice- 
president of marketing and 
later as general merchandise 
manager. 

Industry analystShave sug- 
gested that Gold Circle has suf- 
fered from underfunding and a 
lack of interest from its depart- 
ment store-oriented parent.

Personal care appliances 
have been the stellar perform- 
ers in electrics housewares— 
evident in the PMA not only by 
the high standing of each classi- 
fication but also by the large 
number of models that showed 
up, 21 for styler/dryers and 13 
for curling wands. 

This broad array of items al- 
lowed discounters to feature 
the merchandise in promotions 
while also maintaining a basic 
mix for maximum everyday 
profits. 

Four new styler/dryers made 
the chart, with one, Georgie 
1200W compact, No. 12, spot- 
ted as a low-priced unit at an 
average retail of $11.70. The 
other three were positioned as 
mid-point items: Conair 1200W 
Pro Styler w/brush, No. 1, Sun- 
beam 1200W Win-Aire, No. 3, 
and Clairol 1200W Shoot the 
Breeze, No. 5. 

The Conair unit checked out 
as the top item partly due to the 
brush attachment which is used 
to help style the hair while dry- 
ing. 
an have tied into 
consumers interest in using a 
brush to style the hair by devel- 
oping a curling brush as an al- 
ternative to the curling wand. 

The curling brush started to 
become an important personal 
care electric about six months 
ago and caught on big in the last 
quarter; four models made the 
overall curling wand listing and 
two—the Northern and Norel- 
co units—were among the five 
new items in the category. 

More importantly, curling 
brushes captured the top two 
spots and four of the top seven 
listings. This occurred despite 
the fact that manufacturers 
have tagged curling brushes as 
the top-priced items in their 
curling wand line. 

The No. 1 item in curlers was 
a Windmere Curling Brush. Its 
$8.68 average retail price is al- 
most double the tag of the other 
two Windmere items that made 
the report. The same is true for

for lower-priced goods. Four

Ekco regular cookie sheets also 
copped spots.

with the bigger, the better. 

In food storage items, for ex- 
ample, the top sellers included 
such products as a Lustro-Ware 
70-oz. round decanter No. 7, 
and an Eagle 80-o0z. oblong Su- 
perseal food container. The size 
scene in other plastics included 
a Lustro-Ware ll-qt. heavy 
duty pan, No. 4 and a Tucker 
22-gal. trash can, No. 9. 

The bath shop is one of the 
most basic categories, showing 
little change in best-selling 
items. It’s the step-up items 
that discounters look to for add- 
ed dollars and margin. One 
showed up on the report as No. 
20, a Donner towel bar set in 
chrome. 

Fashion is the big interest in 
Rubbermaid as discounters and 
other retailers track movement 
of the different colors offered 
for an item. The report has 
chocolate and gold with seven 
items each, while almond has 
three. Failing to score was avo- 
cado, indicating the trend away 
from this hue toward the earth 
tones. 

But this doesn’t tell the en- 
tire story. Three items showed 
up in all three of these shades. 

ey were a self-closing waste- 
basket, a 10%-in. high rectan- 
gular laundry basket and a 
deluxe dish drainer. In the first 
two cases, the chocolate color 
items had the highest unit 
movement, followed by gold 
and then almond. The deluxe 
dish drainer color movement 
was slightly different with gold 
first, followed by chocolate. 


Different Strategy 


What seems to be happening 
is that for items that don’t have 
to coordinate with previously 
purchased goods, chocolate 
comes our on top. But when 
color coordination is a consider- 
ation, gold becomes more im- 
portant because of the goods in 
these shades already in the 
kitchen. 

Rubbermaid isn’t the only 
category where fashion is a vI- 
tal consideration. Corning 
Ware is another area, with the 
interest focused on the three 
different patterns. Spice cap- 
tured seven listings while Corn- 
flower and Wildflower took four 
each. 

A key to Cornflower’s strong 
showing is its lower price as 
compared to the same item in 
the other two designs. A case in 
point is the Menu-ette set, 
where the Cornflower offering 
was No. 1 while the Spice de- 
sign captured No. 4 and the 

ildflower No. 6. The Corn- 
flower edition costs about $4 
less. 

But for items with a smaller 
cost spread, the other designs 
ranked higher than Cornflower. 

Clear glass is the sales leader 
in Pyrex cookware. Five clear 
glass cookware items made the 
chart, while amber-colored 
Fireside cookware only ac- 
counted for three listings.

ean while a Loma 32-gal. offer-

nant, plastics continued to be 
Republic’s Freezette line, 
which captured 11 places.

bage cans was also seen in the

as the average retail—than

enable discouriters to step up 
successfully in housewares.

7 and an Ekco 24-in. die-cast

manufacturers haven’t had any 
problem delivering goods, 
Corning Glass is an exception.

ware dominates and movement 
for the merchandise would have 
been even greater if it weren’t 
for supply problems for most 
clear Pyrex items.

PRODUCT MOVEMENT AUDIT 


Some No-shows Prefer Distribs 


The National Housewares Manufacturers Association as- 
serts that it's important to attend the January housewares 
show to see firsthand what's new. But some electric house- 
wares buyers don't agree and expected to miss the show. 

One merchandiser for a Midwest discounter—who also 
buys consumer electronics—summed up the situation by 
noting that his electric housewares distributor will show him 
the new items and report the latest deals a week or two before 
the show “so why should | waste my company’s money and 
my time when | have other things to do?” 

He plans to attend the Consumer Electronics Show be- 
cause “that's the only place to see the new products and make 
deals with manufacturers. There aren't any consumer elec- 
tronics distributors.”

Korvettes to Follow Firings With Turnaround Program 


Ravi ona Nicholas Palihnich (right) and DSN's publica- 
tion director Stu Horton discuss Korvettes merchandising prob- 


lems during a tour of the Douglaston, N.Y., store. 


(DSN photo) 


NEW YORK—Korvettes as- 
serts it is going to do more than 
just fire employees to turn it- 
self around. 

The 50-store discounter at 
presstime was due to reveal the 
new financial and merchandis- 
ing program that is at the heart 
of its turnaround effort. 

Earlier this month Korvettes 
dismissed 300 employees—in- 
cluding six vice presidents—to 
bring to 1,500 the number let go 
since April 1979 when Agache- 
Willot acquired the chain from 
Arlen Realty & Development 
Corp. for $35 million. 

(Agache-Willot since then 
has pumped in about $60 million 
to maintain Korvettes in the 
face of a number of financial 
problems, including a lack of 
confidence among some ven- 
dors. ) 

The firings, which reduced 
Korvettes’ employees to about 
8,500, were a vital element in 
the first stage of the turn- 
around effort, which focused on 
reducing expenses. 


UFCW’ Local 888 Wins a Mays Election 


Woolco Fights New Rule Allowing Unions 
To Approach Workers on Store Property 


NEW YORK—Woolco has 
launched a legal attack against 
a ruling that allows a union for 
the first time to solicit workers 
on store property. 

The discounter has filed an 
exception to the decision (made 
by National Labor Relations 
Board administrative law judge 
Stanley Ohlbaum) which allows 
a union to distribute literature 
and talk with cierks on side- 
walks in front of stores and in 
in-store public restaurants. 

The ruling in favor of Local 
101, International Brotherhood 
of Craftsmen, Professional 
Workers and Allied Trades 
(IBCPW), came at the same 


time that the NLRB, in a sepa- 
rate action, certified Local 888, 
United Food & Commercial 
Workers (UFCW), as the bar- 
gaining agent for clerks inJ. W. 
Mays’ 14th Street, New York 
City, store. 

A Local 888 petition for rep- 
resentative elections at Mays’ 
stores in downtown Brooklyn 
and in Jamaica, N.Y., is pend- 
ing before the NLRB. 

The union won an election at 
Mays I4th Street store by a 280 
to 50 vote, with 104 ballots chal- 
lenged by the discounter. It was 
the first time in almost 30 years 
that a union won a representa- 
tive election at a major retail

NEW RINK’S. Gray Drug has 
opened a new Rink’s discount 
store in Marion, Ohio. The 
75,000-sq.-ft. unit has new fix- 
tures, a yellow and orange 
decor, and improved depart- 
ment identification. 


WOOLWORTH PROMO-

JEWELCOR DIVESTMENT. 
Jewelcor suffered a pretax 
loss of $131,500 from the sale 
of its 50% interest in Jewelcor 
Dai’ei, which had one show- 
room in Hawaii, to Dai’ei, a 


major Japanese retailer. Jew- 
elcor was owed $807,000 in 
cash and inventory, and re- 
ceived $550,000 in cash and 
$152,000 in inventory, for a 
deficit of $105,000. 


SWITCH. Jack Doyle, re- 
gional vp for Target in Texas, 
has joined Gold Circle as se- 
nior vp of store operations. 


TOWERS SHIFT. Towers, 
the seven-unit catalog show- 
room division of Gaylords, has 
switched coordinators, going 
from Jewelcor to Creative 
Merchandising. The move will 
pit Towers against two other 
Creative members, Basco and 
Dahlkemper in the Pitts- 
burgh market and Basco in 
Wilmington, Del.

Korvettes executives con- 
firmed that the second stage— 
the financial and merchandis- 
ing changes—will include the 
closing of some stores and con- 
verting of excess space in oth- 
ers. 

The executives have em- 
phatically denied persistent re- 
ports that as many as 15 stores 
would be closed and that units 
outside of the Metro New York 
Area would be cut back most 
heavily. 

A pelvenas told DSN: “We 
deny any wholesale closing of 


stores outside of New York and 
any plan to become just a metro 
New York chain.” 

He asserted: “‘Korvettes 
plans only a small number of 
closings. We are in the midst of 
reviewing Christmas sales and 
are holding discussions with 
landlords, so we can’t tell the

to be more moderate than 
feared.

spokesman. “I haven’t figured 
out what the increases average 
out to, but it is a lot less than I 
anticipated. Some items in- 
creased in price, but others de- 
creased.” 

A Heck's buyer, the first rep- 
resentative the chain has ever 
sent to the show, said prices for 
calculators and LCD watches 
would be lower for 1980. 

“We’ve always gone in and 
out with LCD's and we were of- 
fered a very exciting price for a 
Casio chrono alarm. The cost is 
about $19 so we'll sell it at 
$29.85 everyday and $5 less on 
ad. That's a fantastic price for a 


chrono alarm. It has a plastic 
band, but at that price I don’t 
think that will hurt it.” 

Heck’s also committed itself 
at the show to a pocket-sized 
printing calculator on an in- 
and-out basis at tax time. The 
calculator, made by Canon, has 
a display as well as the printing 
capability, and will retail for $69 
everyday and $54 on promotion. 

While exhibitors displayed 
many new high-end products, 
most new offerings of interest 
to discounters were derivations 
of existing merchandise. 

“At some past shows, there 
were whole new lines that we 
could go with, but this year’s 
show was limited mostly to re- 
finements,” a Gaylords spokes- 
man Said.

manufacturers sought to whet 
discounters appetites with pri-

GREEN L&G YEAR. Buyers 
look for 1980 to be a banner 
year in lawn & garden sales. 
Last year's move to higher-ticket 
mowers and trade-up string 
trimmers is expected to inten- 
sify, though mower costs are up. 
Patio goods are also looked to 
for exceptional volume this year, 
as chains move to better lines of 
furniture and stock up on gas 
grills and accessories. (P. 14)

ment of family reading centers 
is increasing. Discounters are in 
some cases uniting sku’s that 
were dispersed throughout the

creasing space for books. Hard- 
cover best sellers are in vogue, 
particularly at trade-up chains.

PRODUCT MOVEMENT AUDIT 


Diet Items Hot: 
New Line Seen 
Fattening Sales 


By M. Raymond Prendergast 
President, 
Boston Distributors 

Diet products have been one 
of our fastest-growing catego- 
ries with a 35% increase in sales 
last year, as reflected in the 
Product Movement Audit for 
Nov. 12 to Dec. 7, 1979. 

Nationally the diet market 
has shown 30% sales increases 
annually since 1974. This year is 
sure to be the biggest ever due 
to an unprecedented number of 
new-product entries. We are 
projecting a 50% increase in 
sales, primarily because of 
Menley & James entry into this 
market. 

The maker of Contac is intro- 
ducing a full line of capsules, 
tablets, and drops that will be 
marketed under the name of Di- 
etac. The strong packaging, 
capitalization on the Contac 
name, and an advertising ex- 
penditure greater than that for 
the total category in 1979, 
should make Dietac a market 
leader in the 80's. 

We anticipate that the new 
entries will not detract sub- 
stantially from the current 
best-sellers, but will garner 
new users from this virtually 
untapped market. We expect 
Thompson Medical’s Dexatrim 
and Prolamine to continue to 
show increases this year. Dex-

Readied by NMRI 


PHILADELPHIA—The 
National Mass Retailing In-

sonnel conference Feb. 11-13 at 
the Fairmont Hotel here. 

Conferences and seminars 
will be conducted on several 
topics focusing on personnel re- 
quirements in mass retailing, 
including: training programs; 
bonus plans; attitude surveys; 
executive compensation alter-

decentralized training; em-

in training; recruiting; commu- 
nication; staying nonunion; in-

compensation.

The conference ends on

confidential. Registration can

Discounters Split on Inventory Strategies 


Natiowide DSN Report 
Two major positions are 
evolving as discounters face 
economists’ predictions of flat- 


tened consumer spending for 


the first half of 1980. 

The dominant approach, 
taken by discounters such as 
Heck’s, Gee Bee, ALCO, Mur- 
phy’s Mart, Prange-Wage and 


Clover, is to inflate inventories 
at a rate slower than that of in- 
flation.

units will allow an easier com-

increase volume by chain distribution, but 
are uncertain how to make the leap.

stroying their image and customer base.”

brand began as an upstairs resource, but gave

mass merchants. Dittos are now in Target, 
Gold Circle and T.G. & Y., and the manufac-

company doing it. There are

in a staggered fashion because 
of these physical limitations, 
not because of any cost limita- 
tions.”

Category. I’ve had people come up to

ment.”

OY FAIR

Nationuide DSN Report 

Buyers will be arriving at the Toy 
Fair next week in a strong open-to- 
buy position, as a result of a healthy 
Christmas season that left them 
with many clean-outs, generally low 
inventory levels and a limited num- 
ber of markdowns. 

In 1979, as in 1978, the toy depart- 
ment was paced by sales in a rela- 
tively new area, electronic games. 
Virtually all chains contacted said 
that this expanding classification 
ran well ahead of all others. 

Consumer interest in such ver- 
sions as Merlin and Simon was ex- 
ceptionally strong. In addition, elec- 
tronic sport games—in particular, 
the football version—were also in 


high demand, and merchandisers 
say they are looking to electronic 
games for continued growth in 1980. 

However, these same buyers are 
quick to point out that the magic of 
this classification could be undone, 
either by supply problems or by 
steep price increases from manufac- 
turers. 

Other trends that emerged from 
interviews with buyers and manu- 
facturers included: 

@ The steady performance of most 
basic toy categories, especially 
plush, preschool and miniature 
wheel goods; 

e@ The apparent success of radio- 
controlled products, but only in 
chains where they were demon- 


80's View: Electronic Games Still Tops, 
TV Dolls Down, Space May Rebound 


What is the market outlook for 
toys in 1980? 

According to buyers and 
manufacturers, electronic 
games will lead the department 
once again this season. 

In addition, TV dolls should 
continue to lose market share, 
while space figures may rebound 
with the opening of a new Star 
Wars movie. 

Basic items are expected to re- 
peat their strong 1979 perfor- 
mance, as consumers look for 
more play value and durability in 
the toys they purchase. This au- 
gurs well for staples like regular 


dolls, plus, preschool toys, 
board games and miniature 
wheeled goods—but it could 
spell trouble for the high-end ra- 
dio-controlled products. 

Overall, price increases in the 
department will range from 5% 
to 20%, depending on the cate- 
gory. Supply shouldn't be a 
problem, except in some of the 
electronic games. If the econ- - 
omy softens even further, indus- 
try sources expect the public to 
defer major purchases and 
spend more time in the home. 
And that should add up to an- 
other big year in toys. 


2 BRS * és Gea F r fy 
i “3 6 GRRE * , Z 


skool toys is at Woolco, Arlington, Tex. 


Old standards like preschoo! toys fared better than 
space-related items and TV dolls. This display of Play- 


strated; and 

e The continued resilience of board 
games, in spite of a strong challenge 
from their electronic rivals. 

In fact, one industry source as- 
serted that sales volume in board 
games has increased—not fallen 
off—as a result of the electronic 
competition. 

As always, this category was led 
by the old standards, such as Scrab- 
ble, Life, Clue and Monopoly. Some 
of the newer introductions were hot 
as well, but it is too early to tell if 
they will be able to match the perfor- 
mance of the classic games. 

Among the losing categories for 
1979, the only sure disappointments 
came in space-related toys and the 
television (or licensed) dolls. 

“There was not much action in 
space this year,” an Alexander’s 
source said. “Not much is new in 
Star Wars figures, and the Buck 
Rogers didn’t do what was ex- 
pected. 

“I think the category died because 
the manufacturers didn’t revive it. 
They didn’t time it to come out with 
another movie this season. It may 
pick up when there is the sequel to 
Star Wars.” 

At Clover, a merchandiser re- 
ported better results with Star 
Wars, although the derivatives—in- 
cluding Star Trek, Battle Star Gal- 
lactica and Black Hole—were not as 
exciting because “the kids couldn’t 
relate to it.” 

And even at chains where the 
space-related toys were a success, 
the volume was not in the larger 
Star Wars figures, but rather in the 
lower-margin small-size characters. 


Healthy Christmas Sales Strengthen Open-to-Buy 


Whereas a lack of successful new 
promotions hurt the space category, 
high price points may have been the 
undoing of television dolls in 1979. 

A number of chains reported that 
sales in the licensed goods lagged 
behind the regular dolls and plush 
volume, and at least one discounter 
believes that future price increases 
will kill the classification completely. 

In the radio-controlled area, 
where margins can be as high as 
40%, a number of discounters were 
able to turn a healthy profit. 

The key to this classification, mer- 
chandisers say, is that the various 
products must be demonstrated for 
the customers—otherwise, there 
will be resistance to the high price. 

“We bought into the radio-con- 
trolled products cautiously in 1979, 
but we will be going back into it,” 
said a spokesman at Kansas-based 
Davids. “The margins are good, and 
r/ecan make us a little different from 
our competition.” 

At Alexander's, products in the 
$25 to $40 range did well, while the 
G.I. Joe’s chain in Oregon had price 
points as high as $125. Some buyers 
decided to go with imports, while 
Mattel, Precision and Ideal were 
generally the most popular domestic 
brands. 

As for the more basic categories, 
including regular dolls, plush, pre- 
school and miniature wheel goods, 
merchandisers reported that these 
old reliables again matched expecta- 
tions. 

In contrast to the TV dolls, where 
Christmas sales were a major disap- 
pointment, chains had much better 

(Continued on page 27) 


The impact of toy specialist discount chains 
can be seen in the decreased turns and shrink- 
ing gross margin in toy departments. The 
highly promotional specialists have grabbed a 
significant share of the market, and increased 
promotional pressure against discounters in al- 
most every market area. 

The response by discounters in recent years, 
which may reverse the trends of the 1970's, has 


~ Discounters Emphasize Basics to Offset 
Stiff Competition From Specialty Chains 


been to increase the emphasis on basics like 
plush, board games and preschool toys, and 
more intensive merchandising of other higher- 
margin lines in hobbies and low-ticket toys. 
Electronics footballing has also diminished 
gross margins in the department, but year-long 
sales of the most popular items at everyday 
prices can help offset the impact of Christmas 
season promotions.

Added Soft Goods Improve Margin: Some Trim Mix 


Nationwide DSN Report 
Faced with an uncertain economy, 
rising leather and vinyl prices and 
high interest rates, sporting goods 
merchandisers are particularly in- 

ventory-conscious this winter. 


80's Outlook: 
Price Hikes, 
Apparel Boom 


The market outlook for sport- 
ing goods in 1980 includes: 
e Average price increases of 
20% in leather balls and gloves 
and smaller hikes in vinyl and 
plastic items such as rods and 
coolers; 
@ Increased importance of ac- 
tivewear as retailers work to im- 
prove gross margins; 
@ Camping, fishing and hunting 
will be vulnerable to the avail- 
ability of gas this spring and 
summer; 
@ fxercise equipment will con- 
tinue in popularity. Racquetball 
should also enjoy increased sales 
while tennis will continue to 
level off; 
@ In ball games watch for soccer 
to enjoy growth, possibly at the 
expense of football and basket- 
ball.

v nate 2 


Many are trimming assortments 
and staying away from high prices in 
order to insure turnover. Others are 
increasing their soft line mix in 
order to improve the department's 
gross margin. 

Weather is another factor in this 
seasonal business. A mild winter in 
Venture’s markets has kept turn of 
outerwear slower than expected, ac- 
cording to buyer Dennis Rising. 

“I expected more rapid move- 
ment, but I suspect we’ll come out 
clean. We’re trimming a lot and try- 
ing to get very basic.” 

ALCO is controlling inventory by 
cutting high-ticket long guns and re- 
ducing ammunition sku’s, which add 
up to a large investment, according 
to buyer Dave Huscher. 

At Ciover, buyer Dennis Henning 
is trimming slow-moving basket- 
balls from seven to at least five sku’. 

Soaring leather and vinyl! costs 
further muddy the inventory pic- 
ture. Henning pointed out that in 
baseball gloves, fer example, he 
would have 10% fewer units on the 
floor to maintain the same dollar in- 
ventory. 

Huscher said that chains can no 
longer afford to swallow price in- 
creases. 

“The game is over on being able to 
shave prices and absorb higher 
costs,” he declared. “Discounters 
used to think they could reduce mar- 
gins and sell more merchandise to 
make the same amount of money, 
but that doesn’t work in sporting

margins.

goods any more. If you can’t in- 
crease turns, you can’t reduce mar- 
gins.” 

Sporting goods buyers see ap- 
parel as a way of loosening the gross- 
margin squeeze. At Clover, ac- 
tivewear represents 30% of the mix, 
“so I can ‘give away’ sneakers and 
tennis balls,” according to Henning. 

Bradlees carries soft lines to an 
industry extreme—45% of the mix 
compared to 5% three years ago. 
Bradlees’ markups of 35% in hard 
goods and 51% in apparel, as esti- 
mated by DSN, are fairly typical. 

Other chains are shying away 
from commitments to apparel be-

While discounters are watching 
the prices of most hard goods cate- 
gories, some are experimenting 
with better lines of fishing tackle. 

“There is a definite trend to up- 
grade,” observed James Sylvester of 
Stem Distributors. “The customer 
who once spent $5 on a rod is now 
willing to pay $15.” 

Discounters have benefited from 
the decline in price of graphite and 
are now able to offer such rods at

Gee Bee to Add 
2 Pa. Units by ’81 


JOHNSTOWN, Pa.—Gee 
Bee will open two new discount 
stores in Pennsylvania by 1981, 
one in Pittsburgh and the other 
in York. 

The Pittsburgh site, in the 
Southland Shopping Center in 
Pleasant Hills, is a 90,000-sq.- 
ft. former J. C. Penney. It will 
be completely remodeled and 
refurbished, and is scheduled 
to open in the spring of 1980. 

An 80,000-sq.-ft. Gee Bee 
store will also be opened in 1981 
west of York, in the newly an- 
nounced Crown American West 
Manchester Mall. These open- 
ings will bring the total number 
of stores in the chain to 18.

Retail Execs’ Pay Low, Lags Behind Other Industries’ 


NEW YORK—Salaries of 
executives in retailing—par- 
ticularly mass merchandis- 
ing—are low and are continuing 
to lose ground in relation to 
other industries, according to a 
report by Arthur Young, the 
accounting firm. 

Edwin Mruk, managing di- 
rector of the firm’s executive re- 
source consultant division, told 
an elite group of discounting ex- 
ecutives at the recent Top Man- 
agement Conference sponsored 
by the National Mass Retailing 
Institute that retailing’s sal- 
aries lag behind other indus- 
tries at each level of manage- 


ment. He warned that if the 
industry is to attract the execu- 
tive talent it will need to thrive 
in the 1980’s, compensation 
packages will have to be revised 
to become more competitive. 

Mruk blamed the top execu- 
tives of retail companies for al- 
lowing the industry to lose its 
allure to young men and wom- 
en. 

“This picture of compensa- 
tion in the retail industry is ad- 
mittedly dismal and dispirited. 
In the 50's and the 60's retailing 
was one of the highest-payin 
industries and could attract tal- 
ented, bright, hard-working,

Unique Mix Helps Make Mervyn’ Coast Apparel Star 


By Judith Crown 


HAYWARD, Calif.—Mervyn’, wield- 
ing a unique merchandise mix, combined 
with sophisticated computer technology 
and disciplined operations, is continuin 
to shake up the moderate-priced appare 
market on the West Coast. 

Executives say the chain offers value 
by promoting but not discounting—that 
an entire wardrobe can be purchased for 
under $200. 

The assortment comprises a narrow 
and deep assortment of basics: Levi 
Strauss and private label merchandise, 


which are heavily promoted, and other 
key mainstream brands that are offered 
mostly at full price. 

The 60-unit chain headquartered here 
did estimated sales last year of $641 mil- 
lion. 

This provides tough competition for 
upscale discounters like Gold Circle 
which are unable to offer national brands, 
and off-price chains like Atherton’s Pic-a- 
dilly, which cannot offer depth or con- 
tinuity of merchandise. 

Mervyn’s has been one of Dayton Hud- 
son’s strongest suits since it acquired the 


chain in 1978. Mervyn’s and Target have 
been pacing the parent’s sales gains and 
are the strongest contributors to its bot- 
tom line. Mervyn’s had sales increases of 
34% for the first nine months of 1979, 36% 
in December and 32% in January. Every 
store is profitable, according to spokes- 
man Lizette Weiss. 

Mervyn's plans to double in size within 
the next five years—mostly within its 
current markets in California, Arizona, 
New Mexico, Nevada and Oregon, with 
expansion into new trading areas in
