vival efforts so far on closin 
unprofitable stores—14 have al- 
ready been shut—and is re- 
turning toward discount store 
merchandising. 

The other major element in 
the plan, arranging additional 
financing, was being pursued at 
presstime by Korvettes’ parent 
Agache-Willot, according to 
the retailer’s chairman Alain 
Mathieu. 

The radical store surgery, 
with at least two more units ex- 
pected to be closed, and a “re- 
turn to the concept of basic 
value that was the foundation of 
the company’s original success” 
support DSN’s analyses of the 
basic problems faced by what 
had been a 50-store chain (see 
DSN, Nov. 5, 1979, p. 1; Jan. 28, 
1980, p. 1). 

But Korvettes’ need to ar- 


range additional financing, 
after Agache-Willot purchased 
the chain from Arlen Realty & 
Development Corp. ll months 
ago for $35 million and then 
umped in more than $30 mil- 
ion in working capital, points 
up the the seriousness of the 
problems facing the chain. 
Nicholas Palihnich, Kor- 
vettes president, asserts the 
chain will be profitable by 1981. 
He made this projection in re- 
sponding to a series of ques- 
tions posed by DSN after the 
retailer released broad details 


of an extensive marketing and 
operational program to “turn 

orvettes around by generat- 
ing more profits from fewer 
stores.” 

The twin tracks Korvettes is 

ursuing simultaneously call 
or (1) reducing costs by closing 
unprofitable stores, leasing out 
excess space, consolidating 
warehousing, cutting back on 
headquarters and store work 
forces, and streamlining adver- 
tising; and (2) redirecting mer- 
chandising to become “a promo- 
tional department store” by 


“carrying lower-priced lines in 
important areas and promoting 
items more aggressively.” 

This year could answer the 
questions of whether Kor- 
vettes’ new program is the an- 
swer to its problems, whether 
it has enough time to do the job, 
and stnechag it bg have the

FORK IN THE ROAD? After a 
decade of automotive sales 
growth, discounters may see a 
slowdown. They expect de- 
creased consumer spending on 
most nonessential auto prod- 
ucts, due to soaring petroleum 
prices and a lagging economy. 
However, as DSN's Spring Car 
Care Buy-in section reports, 
there are many potential bright 
spots. The increasing trend 
among consumers to maintain 
their vehicles better, rather than 
buy new ones, should further 
spur volume in items useful to 
the do-it-yourselfer, and prod- 
ucts that will make cars run 
more efficiently or increase gas 
mileage. The latter have already 
shown a yearlong gain in move- 
ment, according to the latest 
Product Movement Audit. A 
possible downbeat note is being 
sounded with respect to the car 
stereo boom, where at least a 
few chains have cut inventory.

Retail Executives’ Pay Low

the more the executive should 
—— if that person is success- 

While retailing as a whole 
also trails other industries in 
the use of stock plans as a re- 
ward to executives, mass mer- 
chandisers have a far better 
record than other retail seg- 
ments. Other than in the retail 
industry, Mruk said, approx- 
imately 70% of publicly owned 
companies have stock option 
plans. 

Only 39% of publicly owned 
retailers have similar plans but 
when mass merchandisers are 
considered alone 73% have such 
plans. 

Mruk predicted that retailers 
will increasingly turn to option 
plans and other stock-related 
means to supplement base sal- 
aries in the 1980's. 

But while retailers must play 
catch-up ball to again become 
competitive in compensation 
programs, other pressures will 
make the task difficult. 

“Clearly the recessionary 
economy, coupled with continu- 
ing double-digit inflation, has 
‘80 corporate managements 

etween the proverbial rock 
and a hard place with respect to 
executive pay. The rock is the 
executive's need for more dol- 
lars to fight inflation. The hard 
place is the company’ ability to 


pay in a period when corporate 
performance may well decline. 
Add to that a Government pres- 
sure to restrain pay increases, 
which will probably stay with 
us in one form or another.” 

Executives, especially chief 
executive officers of companies 
in all industries, have actually 
experienced a decrease in real 
compensation—aftertax in- 
come adjustd for inflation—in 
the period from 1972-78. Retail- 
ers, whose total compensation 
has increased at a slower rate 
than the overall average, were 
especially affected. 

or the top executive group, 
which Arthur Young defines as 
the ceo, chief financial officer, 
treasurer and controller, the 
average salary increase in 1978 
was 12.2% in retailing while the 
average for all industries was 
13.6%. The differences found in 
earlier studies was even great- 
er. In 1976 retailers in the top 
executive group received aver- 
age increases of 10.1% com- 
pared to 14% as the all-industry 
average, and in 1974 the figures 
were 3.7% for retailers and 
11.8% overall. 

From 1970 to 1978, of 24 in- 
dustry groupings, the average 
total compensation of retailing 
ceo’s dropped from a ranking 
No. 1 to 14th while the top ex- 
ecutive group. dropped from 
third place in 1972 to 18th.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, FEBRUARY 25, 1980 


By Miles W. McBurney 

After years of accelerating sales, 
discounters in the auto aftermarket 
say they may see a slowdown in 1980. 

Encumbered simultaneously by a 
poor economy and out-of-control pe- 
troleum prices, merchandisers an- 
ticipate decreased consumer spend- 
ing on most nonessential automotive 
products. 

The bright spot in the picture 
focuses on automotive basics needed 
by consumers to run their cars, par- 
ticularly products which will help in- 
crease gas mileage. Chain spokes- 
men report that higher-mileage 
motor oils are increasingly popular 


and anticipate high demand for 
tune-up parts and tools this spring. 

However, accessories such as car 
stereos, the hottest high-ticket mer- 
chandise of the late 1970's, are cool- 
ing off rapidly for some discounters. 
Other accessories, of the nonfunc- 
tional, dress-up variety such as rac- 
ing mirrors or wheel covers, are 
being cut back in the expectation of 
lessened demand. 

“Generally, we'll be happy just to 
meet last year’s sales figures,” said a 
buyer at Fisher’s Big Wheel. “I ex- 
pect it to be a very basic year. We’re 
being very cautious with inventory 
levels and have been since last fall. 


The Outlook: Functional Basics 
To Gain as DIY Trend Widens 


The market outlook for automotive in 1980 includes: 
e A decline in the appeal of dress-up accessories as consumers are 
forced to defer nonessential purchases. 
@ Modest gains in functional basics such as spark plugs, filters, tools 
and similar merchandise as consumers increasingly turn to DIY for 


routine maintenance. 


e A continued surge in the body repair category and strength in the 
middle price range of waxes as consumers seek to maintain the ap- 
pearance of their present vehicles. 

® Sharply higher prices for motor oil—about 20% at retail—with 
increases coming in rapid succession through the spring and summer. 
Sales volume will creep upward while unit volume shrinks as consum- 
ers stretch change intervals and reduce their driving. 

@ Fuel-saving merchandise, from inexpensive additives to radial tires, 
will assume greater importance as consumers try almost desperately 


to reduce energy costs. 


® Car stereo, which was a major growth area both in units and tickets 
at the end of the last decade, will begin to slow for some discounters, 
accompanied by a return to more basic merchandise. 


We began controlling inventory lev- 
els in October and cut back more in 
December. If we had 12 items on a 
peg, for instance, we might have cut 
back to eight in October and six in 
December.” 

However, Big Wheel, unlike some 
other chains, is reducing stock 
rather than selection to meet the 
changing market conditions. “We 
don’t plan to drop anything,” the 
spokesman said. “You could say 
we're going with breadth without 
depth.” 

While buyers are predicting a rel- 
atively strong year for basics, they 
also face challenges from that mer-

Challenges Face Automotive After Decade of Growth 


The decade of the 1970's saw automotive as- 
sume an increasingly important role as a traffic 
builder for discounters with the size of depart- 
ments, turns and sales per square foot showing 
substantial gains. 

However, as the promotional importance of 
the department grew and price competition 
from within the general merchandise discount 
industry as well as specialists intensified, both 
initial markups and gross margins declined 
from 1970 levels. 

Average department size is now almost half 
again what it was in 1970, but has been holding 
relatively level in the last half of the decade. 
Turns have grown slowly but steadily from 3.7 
in 1970 to 4.7 in 1979. 

The most dramatic gains have come in sales 
volume, with sales per square foot almost dou- 
bling in five years. A major factor in this in- 
crease has been the inclusion of increasing 
amount of high-ticket merchandise from CB ra- 


stereo in the last few years. The DIY trend in 
auto maintenance has also increased tickets as 
has sharpening of self-sell sales techniques and 
packaging. 

At the opening of the decade, auto depart- 
ments often were limited to motor oil, low-end 
waxes, air fresheners, chemicals and similar in- 
expensive merchandise. In the intervening 
years whole new lines of merchandise were de- 
veloped for the DIY consumer who shops dis- 
count stores. Categories such as body repair 
evolved from modest beginnings, and lines such 


as shock absorbers, mufflers, customizing kits 
and others were almost reinvented for the back- 
yard mechanic. 

With a new decade begun, discounters have 
established themselves as major retailers to the 
DIYer, an increasingly vital market position, 
but face new challenges as the nature of the 
automobile and America’s attitude toward it 
change drastically. But much-altered designs, 
more-complicated maintenance and fuel econ- 
omy considerations present opportunities for, 
as well as obstacles to, continued growth.

Fuel Worries Boost Movement 
Of Additives, Engine Cleaners 


MADISON HEIGHTS, Mich.—The impact of America’s real 
concern about fuel supply and prices can be seen by compar- 
ing the current Product Movement Audit with last years. 

ile both reports naturally share an emphasis on winter 
seasonals, the 1980 PMA shows significant growth in prod- 
ucts which make engines run better and conserve fuel. 

A full 30% of the current top 100 are chemical additives, 
engine cleaners or tune-up kits and parts. In 1979, similar 
products accounted for 25% of the listings and benefitted 
from strong promotions aimed at reducilvg a large inventory of 
Autolite spark plugs. 

Buyers for discount store chains ‘cea that these gas- 
saving basics will continue strong through the spring and 
summer. If true, this means oils, filters, chemicals and tune- 
up accessories will take nearly half the listings in the top 100, 
leaving seasonals and especially high-ticket promotional ac- 
cessories in a diminished position of importance. 

That retailers cannot simply eliminate promotional ac- 
cessories is underscored by the 1980 positioning of the im- 
ported 2-ton hydraulic floor jack. It placed first on the current 
PMA while last year the highest positioning for a high-ticket 
accessory was sixth for a 1/2-ton jack. 

A Jamesway spokesman, noting that store traffic figures at 
the start of 1980 were below 1979's, said his sales of impulse 
items have suffered. As a result, he said, promotions this 
spring and summer in the auto department must be geared to 
maximize traffic and image. 


Bug Removers, Air Pumps Cited 


Promotions will be run with both high- and low-ticket items 
and on merchandise which can be tied into other depart- 
ments. The Jamesway spokesman cited bug removers as 
good low-ticket items to build traffic in the auto department 
and foot-operated air pumps as higher tickets that can benefit 
a department such as sporting goods as well as auto. 

A spokesman for ALCO added that his 1980 plans include 
sticking with similar, functional accessories for promotions 
rather than dress-up merchandise which is expected to suffer 
because of economic pressure on consumers. 

While hydraulic jacks are unquestionably high-ticket ac- 
cessories they are also very functional, and as buyers at 
chains such as Heck’s and Pamida note, the always-vital do- 
it-yourselfer will become even more important. 

The weakening of nonfunctional accessories is illustrated 
by the comparative rankings of air horns. Last year they were 
17th in dollars produced while this year they slipped back to 
56th. On the other hand, auto ramps, which were 26th last 
year moved up to 18th in the current listing. 

That motorists are keeping their cars longer before replac- 
ing them was apparent last year, with the numerous rankings 
of replacement headlights, battery chargers, booster cables 
and especially conventional tune-up kits. If confirmation of 
that trend were needed—beyond shrinking new car sales 
figures—it is contained in the current rankings. 

Discount chain buyers are confident that this development 
will translate into sales gains for car waxes and especially 
body repair compounds and accessories this spring.

Plush Bears, Frisbees, Lunchboxes, T-shirts Affected 


DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, MARCH 10, 1980 


Licensees, Not Buyers, Are Stuck in Olympics Boycott 


Nationwide DSN Report 
There will be few Mischa bears in toy 
departments this spring, and T-shirts, 
Frisbees, lunchboxes and posters with the 
logo and the mascot of the 1980 Moscow 
Summer Olympics are fast becoming col- 


Mischa, mascot of the Moscow Summer 
Olympics, is laughing on the outside. 


lector’s items. 

The United States boycott of the Sum- 
mer Games has dashed the well-laid plans 
of many manufacturers who obtained li- 
censes from the U.S. Olympic Committee 
or through the Moscow Organizing Com- 
mittee in order to cash in on the Olympic 
theme. 

“The initial reception [to Olympic mer- 
chandise] was fantastic, but then some 
cancellations came in and now no one 
wants to talk about it or see it,” said a 
spokesman for Chestnut Hill Marketing 

0. near Boston, a national sales and mar- 
keting company that handles posters and 
T-shirts. 

Most discounters won’t be stuck with 
merchandise because President Carter an- 
nounced plans for the boycott well before 
most buyers placed orders. 

_ALCO, for example, looked at merchan- 
dise, but didn’t plan an Olympic theme 
and made no commitments to manufactur- 
ers.

a, noted apparel buyer Tony Tiren- 

i. 

A Gold Circle stationery buyer said: “No 
retailer who has any sense will invest in an 
Olympic line knowing we might not go.” 
But buyers agreed that manufacturers 
who invested in an Olympic line are in a 
quandary. 

Some manufacturers oriented toward 
the discount market who obtained licenses 


for Olympic lines are R. Dakin & Co. 
(plush Mischa bears), Stuart Hall and 
Mead (stationery Pgs mars The Shirt 
Shed (T-shirts) and Adamstown Hosiery 
(athletic socks). Buyers say H&BA items 
with the Olympic seal will probably fare 
better than novelty merchandise. 

Naturaliy, those manufacturers who are 
further along in production are the most 
vulnerable. For example, Stuart Hall is 
well into production of a line of school sup- 
Se item is a record book with a 

lank chart for entering the names of gold 
medalists and their winning times. 

“We may have a collector’s item,” con- 
ceded executive vp Charles Hanson. 
“We’re waiting to see the outcome. We 
have other more important properties.” 

Mead, another licensee, developed a 
school supply line with track and field 
scenes trimmed with a red, white and blue 
border, but without the Olympic logo. 

“We repositioned it as a sports line,” 
explained associate market manager Blod- 
win Carter. “The question of the logo came 
up in planning, and leaving it off seemed to 
be the prudent business thing to do. We 
had hoped to capitalize on the excitement 
of the Olympic Games—it is a small but 
important part of our line. But we won’t 
live or die on it.” 

A spokesman for Dakin said the com- 
pany was not manufacturing, but was still 
taking orders, for its Mischa bears.

Energy Plan Could Close Stores Day Each Week Tradeway 


By Ken Rankin 

WASHINGTON—The Car- 
ter Administration’s new 
“standby” Federal energy con- 
servation plan includes provi- 
sions which could force many 
discount stores to close their 
doors at least one day each 
week. 

The controversial plan calls 
for a “compressed work- 
week”—one day shorter than 
normal operations—to cut gas- 
oline consumption during the 
next major energy crisis. 

The Federal restrictions 
would only take effect in states 
that fail to implement effective 
energy conservation programs 
of their own, but Department of 
Energy officials told Discount 
Store News that as many as a 
dozen or more states could fall 
into that category. 

In issuing the new Federal 
emergency plan, Government 
energy regulators maintained 


that “retail sales. . . should not 
be significantly affected by a 
compressed workweek,” be 
cause “research on the effect of 
Blue Laws [i.e., Sunday clos- 
ings] on aggregate retail sales 
has shown that total weekly re- 
tail sales are not significantly 
affected by such restrictions.” 
Retail industry leaders dis- 
agree, however. Although the 
new Federal “compressed 
workweek” approach would ap- 
ply equally to oe 
and service industries as we 
as retailing, chain store opera- 
tors are expected to raise the 
most strenuous objections. 
The one-day-a-week shut- 
down plan is still in the proposal 
stage—D.0.E. officials don’t 
expect to issue final regulations 
until after a series of hear- 
ings—but other provisions of 
the new Federal standby pro- 
gram were issued in final form. 
Among those final new “in- 


terim” emergency conservation 
mandates: 

@ Reactivation of those contro- 
versial building thermostat 
ceilings set to expire; 

@ New odd-even and dollar 
purchase restrictions on gas- 
oline sales; 

e Tighter enforcement of the 
50 m.p.h. national speed limit; 
@ Requirements that stores 
with 100 or more employees de- 
velop their own programs to en- 
courage car pooling and other 
energy-saving types of trans- 
portation for workers. 

D.O.E. considered, but re- 
jected a number of other 
standby energy conservation 
mandates, including re- 
strictions on retail store light- 
ing. Department officials 
noted, however, that individual 
states may wish to consider in- 
cluding such restrictions in 
their own local emergency con- 
servation plans.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, MARCH 10, 1980 


NEW YORK—Those dis- 
counters troubled by high 
shrinkage rates most likely 
have only themselves to blame, 
a loss prevention study pre- 
pared for the National Mass Re- 
tailing Institute indicated. 

The study, done by Arthur 
Young & Co., the accounting 
firm, concluded that chains that 
have decreased their theft 
losses make a bigger financial 
commitment to security than 
chains with significant shrink- 
age problems.

“Companies that have been 
successful in keeping shrinkage 
levels low have paid a price for 
it. The most direct measure of 
the expense of their investment 
is the size of their security bud- 
get expressed as a per cent of 
sales,” the Arthur Young re- 
port stated. 

In a survey of 51 discounters 
with a total of 5,600 stores, 
shghtly more than half of the 
low-shrinkage companies 
(those in which the rate was 
less than 2% of sales) spend at 
least one-third of a per cent of 
sales for security. Only about a 
third of the high-shrinkage 
companies (with rates in excess 
of 3% of sales) spend a propor- 
tionate amount. 

The greater investment by 
low-shrinkage discounters is 
applied to more formalized se- 
curity programs and to a 
greater 1eliance on personnel to 
control losses rather than de- 
vices such as electronic tags 
and limited-access sales areas. 

In addition, companies that

owever, simply assigning

Orleans, will feature such diverse speakers as baseball Hall- 
of-Famer Willie Mays; CBS newsmen Morley Safer and Andy

Orleans native (and premiere musician) Pete Fountain.

Luria Has Record 


Half-Year Results 


MIAMI LAKES, Fla.—The 
opening of six showrooms out- 
side of the Greater Miami area 
helped cataleger L. Luria & 
Sons record half-year sales and 
income gains of more than 20%. 

Sales for the six months 
ended Dec. 31, 1979, jumped 
36.2% to $42,878,189 from $31,- 
485,342. Income in the period 
went up 21.7% from $1,655,451 
to $2,014,021. 


The half-year gains were 
sparked by a big Jump in vol- 
ume in the quarter ended Dec. 
31, 1979. Sales in that period— 
which included key Christmas 
holiday volume—were up 
42.4% to $31,812,917 from $22,- 
347,071. Income increased 
21.5% to $1,805,156 from $1,- 
485,952. 


The key holiday quarter in 
1979 accounted for 74.2% of 
Luria’s six-month volume while 
the period in 1978 posted 71% of 
the half-year sales.

Expanded Show 
Set For May 18-21 


NEW YORK—The National 
Stationery Show has expanded 
to all four floors of the New 
York Coliseum for its exposi- 
tion to be held May 18-21. 

Hours for the show will be 
Sunday, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.; Mon- 
day and Tuesday, 9 a.m. to 6 
p.m., and Wednesday, 9 a.m. to 
D p.m. 


Jamesway's Sales 
Up 20% For Year 


SECAUCUS, N.J.—James- 
way reported record sales of 
$242 million for the fiscal year 
ended Feb. 2, 1980, not includ- 
ing leased department volume. 
The total is a 20% increase over 
the previous year’s sales of $202 
million. 

Net income is expected to be 
in excess of last year’s $5.8 mil- 
lion, but not in proportion to 
the sales increase.

PRODUCT MOVEMENT AUDIT 


Fragrance 
Biz Swells 
Hot 25% 


By M. Raymond Prendergast 
President, 
Boston Distributors 

A better-balanced merchan: 
dise mix with a greater empha: 
sis on single-bottle rather thar 
gift-set sales spurred a 25% 

owth in fragrance volume for 
Christmas 1979. 

Increased representation oj} 
women’s fragrances and 
greater use of Christmas mer: 
chandisers and stocking stuff: 
ers also contributed to our gain. 

Women’s single-bottle fra: 
grances showed a 35% sales in- 
crease over 1978 with Charlie 
again leading the Product 

ovement Audit for December. 
Holiday sales of this brand, 
however, declined and 1980 wil! 
undoubtedly see a tightening o* 
the line. 

Cachet and Jovan Musk re- 
mained strong in the single- 
bottle segment, ranking No. 3 
and No. 4, respectively. Enjoli, 
Charles of the Ritz’s 1978 entry, 
established a significant in- 
crease due to greater avail- 
ability of the product. 

Enjoli’s sell-through for us 
was nearly 100%, and it ranked 
No. 5. Matchabelli’s Windsong 
and Revlon’s Jontue demon- 
strated strong sales as did Avi- 
ance. Matchabelli’s commit- 
ment to the support of Aviance 
finally speoind to be paying 
off as the brand placed in the 
top 10 for the first time. Of the 
new 1979 entries, Chimere 
(Matchabelli) and Oleg Cassini 
for Women (Jovan) will be sure 
winners in 1980. 


More Winners 


Value sets under $7.50 domi- 
nated the gift category in 1979 
with Enjoli setting the pace asa 
new fragrance entry. Coty, 
with Emeraude and Wild Musk 
taking four positions, held onto 
its leadership of the gift seg- 
ment. Matchabelli was close 
with Windsong and Cachet gar- 
nering three spots. Dana’s Tabu 
and Jean Nate also placed in the 
year’s 10 best sets. 

Jean Nate again controlled 
the bath market with five en- 
tries on the PMA. Jovan, Char- 
lie, Enjoli and Windsong also 
scored well in this strong 
growth category. 

Cachet and Windsong won 
the top two positions in the 
stocking stuffer listing. A more 
definitive description of this 
valuabie selling size is “impulse 
or trial size.” Consumers, espe- 
cially the young, react favora- 
bly to the lower price points as a 
means of sampling a new fra- 
grance. 

The men’s gift-set category 
showed only a 10% increase in 
dollar volume in December. Al- 
though Old Spice retained its 
No. 1 position, the franchised 
lines showed the greatest 
growth. English Leather 
(Mem) and British Sterling 
(Speidel) had exceptionally 
strong brand shares.

Color Photo Lab Part | 
Of Lucky's Picture 


DUBLIN, Calif.—Lucky 
Stores has opened a pho- 
tofinishing laboratory in La Mi- 
rada, Calif., that will serve 
almost 200 company stores, in- 
cluding the three dozen Gemco 
discount stores in southern Cal- 
ifornia. 

The facility, called Horizon 
Custom Color Labs, is geared 
to handle more than 4,000 rolls 
of films a day. It processes only 
110, 126 and 135 color film. 

Black and white film, movies 
and slides are processed for 
Gemco and the other stores op- 
erated by Lucky by an outside 
photo lab.

Discounters Plan Nearly 300 More DIY Departments 


By Miles W. McBurney 

Many of the leading chains in dis- 
counting have made major new com- 
mitments to capture an expanding 
share of the home improvement mar- 
ket. 

Discounters began 1980 with more 
than 1,500 home improvement de- 
partments, approximately 300 more 
than were in operation a year ago. 
Present plans call for nearly 300 de- 
partments to be added in the 1980 
DIY census year (Feb. 1, 1980, to 
Jan. 31, 1981). 

While 1,800 home improvement 


departments is a formidable retail 
force—one that has the home center 
industry sitting up and taking no- 
tice—discounters can really be di- 
vided in two categories: K mart and 
everybody else. 

K mart is currently operating 916 
building material departments 
averaging about 4,400 sq. ft. A chain 
spokesman said that 100-125 addi- 
tional departments (all in stores 
other than the 40,000 sq. ft. 
Group 9s) will be opened this census 
year, some as large as 7,500 sq. ft. 

Besides their sheer numbers, 


K mart runs some of the most com- 
plete home improvement sections in 
the discount industry. When build- 
ing material departments, with 
their paneling, lumber, shelving, 
plumbing fixtures and other mer- 
chandise are added to related DIY 
departments such as hardware, 
paint, electrical and lawn “and gar- 
den, a K mart store’s approximately 
20,000 sq. ft. of DIY space is com- 
petitive with the area of many home 
centers. 

In the second tier of home im- 
provement discounters, the major 
forces are T.G. & Y. and a hard- 


cessful of discounters, in 1979 dis- 
continued all 52 of its broad-line 
home improvement departments 
and Bradlees may be on the verge of 
a similar move. 

A Wal-Mart spokesman said that 
bulky, hard-to-handle materials 
such as lumber and fiberglass in- 
sulation simply weren’t sufficiently 
productive in the chain’s relatively 
small stores. The departments were 
dropped, and the space saved was 
divided among expanded hardware 
departments and pet seasonal de- 
partments in those stores. 

Bradlees, which operates 15 home 


charging Woolco. improvement departments, has sus-

Hardware Sales/Ft. Rise /2% in 3 Years 


Long one of discounting’s more basic and sta- 
ple departments, hardware evolved slowly 
through the 1970's. 

At the close of the decade, department size 
was significantly larger than at the beginning, 
but smaller than in the middle years, after 
which some product lines were broken out into 
other departments—notably home improve- 


More significantly, while initial markups and 
gross margins remained stable with slight in- 
creases, sales per square foot rose more than 
72% through the last half of the 70’s. Discount- 
ers and their customers turned from low-end 
product lines to higher-ticket goods of better 
quality as the do-it-yourselfer gained long-term 
interest in home repair activity to beat the ris- 


ment. ing cost of professional help.

Nearly 300 More DIY Depts. Set 


(Continued from page 57) 
choose to concentrate more on home 
“decor” than do-it-yourself improve- 
ments. 

Nonetheless, most discounters in the 
business are looking to home improve- 
ment to be one of the most successful 
categories in 1980 with several factors 
buoying their optimism. 

e economics of DIY is forcing an 
ever-growing number of householders 
to try their hand at their own repairs 
and improvements; energy costs are 
making better weathe nt Me impera- 
tive, and first-time DIYers are discover- 
ing that most projects are easy to 


perform and sometimes even become 
recreational. 

While inflation is squeezing dispos- 
able incomes even harder, consumers 
view maintenance of their homes as a 
necessity. “A home is the No. 1 priority 
for people. ... People will spend on 
their homes because they have to,” a 
spokesman for Rink’s said. “Our job is to 
see that they spend at our stores.” 

A spokesman for Jamesway said: 
“Home improvement will probably be 
the single biggest growth area in our 
stores for the _ ee future.” 

Not only are DIY repairs less expen- 
sive than professional contractors, he 


said, but consumers are inclined to im- 
prove the homes they presently own 
rather than purchase another. 

“Consider the cost of new homes. Not 
just are materials and labor higher, but 
also mortgage rates are at record levels. 
Rather than being able to afford a new 
home, people are forced to add on to 
their present homes,” he explained. 

One of the staple categories in home 
improvement is energy savers—from 
fiberglass insulation to weather strip- 
ping, storm doors and windows, pipe 
wraps, timer thermostats and any other 
product that will reduce heat waste and 
conserve fuel. 

Retailers in more temperate markets 
report steady growth in energy savers 
as well as do discounters in the colder 
North. 


A Sunbelt discounter like T.G. & Y. 
noted that despite a relatively mild win- 
ter in its regions, insulation sales this 
year have shown healthy gains. 

Others agree, reasoning that the 
prospects for this kind of merchandise 
will no longer fluctuate according to cur- 
rent weather patterns but will continue 
to gain as fuel becomes more expensive. 
Fuel consumption may be lower, but. 
costs still rise, they note. 

“We’re having a mild winter this year 
and people are still seeing their heating 
bills go up because of the cost of oil,” the 
Rink’s spokesman said. 

Fiberglass insulation remains the key 
to projecting a good image in energy 
savers, and discounters reported this 
season that shortages eased, allowing

Aggressive Promotion Is Key 


Rink’s: DIY to Grow Despite Economy 


TOLEDO, Ohio—Despite 
economic pressures that may- 
hold down other merchandise 
categories, home improvement 
will continue to grow a 
out 1980, a merchandiser for 
Rink’s predicted. 

“If we’re aggressive in pro- 
moting home improvement, 
this will be a good year for us,” 
said Jerry Sommers, the 
chain’s merchandise manager 
for the category. 

“A home is the No. 1 priority 
for people. Home improve- 
ment, from nuts and bolts and 
screws to hand tools and plumb- 
ing and hardware and every- 
thing else is very recession 
resistant. People will spend on 
their homes because they have 
to,” he said. “Our job is to see 
that they spend at our stores.” 

Of particularly high potential 
will be products related to en- 
ergy saving. While merchan- 
dise in this group has benefited 
in recent years by the steady 


rise in energy costs, the quick- 
ening pace of fuel price in- 
creases has led to ever-greater 
optimism by home improve- 
ment retailers. 

“I’m still excited about en- 
ergy savers,” Sommers said. “I 
think they’re going to stay very 
big for us. We’re having a mild 
winter this year and people are 
still seeing their heating bills go 
up because of the cost of oil. 

As a result, sales of weather 
stripping, fiberglass insulation 
and other products that can 
help ease the energy-cost di- 
lemma, such as wood-burnin 
stoves, have steadily increased. 

Rink’s, which introduced 
stoves in its stores last year, 
carried six sku’s this season 
with good results, especially in 
the fall and early winter, Som- 
mers said. 

Fiberglass insulation, which 
two years ago was virtually un- 
available, is now carried as a 
year-round product with some

The high cost of borrowing will 
put ever-greater pressure on

amine their mix to pare down 
slow-turning sku’s. 

An example is lauan-backed 
wood paneling. “Where before 
we might have about 10 dif- 
ferent panels in a store, now we 
might have six or eight,” the 
merchandiser said. 

Rink’s includes home im- 
provement departments in each 
of its 42 stores, with four more 
to be added by April. At least 
one additional store is sched- 
uled to open in the next year. 

Department size averages 
5,000 sq. ft., although the 
newer stores are slightly 
smaller than the approximately 
80,000 sq. ft. of existing units. 

“The newer departments will 
have to be slightly smaller be- 
cause everything will be com- 
pacted in these stores,” Som- 
mers said. “They’ll have the 
same merchandise, however, 
because we'll go a little higher.”

ignated as home improvement 
are separate departments for 
paint and hardware, adding ap- 
proximately 4,000 sq. ft. of sell.

Rink’s and Jamesway re- 
ported that customers snapped 
up their enlarged lines of stoves 
during late-summer and early- 
fall promotions. “We didn’t have

We were completely wiped out 
after the first two promotions,”

Discounters also theorize 
that consumers are becoming 
more committed to DIY im- 
provements by virtue of the 
changing patterns in tool pur- 
chases. Rather than purchasing 
for price alone, consumers 
seem to be more concerned 
about quality, leading merchan- 
disers to believe that consum- 
ers are making a long-term 
commitment both out of neces- 
sity and as converts to home 
repair as a hobby. 

Most discounters report that 
the greatest interest is gener- 
ated by their mid-priced lines of 
better imported tools and some 
domestic brands. 

“The middle of the road is 
where we find the action in 
hand tools,” a Rink’s merchan- 
diser said. “Most American- 
made tools are very expen- 
sive—you can pay $8 or $9 for 
pliers. You can get a good im- 
port for half the price with 90% 
of the quality and that’s where 
we want to be.” 

Perhaps as important a 
motivation for growing num- 
bers of DIYers as cost savings is 
the recreational aspect of work- 
ing with their hands. “They 
may have been forced into DIY 
by necessity, but many of them 
stay with it because it’s fun,” a 
Woolco spokesman said. “They 
redo a room and they’re proud 
to show their neighbors what 


they accomplished.”

Macks Joins Up: Latest Variety Chain to Open Discounter 


By Judith Crown 

Macks becomes one of the 
last major variety store chains 
to turn to discounting with the 
opening of its first Maxway 
store this month in Sand- 
ersville, Ga. 

The Maxway debut comes 18 
years after Kresge made the 
switch and shaped the face of 
discounting. During the 1960's 
and 1970’s, Woolworth, 


A & & a <A Mart, A. L. 
Duckwall, G. C . Murp ¢ Pani 
Sterling Stores saw that 
growth would come with high- 
volume, low-margin opera- 
tions. They concluded, some re- 
luctantly, that variety stores 
were a ying breed. 

During the mid-1970’s, 
Macks, headquartered in San- 
ford, N.C., found its variety 
stores squeezed by discounters 


and dollar and drug chains. 
This contributed to a slowdown 
in earnings and 5.9% profit dip 
in 1978. 

For the first three quarters of 
1979, sales increased 23% to 
$42. 2 million and earnings were 
up 61% to $870,336. The chain 
operates 99 variety stores. 

Macks executives regret not 
having moved to discounting 
sooner, but note they have

DALLAS—Twenty thou- 
sand people turned out for the 
annual home center show held 
here early this month, but dis- 
counters were barely visible in 
the crowd. 

Although tool, paint and sun- 
dries, plumbing and electrical 
vendors rented more booth 
space than ever before, dis- 
counters still think of the show 
as too building-material ori- 
ented for their needs. 

However, among the dozen or 
so discounters that did come 
out the reactions were more 
than favorable. 

“It’s a show that gets better 
rag oe said a spokesman 
for Gold Circle who said he at- 
tended the show each year to 
keep abreast of what's happen- 
ing in home improvements. 

‘It was a good working 
show,” reported Rick Giordano, 
buyer, Fisher's Big Wheel, New 
Castle, Pa. “It gave us a chance 
to take care of any problems we 
had with our vendors.” 

Giordano and the other dis- 
counters who went to Dallas 
agreed that the home center 
show would never replace the 
giant hardware show in Chi- 
cago. However, they all pointed 
out that the slower pace of the 
former gave them a chance to 
stop in at the booths of the 
smaller vendors they never 
have time to see in Chicago. 


“The more hard lines vendors 
they get,” predicted Giordano, 
“the bigger the following they'll 
get.” 

“It was an excellent show,” 
assessed Larry Shapiro, divi- 
sion merchandise manager, 
Gold Triangle, Hialeah, Fla.

cause the hardware show was 
becoming too “nuts and bolts 
oriented. 

“This show gives me a chance 
to look over the big-ticket do-it- 
yourself products, like kitchen 
cabinets. 

The one single complaint

of new products. Some dis-

hardware show to offer new 
items. Others felt that the rapid 

owth of the do-it-yourself 

usiness over the past five 
years had finally caught up with 
the industry.

ucts—although their opinion of 
the show remained high.

End of Minimum Pricing 
For Booze Due in N.J. 


TRENTON—Barring fur- 
ther court intervention, min- 
imum pricing of alcoholic bev- 
erages is due to end this month. 


Minimum wholesale and re- 
tail prices, opposed by con- 
sumer groups and state agen- 
cies, but strongly supported by 
distributors and most retailers, 
were struck down by the State 
Supreme Court last month. 
The court, however, stayed en- 
forcement of its decision until 
Maren 11 to allow minimum 
price supporters time to file for 
a rehearing or to appeal to the 
United States Supreme Court. 


In addition, legislators in the 
State Senate and Assembly 
have filed bills to reinstitute 
minimum prices through at

Outlook For 1980: 
Price Increases, 
More Accessories 


The 1980 outlook for camera 
and photo includes: 
e Higher retail prices on film 
and photo finishing as manufac- 
turers pass along recent surges 
in material (particularly silver) 
and labor costs. 
@ Stepped-up consumer and 
discounter interest in 35mm 
cameras, particularly single lens 
reflex cameras (SLR’s) as manu- 
facturers continue to presell the 
TV viewing audience with heavy 
ad schedules. 
@ Increased stocking of profit- 
able camera accessories—gad- 
get bags, straps, lenses, flashes 
and the like—for bottom-line 
protection. 


While catalogers like Service Merchandise, Fishkill, 
N.Y., have increased their selection of accessories to 
boost mar ins, discounters suspect that recent price 
hikes will force showrooms to alter their giveaway 


price strategies.

Discounters Top $2 Billion in ’79, Up 16%; 
Use of Lessees Down Sharply in Decade — 


Last year, discounters’ photo department 
sales topped $2 billion—a 16% increase over the 
previous year—evidence that the decision by 
91% of the country’s discounters to own and 
operate their own departments was paying off. 
In 1970, only 63% of the chains were running 
their own photo departments. 

While department turns and margins have 
remained fairly constant over the past decade, 


sales per square foot have more than doubled. 
Dealers attribute this improvement to the addi- 
tion of more sku’s of high-profit accessories and 
to increased consumer demand for photo finish- 
ing which carries margins of about 30%. This 
improved performance coincides with a shrink- 
ing sales floor. Discounters decreased their spa- 
tial commitment to the category by more than 
20% over the last 10 years.

By Arthur Markowitz 

There’s going to be fewer cata- 
logers, but stronger ones. 

The net result is that the industry 
will continue to show strong growth, 
hitting $8 billion this year, up about 
15% from $7 billion last year, accord- 
ing to DSN estimates. 

The top three dozen chains— 
those with $16 million and over in 
volume—will account for an esti- 
mated $4.7 billion, or about 59% of 
the volume. 

DSN last year tracked 27 cata- 
logers with $16 million and over in 
sales and they accounted for $3.8 bil- 
lion or just over 54% of the industry’s 
total volume. 

A sharper indicator of the trend 
toward the top chains capturing a 
greater share of the industry’s vol- 
ume can be seen in a comparison of 
the sales of the six leading cata- 
logers. DSN estimated they will do 
$3.2 billiom in their current fiscal 
year, up 18.5% from an estimated 
$2.7 billion. 

The contraction under way in the 
industry includes about a dozen 
Dahnken franchisee members cle- 
ing down shop, joining about an- 
other two dozen small companies 
that have either shut their doors or 


reverted to their jewelry store or 
tobacco distributor roots. 

Corr-Williams, a privately held to- 
bacco distributor that had seven 
small showrooms in Mississippi and 
Louisiana before cutting back to 
just one, exemplifies the contrac- 
tion. 

One executive explained: “We 
were too small and we faced too 
strong competition; H. J. Wilson 
just overwhelmed us.” 

He asserted that “our catalog 
prices averaged 5%-10% less than 
Wilson, but we couldn’t carry $1 mil- 
lion in inventory in our 2,500-sq.-ft. 
units as Wilson did in its larger 


showrooms.” 

Wilson, he added, “got there first 
with the larger showrooms; we could 
have switched to larger units if we 
had. several million dollars, but we 
don’t.” 

Wilson is No. 4 among catalogers 
in volume. But the stronger cata- 
loger doesn’t have to be as large as 
Wilson to impact smaller chains. 

Two-unit Key Distributing plans 
to open in North Huntington, Pa., to 
get out of the highly competitive 
Pittsburgh market where it has one 
showroom that has to face Basco, 
David Weis, J. Dalhkemper, Catalog 
Discount Sales, and Towers, chains 


Biggies to Get Fatter as Number of Operators Slims 


whose volume ranges from $100 mil- 
lion down to $16 million. 

Getting out of the business is one 
way the catalog industry is contract- 
ing. The other method that could 
spread is acquisition of smaller 
chains. (Modern Merchandising 
bought Dolgin’s and Leeds in the 
last two years and Service Merchan- 
dise took over Value House in 1978.) 

While catalog executives agreed 
that acquisitions were a quick way to 
grow and get into new markets, no 
one expected to see any major take- 
overs this year.

More Chains Meet Competition With Different-Price Editions 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Catalogers are stepping up their 
use of differently priced versions of 
their main book, as competition 
among them heightens, and a grow- 
ing number of chains open show- 
rooms in the same markets. 

The catalogers already using dif- 
ferently priced editions include the 
industry’s top five chains—Service 
Merchandise, Best, Modern Mer- 
chandising, H. J. Wilson, and Ar- 


dan—along with Consumers Dis- 
tributing, Naum and Century 
House. 

Most of the catalogers declined to 
discuss the fact that they issue dif- 
ferent editions of their book because 
they don’t want their competition to 
know this, nor do they want com- 
petitors to get copies of the various 
versions to check out their pricing 
program. 

But the Big Three—Best, Service 


and Modern—have readily acknowl- 
edged that they use different edi- 
tions, with the markets served by 
each version easily identified in the 
case of Best and Modern. 
Executives of the three chains 
each cited competition as the reason 
for using different editions. A Best 
executive explained that the dif- 
ferent editions “give us margin flex- 
ibility to meet competition by allow-

=, Discounters Respond to Carter, 
7m ~a scrutinize Credit-Card Setups 


WASHINGTON—Dis- 
counters are scrutinizing their 
credit card programs in re- 
sponse to President Carter's re- 
cent call for tighter controls on 
consumer credit. 

“Our attorneys are currently 
studying the usury law require- 
ments in each of the states 
where we have stores,” said 
Richard Baum, Woolco’s direc- 
tor of retail credit. “At the same 
time, we are studying our com- 
puter needs to learn how long it 
will take us to implement any 
changes.” 

However, he noted: “Our 
efforts today are to have our 
customers pay by cash.” The 
credit director added that 
Woolco’s policy is to first em- 
phasize cash payment, then 
promote its layaway program 

and after that its credit. 

"Only 10% of Woolco’s sales are 
derived from credit card pur- 
chases, according to Baum. 

While most discounters reac- 
tions were supportive of the 
President, those who would be 
making credit rogram changes 
said they would wait until the 
oe were more clearly 

efined before making any 
moves. 

At T.G. & Y , Harold Plunk, 
senior vice president of admin- 
istration, told Discount Store 
News: “We don’t have our own 
credit program and bank cards 
make up a small percentage of 
our sales. We do not anticipate 
any negative impact due to 
credit restraints.” 

Still, Plunk said, he found it 

“encouraging to have the Presi- 
dent take a positive approach to 


economic conditions.” 

A spokesman at the National 
Mass Retailing Institute re- 

ported that it was too soon after 
the President's talk to get a con- 
sensus of what _—— chains 
would be doing to com 

At the Association o neral 
Merchandise Chains, president 
Edward T. Borda pointed out 
that most of the association’s 
members do not have extensive 


credit programs. He agreed 
with those discounters who 
said they were waiting to learn 
the details of the Administra- 
tion’s new program before de- 
ciding what steps to take. 

Teck Shewmaker, president 
of Wal- Mart, noted that “the 
effect on our business won’t be 
great because we don't have our 
own credit program.”

{ Spotlight on: Up-and-Coming Category )) 


More Discounters TTT} 


Carry Luggage 


Discounters are in- 
creasingly adding luggage 
to their merchandise mix 
and often using platforms 
to achieve the effect of this 
display at Caldor, White 
Plains, N.Y. 

Caldor gives luggage 
up-front prime real estate 
between photo and gift- 
ware. Other chains mer- 
chandise luggage with 
sporting goods or set it off 
from other hard goods. 

Luggage offers high- 
margin, high-ticket sales, 
and smaller carry-on bags 
can turn fast. They are get- 
ting more space at the ex- 
pense of three-, four- and 
five-piece se’s. 

In luggage, discounters 
are able to stand behind 
national brands (such as 
Samsonite and American 
Tourister), a luxury they 
don't enjoy in apparel. 

_ Luggage, not surpris- 
ingly, appears to have the 
best acceptance by 
chains in metropolitan 


areas. (DSN photo)

ANNUAL REPORT. DSN's ex- 
clusive Product Movement Au- 
dits wrap up the results for 1979. 
The top-moving products in key 
merchandise categories are 
tracked and the significance of 
purchasing trends is explored. 


AUTOMOTIVE. The basics in 
this category will have to carry 
the load for discounters in 1980 
as the sales of dress-up ac- 
cessories slumped last year, a 
development expected to con- 
tinue this year. (P. 35) 


ELECTRIC HOUSEWARES. 
Practicality will be the key as 
consumers defer nonessential 
purchases in 1980. (P. 26) 


H&BA. Bar soaps developed 
into a major dollar producer for 
discounters last year with de- 
odorants also showing good 
gains. These products, with 
nome permanents, promise to 
do well in 1980. (P. 64) 


HARDWARE. To no one’s sur- 
prise, home improvements, es- 
pecially energy savers, were the 
hot products and will be for the 
foreseeable future. (P. 44) 


HOUSEWARES. Novelty value, 
especially coupled with fashion, 
fueled this category in 1979. Un- 
like many other departments. 
trade-up products look strong 
here. (P. 18) 


SPORTING GOODS. Family 
activities, lawn games, fishing, 
camping and similar pursuits, 
will continue to lead. (P. 66) 


TOYS. Play value will be the key 
to merchandising toys. Con- 
sumers in 1979 showed they 
want that attribute in toys, 
whether low-ticket basics or ex- 
pensive electronics. (P. 60)

Different Emphasis 


The region’s lifestyle has re- 
sulted in low-cost traditional 
ironstone dinnerware continu- 
ing to be popular. Bacar lists six 
20-pe. Royal China sets, includ- 
ing five designs that debuted on 
the audit. 

Fashion is a major selling fac- 
tor for glassware, with the bet- 
ter-selling styles trending to- 
ward simple designs in either 
one or two hues or cut of the 
glass. 

Gold Aster was the new de- 
sign for beverageware that 
made the HalMar and Myron 
Nickman reports while Chival- 
ry was the cut glass style for 
wineglasses that showed up on 
the HalMar and Bacar audits.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, APRIL 7, 1980 


(Discount Store News.) 


LA | 


6th Annual 


Product Movement Audit 


Corning Removal 
Of Retail Prices 
Bothers Chains 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Corning Glass’ decision to 
drop retail prices from its 1980 
first-half catalog has created 
competitive pricing problems 
for discounters and other retail- 
ers. 

A Corning Glass executive 
asserted that the prices were 
dropped from the catalog be- 
cause the end of fair trade 
meant that no one sold goods at 
the listed prices. 

But discounters offered addi- 
tional reasons for the manufac- 
turer's move. 


Another Perspective 


One merchandiser noted that 
elimination of the prices would 
help distributors maintain their 

rofits despite the loss of some 

usiness from chains who will 
buy direct. Lack of the catalog 
ee means “I don’t have a 

enchmark price against which 
I can compare prices from dif- 
ferent distributors to see who's 
giving me the best deal.” 

He explained that the =— 
price was the basic price quote 
by distributors who then cited 
various discounts for such fac- 
tors as advertising and quan- 
tity buys to come up with the 
final charge for the merchan- 
dise. 

Another merchandiser point- 
ed out that Corning Glass 
raised its prices at the end of

cookware is seen in Zodys, 
Slauson Avenue, Los Angeles, 
in merchandising of stainless 
steel and high-end, nonstick 


goods. (DSN photo)

6th Annual 
Product Movement Audit 


Styler/Dryers, 
Drips Vie For 
Electrics Lead 


Styler/dryers and drip cof- 
feemakers this year are again 
expected to vie for the top spot 
in small-electrics productivity. 

Overall, electric housewares 
sales are seen as remaining flat 
due to the uncertain economy 
and consumers focusing their 
buying on essential goods. 

These projections reflect 
trends evident in the electrics 
field for the past few years, and 
are also seen in the Myron 
Nickman small-appliance Prod- 
uct Movement Audit reports. 

The productivity battle be- 
tween styler/dryers and drip 
coffeemakers has been going on 
for the last half-dozen years. It 
shows up in a comparison of the 
PMA for last year with the au- 
dit for 1978. 

In the 1979 audit (see chart), 
the two categories split the 
overall top honors with styler/ 
dryers No. 1 in unit movement 
and drip coffeemakers captur- 
ing the greatest dollar action. 

In the previous PMA, styler/ 
dryers were No. 1 in both unit 
and dollar movement, with drip 
coffeemakers No. 2. 

As for the flat sales outlook, 
this is expected to be a repeat of 
last year. The 1979 report 
showed a slight 3.4% drop in 
overall dollar volume to $4.2 
million from the previous audit, 
while unit movement fell 14.7% 
to 246,388 despite 10 more sku’s

6th Annual 


Product Movement Audit 


Styler/Dryers, 
Drips Compete 


(Continued from page 27) 


total dollar movement. 

Drip coffeemakers recap- 
tured the top spot in total dollar 
movement as this classification 
continued to be used as a popu- 
lar gift, particularly for new- 
lyweds and students off to 
college for the first time. Its 
acceptance as a gift was aided 
by the introduction of units that 
made just small quantities at 
one time; these models are 
geared to the needs of singles 
and couples, demographic 
groups that are forming an in- 
creasingly important segment 
of the population. 

Fad and fringe items have 
long been important for the 
electrics business. Despite con- 
sumer reservations about these 
products, a new item can cap- 
ture sales during its initial in- 
troduction. 


Promising Area 


The specialty electrics classi- 
fication is an example. Hot air 
popcorn makers—which be- 
came available in mass quan- 
tities last year—captured the 
top two spots and No. 6. 

The mini-deep fat fryer, 
which had been a key item in 
the 1978 audit, showed up in 
only four places. Only two hot- 
dog cookers made the report 
and hamburger makers—once 
the hottest electric—didn’t 
score at all. 

Food processors were the 
only new classification on the 
1979 audit. Its inclusion reflects 
the impact it made as a rela- 
tively new item that is in- 
creasingly being used as a gift. 
The higher average retail price 
for food processors resulted in 
low unit movement, but the 
total dollar movement was high 
enough to make the six-sku 
classification ninth in this au- 
dit. 


Balance Is Achieved 


Most of the classifications 
tracked by the audit are basics, 
with little change in overall 
standing and few new items. 

Toasters, for example, 
ranked No. 5 in both total unit 
and dollar movement, while in 
the previous report it was No. 5 
in units and No. 3 in dollars. 
Slow cookers were No. 8 in both 
measurements, having been 
No. 7 in total units and No. 5in 
total dollars in the 1978 PMA. 
Only two items showed up for 
the first time on the toaster re- 
port while only one debuted on 
the slow cooker chart. 

Irons ranked No. 6 in both 
measurements in both PMAs. 
Four lightweight irons debuted 
on the latest report, as these

Product Movement Audit 


Basics Rule 
Auto More 
Than Ever 


By Miles W. McBurney 

Although the biggest dollar 
producer in 1979 was a high- 
ticket promotional accessory, 
the annual Auto Product Move- 
ment Audit was dominated by 
basic, generally low-priced 
merchandise. 

The figures from distributor 
Allied Accessories and Auto 
Parts Co. indicate that predic- 
tions that 1980 will be a year of 
conservative purchasing pat- 
terns by consumers are well 
founded. While basics have al- 
ways been the foundation of dis- 
count stores auto departments, 
as 1979 ended accessories, es- 

ecially dress-up items, were 
urther reduced in importance. 

One note that should be made 
of products listed in this PMA 
concerns Motorcraft spark 
plugs. In 1978, Allied carried 
Autolite as the original equip- 
ment replacement for Ford 
products, but in 1979 Autolite 
was replaced by Motorcraft. 
While the chart indicates that 
the Motorcraft numbers were 
unranked the previous year, in 
fact the Autolite equivalents 
achieved approximately the 
same rankings. For example, 
the BRF-42 and ARF-52 plugs, 
ranked fourth and sixth in this 
report, placed fifth and fourth, 
respectively, for 1978. 


Sales Improve 


Spark plugs generally, as 
well as tune-up kits, chemicals, 
and oils, were the strongest 
performers in 1979, in some 
cases recording significant 
gains. 

Oil, especially, showed gains 
in 1979 because retailers were 
forced by rapidly rising prices 
to seek out comparative bar- 
gains from other than their nor- 
mal supply channels. Allied 
president Herbert Rechter re- 
ported that motor oil was not 
ames a Major product line 
or the distributor, a that re- 
tailers shopping for price near 
the end of the year aided his 
movement of Valvoline, Quaker 
State, and especially Pennzoil. 


Rechter attributed this 
growth to the fact that these 


companies, particularly Pen- 
nzoil, were slower in raising 
their prices than many other 
major brands. In the case of 
Pennzoil, the 1OW-30 multi- 
grade rose from No. 38 in 1978 
to No. 26 last year and the 
1OW-40 multigrade gained even 
more ro? going from No. 
72 to No. 5l. 


The Valvoline and Quaker 
State 1OW-40s both improved 
their showings, with Valvoline 
capturing third place in dollar 
movement, while the Quaker 
State 10W-30 held firm in its 
strong 12th-place finish. 


Spark plugs captured more 
than one-fourth of the top 25 
places in this annual report, 
with Motorcraft numbers tak-

Discounters are again looking 
for Rain Dance and similar 
competitive products from ma- 
jor manufacturers like Turtle, 

imoniz and Starbrite to gener- 
ate the most movement, both in 
terms of units and dollars, in 
1980. 

While the $4-$6 price range 
for wax in previous years was 
considered the premium price 
range, this year polymer pol- 
ishes retailing for as much as 
$20 or more will hold top-ticket 
honors. While most discounters 
will stock at least one polymer 
brand, the price plus the com- 
plexity of application have left 
many discounters skeptical 
about consumer acceptance. 
Nonetheless, simply because of 
novelty and price, some poly- 
mer products are all but certain 
to make the top 100. 

The older-style round head- 
lamps continued to outperform 
the rectangular sealed beams 
adopted by manufacturers for 
most late-model cars. In fact, 
there has been little change in 
the rankings for the three top 
headlamps. 


Adding It Up 


The 6014 sealed beam, which 
still is used in some new cars, 
continued in second place. The 
next highest ranked headlight 
dropped slightly from No. 16 to 
No. 20 while the rectangular 
4652 low beam crept upward 
from No. 42 to No. 39. The rec- 
tangular light will continue to 
gain ground slowly in 1980. 

Accessories, despite the No. 
1 ranking of the two-ton hy- 
draulic jack, took few spots in 
the top 100. Only 10 items 
among the 100 listed can be con- 
sidered moderate- to high- 
ticket accessories, and only 
three of them qualify in any way 
as dress-up items. 

The three dress-up products, 
in order of ranking, were air 
horns, the chrome solar shield 
and amber quartz driving 
lights. 

The air horns, in 1978 a popu- 
lar promotional accessory, 
dropped from No. 25 to No. 47 
on he list with an everyday 
price point of $29.99. The solar 
shield, at $13.99, placed No. 61 
after failing to make the i 100 
in 1978, and the amber light 
barely qualified with a ranking 
of No. 100 at $16.99. 

The seven remaining accesso- 
ries, in order, were the jack, 
auto ramps, the Coleman air 
compressor, the three-section 
antenna with booster, a me- 
chanics creeper, a 4-sq.-ft. 
chamois, and a three-section 
ball spring antenna. 

Most of these items serve a 
clear function for the DIYer in 
maintaining the appearance or 
performance of his car. These 
types of accessories will be the 

romotional products that 
Lasers expect to be most suc- 
cessful in 1980 while strictly

For Empire Crown 


EDEN PRAIRIE, Minn.— 
Empire Crown, auto s ecialty 
chain and lessee in discount 
stores, recorded a 28% increase 
in profits last year. 

Although sales rose only 7% 
from almost $23.7 million to 

| $25.4 million, the chain in- 
creased earnings from $316,764 
to $406,392. Income per share 
rose from 30¢ in 1978 to 43¢ in 
1979. 

Empire Crown, which earlier 
this year backed out of its pro- 

osed acquisition by the 

hitlock Pons, operates 37 
Crown Auto stores, and 14 au- 
tomotive departments in dis- 
count stores in Minnesota and 
Wisconsin. Whitlock has filed 
suit to force the company to 
agree to a merger.

Betty White Hike 


Cataloger’s Sales 


ORLANDO, Fla.—Brand 
Distributors used a TV person- 
ality in two commercials that 
helped the cataloger boost 
fourth-quarter holiday sales by 
30%. 

The cataloger, switching co- 
ordinators, joined Jewelcor too 
late to use the group’s 1979-80 
book. But it was able to run two 
Jewelcor-produced jewelry TV 
commercials that featured 
Betty White as the spokesper- 
son. 

A Brand Distributors execu- 
tive asserted that the two TV 
commercials were the key ele- 
ments in the company’s Decem- 
ber 1979 sales Jumping 30% 
despite competition from three 
new L. Luria & Son showrooms 
plus four Leeds units and one 
O. G. Wilson store. 


Different Strategy 


“We needed something dif- 
ferent to draw shoppers, and 
using a celebrity like Betty 
White in TV ads attracted at- 
tention,” he said. 

Jewelcor is one of anumber of 
catalog coordinators that have 
developed their own TV ads for 
members that have a common 
product sell but an introduction 
and sign-off specifically geared 
to the showroom chain. 

While the coordinators use 
co-op monies for the TV com- 
mercials that feature name 
brands in such categories as 
housewares and sporting goods, 
Jewelcor itself funded the two 
ads that promoted jewelry as 
there aren’t any branded prod- 
ucts in that category.

750—and Milton Bradley's Big 
Ben puzzle.

ture Buggy, another basic boys’ 
action toy, was the highest dol- 
lar producer in that category, 
while Milton Bradley’s Simon 
led the electronics with retail 
volume of $624,750. 


Gain Ground 


Electronics cannot yet be 
called a basic category in the 
toy department—that day has 
not yet arrived—but the high 
play value of many electronic 
oe is making them year- 
ong fast sellers. 

lectronic games are ex- 
pected to lead the toy depart- 
ment again this year in total 
volume and in percentage sales 
gain, in spite of nin | prob- 
ems and anticipated price 
hikes from the manufacturers. 

At the recent Toy Fair in 
New York, electronics were the 
star attraction at most sales pa- 
— with higher tickets the 
rule. 


Another Consideration 


Many electronics now bridge 
the age groupings, using sepa- 
rately packaged and merchan- 
dised software to adapt the 
basic unit to different games. 
The feeling among manufactur- 
ers is that parents will spend as 
much money as usual (perhaps 
on fewer items), and that an 
electronic that appeals to botha 
preschooler and a preteen will 
overcome price resistance by 
its versatility. 

The consumers’ search for 
play value, durability and value 
in toys should also bring more 
of them to presold basic games 
and toys like Monopoly, minia- 
ture wheel goods, non-TV 
dolls, old favorites in —— 
and good quality plush. 

Electronic games that appeal 
to a single-age group, or offer 
limited play value may suffer 
this year, as may the less- 
sturdy, high-ticket lines like 
race sets and radio control toys. 

Overall, however, the stay-at- 
home trend and increased con- 
sumer awareness of play value 
add up to a rosy future for basic 
toys—and that translates into 
better gross margins for retail- 
ers as the basics become a 
greater portion of the business. 

Board games, once thought 
vulnerable to volume erosion as 
more consumer dollars went to 
high-ticket electronics, have 
not faltered. The continued 
strength in the old favorites

1979 experienced a sales gain in 
toys, leading to some specula- 
tion that progress is being 
made in spreading the volume 
over the entire year, depending 
less on highly promotional 
Christmas-season selling for 
volume.

need not wait until Christmas.

Product Movement Audit 


Bar Soap Sales 
Up Over 30%; 
6-Pack Tops 


By M. Raymond Prendergast 
President, 
Boston Distributors 

Bar soap has finally found a 
home in ia discount depart- 
ment store. 

Our sales in this classification 
were up more than 30% in 1979 
as most of our customers real- 
ized that they could use soap to 
draw customers without suffer- 
ing a significant margin loss. 

ong a mainstay of the food 
trade, bar soap special packs 
can be priced for profit and still 
stimulate strong impulse sales. 
Merchandising is the key to 
success. We suggest dumping 
soap in wire bins in the gondola 
run or on endcaps. Manufac- 
turer specials such as multi- 
packs and off-labels will sell the 
product for you if displayed in 
this manner. 


Leading Brand 


Our leading sku in 1979 was 
Zest’s 6-pack followed by Dial 
bath size in a 4-pack bundle. By 
serge in the No. 5 position 
with the single bar pack, Dial 
was again our leading brand. 
The most exciting entry in the 
soap market this year is Min- 
netonka’s Soft Soap. This prod- 
uct looks good, is priced right 
and makes sense. It will be 
some time before it can draw 
customers the way Dial can, 
however. 

Deodorants, another impor- 
tant draw for the mass mer- 
chant, showed us more moder- 
ate sales growth (15%) in 1979. 
Right Guard 10 oz. and Sure 6 
oz. led our PMA, illustrating 
the fact that aerosols are far 
from dead. 

The roll-on segment was 
again led by Ban with Sure and 
Secret also scoring well. Al- 
though not placing in the top 
20, Dry Idea and Tickle showed 
significant increases in 1979. 

The stick category will prob- 
ably show the greatest growth 
this year as several manufac- 
turers are introducing solid 
antiperspirants. Procter & 
Gamble has solid entries for 
both the Secret and the Sure 
brands, and initial sales are en- 
couraging. Faberge, whose 
Brut 33 Stick was our fastest 
growing sku last year, has 
added an antiperspirant to its 
line. 

The sanitary napkin category 
promises to continue its strong 
growth pattern in 1980 with re- 
cent introductions spurrin 
real increases. Personal Prod- 
ucts’ new entry, Sure & Natu- 
ral, is superior to its tremen- 
dously successful Stayfree 
Maxi Pads. Stayfree held three 
out of our top five positions in 
1979. 

The other two spots were, of 
course, held by Tampax, the pe- 
rennial tampon leader. This 

ear Procter & Gamble will give 

mpax a run for its money 
with its rollout of Rely Tam-

6th Annual 
Product Movement Audit 


Ready-to-Fish 
Combinations 
Make Splash 


Hunting and fishing basics 
and a wide assortment of Cole- 
man products dominated the 
1979 Stem Distributing annual 
sporting goods Product Move- 
ment Audit. 

Air-powered guns made their 
usual strong showing on the list 
also, while a total of 10 spots 
went to products not in those 
four categories. 

Twenty fishing items were 
listed, including many of the 
popular Zebco and Daiwa rod 
and reel combinations. The pro- 
motional appeal of these pre- 
packaged mh and reel combina- 
tions, which offer ready-to-fish 
convenience with balanced 
equipment, has enhanced their 
value to the consumer seeking 
an inexpensive activity for fam- 
ily outings. 

With gasoline in short sup- 
py, and travel vacations often 

eyond the consumers financial 
reach, fishing in local waters 
has av a surge of popu- 
larity. The packaged combina- 
tions are ideal for that market. 

Shot shells dominated the 
ammunition sales last year at 
Stem, and may also have bene- 
fited from the consumers’ 
search for inexpensive sporting 
activity. 


Shifting Gears 


Those who already own a 
shotgun, hand gun or rifle can, 
with a few dollars worth of 
shells and a few hours of free 
time, enjoy target shooting and 

linking with their family or 
riends. A shooter unable to 
take his family to some vacation 
spot because of the cost could 
spend several days of his time 
off plinking—especially with 
his 22-caliber rifle or hand 
gun—at a fraction of the cost of 
traveling. 

The extremely mild winter 
weather in most of the country 
did some harm to the hunting | 
apparel business, but appar- 
ently had little effect on am- 
munition sales. The bulk of the 
ammunition sold in discount 
stores is for practicing and for 
plinking, not for the actual kill- 
ing of game—and the shooters 
practiced and plinked as much 
as always in most markets. 

Coleman product sales have 
benefited from the same gas- 
oline ata, ar and inflationary 
pressures that have put long- 
distance travel out of the pic- 
ture for many consumers. 


While fewer campers will be 
driving hundreds or thousands 
of miles to visit national parks 
and other attractions, many 
more families will be opting for 
the outdoor life as an inexpen- 
sive alternative to motels and 
hotels. 


Whether the trip is 10 miles 
or a thousand, the family that is 
camping still needs lanterns, 
sleeping bags, coolers, cook 
stoves and tents. Even if all

Different Emphasis 


While the trend in 1980 has 
been to trim inventories to keep 
only the fastest-turning mer- 
chandise on the shelf, some cat- 
egories have increased in as- 
sortment. Running counter to 
the trend to smaller assort- 
ments and lower stock levels 
are fishing tackle and exercise. 

Exercise, especially the 
firmly established physical fit- 
ness category, is still a growth 
category for discounters. Mid- 
dle- and high-ticket benches 
and exercise bikes are the 
mainstay in exercise volume, 
while the low-ticket accessories 
and apparel sku’s add profit dol- 
lars. Most basic exercise equip- 
ment is purchased by men, 
under 25 years, while the 
women tend to spend more on 
apparel and fad reducing equip- 
ment. 


Successful Trade-up 


The trend to upgraded fish- 
ing equipment has helped that 
category retain its growth this 
year, aS new rod combos and 
more sophisticated reels attract 
freespending, dedicated sports 
fishermen. Combinations still 
do 35%-50% of the fishing 
tackle volume at most chains, 
but trade-up opportunities 
abound in the category. Sports- 
men with little to do this sum- 
mer except stay home are likely 
to spend their available recrea- 
tion dollars on new and better 
equipment. 

Also aiding the continued 
growth in fishing equipment is 
the unabated flow eae baits, 
a necessary part of the mix in 

fishing department and 
able to hook most browsers for 
one or more sales each visit. 


More Important Role

ing a more important factor in 
discount stores too, at least “ad 
the coastal chains and es 
cially for those in the Sunbe . 

Salt water fishing is even less 
expensive than fresh water 
fishing in most locales, since no 
license is required, and is as 
easily accessible from the nu- 
merous free docks, fishing

The air guns listed on this 
year’s chart are another indica- 
tion of increased togetherness 
in American families seeking 
inexpensive leisure activities. 

A father and son (or daugh- 
ter, less frequently) can spend 
many enjo Able ternoons to-

or backyard plinking with an 
air-powered rifle or hand gun, 
at minimal expense. Ammuni- 
tion for the air guns is very in- 
expensive—and recoverable 
when a trap is used—and the 
guns are sophisticated enough 
so even dad can enjoy tne sport. 

More good news for the bot- 
tom line in sporting goods de- 
partments comes from the ap- 
parel side, where runnin 
shoes, warm-up suits an 
sweatsuits are adding moder- 
ate to high tickets and high 
gross margins. 


More Emphasis 


At some chains, apparel 
items now constitute 30% or 
more of the sporting goods vol- 
ume, and growth opportunities 
are available in gym suits, spe- 
cialized shoes and apparel for 
specific sports and apparel ac- 
cessories for sportsmen. 

The end result of the apparel 
business is a gradual easing of 
the gross margin crunch that 
had characterized sporting 
goods in recent years. Gener- 
ally less promotional merchan- 
dise mixtures, selective sku 
cuts in some areas, concentra- 
tion on higher-margin ac- 
cessory items in hard and soft 
sporting goods lines and a 

owing consumer preference 

or basic, family-oriented lei- 
sure equipment may produce 
an average departmental gross 
margin of 30% soon.

ing with its 2-pack men’s 
shaver. The profitability of trial 
sizes for the retailer, and the 
manufacturer's accessibility to 
new users, have maintained 
trial sizes as an ongoing depart- 
ment in the discount store. 


New Strategy 


Many manufacturers are now 
making trial sizes of estab- 
lished brands available on a reg- 
ular basis. New-product intro- 
ductions accompanied by trial 
sizes have also become accepted 
practice in the industry. 

Merchandising of the trial 
products is the key to success, 
as the sale is almost entirel 
impulse. Wire baskets on end- 
caps or at the checkouts have 
yielded the best results for 
stimulating everyday sales. Ex- 
ceptional values to the cus- 
tomer, which are available on 
occasion, will yield tremendous 
sales if promoted in print ads. 


Gemco/Memco Bows 


In Tucson, Las Vegas 


BUENA PARK, Calif.— 
Gemco/Memco entered two 
new markets as it opened four 
stores to boost its count to 76. 
The chain projects passing the 
80 mark in 1980. 

The two new markets for the 
Gemco nameplate are Las 
Vegas, Nev., and Tucson, Ariz., 
where 102,000-sq.-ft. units 
were unveiled. Each market 
will get another Gemco this 
year, an executive said. 

Gemco/Memco’s parent 
Lucky Stores already has su- 
permarkets in both markets, 
giving the company a base from 
which to develop customers for 
its membership discount 
stores. 


Still Developing 


Gemco’s move into Tucson ex- 
tends its Arizona operation to 
the state’s second largest city. 
There are Gemco units in Phoe- 
nix and the suburbs of Glendale 
and Tempe, the largest market 
in Arizona. 

The other two Gemco/Memco 
openings were a 104,000-sq.-ft. 
Memeo in Baltimore as the sec- 
ond in that city with another 
due this year, and a 102,000-sq.- 
ft. Gemco in Riverside, Calif. , 
the second in that Los Angeles 
suburb.

ames Hyman, vice president

without a department store

With increased competition 
from catalog showrooms in 
hard lines, upscalers clearly 
have to offer customers a rea- 
son other than price to shop 
their stores. 

“We’re still in a price busi- 
ness,” observed David Snell, 
vice president of marketing and 
sales promotion, Gold Circle. 
“We have to be, in H&BA and 
household chemicals. They are 
hot tonnage items on which we 
are very competitive and that 
we stand by. But we have to 
identify what we do well, and 
low price is not one of the main 
reasons customers shop our 
stores.” 

Gold Circle’s strongest soft 
lines stores do 45% of their 
sales in wearables and an addi- 
tional 10%-15% in domestics. 
Richway does approximately 
40% in soft lines overall while at 
Bradlees, apparel and domes- 
tics together do 60% of sales. 

Clearly the main stumbling 
block to successful apparel mer- 
chandising is the unavailability 
of most national brands—a par- 
ticular sore spot among mer- 
chandisers at the chains. 

“Brands give us credibility,” 
said Jack Heilpern, vice presi- 
dent for soft lines at Richway. 


Questionable Practice 


“Our stores are beautiful— 
there’s no reason we shouldn’t 
have Arrow shirts or Jockey un- 
derwear. We are a logical outlet 


for mass-produced brands—not 
necessarily designer labels. 
The manufacturers should see 
our distribution potential—but 
they have an ego problem.” 

Most of the trade-up group 
have stressed the brands they 
do have, like Wrangler, Hanes, 
Dickie and Fruit of the Loom. 
Target promotes Ditto jeans. 
— and Target buy Levi's 
through secondary sources, 
and Target caused a mild up- 
roar when it promoted Calvin 
Klein, Gloria Vanderbilt and 
Sasson jeans. While most mer- 
chandisers are open to off-price 
buys of hot brands to generate 
traffic, they recognize their 
bread and butter is in fashion, 
continuity and selection. 

While the department store 
children may have inherited 
their soft lines orientation from 
their founders, the second gen- 
eration of middie management 
has several origins. Buyers and 
store managers are from Sears 
and Penney, other discounters 
or specialty chains. 

“All our key people are not 
out of the department store but 
out of the discounter,” said 
Richway’s Heilpern. 

Upscale discounters now ap- 
pear to use the resources of 
their parent rg Sg for op- 
erations rather than merchan- 


— 
e have gotten support ser- 
vices from Rich’s, but they have 
no influence in our merchandise 
strategies,” said John Weit- 
nauer, chairman of Richway. 
Snell pointed out that Gold 
Circle may draw on the exper- 
tise of Federated’s planners, 
but noted: “We first must define 
what we want—as we do that, 
the solutions become obvious.” 
As the second and third gen- 
erations of upscale discounters 
talk to each other and learn 
from each other’s mistakes, 
their stores are likely to look 
more and more alike.

| Celebrity Posters Win Starring Role in Profit Pic 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Fast turns and fat margins are just part 
of the reason so many discounters are add- 
ing celebrity posters to their music depart- 
ments. 

Fully serviced displays, returns of un- 
sold stock and traffic-pulling popularity 
make the posters—which are seldom pro- 
moted—profit centers within the depart- 
ment. 

Sales of posters, including such other 
types as scenics, reproductions and ani- 
mals, comprise as little as 1% of the space 
in many music departments, but contrib- 
ute a greater proportion of the total sales. 

In traditional chains, for example, pos- 
ter sales generate 2%-4% of Woolco’s music 
department sales and approximately the 
same percentage of T.G. & Y.’s stationery 
department volume. Sales at more youth- 
oriented tradeup chains such as Bradlees 
probably exceed those figures—due in 
part to the younger shoppers and in part to 
the broader assortment generally carried 
by the tradeup chains. 

Sales of celebrity posters were esti- 
mated to be $100 million nationwide by one 
distributor, who sells 75%-80% of his stock 
through discount department stores. 

“Some may claim the $100 million figure 
for the industry, but I don’t believe it’s that 


big with returns,” said Charles Staley, 
Woolco’s music department buyer. (Post- 
ers that do not sell can be returned to the 
supplier.) “But celebrity posters are sell- 
ing well, even when compared to the im- 
act of Farrah Fawcett posters.” Farrah’s 
sa set unprecedented sales records 
in the poster industry. 

Posters of Bo Derek, star of the movie 
“10,” and John Snyder, of TV’s “Dukes of 
Hazzard” are Woolco’s top sellers now. Sta- 
ley features them in promotional dumps 
with 24, 48 or 72 one-of-a-kind shots. The 
dumps, like the permanent displays, are in 
the music department because so many 
posters stars are from the recording indus- 
try. Staley maintains a permanent wood 
display from Western Graphics of Eugene, 
Ore., his chief supplier. It contains a basic 
assortment of about 400 celebrity, scenic 
and lesser-personality posters. Posters are 
stocked with number codes corresponding 
to a leaf-turning display above. 

The gross margin of posters is double 
that of records and tapes at Woolco’s music 
department. Records get up to 25%, while 
celebrity posters return 40%-50%. 

“The permanent display takes no more 
than about 10 sq. ft. in 1,000 sq. ft. of floor 
space, and it produces 2%-4% of the total

walk, Ohio. Self-service, high margins 
and six turns a year attract retailers.
