U.S. May Urge Gen. Mdse. Chains to Ice Prices 


WASHINGTON—Carter 
Administration officials may 
soon begin pressuring the na- 
tion’s largest discount and 
other general merchandise 
chains to freeze prices on key 
lines, White House consumer 
aides told Discount Store 
News. 

The plan calls for letters from 
Presidential Consumer Affairs 
Adviser Esther Peterson to 
dozens of chains urging them to 
impose voluntary price ceilings 


to “ease the inflationary pres- 
sures that are causing such 
hardships for all consumers.” 
Peterson used just such an 
approach last month with food 
retailers, firing off letters to 50 
major supermarket chains ask- 
ing them to put a temporary 
cap on food price hikes. Nearly 
a dozen top grocery chains, in- 
cluding industry giants like 
Safeway, A&P and Grand 
Union, responded promptly 
with price freezes and the 


White House campaign began 
to snowball. 

At presstime Peterson had 
already expanded the volun- 
tary price moratorium effort to 
nonfood firms (letters were 
being sent to scores of dru 
store chains as well as food an 
pharmaceutical manufactur- 
ers), and plans were in the 
works to broaden the campaign 
further.

Maloney's Readies Remodel, Plans Scale 


MOUNT STERLING, Ky.— 
Maloney’s will remodel its 
25,000-sq.-ft. Jackson, Ky., 
store next month to fit the pro- 
totype unit opened late last 
year in Norton, Va. 

The 14-store Southeast re- 
gional discounter will open a 
scaled-down 12,000-sq.-ft. unit 
in Stanton, Ky., this fall, which 
varies from the prototype by 
cutting back soft goods. The 
new store is one of three that 
Maloney’s projects opening this 
year in its tristate market area 
of Kentucky, Virginia and West 
Virginia.

remodeled to follow the new 
—— was the unit in Ir- 
vine, . The store was en- 
larged from 18,000 sq. ft. to 
30,000.

discounter expects to expand 
them eventually to fit the pro- 


totype. 
the Jackson remodeling in-

Burn Concerns 


Should Boost Sunscreen Sales 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Increased advertising and promo- 
tional support, and growing consumer 
awareness of the hazards of excessive 
exposure to the sun are expected to 
boost sales of sunscreens this spring and 
summer. 

While screens have not formerly been 
strong H&BA sellers, because people 
wanted to get deep tans, increased con- 
sumer awareness is prompting many re- 
tailers to boost their assortment in the 
category. 

Jamesway has increased its merchan- 
dising of the screening products. Ven- 
ture recently experienced a 40% gain in 
sales, attributed, by a buyer for the 
chain, to stepped-up media promotions. 


Regional factors and weather play a 


large role in determining a chains sun- 
screen/tanning lotion mix, with Sunbelt 
and resort-area stores getting the lion’s 


share of sales. 

Basic mixes dominate the Northern 
and inland stores. T.G. & Y. and 
K mart, for example, place heavy em- 
phasis on Coppertone (which one buyer 
estimated did 70% of T.G. & Y.’s busi- 
ness). K mart pushes private label 

oods mixed with major national 

rands. 

The merchandise mix at S. E. Nich- 
ols is varied by region, with some bou- 
tique-style lines doing well in surnmer 
resort areas, but highly advertised na- 
tional brands dominate chainwide. 


same time.

when purchased through diverters.

grances vary in assortment according to 
season—Venture’s assortment in up-

or more for Christmas, Father’s Day 
and Mother's =

rypick.

Francisco had already a:

and its finance charge on credit 
cards as high as 21%, after June 
1. Bank of America, the coun- 


try’s largest bank, unveiled 

lans to ask cardholders for a 
$12 annual membership fee, 
effective June 5; and Citibank 
raised the cost to member mer- 
chants extending credit on its 
Visa cards and MasterCards 
from 4.3% to 5.3%. 

All of that had discounters 
admitting they could be feeling 
the pinch by fall. 

On another front, the Fed- 
eral Reserve ruled March 14 
that lenders must set aside 15% 
on outstanding balances of new 
credit excluding secured loans.

credit cards for a number of dis-

Gibson’s Shutters 7 Company-run Stores 


SEAGOVILLE, Tex.—In a 
move designed to help keep its 
remaining stores afloat, Gib- 
son’s is closing even more com- 
pany-operated units. 

The recent closings leave 
Gibson’s with only 27 stores still 
owned and operated by head- 
quarters (at midyear last year 
it owned and operated 41). 

“This was done to reinforce 
our financial structure,” said 
Art Scateni, vp of advertising 
and sales promotion. “These 
were marginal units. If you are 
not getting the turns on inven- 
tory dollars in an era of 20% 
money, you can’t hold the mar- 
ginal stores.” 

The closings will knock near- 
ly $15 million from the com- 
panys volume, by DSN’s esti- 
mate, pulling Gibson’s sales 
from owned units well under 
$100 million a year. 

(Gibson’s also franchises its 
name to over 350 independent 
operators. ) 

Scateni said Gibson’s “will 
put the money into the stores 


that are performing for us. This 
will help them and will aid our 
cash flow.” 

The stores being closed are in 
Fort Worth (three), Terrell and 
Greenville, Tex.; Longmont, 
Colo., and Rosewell, N.M. 

Gibson’s owns most of its 
store sites, and it will be the 
company’ option to lease or sell 
the locations. Scateni empha- 
sized that the closings were not 


part of a move to abandon dis- 
count retailing at Gibson’. 

The necessary evil of closin 
stores is largely a result of stiff 
competition from K mart, Tar- 
get and Wal-Mart, according to 
store managers and local ob- 
servers. 

Wal-Mart, particularly, often 
chooses sites across the street 
from Gibson’s units and man-

Sales Unaffected by Credit Crackdown . . . So Far 


Consumer Financing, Surcharge 
Problems in Major Appliances 


Nationwide DSN Report 

The consumer credit crunch 
has created uncertainty in the 
major appliance market, but 
any downturn in sales isn’t ex- 
pected to become evident until 
the fall. 

Two big problems face the 
handful of eeuien (inelud- 
ing K mart, Woolco, Nichols, 
Jefferson, Times Square 
Stores, FedMart and Zodys’ 
lessee Wards) that carry major 
appliances. The concerns are 
(a) finding a credit source for 
customers who want to buy the 
high-ticket brown and white 
goods; and (b) paying the sur- 
charge now being charged re- 
tailers by some consumer 
credit companies on time pay- 
ment plans. 

The Association of Home Ap- 

liance Manufacturers had 
orecast that manufacturers’ 
shipments of all types of white 
goods this year would total 32.9 
million units, down slightly 
from the 33.2 million shipped 
last year. An association execu- 
tive said an updated forecast 
would be issued sometime this 
month. 

The first quarter’s actual re- 
sults showed January ship- 
ments up 11%, February up 3% 
and March down 11%. 


— 


The executive said that the 
March decline could indicate 
some weakness but it was too 
early to tell because “it’s not un- 
usual to have month-to-month 


swings up or down.” 

A FedMart executive noted 
that there hasn’t been any fall- 
off in sales. The credit crunch 
might help discounters, he add- 
ed, as consumers could turn to 
discounters because they 
charge lower prices than other 
— appliance retailers. 

Times Square Stores ex- 
ecutive added: “So far there 
hasn’t been any signs of weak- 
ness in major appliance sales. 
As the cost of money goes up, 
however, you can expect a 
drop.” 

Any drop that does occur 
wouldn’t become evident until 
around September, a Nichols 
executive said. “The spring and 
summer aren’t the biggest sea- 
sons for major appliance sales,” 
he explained, “and at this stage 
there haven’t been any signs of 
a downturn.” 

Some K marts have had to 
find new credit sources for the 
time payment plans used by 
consumers because some fi- 
nance companies have dropped 
financing of this type.

Housewares: Discounters No. 1, Catalogers Gain 


CHICAGO—Discounters 
are still No. 1 in housewares, 
while catalog showrooms and 
drug stores have increased 
their market shares. 

Discounters accounted for 
29% of manufacturers total dol- 
lar sales to retailers in 1979, 
compared to 33% in 1978. 

Catalogers had a 12% share 
and drug stores 10% in 1979, 
compared to 9% and 5%, re- 
spectively, in 1978. 

Those were among the find- 
ings of the 13th annual National 
Housewares Manufacturers 


Association industry survey. 

The discounters share didn’t 
include purchases from whole- 
salers such as housewares/ 
hardware distributors, so that 
the total amount of housewares 
sold by discount stores was 
much higher than the 29% 
share reported in the survey. 

Retailers, overall, accounted 
for 74% of manufacturers sales, 
up three percentage points 
from the 71% share reported in 
last year’s survey. 

The wholesalers’ share fell to 
26% from 29%, reflecting the 


growing trend of discounters 
and other retailers to buy di- 
rect as much as possible, espe- 
cially on nonelectrics. 

The survey listed housewares 
manufacturers sales in 1979 at 
$15,579,000,000, up 15.6% from 
$13,479,000,000. 

Retailers’ share in dollars 
amounted to $11,528,460,000, 
up 20.5% from $9,570,090,000. 

The wholesalers’ dollar vol- 
ume was $4,050,774,000, up a 
slight 3.6% from $3,908,- 
910,000.

High-Flying Toys ‘R’ Us |s Wary of Petrie Takeover 


SADDLE BROOK, N.J.—Toys ‘R’ Us remains 
the undisputed king of the specialty toy retailers, 
yet its outstanding success is also the source of wor- 
ry—of a possible takeover by the women’s apparel 
specialty retailer Petrie Stores. 

The Secaucus, N.J.-based Petrie began to acquire 
Toys ‘R’ Us stock at the end of 1978 and continued 
throughout last year. Petrie now owns 23% of the 
outstanding stock, amounting to 2.03 million shares. 

Petrie’s interest in the toy chain is understanda- 


ble; from 1974 to the present, Toys ‘R’ Us has re- 
corded an average compound annual growth rate in 
excess of 25%. Last year, the chain’s sales volume 


was $480 million, an amazing 37.5% increase from 
the year-before volume of $349 million. 


Toys ‘R’ Us chairman and founder Charles Laza- 
rus, who has been opposed to takeover in the past, 
has an escape clause in his contract, as do three 
other senicr members of the chain’s management. 

This clause states that Lazarus can terminate his 
employment contract six months after any buyer 
acquires 30% or more of Toys ‘R’ Us stock. If (and 
only if) he exercises his option, the other manage- 
ment members with similar clauses may also exer- 
cise their option. All would be eligible for a year's 
compensation after their termination with the com- 
pany. 

It is still possible that Petrie wants the stock for 
investment purposes only. Securities analysts at

Computer Outlets Spark Radio Shack Sales to $1.2B 


FORT WORTH—Radio Shack, leader in its spe- 
cialty field, is on an upswing with no downturn in 
sight. And when it comes to consumer electronics, 
president Lewis Kornfeld does not think discounters 
can jump on the success bandwagon. 

The company’s growth—reflected in a 12% in- 
crease in sales in 1979 to $1.2 billion, and an 18% 
increase in this year’s fiscal third quarter to $739 
million—has come from its new computer-oriented 
outlets. These centers offer Radio Shack computer 
systems to businessmen. Kornfeld said the trained 
sales and service personnel, which he calls the keys 
to consumer electronics sales, are an advantage 
unique to specialty chains like Radio Shack, and not 
offered to discounters. 


Not unique are the financial worries that come 
with paying for high-ticket inventory in these infla- 
tionary times. Kornfeld said borrowing money at 
20% to purchase inventory is now one of the com- 
pany’s major concerns. 

Earlier in its history, Radio Shack financed expan- 
sion through franchising arrangements. More re- 
cently, however, it found them largely unprofitable. 
It hasn’t granted one in eight years. 

“Franchises, which for us first looked like a rela- 
tively low-cost way to grow, looked later like an 
inhibitor, policywise,” Kornfeld said. “We haven't 
tried to cut them out; we offered them a different 
arrangement. The hard core [1.8%] stayed.”

Herman’s Slows Expansion as Mild Winter Trims Sales 


CARTERET, N.J.—Herman’s, still the largest 
sporting goods specialty retailer in the ge by 
volume, is slowing down its expansion rate of the 
previous two years for 1980. 

After adding a dozen stores two years ago and 19 
last year, Herman’s plans to open only six this year. 
The lower expansion rate will place less of a strain on 
Herman's cash flow. 

The slowdown in expansion plans accornpanies a 
slowdown in the growth rate of sales. While the store 
base increased 28% during the last year at Her- 
man’s, sales were up only 14%. 

Sales at the 88-unit division of W. R. Grace, a New 
York-based conglomerate, were $195 million last 
year. Year-before sales at Herman’s were $171 mil- 


lion. 

W. R. Grace chairman Felix Larkin admitted in a 
report to shareholders that “Herman's had a difficult 
year as mild winter weather and gasoline shortages 
plus the cost of store openings adversely affected 
sales and yen performance.” 

While the openings last year included entry into 
Pittsburgh and Columbus, Ohio, markets, Herman’s 
will reportedly focus on ski markets in its Northeast 
stronghold for future units. 

Management at the chain said that sales of cross- 
country ski gear were particularly strong in 1979. 
Other outstanding categories for the chain were rac- 
quetball equipment, rugged outerwear and roller

Western Auto Does $698M Despite 450 Closings 


KANSAS CITY, Mo.—Western Auto, the giant 
specialty chain, continued to close stores in 1979, 
finishing the year with 3,450 outlets, down from 
more than 3,900 the year before. The chains will 
close an additional 50 units by the end of this year. 

In sales, however, this subsidiary of Beneficial 
Management Services continued to lead the field 
with §698. 1 million reported for fiscal 1979. 

Still, “we’re pessimistic about 1980,” reported Ken 
Brown, controller. “We’re located predominantly in 
rural markets and our farmer customers are really 
feeling the pressure of the high interest rates.” 

Only 200 of the chain’s stores are located in major 
market sites. 


“We are not willing to make a capital investment in 
new stores at this time,” Brown said, adding that the 
store closings represent chain efforts to streamline 
itself and improve sales performance. 

Adding to the company’s pessimism is its de- 
pendence on installed sales for a considerable por- 
tion of its volume. 

We rely too heavily on installation services to be 
buoyed by the news that most auto chains prosper in 
recessionary times when more consumers do repair 
projects themselves, Brown said. Even worse, the 
chain’s Tepes also relies heavily on big-ticket 
sales (< spliances, TV’s). Brown declined to comment 
on what percentage of sales came from those items. 


H&BA Discounting to Boost Revco Volume Over $1B 


TWINSBURG, Ohio—Revco is set to become the 
first discount drug specialty chain to break the $1 
billion volume mark by doing what it does best: 
discounting health and beauty aids. 

The company is projected to generate $1,050,000, - 
000 in sales in its current ieee year, a 13.2% jump 
from the $927,533,000 reported for the fiscal year 
ended June 2, 1979. 

That volume was a 17.1% increase from the pre- 
vious fiscal year’s $792,033,000. Net income regis- 
tered a slightly smaller 14.5% boost, going to 
$33,636,000 from $29,376,000. 

Revco’s percentage gains in sales and earnings 
outpaced the percentage increase in stores during 
the two fiscal years; the count went to 1,143 from 


1,030, an 11% increase. 


The chain, besides aiming for a new sales plateau 


this year, is continuing the fast-paced expansion that 


saw it open the doors of about two new stores a 
week. 

The store expansion program calls for Revco to 
unveil 80 new units during the last half of the year to 
maintain its status as the discount drug chain with 
the greatest number of units. 

The 1,250 units in operation at the start of May 
1980 include about 40 stores opened so far this year. 

Revco, which has stores in 24 states and has focused 
heavily on markets east of the Mississippi River in 
past years, will emphasize Sunbelt areas this year.

Oshman’s Revives 
AF Picks Dallas 
For Second Unit 


HOUSTON—In a year of 
healthy sales increases and 
modest expansion in store num- 
bers, Oshman’s caught the eye 
of sporting goods shoppers by 
bringing back the Abercrombie 
& Fitch name. 

Oshman’s opened a 16,000- 
sq.-ft. Abercrombie & Fitch 
unit in Beverly Hills, Calif. , last 
year, and plans to open a 
26,000-sq.-ft. store in Dallas. 

“We do have expansion in 
mind,” Oshman’s president 
Marvin Aronowitz told DSN, 
“but the Abercrombie & Fitch 
stores are not stamped out by 
cookie cutiers. Obviously, we 
will not expand them at the 
same rate as the Oshman’s 
stores.” 

Despite the high-ticket glit- 
ter at Abercrombie & Fitch, 
the company’s volume still 
comes primarily from its typi- 
cal 11,000-sq.-ft. Oshman’s 
stores. 

With four more units than 
last year, Oshman’s 91 stores 
have kept it the largest sport- 
ing goods chain in the country 
by store number, despite a 19- 
store building spree by Her- 
man’s last year. 

Aronowitz said the new 
stores this year will be in new 
and existing markets. Texas 
and California are likely sites 
for the bulk of new stores, while 
Florida is also in Oshman’s ex- 
pansion plans. 

The chain, which had been in 
the northern Florida market 
before, opened in Miami at the 
end of March. Aronowitz said: 
“We are looking at Fort Lauder- 
dale, a nothing has been 
signed yet there.”

Remodeling Helps Doll Up Pep Boys Biz 


PHILADELPHIA—Pep 
Boys, the second-ranked spe- 
cialty automotive chain, closed 
fiscal 1979 (ended Jan. 31, 1980) 
with $181.9 million in sales, a 
17% increase over the previous 
year’s volume. 

According to a chain spokes- 
man, management credits re- 


modeling and remerchandising 
efforts with much of the boost 
in sales. Last year, he noted, 
the chain remodeled, and in 
some cases enlarged, 20 out- 
lets—most of which were lo- 
cated in the older East Coast 
markets where the chain got its 
start 55 years ago. 


Cost of Money Makes Empire-Crown 


‘Very Cautious’ on Building Inventories 


EDEN PRAIRIE, Minn.— 
Empire-Crown, discount store 
lessee and specialty outlet 
chain, has been growing stead- 
ily in the five years since its 
takeover of Crown Auto in 1975, 
and last year was no exception. 

Sales for the then 50-unit 
chain topped $25 million in fis- 
cal 1979, ended Dec. 31, up from 
$23 million the year before. The 
chain currently operates 52 
stores and 14 leased depart- 
ments in Wisconsin and Min- 
nesota. 

“We’re saying we’re reces- 
sion proof,” said Richard 
Roderick, vice president of fi- 
nance, “but with the cost of 
money so high we’re really 
going to be very cautious—par- 
ticularly about building inven- 
tory.” Roderick did say, how- 
ever, that the chain may expand 
its hard parts mix slightly. 

The current prototype for its 
stores is 7,000 sq. ft. of which 
3,000 sq. ft. is sales space. The 
rest of the space is given over to 
service bays. 

Nationally branded products 
tend to be the rule in both the 
company’s leased departments 
and freestanding specialty out- 
lets. The closest equivalent to 
private label products is the 
company’s inventory of tires 
and batteries. 

Empire-Crown is one spe- 
cialty chain that could not sur-

Hear Flat Sales Slow Zale Growth 


DALLAS—Zale Corpora- 
tion’s sporting goods division, 
reportedly experiencing disap- 
pointing sales, has slowed 
growth plans for 1980. 

After opening five new units 
in its last fiscal year, Zale plans 
only one additional sporting 
goods store this year, according 
to a company spokesman. 

The five additions, all in ex- 
isting markets for Zale, were in 
Phoenix, New Orleans, Dallas, 


San Antonio and Austin, Tex. 
They brought Zale’s total to 37 
sporting goods stores. 
However, reports last year 
by analysts at securities firm 
Merrill Lynch cited continuing 
poor performance in the sport- 
ing goods division at Zale, with 
sales flat compared to year-be- 
fore figures, and even a 4% de- 
cline in store-for-store sales at 
midyear although this report- 
edly improved later in the year. 


Expansion Plan Play World Studies Rebuilding 


Under Singer; Three Units Shut 


FARMINGDALE, N.Y.—It 
has been a year of changes at 
Play World, including the clos- 
ing of three stores and the in- 
stallation of a new president, 
and the toy specialist is looking 
to rebuild. 

The Long Island chain is 
down to a dozen units from 15 
last year, but is currently 
choosing sites for one or possi- 
bly two more units, according 
to a spokesman at the company. 

(Play World’s Elmont store 
was destroyed by fire, while the 
Smithtown and Massapequa 
stores were shuttered.) 

Play World’s parent company 
Greenman Brothers announced 
midway through last year that 
it was beginning “an aggressive 
rebuilding program,” and it im- 
ported Carey Singer as the 
chain’s new president. 


After hiring Singer, the par- 
ent company said it would make 
a greater investment in inven- 
tory for its Play World stores. 
Another move begun in mer- 
chandising at the chain was to 
phase out housewares from the 
merchandise mix. Housewares 
had been included in the stores 
stock because it appealed to the 

rimarily female customer and 

ecause it was seen as a possi- 
ble way to attract traffic in the 
off season for toys. 

“We found that phasing out 
the housewares and installin 
more toy product has helpe 
our return,” Singer told DSN. 
“We lost a little counterseason- 
al business, but we more than 
made it up on our return by 
going with the toys.” 

Play World, which also oper- 
ates leased toy departments in

Circus World, 
Tops in Units, 
Unwraps 23 


TAYLOR, Mich.—Circus 
World’s ambitious expansion 
program has led to an increase 
of 23 units since last year, mak- 
ing it the largest toy specialty 
retailer by store number. 

The 111-unit chain, which will 
reach 120 stores by December, 
according to a company spokes- 
man, is still smaller than Toys 
‘R’ Us and Child World in sell- 
‘ing space, however. 

Stores are all in mall loca- 
tions and the prototype size is 
3,000 sq. ft. New markets bro- 
ken into last year include Waco, 
Lufkin and Midland, Tex.; Port 
Richey and St. Augustine, Fla. 

Future expansion includes 
Midwest locations in existing 
markets, but concentration will 
primarily be in the Sunbelt.

Booming Rite Aid 
Hypos Pharmacies 


SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa.— 
Rite Aid continues to be one of 
the fastest-growing specialty 
drug discounters and plans to 
open 50 stores through the end 
of the year to hit the 870-unit 
mark. 

The company opened 46 
stores during the first five 
months of the year after ending 
1979 with 774 units. 

All new stores will include 
pharmacies as part of Rite Aid’s 
program of positioning itself as 

ll-service drug stores, rather 
than just a discount health and 
beauty aids chain. Pharmacies 
were also added to older units 
that didn’t have this facility and 
only 68 stores are expected to 
lack Rx counters because of low 
volume or small size. 

The chain is going with 6,700 
sq. ft. of space as its prototype 
and expects to remodel about 
80 units this year, with a num- 


ber being enlarged to this size. 

The chain’s expansion should 
enable it to hit a projected $950 
million in sales in the new fiscal 
year, up 17.1% from $811 million 
during the fiscal year ended 
March 1. 

The volume in the completed 
fiscal year was a 26.7% increase 
from the $640 million in the pre- 
vious fiscal year and the per- 
centage gain was slightly ahead 
of the 23.5% boost in net profits 
which went to $30.2 million 
from $24.5 million. 

Chain executives have tar- 
geted a 10% annual growth rate 
in units so that Rite Aid should 
break the 1,000-store mark by 
1983, the second specialty drug 
discounter to do so. 

A key support for this growth 
was Rite Aid’s opening of a 
210,000-sq.-ft. distribution cen- 
ter in Charlestown, W.Va., to 
service its Southern States 
thrust. 


7 


“ 


Rite Aid has also speeded " 
its remodeling program, wit 


the 80 stores due to be updated 
this year being a 33% jump 
from the 60 modernized last 
year. 

Rite Aid spots its stores in 
shopping centers to draw cus- 
tomers from the high traffic; its 
inclusion of pharmacies is 
geared to offering these cus- 
tomers the full range of prod- 
ucts and services of a drug 


store, rather than just a dis- 
counted H&BA mix. 


Longs to Step Up 
Expansion; Plans 
13-18 Per Year 


WALNUT CREEK, Calif.— 
Longs, a pioneer West Coast 
discount drug chain, plans to 
step up its expansion from 15 to 
18 stores a year from the nine- 
or 10-unit pace maintained for 
the past half decade. 

e 130-store chain set the 
stage for this move by building 
13 new units last year to end up 
with a net gain of 10 stores as 
two smaller Longs were re- 
placed and one closed. 

The chain’s more aggressive 
growth included jumping into a 
new market—Nevada—last 
year to expand its coverage to 
six states; the others are Cal- 
ifornia, Oregon, Arizona, Ha- 
waii and Alaska. 

Longs is a highly decentral- 
ized chain and this merchandis- 
ing and operational approach 
has enabled the company to 
generate about $5.9 million in 
sales per store. 

In the fiscal year ended Jan. 
31, Longs’ sales amounted to 
$773 million, a 16.4% jump from 
the $664 million produced in the 
previous fiscal year. 

Net earnings showed a 
slightly smaller percentage in- 
crease, going up 13.1% to $26.7 
million from $23.6 million. 

The decentralized merchan- 
dising and operational program 
focuses on the store manager 
and the district manager mak- 
ing the day-to-day business de- 
cisions, including buying mer- 
chandise, setting prices and 
taking markdowns. 

All stores except the dozen 
units in Hawaii buy goods di- 
rect, thereby avoiding the need 


for central warehousing.

Editorial 


1980: 


THE YEAR OF 
THE DISCOUNTER 


( Discount Store Ne ws ) 


Welcome to the NMRI convention! 

We’ve probably never needed it 
more than we do today. The horizon is 
ominous, especially when the most re- 
cent past (April sales, for instance) is 
analyzed. 

This is, indeed, a “Time of Change.” 

But there’s no reason that a group of 
this nation’s most dynamic retailing 
executives, putting their heads to- 
gether for a week in New Orleans, 
can’t figure out some surefire ways to 
lick this economic monster. 

Today, discounting is an industry of 
retailing professionals. This group in 
New Orleans represents the best mass 
merchandising brains in the world. 


And, happily, these brains are here 
to be ares | 

Also available for the asking are the 
knowledge and ‘ry of plenty of 
smart suppliers. In most cases, these 
manufacturers have lived with dis- 
counting, enjoying the industry’s good 
times and weathering its storms. 

We call 1980 the Year of the Dis- 
counter. We consider the 80’s to be the 
Decade of the Discounter. This will be 
true, regardless of how bleak the econ- 
omy turns. It will be tougher, for sure. 
But consumers, nevertheless, will 
continue to recognize that value and 
price are synonymous with discount 
store. 


Let’s Make the NMRI Convention a Time For Action 


The job will be to convert sales to 
dollars. That’s why the 80’s also will be 
a decade of control. Existing stores 
will become more productive through 
better assortment editing. Discount- 
ers—and their sources—will know the 
best-selling items and planogram their 
floor space with that in mind. 

Computers will more and more play 
a part in manpower deployment and 
energy usage, as well as measure sales 
at store level. 

Replenishment techniques that en- 
hance turnover will need to be devel- 
oped jointly by discounters and their 
suppliers. Personnel and manpower

Census Results For Use in ‘ene? 
Merchandising, Site Picking jj Kalle 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Officials of discount store 
chains throughout the nation 
say they expect the 1980 census 
results to be of great value in 
long-range planning, but are 
cautioning their staffs not to 
abandon traditional methods of 
determining market composi- 
tion. 

If the breakdowns on popula- 
tion age, size and income are as 
complete as in previous years, 
they say, the information will be 
an important tool in site-selec- 
tion decisions and determina- 
tion of merchandise mixes. 

But the results will be as 
much as two years old by the 
time they are released by the 
U.S. Bureau of Census in late 
1981 or early 1982—a better 
base than the figures provided 
in the 1970 census, but still in- 
adequate and in need of updat- 
ing by the traditional methods. 

ost major chains surveyed 
at presstime said they have 
been using the results of the 


1970 census updated by a wide 
variety of techniques, as a 
means of making store location 
and marketing decisions. 

Officials of K mart said that 
they use the Editor and Pub- 
lisher Market Guide, in addi- 
tion to checking with local 
chambers of commerce in order 
to update the population fig- 
ures of the areas in which their 
stores are located. 

Other chains, such as Pa 
Less Drug Northwest, head- 
quartered in Beaverton, Ore., 
said they use techniques such 
as aerial photography to update 
the 1970 census results. _ 

Still other chains routinely 
check with local utilities for the 
number of new hookups in a 
given area, and ask municipal 
building permit issuers for to- 
tals on the number of new per- 
mits. 

“We’re all waiting for the re- 
sults with bated breath,” ex- 
plained John Thompson, whose

R. Gibson Fights FTC Subpoena 
Requiring Firm’s Quarterly Report 


WASHINGTON—Richard 
Gibson has filed a motion with 
the Federal Trade Commission 
to quash a subpoena requiring 
his company, Gibson Products, 
Longview, Tex., operator of 14 
franchised discount stores, to 
send the agency its quarterly 
report. 

Gibson is a son of H. R. Gib- 
son, founder of Gibson’s, Sea- 
goville, Tex., which both fran- 
chises and operates discount 
stores. 

Richard Gibson’s motion fol- 
lows on the heels of an FTC 
order against H. R. Gibson’s 
firm to restrict its trade show 
operation which the FTC 
claimed violated provisions of 
the Robinson-Patman Act. The 
case is being appealed by Gib- 
son's. 

The motion to quash involved 
only the independent firm 
owned by Richard Gibson, who 
was not involved in the earlier 
FTC investigation. Apparently 
there is no connection between 
the two FTC actions. 


According to FTC officials, 
its request was part of the 
agency's program to obtain 
quarterly reports from all com- 

anies in retailing and other se- 
ected categories that have as- 
sets of more than $25 million. 

Gibson opposed the request, 
in part because his firm “does 
not maintain any records on a 

uarterly basis,” according to 
the motion filed with the FTC. 
Therefore, he would have to es- 
timate much of the information. 

The motion also declared that 
the FTC does not have the au- 
thority to issue such a request 
“since the report sought is a 
quarterly report and is neither 
an annual or a special report 
under the limited authority 

iven to the Federal Trade 
ommission.”

(DSN photo) 


Gals See Discounters Taking Food Plunge 


PHOENIX—Twenty-eight 
per cent of 200 women polled by 
the National Advertising Bu- 
reau anticipate that discount 
stores will add complete food 
markets to their mix in the 
coming decade, thereby in- 
creasing their one-stop shop- 
ping capabilities and becoming 
attractive competitors for food 
dollars. 

The research, part of a study 
undertaken by the NAB to an- 
ticipate consumer attitudes to- 
ward food buying in the 1980's, 
found that the food shopper 
“has become extremely price 
conscious—more so than at any 
time since the 1930’s—and per- 
haps more willing to change her 
food store than ever.” 

Interview results were com- 
pared with comments by top 
executives of six major western 
food chains. 

In general, food shoppers ex- 
pect to see higher prices in the 
coming years, but they also ex- 
pect greater preparation conve- 
nience and more help from 
retail advertising. At the same 
time, many anticipate that a se- 
ries of competitive develop- 
ments will take place in food 
retailing—among them, a 
stronger bid for food dollars by 
discounters—to persuade them 
to shift store allegiances. 

For example, 43% of those 
polled expected to be swayed by 
a “second” retailer’s efforts to 
better advertise prices and sav- 


( Spotlight on: Upscale Presen tation ) 


Jefferson Gives Jewelry SS 
‘Corner Window’ Setting [ane 


Jefferson, as in its Lauderdale Lakes, Fla., store, has developed an upscale 
presentation for jewelry that uses glass and chrome showcases to display dia- 
monds, other jewelry and watches. Corner “window” displays (inset, left), are used 
to play up new items, current fashions and advertised goods. 

These “windows” are changed every four to six weeks to give the displays a new 
look and to tie in with holidays and seasonal changes. The “windows” don’t play up 
prices of the goods on display except for items that are being promoted. The jewelry 
area, which is carpeted, is on a main aisle and provides a counter where customers 
can sit and examine big-ticket items such as diamonds.

325 units by the end of the year,

In addition, 400 other poten-

growth. 


Still Developing 


According to a Wal-Mart ex- 
ecutive, however, the chain is 
not relying on its expansion 
program exclusively to boost 
chain sales. Last year, im- 
‘ete operating procedures 

elped boost same-store sales 
by 16%. 

Another chain gearing up ior 
a flood of new store openings 
this year and next is Jefferson, 
the discount branch of Mont- 
gomery Ward, which has added 
approximately 30 stores 


In 1979, the Miami-based 
chain absorbed Almart, added 
several units vacated by the 
now defunct J. M. Fields, and 
took over another two dozen 
stores that once belonged to 
Two Guys, Murphy’s Mart and 
Ward. Those outlets will be 
opened under the Jefferson 
banner during 1980 and 1981. 

On the downside, two trou- 
bled chains to watch for addi- 
tional closings this year are 
Two Guys and Korvettes. 

The new board proposed for 
Vor.iado, Two Guys parent cor- 
poration, will be controlled by 
outside real estate interests 
who have expressed the desire 
in the past to close down stores 
and sell off the chain’s lucrative 
properties outside the metro- 
politan New York/New Jersey 
area. 

And earlier this year, Kor- 
vettes closed four Baltimore 
stores and 10 more in New 
York, New Jersey, Pennsylva- 
nia and Virginia. The chain is 
also expected to shed its last 
Philadelphia store, and ma 
shut down its three New Yor 
City locations. 

The closings are part of Kor- 
vettes lith-hour struggle to re- 
gain profitability and recapture 
lost market share. 

Merchandising efforts that 
accompanied the store closings 
are aimed at putting the chain 
back in the “basic” discount 
store business at which it ex- 
celled in the 60's and early 70's.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, MAY 19, 1980 


“ 


Liscount Store News 


CONVENTION PERSPECTIVE — 
NATIONAL MASS RETAILING INSTITUTE 


Kenny, Walton Warn Discounters 


Trade-up Trend May Open Door to Bargain-Outlet Foes 


NEW ORLEANS—What do dis- 
counters see coming in the 1980’s—‘“A 
Time of Change” is the NMRI theme— 
that will force changes in the industry? 

Competition, first and foremost, will 
be changing. Not only will there be 
changes in other segments of retailing, 
but intra-industry competition will in- 
tensify. 

As one convention speaker put it, 
“There are no undiscovered cities and 
everyone knows about Taiwan. Dis- 
counters can no longer rely on unique 
merchandise assortments or store loca- 
tions.” 

Trading up in merchandise and pre- 
sentations that has taken place in recent 
years has both a positive and a negative 
side. Jefferson’s president David Kenn 
Sees another type of competition devel- 
oping as a result of trade-ups. 

“Discounters faced three tiers of com- 
petition in the 1970's, from department 
stores, specialty shops (including the 
catalogers) and general merchandise 
chains such as Sears and Penney,” 


“Discounters faced three tiers of com- 
petition in the 1970's, from department 
stores, specialty shops and general 
merchandise chains. . . ."—David 
Kenny, President, Jefferson. 


Kenny said. “As discount stores have 
traded up, they have created a price 
vacuum Presi and a fourth layer of 
competition is emerging in the 1980's. 
Price-conscious customers are going to 
shop at places like flea markets and 
other types of stores that can undersell 
discounters.” 

Wal-Mart chairman Sam Walton 
agreed. “There are a lot of us who are 
thinking about the trade-up route, but 
we must be careful to remain true dis- 
counters. Otherwise the trade-ups 
could go too far, and the trend of the 
food industry could be followed, with 
bare-bones, bargain-store competition 
emerging.” 

One of the great positive effects of 
trading up has been in consumer accep- 
tance, which some discounters see as 
the prime benefit moving into the 
1980's. 

“We have gained consumer accep- 
tance that we did not have in the 1960's 
and have also gained in professionalism 
of our operations as an industry,” said 
S. E. Nichols president Manfred 
Brecker, “and for the first time we re- 
ceived a fashion image in the late 1970's. 
This will be a great benefit for those 
who are able to exploit it in the 1980's.” 

Expansion of store numbers has tra- 
ditionally accounted for much volume 
growth, but several discounters and 
analysts predict that growth of store 
units will slow in the 1980's. 

“T still see more consolidation and ac- 
quisitions as some weaker sisters in the 
industry will be squeezed out,” Kenny 
said. Brecker, noting the high cost of 
building today, said “there will be less 
building in the years to come, and be- 
cause people can’t afford to build, there 
will be more takeovers.” 

High interest rates in recent months 
have slowed many chains’ expansion 
plans, although this is seen as a short- 
term problem and not a long-term 
obstacle. 

“Immediately, the cost of money has

were not cut, they were just put on the

While the cost of money is expected to 
tail back down from present levels, the 
cost of building is not likely to. 

“The No. 1 problem coming at us is to 
be able to build or rent a store at a 
reasonable cost or rate,” said James- 
way'’s chairman Herb Fisher, comment- 
ing on changes to come in the next few 
years. 

“There has been some talk of fluctuat- 
ing mortgage rates, which is frighten- 
ing,” Fisher said. “Iwo things we are 
doing to overcome the problem is to re- 
duce the specifications on our stores— 
making them without frills and cutting 
down on lighting and air-conditioning, 
for example—and trying to develop new 
ways to finance expansion. We are con- 
sidering such things as joint ventures 
with developers.” 

Discounters are split on the point of 


ownership of stores, however. ALCO’s 
Soelter said: “We do not want to commit 
our capital to buildings; we would 
rather have it in merchandise.” 

Discounters agree that productivity 
from existing units becomes a challenge 
in a time of continued inflation and high 
cost of additional units. Changes in both 
operations and merchandising are on 
the way for the 1980's. 

Soelter said ALCO’s management is 
looking forward to the deregulation of 
the trucking industry to allow the chain 
to haul merchandise that is not its own, 
since the chain must make deliveries to 
faraway stores. 

Jamesway’s Fisher said his chain is 
purchasing its own telephone system, 
cost-justified because of its adaptability 
to the company’s needs and long-term 
savings. Jamesway is also installing ter- 
minals at the receiving docks of new 
stores (also equipped with POS sys- 


tems) to eliminate the hand paperwork

anization and computer sup- 
port, noted that the emphasis 
on precommitment buying had 
enabled the chain to achieve 
better results with fewer peo- 
ple. The system also served to 
reduce warehouse sku’s, he 
said. 

Glass will cover backroom 
productivity, focusing on devel- 
opment of a flow-through sys- 
tem. “The backroom should be a 
processing area,” he said. “Mer- 
chandise should be received, 
marked, and then flow right on 
through to the floor. Too many 
backrooms are used simply for 
storage, and this keeps produc- 
tivity down.” 

Glass also urged specializa- 
tion of backroom personnel. 
“People should be trained for 


particular jobs,” he said.

EDP to Play Ever-Increasing Role in Management and Merchandising 


Nationwide DSN Survey 

A recently completed point- 
of-sale (POS) terminal systems 
Survey completed by Touche 
Ross & Co. and Discount Store 
News has underscored the in-

the 1980's. 

In both operational and mer-

data will play an ever-increas-

and assets, and fine-tuning as- 
sortments to meet the needs of 
customers’ rapidly evolving 
lifestyles.

Four Discounters Freeze Prices 


On Some Food and Drug Items 


NEW YORK—Four major 
discount chains with more than 
250 stores nationwide have im- 
posed price freezes on some 
food and drug items as part of a 
volunt Federal program to 
nidela the consumer against 
skyrocketing inflation. 

The chains—Fed Mart, 
Rink’s, Venture and Target— 
imposed the price freezes last 
month in response to a request 
from the ite House. They 
will remain in effect 60 to 90 
days. 

The products and prices 
frozen vary from chain to chain, 
and include basic items such as 
spaghetti, tomato sauce and 
shampoo at FedMart, and ge- 
neric prescription drugs and 
other items at all four chains. 

“We’re not sure if we can 
keep it up after 90 days,” ex- 
plained William E. Sliney, Fed- 
Mart executive vice president, 
“but taking this stand is some- 
thing we felt we had to do to 
carry on the fight against infla- 
tion.” 


plying with the White House 
request. 

However, they said they are 
absorbing the increases passed 
along by other manufacturers, 
and writing letters to them urg- 
ing that they also participate in 
the voluntary price-freeze pro-

“We had some increases that 
were scheduled to take effect 
April 1,” said Stan Heller, Ven-

going to take a stand and ab- 
sorb these increases.”

Catalogers’ '79: Biz Up, Net Down 


Nationwide DSN Report 

The year 1979 was a mixed 
one for catalog showrooms, 
with sales generally up—sub- 
stantially so for a number of 
chains—but income down for 
most companies. 

While none of the top publicly 
held catalogers reported a loss, 
only two, Best and H. J. Wil- 
son, recorded higher earnings. 
The former was up 11.3% and 
the latter 12.9%. 

Sales increases ranged from 
12,5% for Jewelcor to 38.2% for 
Service Merchandise, and hit 
62.7% for the United States di- 
vision of Consumers Distribut- 


ing. Earnings declines ranged 
from 12.4% for Service Mer- 
chandise to 92.5% for Sam Sol- 
omon. 

The mixed results, together 
with continued weaker perfor- 
mances in the first quarter of 
1980 and the industry’s greater 
share of the general merchan- 
dise retail market, mean that 
the 1980 recession will impact 
catalog showrooms more than 
the one in 1974. 

Catalog executives explained 
that the industry was so small 
six years ago that the recession 
passed by the showrooms. But, 

(Continued on page 158) 


The Administration's call for a price moratorium on selected 
product lines comes on the heels of similar White House 
requests involving supermarkets and drug chains earlier this 
yeer. 

Ir, her letter—which will be sent only to the 50-169 largest 
“department store-type” chains—Peterson is not likely to set 
any ground rules for voluntary compliance by the chains, but 
will urge the broadest price freeze possible to help consum- 
ers cope with inflation. 

Large department store and a merchandise chains 
will “definitely” be the targets of Peterson's program, but it's 
still not “100% sure whether we will include discount store 
chains as well,” a White House official told Discount Store 
News. 

“We're a little reluctant to ask the discount industry to_ 
participate in this program, because its prices are already so — 
iow,” a Peterson aide said. “But, at this point we're leaning 
toward including discounters anyway.” 

Peterson met privately last month with representatives of a 
number of industry groups (American Retail Federation, As- 
sociation of General Merchandise Chains, National Retail 
Merchants Association, etc.) to map out strategy for the latest 
price-freeze campaign. 

“It was a very positive meeting and | think we'll get a great 
deal of cooperation from this industry,” a spokesman for the 
veteran Presidential consumer advisor told DSN. 

Originally Peterson had planned to send letters to the top 
chains late last month, but an illness disrupted that timetable.

(Continued trom page 1) 
must become more productive. 
Shrink control and warehouse

And, a Government which 
seems not to understand busi-

will have to be contended with 
on a daily basis. These regula-

around all are weighing heavily 
on the minds of many of us. 

That's why it is particularly 
refreshing to be in a position to 
take positive action. We can 
this week. Let’s put our heads 
together, pick each others 
brains and exchange ideas. 

Discounting is an industry of 
achievers. Those achievers are 
in New Orleans this week. To- 
gether, you achievers can begin 
your walk through the 80's in a 
positive manner that leaves no 
room for panic—or failure. 


It's a “Time of Change,” in- 
deed. Let’s look at the 80's as a 
time of opportunity. Discount- 
ing’s message is right. It’s a 
matter of coolly developing the 
controls. 

Good luck.

Will Two Guys, Under Roth, Take Retailing or Real Estate Route? 


By Arthur Markowitz 

GARFIELD, N.J.—Where is Two Guys going? 

Will the financially troubled chain, which just opened its 
first new store in three years, remain committed to retailing 
or eventually go the potentially more profitable reali estate 
route! 

The answer could come at the annual 
meeting, due to be held at presstime, at 
which executives of Interstate Propérties, a 
real estate company headed by Steven 
Roth, were scheduled to take control of the board of directors 
of Vornado, Two Guys’ parent. 

Interstate’ S move to increase its representation from three 
to five of the board’s nine seats—agreed to by the previous 
management group in pe ae 4 end Frederick Zissu’s 
long domination of the company, although he is expected to 
continue as board chairman and chief executive officer. 

Vornado executives asserted that despite the changing of 
the guard, the company is “committed to the development of 
its retail business in its core areas of metropolitan New 
Jersey and New York” and cite the new Freeport, N.Y., 
store as the prototype Two Guys of the future. 

But, trade observers counter that the company, having 
suffered more than $40 million in operating losses during the 

ast four years, would be better off as a real estate firm, with 
its sites and stores developed as shopping centers and leased 
out to other retailers, with Vornado possibly retaining any 
ongoing Two Guys stores.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, JUNE 2, 1980 


Do Much Better Than Sears, Penney, Ward 


Discounters’ First-Quarter Biz Steady But Softening Creeps Into April 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Discount store sales held steady in 
the first quarter, but the weakenin 
economy and an early Easter eaiet 
in a softening pattern developing in 
April. Some chains reported a drop in 
volume for that month against a strong 
April 1979. 

Discounters overall did much better 
than the Big Three—Sears, Penney and 
Ward—each of which had a sales decline 
in April. Only Penney reported a slight 
(0.6%) increase for the quarter. 

The big gains reported by such dis- 
counters as Wal-Mart, up 32%; James- 
way and T.G. & Y., cam with a 23% 
increase, and Caldor and K mart, with 
14% hikes, reflect new-store openings 
by these chains, inflation and small 
same-store increases. 

The small same-store gains for the 
quarter and the mixed April results are 
seen as signs that ripples from the eco- 
nomic downturn are starting to reach 
some discounters. 

Wal-Mart performed the best among 
discounters by recording 32% increases 
for the quarter and April, with the 
month’s sales at $119,000,000. 


Some Mfrs. (More Expected) Ice Prices 


The top discounter, K mart, had a 
14% jump for the quarter and an 11.8% 

ain for April when volume hit 
142,474,000. 

The mixed results were evident at 
Jamesway which had a 23% boost for the 
quarter, but a 5% same-store gain. Vol- 
ume, for the four weeks ended May 3, of 
$78,450,000 was up 12%. 

Among the discounters that had 
quarterly gains, but declines in April, 
were Zayre, Venture and Murphy. 

In Zayre’s case, the 6.8% quarterly 
boost was offset by a 5.9% decline to 


$100,941,000 for the four weeks ended 
May 3. 
A 5.2% quarterly gain for Venture 


culminated in a 2.8% sales decline for 
the four weeks ended May 3, to 
$38,200,000. 

Murphy’s small 1.4% quarterly gain 
ended in a 1.9% drop in April as sales 
declined to $57,000,000 (but from fewer 
stores in this case). 

The Big Three results for the quarter 
had Sears down 0.2%, Ward off 2.6% 
and Penney up 0.6%. Ail three had de- 
clines in Apri: Sears 4.3%, Penney 5% 
and Ward 5.4%.

will solve it for us.” 

The advertisement was fol- 
lowed by a four-page pamphlet 
that was inserted in customers’ 
bags at checkouts in many of 
the Wal-Mart stores, contain- 
ing the same warning and 
adding a list of Senators, Rep- 
resentatives and Congressional 
committee members to be con- 
tacted. 

In both the ad and the 
stuffer, Walton warns that the 
nation is “in serious trouble” 
and suggests that all-out use of 


our vast coal reserves should 
get priority attention in the for- 
mulation of a comprehensive 
energy policy. 

Nuclear power and synthetic 
fuel Toeslosanean are also 
urged, as is energy conserva- 
tion, to “develop a self-suffi- 
cient energy program for 
America, and free us from the 
OPEC oil cartel.” 


See editorial, p. 8. 


Walton reported that early 
feedback to the ad has been 
100% supportive. He plans to 
monitor the public’s reaction, 
seeking confirmation from the 
Congressmen involved (who 
have been alerted to the proj- 
ect), with an eye toward imple- 
menting a full-scale campaign 
in all Wal-Mart stores later on. 

“If the campaign is as suc- 
cessful as I think it will be,” 
Walton explained, “we’ll follow 
it up with specific suggestions 


for new legislation that will en- 
courage formulation of a com- 
prehensive and effective en- 
ergy policy for the country.” 

Asked about the possibility 
of confrontations with ant}- 
nuclear activists, or anticoal 
environmentalists, Walton 
agreed that “some folks will dis- 
agree with my proposals. But 
every businessman has an obli- 
gation to speak his mind on an 
issue as important as this.” 

Walton counters the com- 

laints of environmentalists in 

is ad. He calls for immediate 
industrial conversion to coal; 
more atomic-power-generating 
capability, and faster develop- 
ment of domestic oil production 
on Federal lands. 

He then asks: “Would such a 
program harm the environ- 
ment?” 

“Absolutely not,” claims the 
ad. “Unless these steps are 
taken soon, our people will 
wind up cold, hun and un- 
employed—and what kind of 
environment is that?” 


To Fit Format in 60,000 Sq. Ft. 


By Iris Rosenberg 

HALLANDALE, Fia.—Tignht, innovative merchandising has 
helped Jefferson wedge its basic 100,000-sq.-ft. format into a 
60,000-sq.-ft. store here. 

The unit, which opened last month, is one of 11 J. M. Fields 
stores the Miami-based chain picked up last summer (for $1.4 
million) when the bankrupt discounter auctioned off its hold- 
ings. 

“This isn't a prototype store,” said Joel Peney, senior vice 
president, sales promotion. “We just did what we had to do to 
get all of our classifications into the store.” 

What they did, according to Peney, was to tip the store's 
merchandise mix in favor of soft goods, scaling back on the 
size and sku count of the lawn & garden, toy, sporting oe. 
furniture, hardware and housewares departments. To further 
support the new 60-40 ratio (55 hard lines/45 soft in other 
stores) the chain added higher gondolas (in the cut-back hard 
lines departments), careful planogramming and a new look in 
store design. 

“This is the first time we got away from straight aisles,” 
Peney said of this more complex racetrack presentation which 
allows side aisles to cross over and converge in some places. 

The racetrack takes a conventional course along three 
sides of the store. On the fourth side, however, where the 
store opens directly into the Diplomat Mall, the racetrack 
breaks up into a small network of cross-over aisles. They 
bisect the carpeted men’s, women's and children’s apparel 
departments. 

“The successful layout of the store depended on depart- 
ment accessibility and product exposure,” Peney added. 

Accentuating the new look are several new merchandising 
techniques, some of which are being tested for possible use 
throughout the chain. Others, are new elements that are also 
being added to existing units, according to Peney. 

The new gourmet cookware department, The Creative 
Kitchen, is here. At approximately 800 sq. ft., it may be 
disproportionately large for this store but it is the same full- 
scale department that will eventually be added to all other 
stores, Peney said.

Outlook, in View of Past Trends: 


By ARTHUR MARKOWITZ 
Special DSN 
Housewares Report 

Housewares and electric 
housewares, as basic merchan- 
dise used every day by consum- 
ers, tend to be among the more 
recession-proof products han- 
dled by discount stores and cat- 
~— showrooms. 

ut housewares, in common 
with most other products sold 
by retailers, are prone to sharp 
price increases due to inflation. 

These two seemingly contra- 
dictory trends are evident in 
the National Housewares Man- 
ufacturers Association’s latest 
market study of the house- 
wares industry and a review of 
the past decade of reports. 

The 10-year review shows 
that in 1974, the year of the last 
recession, discounters cap- 
tured a greater dollar and per- 
centage share of manufactur- 
ers’ sales to retailers than in 
1973 ($1.76 billion and 30% vs. 
$1.6 billion and 28%), and the 
discounters’ share was even 
greater in 1975 as the nation 
came out of the recession ($2.27 


billion and 34%). 

Manufacturers sold more 
housewares to discounters in 
the two years vecause consum- 
ers turned to discounters to 
Save money during the 1974 re- 
cession and this buying pattern 
continued into 1975. 

If the 1974 recession is an in- 
dication of what can happen 
during a down year, then dis- 
counters can look forward to 
another strong and steady 
housewares sales year in 1980. 

This outlook is also in keep- 
ing with the decade-long trend 
for discounters, during which 
the industry’s dollar share of 
manufacturers sales to retail- 
ers has wn, cespite varia- 
tions in the industry’s percent- 
age share of manufacturers’ 
sales to retailers. 

In 1979, discounters’ percent- 
age share fell four percentage 
points to 29%. But dollars grew 
20.5%, a pace that was even 
higher than the housewares in- 
dustry’s 16% boost in total vol- 
ume. 

The outlook isn’t as clear for 
catalogers because the industry

recession period when luxuries 
are less important than basics. 

The impact of inflation on the 
wholesaie cost of housewares is 
of basic concern to discounters, 
catalogers and all other retail- 
ers. The latest NHMA market 
study presents a discouraging 
picture for 1980, with manufac- 
turers forecasting 11% as the 
average price increase and with 
53% of those surveyed project- 
ing increases of 10% or more. 

In the past, manufacturers’ 
projections have tended to be 
under the actual increases. The 
1978 projection for the average 
price increase for 1979 was 7.7% 
while the actual average hike 
turned out to be 10.3%. Only 
22% of the manufacturers fore- 
Saw price increases of 10% or 
more but 43% ended up report- 
ing such boosts. 


Closer to Mark 


The recession could result in 
manufacturers’ expectations 
this year being closer to the 
mark than in the past as the 
economic downturn offsets 
some projected increased costs. 
The reasons cited for the higher 
costs this year include inflation, 
15%; higher freight costs, 1%; 
higher overhead, 19%; higher 
labor costs, 19%, and higher 
material costs, 70%. 

The recession could lessen 
the impact of inflation and some 
overhead costs such as interest 
expenses, but not labor, mate- 
rial and freight costs. 


In the last recession, manu- | 


facturers’ projections for price 
increases for 1974 were under 
the actual hikes—a situation 
that doesn’t bode weil for the 
outlock for 1980.

Can Buy Basco 
On Margin Now 


CHERRY HILL, N.J.— 
Basco has been added to the 
Federal Reserve Board's list of 
over-the-counter stocks that 
can be purchased on margin. 

Previously, Basco’s OTC 
stock could only be purchased 
from a broker at its full price. 
Now brokers can make margin 
loans using Basco’s common as 
well as wor: So the stock on mar- 


gin. 
Must Meet Standards 


The Federal Reserve Board 
annually surveys companies 
that aren’t on its list of - 
proved OTC marginable stocks 
to see if the firms meet the 
board’s standards, which in- 
clude dollar value of the share, 
the company’s net worth and 
activity in the stock. 

The board’s move could result 
in increased activity in Basco’s 
stock as investors can now ob- 
tain more shares on margin 
than they could have when the 
stock could be purchased only 
at full price.

Gateway to the 80's 


Farsighted Merchants to Solve Risk/Reward Crisis 


The decade of the discounter has ar- 
rived—bringing with it levels of risk 
and reward seldom equaled in the 
short history of discount department 
store chains. 

This crisis—for that is what such a 
combination of opportunity and dan- 
ger is—will be best resolved by retail- 
ers with sufficient courage, commit- 
ment and ability to attack the prob- 
lems and seize the opportunities. 
Those who plan to “sit it out” with 
“time-tested” approaches will falter 
and fail. 

But the discount department store 
industry is replete with farsighted 
merchants and managers, and as a 
whole has never been better posi- 
tioned to maximize its potential. 

The crisis of double-digit inflation 
will continue to bring downside pres- 
sure on the personal disposable in- 
comes of our customers, and upside 


more consumers to seek out the better 
values offered by discount stores— 
quality name brand merchandise at 
lower prices, and soft-line basics of in- 
creasing quality, attractively priced. 
The crisis of America’s aging popula- 
tion will require retailers to carefully 
track, through extensive consumer 
and market research, the changing 
lifestyles and needs of their custom- 


Discount executives view 
the next 10 years—pp. 13-31. 


ers. But, it also means that the bulk of 
the purchasing power controlled by 
the American consumer will be held by 
upwardly mobile, career-advancing 
homeowners who grew up with dis- 
counting in the years since 1950. 

The crisis of information manage- 


uate data retrieval and fall behind 
their competitors, or implement ex- 
cessive data processing that will bury 
them under an avalanche of under-uti- 
lized information at excessive cost. 
However, the information gathering 
and processing revolution aiso pro- 
vides the capability to obtain item-by- 
item, day-by-day, store-by-store 
tracking of the most productive goods. 
New measurements will evolve, show- 
ing the traffic-pulling power and profit 
production from every sku, from every 
square foot of display and from every 
style of presentation. 

The energy crisis will add to dis- 
counters’ woes with increased store 
operating costs, rising freight bills and 
worse prospects for repressive Gov- 
ernment regulation of in-store en- 
vironments and operating hours. But, 
the energy shortages and price hikes 
will also force consumers to seek the 


stores, with broad assortments and 
convenient suburban and rural loca- 
tions (as well as in-store or next-door 
supermarkets) fill the bill. 

e crisis of Federal tampering with 
the free enterprise system will con- 
tinue to hamper the most-efficient 
least-inflationary distribution of gen- 
eral merchandise, and the efficient op- 
eration of retail businesses. However, 
excessive Government regulation, 
from the tea tax to today, sows the 
seeds of its own defeat. Discounters in 
the coming decade will organize and 
cooperate to whatever extent neces- 
sary to finally convince the Govern- 
ment bureaucracy that sound business 
practices and adequate profit potential 
will produce sound social progress. 

Discount Store News, in this first 
year of a crucial decade, takes a look at 
the future of discounting in a special 
“Gateway to the 80's” section.

—Doug Stinson

downs of mass merchandising 
personally. 

As the newly elected board 
chairman of the National Mass 
Retailing Institute (NMRIJ), 
Godfrey will be as sensitive to 
industrywide problems as he is 
to those in his own backyard as 
chief executive officer of Hart 
Stores. 

Take this current example: 

“Many of our consumers in 
this area work in the coal-min- 
ing industry, and we all think 
there shou.. be more use of 
coal. By motivating our legisla- 
tors to push for more use of 
coal, we can achieve more en- 
ergy, more jobs, higher employ- 
ment and more buying power,” 
Godfrey said. 

The end result would allevi- 
ate inflationary pressures on 
Harts’ customers by attacking 
the root of the problem, 
whether it is a Government 
obstacle, energy shortage and 
expense, or some othcr inf» 
tionary woe. 

This is the same tactic God- 
frey will put to work for NMRI. 
The three trouble spots he will 

“focus on during his term are en- 


ergy, Government relations and 
the development of a uniform 
merchandise marking system 
within the industry.

years behind other industries in 
this last area,” he said, al-

Its Properties to Be ‘Developed’ 


Roundup of Recent Annual Meetin gs 


Future of Two Guys’ Sites Up in Air 


GARFIELD, N.J.—The dis- 
position of Two Guys’ stores and 
sites is up in the air. 

Steven Roth and Frederick 
Zissu, the two top executives of 
Vernado, Two Guys’ parent 
company, told stockholders at 
the annual meeting that the 
chain’s properties would be “de- 
veloped.” 

But they left unanswered the 
type of development planned 
for the sites. 

Roth, chairman of the board 
of directors’ executive commit- 
tee and the key executive at 
Vornado, told DSN after the 
meeting that “I’m not going to 
tell you that we’re going to liq- 
uidate the retail business.” 

He indicated that there was 
too much at stake in the way of 
employees and potential use of 
sites to offer a simple answer to 
Two Guys’ future. 

“I have a big investment in 
Vornado and I don’t plan to lose 
money.” 

Roth is general partner of In- 
terstate Properties, a real es- 
tate firm that won control of 
Vornado in a oy battle last 
year. He would be considered 
the sparkplug in any plan to re- 
vamp Vornado into a real estate 
operation. 

Zissu continued as board 
chairman and chief executive 
officer after his group lost the 


proxy fight. Both sides signed 
an ——— in April institu- 
tionalizing the change of con- 
trol. Interstate also filed a new 
13D statement with the Se- 
curities and Exchange Com- 
mission outlining its plans for 
Vornado. 

Zissu, who answered most of 
the questions raised at the 
meeting, declined to say if 
there were plans to lease or sell 
any stores besides the units dis- 
posed of in the Greater Phila- 
delphia market. 

“If I answer that question, I 
would give information to our 
competitors and I don’t want to 
help them, so I won’t answer.” 

He asserted, however, that 
Vornado has the “strength and 
will and capability to maintain 
its retail business.” 

Roth acknowledged that Vor- 
nado was still interested in leas- 
ing out Two Guys stores outside 
of its core market of metro- 

olitan New Jersey and New 

ork. This is in line with Inter- 
state’s plans contained in a 13D 
statement filed with the S.E.C. 
in 1979 when the real estate 
a= launched its attack. 

The new 13D states that 
there aren't any plans for any 
extraordinary Vornado trans- 
action (such as liquidation) nor 
any material change in capital 
or dividends.

through merchandise refine-

that will keep us in touch with

art of the structure on which

BEVERLY HILLS, Calif.— 
Zodys, the discount division of 
Hartfield-Zodys, is expected to 
perform especially well in the 
coming ee ceepite 
dour economic forecasts. 

That bullish prediction was 
made by Edward D. Solomon, 
— and ceo of Hartfield- 

odys, at the annual meeting. 

Solomon announced record 
sales for the discount division 
and a commitment by the par- 
ent corporation to earmark $11 
million for capital expenditures 
in fiscal 1981. The funds will be 
used to build four new Zodys 
units, remodel seven others 
after the chain’s new prototype, 
and remodel and expand by 20, - 
000 sq. ft. the flagship Holly- 
wood store. 

This signifies the beginning 
of a major four-year corporate 
expansion pro which will 
require an anticipated $40 mil- 
lion-$45 million in capital ex- 
penditures, he added. 


Officials predict sales at the 
end of the four-year period will 
reach $550 alos with total 
units reaching 420 including 60 
Zodys, 100 Hartfields, 160 Shoe 
Stops, 30 Karl’s and 70 licensed 
footwear departments. 

For the fiscal year ended 

‘eb. 1, 1980, the Zodys division 
reported record sales of $304, - 
559,000, up 12.9% over the pre- 
vious year. Comparable same- 
store sales were up 7.1%. 

Total corporate sales, exclud- 
ing licensed departments, were 
$339 million, an increase of 
7.4% over the previous fiscal 
year, with income before ex- 
traordinary items $7.3 million, 
compared to the prior $7.2 mil- 
lion. Licensed department 
sales rose to $74 million vs. $66 
million the previous year.

Higher Cost of Doing Business Hurts 


Nationwide DSN Report 
The higher cost of doing on oll 
ness in the first three months of 
1980 collided with typically slow 
first-quarter sales and a weak- 
ening economy to produce a 
mixed bag of earnings results 
for discount and general mer- 
chandise chains. 

Woolworth (all divisions) was 
at the front of the field this 
year with an impressive income 
gain of 193.2% which included 
adjustments for currency 
translations and overseas tax 
refunds. 

Grand Central, the 30-unit 
chain headquartered in Salt 
— City, also posted high 

for the quarter (boost- 
of by d by $1 140,766 in a oa genie 
gains), exceeding last year's 
quarterly profits by 110.1%.

ever, nedeig reflected a

figures. Earnings dropped 
71.4% from last year’s, netting

On the brighter side, Duck-

Several other chains—Pam-

Film, Flash, Finishing Firm Up Photo Dept. Sales 


Special DSN Photo Report 

Photo department sales are 
staying ie buoyed by un- 
flaggin Bing consumer demand for 
film, flashbulbs and photo- 
finishing service. 

Camera sales, on the other 
hand, showed some of the si ; 
of weakness reported in othe 
high-technology hard lines. 

hese mixed results left 
buyers hoping that this sum- 
mers new products—most no- 
tably a pocket camera with 
automatic on/off flash and an- 
other with fashionably colored 
body casings—will generate 
enough consumer interest to 
bring equipment sales up to 


par. 
In any event, most buyers 
say they've not seen enough of a 
downturn to keep them from 
putting together a full Christ- 
mas program. 
YE . haven't seen a softeni 
ment sales,” “sar 
sing urphy’s Mart camera 
buyer, “except in higher-end 
goods. Low-end products seem 
to be doing well. 
This downturn in higher-end 
oods, however, has not af- 
ected the chain’s Christmas 
emai In ape according to the 
uyer, the chain is currently 


testing SLR’s (single lens reflex 


cameras) in 15 of its stores. 
“It’s the fastest growing seg- 


ment of the camera market,” he 
said, explaining the decision to 
begin se two to five cam- 
eras at each of the targeted 
stores. The top-of-the-line price 
point is $300, he said. 

At Prange-Way, buyer John 
Dankwardt lans to leave the 

“periphe out of his Christ- 
mas buying this year. 

“Right now we’re just count- 
ing on those items with proven 
track records,” he said. By not 
using its full purchasing power 
now, he continued, the chain 


may be able to take advantage 

of some deals later if there is a 

— downturn in the mar- 
et. 

Otherwise, Dankwardt said, 

“photo department sales don’t 
soften as severely or as quickly 
as other departments’.” 

Still, the current economy 
does make it rough for new 
products, which explains Dank- 
wardt’s decision to wait and see 
how they fare in the market be- 
fore he adds them to his mix.

Fishers Big Wheel to Open Six in Mich. 


NEW CASTLE, Pa.— 
Fishers mg, A will open six 
stores in Michigan later this 
year. 

The stores, which will open in 
Albion, Caro, Bad Axe, Sand- 
usky, South Haven and Saint 
Johns, will bring to 12 the num- 
ber of outlets the chain has in 
the state. 

“We thought Michigan pre- 
sented an opportunity for us,” 
said Marshall Hess, president, 
“because we already had stores 
scattered throughout the 
state.” 

The new stores, of which only 
the Albion unit is a takeover 
building, will each total 43,800 
sq. ft. and conform to ‘the 


chain’s usual merchandise pre- 
sentation, according to Hess. 


“We could have reversed our 
expansion plans, and put off 
opening the stores,” Hess said, 
alluding to the current eco- 
nomic picture, “but we are look- 
ing at our long-ran e plans and 
these openings e sense.” 

Like the other markets 
where the chain has stores, the 
Michigan sites targeted for this 
year’s expansion are small 
towns in the lower half of the 
state. In fact, only the Albion 
store has a population of more 
than 10,000 eadale. The other 
targeted towns have an average 
core population of closer to

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, JUNE 16, 1980 


5 


NSUNER 


ELECTRONICS 


SHOW 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Portable televisions and low-cost 
clock-radios loaded with features 
have become hot items in a con 
sumer electronics industry begin- 
ning to feel the pinch of a tight 
economy. 

Discounters said customers, look- 
ing to avoid the skyrocketing cost of 
gasoline and vacationing, are boost- 
ing purchases of products geared to 
at-home recreation. 

Especially strong sellers in the 
consumer electronics area are 13-in. 
color portable and AC/DC black- 
and-white TV sets. 


The Outlook: 
Lower-ticket 
Items to Gain 


The 1980 outlook for con- 
sumer electronics items in- 
cludes: 

@ Stepped-up consumer de- 
mand for portable televisions. 
Thirteen-inch color and AC/DC 
black-and-white models will be 
particularly popular as more 
people seek at-home activities. 
@ Price drops on television 
games. New, more sophisti- 
cated models are due to start 
coming on the market within a 
year, however, and some retail- 
ers may get stuck with obsolete 
equipment. 

@ Fast movement on low-to- 
medium-ticket portable items 
with plenty of features. High- 
ticket items and heavy items 
such as console televisions 
won’t move as fast as the year 
progresses. 


13-in. Color TV's Pace CE Biz as Economy Pinches 


VE jj lf Hi iy: ‘the 
Discounters 


stocking shelves accordingly. 


Almost as hot are the lesser- 
known makes of clock-radios and 
tape decks that can still be pur- 
chased at the same price that brand 
names cost more than a year ago. 

“It was kind of slow last month, 
but we’re really beginning to pick up 
on small-screen portables and on the 
type of things you can carry with 
you,” said a buyer for Fed Mart. 

The optimistic note came amidst 
comments by some discounters that 
the worsening economy may be 
about to catch up to the consumer 
electronics department. 

Already hard hit, said buyers for 
some of the nation’s larger chains, 
are the fringe items—equipment at 
the top and bottom of all lines that 
may be attention getters but that 
never accounted for much in sales. 

Discounters are also reporting 
sales drops in top-of-the-line and 
brand name models of clock-radios 
and home sound equipment. 

“Something’s happening out 
there, and I don’t think its going to 
be fun,” explained Richard Millner, 
an ALCO buyer. “It’s the economy.” 

Most chains surveyed said last 
Christmas went well, but that sales 
have begun to suffer since then. 

“It only hit us in the last four 
weeks,” explained Michael La- 
Comba, of lessee Starlett Stores, 
which sells consumer electronics in 
Treasure City and Laneco discount 
department stores. 

“It could get very, very rough out 
there,” he warned. 

Discounters said they’ve been able 
to minimize the effects of the tight 
economy by recognizing changing 
consumer demand. 

Seeking the greatest value, con- 


sumers are scrambling for the larg- 
est number of features at the lowest 
possible price. 

In the coming months, consumers 


Sy 


Inventory watching, upscale merchandising (a la its Ward parent) give Jefferson an 


edge over an economy that has most CE buyers looking grim. 


are going to be looking for items 
such as weather bands on radios, 
and tape decks that can play both 8- 
track and cassette tapes, according 
to discounters from various chains. 

The net result of the changing 
economy for the chains, said Lowell 
Corbin, vice president of Mr. Wiggs, 
has been a “return to the basics.” 

“We’re taking an introspective 
look at ourselves and asking who we 
really are and how we can best be of 
service to our customer.” 

The new priority, he said, includes 
stocking a heavy percentage of small 
radios and cassette players—the 
kind that can be purchased for rela- 
tively little money and carried 
home. 

In addition Corbin said he’s had 
luck pushing items with a large 


(DSN photo) 


number of features—even if they 
tacked a bit onto the price. Mr. 
Wiggs’ hottest item so far has been 
an AM-F'M radio that plays cassette 
and 8-track tapes. 

ALCO’s Millner is also trimming 
all the fat from department inven- 
tory. He said he’s eliminating all the 
“window dressers’—items carried 
to give customers the impression 
that a complete line is sold, but that 
“do not hold their own.” 

A Gold Circle buyer said his chain 
has been experiencing strong televi- 
sion sales. But he offered another 
reason than the gas shortage for the 
trend: 

“It’s still part of the American way 
of life to keep up with the Joneses, 
and they’re doing it by getting an- 
other television.” 


around the country report increased 
consumer demand for moderately priced stereo sys- 
tems. Barkers, Metairie, La., is among those retailers

At Record Pace; Dirt Style Hot 


DSN Nationwide Report 

Discounters—riding high on 
a growing health craze and on 
popular new styles from Cal- 
ifornia—say they expect to roll 
in big profits as customers roll 
out bicycles in record numbers. 

Unit sales on bicycles were 
reported to have increased by 
as much as 17% last year, and 
some buyers are predicting in- 
creases of 5% to 10% more this 
year. 

Largely responsible for the 
strong sales are styles resem- 
bling dirt bikes that originated 
in California two years ago, and 
are beginning to take the coun- 
try by storm. 

But three- and 10-speed bicy- 
cles, which began to soar in 
sales during the 1979 gas lines, 


are still big sellers. Buyers for 
chains such as Woolco, Hills and 
Gibson’s said they will continue 
to do well.for the foreseeable 
future.

year, more bicycles were sold 
nationwide than cars,” ex- 
plained a Gibson’s buyer, “and 
there’s a good chance this year 
will be even better.” 

Buyers for most of the firms 
surveyed said they expected 
motocross styles to remain 
strong at least through Christ- 
mas and probably well into next 
year.

More Chains Spot Expanded Food Service Up Front 


Nationwide DSN Report 

The familiar snack bar found 
today in many discount stores is 
going the way of other nostalgic 
items from discounting’s vari- 
ety store heritage, if upscaling 
executives have their way. 

The smell of buttered pop- 
corn or roasting franks will re- 
main; so will warm-toned 
counters serviced by a few 
store employees. 

Many discounters already 
have stepped, with ing de- 
grees of confidence an exper- 
tise, into the role of restaura- 
teur. 

Whether through additional 
seating, expanded menus or a 
new theme, discounters are 
moving food service farther u 
front to capitalize on store trat- 
fic—beginning to pick up on a 
trend in department and spe- 
cialty stores, where food ser- 
vices increasingly are geared to 
attract the nonshopping diner. 

So far, however, discounters’ 
development is keyed to in- 


store location and enhancing 
the shopping experience for 
customers, rather than focus- 
~—" nonshoppers. 

y moving their new theme 
restaurants up front, Jefferson 
stores—more committed to the 
department than most chains— 
will become more competitive, 
have longer store hours and a 
more “enticing” atmosphere. 

Jefferson is moving away 
from the snack bar concept to a 
“patio garden” theme. 

Formerly, snack bars were 
located at various spots 
throughout the store. In some 
recently acquired stores, 
Jefferson expanded existing 
up-front restaurant facilities 
and in other buildings will add 
the necessary space. 

Although construction has 
been running behind schedule, 
the first of seven new theme op- 
erations was scheduled to open 
by presstime. 

“Location is the key,” said 
George Seckinger, vice presi- 


Cook's new unit in

erations. “It’s a matter of mov- 
ing it up, ne in the right 
equipment and coming up with 
the right decor.”

Big Chains Reapportion Ad $$; Direct Mail Gains 


Nationwide DSN Report 

A faltering economy and the 
—* costs of doing busi- 
ness are forcing discounters to 
re-examine their ad budgets. 

What most have decided is 
that now is not the time to cut 
budgets (even if the sales fig- 
ures to which ad budgets are 


pegged are showing reduced 


gains due to the lagging econ- 


omy). The time has come, they 


say, to identify nonproductive 
dollars and to shift priorities in 
order to make dollars work 
harder. 

For the larger chains, this 
scrutiny is leading discounters 
to bank more heavily on direct 
mail advertising. 

Many discounters report 
they are relying more on Zi 
code demographics to help 
them locate their customers. In 
these cases, retailers are tak- 
ing preprint inserts from news- 
paper circulation routes and 
mailing them directly to the 
homes and apartments of the 


most desirable target custom- 
ers. Consumer response, the 
say, will offset the higher mail- 
ing costs. 

Among the smaller chains, a 
move is on to beef up insert fre- 
quency schedules, and in some 
instances to improve the look 
and format of the tab by adding 
color or scaling down the num- 
ber of items in the ad. (Here,

tempts by discounters to pro-
