identified by consumers as 
good values, and to keep gross 
margin losses to a minimum by 
limiting the number of promo- 
tional items.)

Court Lets Stand Decision Making 
Chain Liable For Co-op Ad Claim 


WASHINGTON—A blow against co-op advertising was 
struck by the Supreme Court when it refused to overturn a 
lower court decision involving the Pay 'n Save Corporation. 

The Supreme Court recently let stand a decision by the 
Court of Appeals which upheld the strict liability standard 
against the West Coast drug chain. The principles involved, 
however, could apply in the future to discounters and other 


The case arose after the Federal Trade Commission al- 
leged that Porter & Dietsch, manufacturer of the X-11 diet pill, 
the advertising agency which prepared co-op ads, and Pay 'n 
C act which prohibits false and 
misleading advertising. All three were ordered by an FTC 
administrative law judge to cease and desist from advertising 


The decision was appealed and the U.S. Court of Appeals 
for the Seventh Circuit ruled that although Pay 'n Save had no 
active part in the preparation of the co-op advertising, its lack 
of knowledge of the false and misleading claims did not

Planogramming, os be- 
gan to take hold in the discount 


world in the mid-70’s, has now 
become a way of life for most 
chains. 

Major discounters through- 
out the country report that as 
much as 80% of their merchan- 
dise—mostly hard lines—is 
planogrammed. The chains that 
don’t meet that figure say they 
have plans to get there within 
the next few years. 

Hills, for example, said it 
plans to add a fifth full-time 


planogrammer sometime next 
year—four more than it had in 
1976. They will work with the 
company’s five hard lines divi- 
sional merchandise managers. 

Even the smaller chains have 
made major inroads into 
planogrammin 
Gray Drug’s E Dene’ Rink’. for exam- 
ple, plots the positions of most 
products in its 42 stores with 
detailed maps and photo- 
graphs. Rink’s maintains a 
planogram room in its Toledo 
warehouse.

Cost Control Keys Pamida’s 


OMAHA—Expense control 
by new management execu- 
tives has been the key to Pam- 
ida’s bottom-line turnaround 
after a checkered economic 
past. 

It is breathing new life into 
the traditional chain, charac- 
teristically as slow to change as 
some residents in its rural mar- 
kets. 

The overall plan to standard- 


ize stores and centralize buying 
and distribution, initiated un- 
der the presidency of C. 
Clayton Burkstrand, was slow 
to develop. But now the re- 
ional chain seems to have a 
ead start on the “operations 
decade” of the 1980’s. Evidence: 
Earnings on flat sales increased 
nearly sixfold last year, from 
$528,000 to $3,053,000, with 
projections for $10 million this 


the field—chains like Rink’s, 

Zodys and others—the benefits 
have been readily apparent. 

Chain executives said their 
sales have increased, they have 
reached a better in-stock posi- 
tion and—most important of 
all—_the employee time it takes 
to display new products has de- 
creased since planogramming 


began

How Presidential Candidates 
Stand on 10 Retail Issues 


By Ken Rankin 
Special Election Report 


[Lebhar-Friedman, 


parent of Discount Store News, has prepared 


a l election report (pp. 89-92) which details responses 
each of the four major Presidential candidates to 10 critical retail 


eae. A utente poll o 


400 leading executives was followed 


by personal interviews vith each of the candidates. ] 


No matter which of the major 
Presidential hopefuls goes on to 
the White House, the next 
President will be sympathetic 
to some of the retail industry's 
most pressing concerns—and 
not at all sympathetic to others. 

Predictably, President Car- 
ter, Governor Reagan, Sen. Ed- 
ward Kennedy and Rep. John 
Anderson each expressed 
strong commitments to deal 
with the problems of inflation 
and energy shortages on a top 
priority basis. 

All four also voiced support 
for loosening international 
trade barriers despite rising 
protectionist sentiment among 


powerful labor unions and man- 
ufacturing industries. 

And, each of the candidates 
acknowledged the legitimate 
concerns of retailers regarding 
excessive regulation. 

But there were clear differ- 
ences separating the candi- 
dates on a number of retailing’s 
key concerns. 

On the issue of possible new 
mandatory Federal wage and 
price controls—an anti- infla- 
tion “remedy” almost univer- 
sally opposed by business— 
Reagan came down squarely 
against such economic re- 
straints, while Kennedy voiced

Layaway Plans Gain Popularity, 


Nationwide DSN Report 

The downturn in the econ- 
omy is turning layaway plans— 
traditionally just a convenience 
to shoppers—into a valuable 
tool for a growing number of 
discount chains. 

The number of persons buy- 
ing on layaway began to in- 
crease late last year and, say 
discounters, really began to 
soar several months back when 


President Carter announced a 
tightening of personal credit. 
Major discounters such as 
Woolco and King’s have already 
reported substantial increases 
in the number of layaway pur- 
chases and several Midwest dis- 
counters said they plan a major 
ush for this fall to cash in even 
her on the promising new 
trend. 
“We’ve just been doing fan-

tastic,” oe a Woolco ex- 
ecutive. “Things have really 
been starting to peak.” 

Exact statistics, however, 
will not be available for most 
discounters for several months. 

For those who have already 
evaluated the new trend, the 
additional sales brought in by 
layaway plans more than out- 
weigh the cost of storing goods.

Woolco Skeds 30 U.S. Openings in 1980 


HOUSTON—High inflation 
and tight credit are taking their 
toll, but the F. W. Woolworth 
Company predicts that Woolco, 
the nation’s second-largest dis- 
count chain, will finish the year 
with sizable gains both in sales 
and store numbers. 


By January a total of 45 new 
Woolco stores will be opened 
worldwide—30 of them in the 
United States—and sales, up 
by 10.8% in 1979, should again 
rise substantially.

According to one source, the purpose of the proposed sale

Satisfaction-Guaranteed’ Claims 
By Biggies Draw FIC Probe | 


WASHINGTON—Kor- 
vettes, Sears, and Ward are 
among at least half a dozen dis- 
count and general merchandise 
retailers under investigation by 
the Federal Trade Commission 
(FTC) for allegedly failing to 
live up to “satisfaction guaran- 
teed” advertising claims. 

The massive, nonpublic in- 
vestigation was revealed after 
the three firms filed motions to 
quasn the FTC’s orders for in- 
formation. The commission has 
asked for potentially thousands 
of documents relating to re- 
funds and other practices of the 
chains. 


The FTC’s involvement in in- 
vestigating “satisfaction guar- 
anteed” claims dates back about 
eight years when it asked Ward 
and other retailers for informa- 
tion regarding such claims in 
catalogs. 

Lawyers for Korvettes have 
informed the FTC that the “sat- 
isfaction guaranteed” policy 
was discontinued by the new 
owners in 1979 and is “no longer 
being used by Korvettes in the 
stores or advertising.” Kor- 
vettes further told the agency 
that “as a consequence,” it “has 
changed from a department

Discountland Survey: FedMart, K mart Rank 1-2 in Sales per Sq. Fr. 


NEW YORK—A recent 
study of discounter perfor- 
mance in 1979 y # Paine Webber 
Mitchell Hutchins gave top 
marks to four regional chains 
and a national one. 

Using some 60 (statistically 
weighted) financial criteria, the 
study, “1980 Retail Industry 
Statistical Compendium, 
laced Wal-Mart, Caldor, 
COA Industries (Hills) and 
Hartfield-Zodys—along with K 
mart—at the front of a field of 


"ins included in the study 
are discounters who Paine Web- 
ber identified as being “signifi- 
cant competitors and impor- 
tant volume contributors.” Fig- 
ures are based on the fiscal year 
completed during 1979.) 

Results within individual cat- 
egories showed that FedMart, 
with its volume food business, 
ranked first in productivity 
with sales per square foot of 
$199. K mart, industry leader 


in number of stores, sales vol- 
ume and net income, ranked 
second in sales per square foot 
with $128. 

Following those two, using 
the same yardsticks were Glos- 
ser Bros. (Gee Bee) with $116, 
Caldor with $110 and Wal-Mart 
with $95. Jamesway, Zayre, 
King’s and Gaylords all fel be- 
low the industry average with 
sales per square foot of $76, 
$67, $46 and $44, respectively. 

In net income, giant K mart 


set the pace with $343.7 million 
followed by Wal-Mart ($29.4 
million), SCOA ($20.3 million), 
Caldor ($15.5 million) and 
a. ($15.1 million). FedMart 
finished dead last and in the red 
with a loss of $11.1 million, al- 
though the West Coast dis- 
counter/food retailer did record 
the highest sales growth during 
the period: 40.7%. Much of this 
wth, however, was derived 
rom the addition of 22 stores 
since the middle of 1978. 


Expansion-minded Wal-Mart 
saw sales increase by 32.7% last 
year, consistent with the chain’s 
(compounded) five-year growth 
pattern of 40%. 

Hartfield-Zodys, whose av- 
erage sales growth was 4% over 
the past five years, boosted 
sales by nearly 30% last year. 
The sales performance at most 
other chains was consistent 
with the previous five-year pe- 
riod: In 1978, sales for K mart

Another reason why the FTC

Sears has asked the FTC to 
drop its request for information 
on the grounds that the recent

the FTC’s order “is burden-

Shifting Gears 


Ward pointed out that for 
more than five years, it has 
“virtually eliminated” the un- 
qualified use of the “satisfaction 
guaranteed” term in advertis- 
ing. Its outlets were encour- 
aged to use in-store displays 
that make the more limited 
claim: “Satisfaction is our goal.” 

Since 1974, Ward noted, its 
catalogs have not used the “sat- 
isfaction guaranteed” term in 
regard to specific products. The 
term has only been used on cat- 
alog covers in small print, in- 
side catalogs along with a de- 
tailed description of the policy, 
and on only one type of in-store 
sign. 
Ward also pointed out that a 
purchaser can express “any 
reason at all for his/her dissatis- 
faction and obtain a full refund 
of all money paid,” and that 
such obligations are always 
fulfilled. 

Summarizing its contention 
that the FTC’s request is unrea- 
sonable, Ward states that it is 
being asked “to document im- 
plausible interpretations of a 
claim which was ee in- 
vestigated and for which the 
commission has no reason to be- 
lieve consumers have either 
been misled or injured.”

Market Price Well Over Book Value For 4 Chains’ Stock 


Expect Senate Unit Will Approve 
Zimmerman for N.L.R.B. Vacancy 


WASHINGTON—Following Senate confirmation of William 
Lubbers as general counsel of the National Labor Relations 
Board, the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee 
is expected to approve the nomination of Don Zimmerman to 
fill the current vacancy on the board. 

Many of the same business groups that had opposed Lub- 
bers nomination oppose Zimmerman because he will occupy 
a traditionally Republican seat. A liberal independent, Zim- 
merman was formerly a registered Democrat in California. 

At present, he is minority counsel of the Senate Labor and 
Human Resources Committee. As such, he advised the Re- 
publican members, particularly Sen. Jacob K. Javits (R-N.Y.), 
the senior GOP member. 

lf approved, Zimmerman would serve a term that expires at 
the end of 1984.

Middle-of-Road 
Pricing, Promos 
lo Be Stressed 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Discounters are counting on 
middle-of-the-road pricing and 
extensive promotions to sustain 
the small-appliance business in 
the face of a recession. 

Merchandisers reason that 
the midprice range will satisfy 
the overriding consumer de- 
mand for quality, sturdy mer- 
chandise at prices shoppers 
can still afford. 

“The middle-price range is 
strongest in most categories of 
appliances,” said a Matco 
buyer. 

Except for some forays into 
electric scales and quartz heat- 
ers, discounters will largely 
avoid fringe or novelty items for 
the fall and Christmas season. 

The emphasis on middle-of- 
the-road pricing is evident in 
food processors. Zodys, Heck’s 
and Target, among other 
chains, have been heavily pro- 
moting them in the $40 to $50 
range. A Gold Circle merchan- 
diser reported that processors 
priced at $40 and under, with a 
rebate, represented almost all 
movement in the category. 

Since most discounters view 
the processor as an everyday 
item, they are also carrying $69 
and $79 models. But a Magic 
Mart buyer admitted: “These 
price points are just too high for 
most shopoers these days.” 

Others noted that the food 
processor business tends to ac- 
celerate in the fall and the 
Christmas season, which partly 
explains why the category has 
gotten off to a relatively sluggish 
~~ year. ty toh 

“The ery usually takes 
off between Thanksgiving and 
Christmas, and we allocate sub- 
Stantially more space for pro- 
cessors at that time than the 
rest of the year,” noted a buyer 
at S. E. Nichols.

SMALL ELECTRICS SUPPLEMENT 


Curling Brushes Give a Lift to Personal Care Appliance Business 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Curling brushes have helped 
personal care appliances fluff 
up new sales and given more 
body to the classification. 

A Target merchandiser ex- 
plained that curling brushes 
took off immediately, indicating 
that the consumer was ready for 
something new in personal care 
appliances. 

He added that brushes have 
made the hair curling area the 
hottest part of the hair care ap- 
pliance business, but that the 
new item has resulted in a de- 
Cline in curling wand action. 

Sales of styler/dryers, the 
other portion of the hair care ap- 
pliance field, have remained flat, 
discounters and catalog show- 
room merchandisers reported, 
reflecting the maturity of this 
business. 

Pistol dryers are the key 
items, a Jamesway merchan- 
diser noted, because consum- 
ers want “something substantial 
in their hand when they dry and 
style their hair.” 

A MacDonald Showrooms 
merchandiser added that per- 
sonal care appliance sales keep 
growing because of the boom in 
hair care appliances. Curling 
brushes are hot, replacing curl- 
ing irons, while styler/dryer 
sales have been maintained by 
the strong movement in pistol 
models. 


A Major Share 


Hair care appliances (exclud- 
ing hard-hat and bonnet dryers 
and rollers) account for 
50%-60% of the personal care 
business for discounters and 
catalogers, with the remaining 
volume coming from the other 
items used for hair care plus 
such specialized products as 
foot massagers and face and 
body care appliances. 

The sales breakdown reflects 
the two types of merchandising 
programs followed for personal 
Care appliances: Hair care 
items are featured for traffic 
through sharp promotions and 
low margins, while the other 
products are the high profit pro- 
ducers, often carrying margins 
in the 40% to 50% range. 

The greater number of sku's 
carried for hair care as com- 
pared with the other type of per- 
sonal care appliances has re- 
sulted in an overall low gross 
margin but high turn. 

This was pointed up by a 
Frost & Sullivan personal care 
appliance market study issued 
last year which showed that al- 
most half of the discounters sur- 
veyed reported an average 
gross margin for personal care 
appliances that ranged be- 
tween 15% and 25%, while 75% 
of the discounters listed turns 
ranging between three and 
seven. 

Catalog showrooms had 
lower gross margins and didn't 
achieve significantly higher 
turns than discounters, the 
study reported. 

Just under half the show- 
rooms questioned listed an 
average gross margin in the 
10% to 15% range while just un- 
der 60% reported turns ran from 
three to five. 

The report noted that “for re- 
tailers, their final average main- 
tained gross margin is of utmost 
importance. Using all margins 
25% and above as a bench- 
mark, catalog showrooms are 
weakest with only 4% at that 
level. The retailers second to 
department stores [which are 
highest with 54% at that level] 


are discounters at 36%. In over- 
all averages, discounters give 
25.6% off on sale and catalog 
showrooms’ markdown [for 
sales] is 26.5%, only slightly 
higher.” 

he key to the differences in 
productivity between discount- 
ers and catalogers, the study re- 
ported, “are in regular mark- 
downs. Showrooms’ average 
markdown is 19.7% and the dis- 
counters 16.8%, a much greater 
difference [than the ad mark- 
downs]. 

“In conclusion, catalogers 
showrooms are selling a greater 
percentage of their personal 
Care appliances on sale and dis- 
counters are doing more busi- 
ness at the regular price.” 

The study asserted that there 
“are some important contribut- 
ing factors to this phenomenon. 
Showrooms place these prod- 
ucts on sale frequently and use 
them as traffic builders. Also, 
showroom sales are often of the 
planned purchase sort [due to 
the use of the catalog by shop- 


ers]. Discounters have a broad 
ine of goods and are in a better 
position to attract impulse pur- 
chases. In addition to achieving 
higher average gross margins in 
personal care appliances, dis- 


et had a higher inventory 
urn.” 

_ Discounters greater pi.duc- 
tivity in personal care avoli- 
ances is also evident from a 
number of other portions of the

Discounters, More 
Than Catalogers, 
Utilize Distributors 


Discount stores and catalog 
showrooms follow different dis- 
tribution plans for personal care 
appliances, both on the buying 
and receiving ends. 

Discounters rely more on dis- 
tributors than do catalogers. 
Mass retailers tend to ship 
goods to stores and chain ware- 
houses while showroom opera- 
tors favor direct delivery. 

These two different distribu- 
tion patterns were evident in the 
Frost & Sullivan study of the per- 
sonal care appliance business. 

The study noted that while 
discounters and catalogers “fol- 
low much the same purchase 
patterns. . . the vast majority— 
45.7% of catalog showrooms— 
purchase directly from the 
manufacturers. Purchasing 
through manufacturer reps is 
another way of purchasing di- 
rectly, and catalog showrooms 
do this to a high degree also.” 

Discounters, the study 
added, “are more likely to use 
independent distributors, buy- 
ing groups and buying services 
than catalog showrooms.” 

But, the heavy reliance on di- 
rect purchase by yr i and 
use of distributors by discount- 
ers still allow for the two types of 
retailers to obtain large 
amounts of merchandise 
through other channels. 

The study noted that 21.3% of 
discounters used distributors, 
and obtained only 64.6% of their 
merchandise from this source. 
The 26.2% of discounters buy- 
ing direct purchased only 59.4% 
of their goods this way. 

On the cataloger side, the 
45.7% that bought direct ob- 
tained 73.5% of their merchan- 
dise from the manufacturers; 
the 14.3% that used distributors 
purchased 83% of their goods 
from this source. 

The end point of the distribu- 
tion process is more clearly de- 
fined. Sixty-five per cent of the 
catalogers had personal care 
appliances sent direct to their 
showrooms, while only 32% of 
the discounters bought direct 
for the stores. Fifteen per cent of 
the catalogers and 18% of the 
discounters had goods go right 
to their warehouses. Mean- 
while, 47% of the discounters 

sent goods to the stores and 
warehouses as compared with 
only 19% of the catalogers that 
had merchandise flow to the 
showrooms and the main ware- 
house.

PRODUCT MOVEMENT AUDIT 


Value Is King: 
$10-$20 Items 
Crown Electrics 


By Howard Bobroff 
President, 
Myron Nickmen Distributors 
etailers’ cutback to basics 
and lower-priced items to main- 
tain a slim but productive traf- 
fic-appliance 4 
mix in the face 
of the weaken- 
ing economy 
was evident in 
the Product 
Movement Au- 
dit for Jan. 1- 
May 29. Sta- 
les, particu- : 
arly those in the “magic” $10 to 
$20 range, dominated the re- 
port. 

The push to become lean be- 
came especially noticeable in 
the June post-audit period as 
retailers reported traffic appli- 
ance inventories were higher 
than desired. However, the 
trend toward an inventory cut- 
back wasn’t a question of just 
dropping higher price points, 
but rather of focusing on val- 
ue—offering customers items 
and features at price points that 
will attract sales. 

Discounters can expect some 
help from manufacturers this 
fall in establishing value as a 
selling factor. 

For one thing, rebates will be 
extensively offered by manufac- 
turers—and, just as important, 
producers plan to heavily pro- 
mote the rebates. 


Smaller Price Hikes 


Manufacturers have indi- 
cated that the weakening econ- 
omy has resulted in smaller 
price hikes, due to be posted at 
the housewares shows. The em- 
phasis on the manufacturer 
end—similar to the effort 
among retailers—is to move 
merchandise, with the closing 
down of production lines the 
last resort. 

Besides rebates, manufac- 
turers will be offering special 
promotional models and new 
designs to help move goods. 
This merchandising approach 
should be evident at the shows, 
where a number of producers 
plan to introduce special mod- 
els of food processors designed 
to retail at under $40, and 
where a new look that features 
a tall silhouette is due to be 
shown by at least one manufac- 
turer. 

The focus on basics and 
lower-priced electrics means 
that personal care appliances 
and gift-oriented goods such as 
hot-air nigep pumpers will 
be big this fall and during the 
holiday gift period. 

A number of retailers have 
indicated that hair care appli- 
ances and the hot-air pumpers

MacDonald Biz Up; Operating Net Dips 


DAYTON, Ohio—Mac- 
Donald catalog showrooms 
boosted sales 5.7% but experi- 
enced an 82.9% drop in opera- 
tional income for the fiscal year 
ended Feb. 3. 

Sales went to $25,461,697 
from $24,089,273, but opera- 
tional earnings dropped to 


$198,597 from $1,163,473. 

The chain, a division of the 
E. F. MacDonald Co., has 
switched from the Jewelcor 
group to Merchandisers’ Asso- 
ciation Inc., in a move to in- 
crease showroom volume by 
using a catalog geared for $5 
million-plus sales.

Rebates Planned 


A number of producers plan 
to offer rebates for hot-air pop- 
corn makers this fall that 
should make these units retail 
for around $20-$22 after re- 
bates. 

Irons, interestingly, were the 
No. 5 classification in both unit 
and total dollar sales. This 
showing denotes a strong re- . 
bound due to the greater use of 
cotton in clothing and the devel- 
opment of the lightweight iron. 

Three lightweight irons were 
among the 10 that made the 
PMA (a travel iron also made 
the report), indicating the im- 
portance that this type has as- 
sumed. Proctor-Silex, which 
has a steam iron that was No. 1 
on the report, is due to intro- 
duce a new line of lightweight 
irons; only Hamilton Beach and 
Sunbeam lightweight models 
made the report. 

The other basic electrics— 
toasters, slow cookers, mixers 
and blenders, showed action on 
the report mainly within-the 
magic $10-$20 range. Four of 
the six toasters, for example, © 
were ‘agged under $20, with 
two under $15. 

It’s in these staples that the 
combination of feature and 
price to show a value is impor- 
tant for everyday sales, espe- 
cially as discounters and other 
retailers tend to promote these 
items less often. 

Food processors have slowed 
down—only four models made 
the PMA—and price has be- 
come the key to sales. Manufac- 
turer awareness of this is be- 
hind the plan to offer models 
and rebates that will make food 
processors go out at under $40.

(Continued from page 73) 
change with new patterns; as is 
customary, the changes apply 
to 8-pc. gift box sets, rather 
than bulk or 4-pack glassware. 

Because of the high cost of 
packaging, gift box sets have, 
as a classification, suffered in 
sales in recent years. A number 
of manufacturers will try to 
counteract this situation at the 
housewares show by coming 
out with simpler, less-fancy 
packaging for the gift box sets. 

The area to watch for in- 
creased sales is multiple sets, 
primarily 24-pe. offerings, be- 
cause they represent a recog- 
nizable value to consumers. 
Retailers will be looking for 
more and more promotions to 
stimulate flagging sales and 
they will want to promote from 
within their basic assortment. 
Manufacturers of such basics as 
glassware can be expected to 
have special price promotions 
for the fall. 

No 8-pe. beverage gift box 
set made the PMA, indicating 
the weak demand for such mer- 
chandise. Wineglasses and 
glass containers dominated the 
listing.

Jamesway Net Falls 


Despite Sales Rise 


SECAUCUS, N.J.—James- 
way declared a regular quar- 
terly cash dividend of 3¢ per 
share on outstanding common 
stock at its recent annual meet- 
ing here. The dividend is pay- 
able July 11 to stockholders of 
record as of June 26. 

Herbert Fisher, chairman of 
the 62-store regional chain, 
said higher sales and earnings 
were projected, despite first- 

uarter results. While sales for 
the quarter showed a 24% in- 
crease, net earnings dropped to 
$192,000—a 61.5% decrease 
from the same period last year. 


The Reason Why 


Fisher said the main reason 
for the drop was that antici- 
pated store-for-store income 
gains failed to materialize. 

Total sales were $55,286,000, 
up from the $44,586,000 re- 
ported in the first quarter of 
1979. 

Net earnings per share 
dropped to 7¢ this quarter from 
the 18¢ reported last year.

Further Attempt 


Corning, besides adding 
Strawberry to the Expressions 
line, was set at presstime to 
show Dimension IV as a brand 
new line at the housewares 
show. The line is another exam- 
ple of the company’s merchan- 
dising plan of going after con- 
sumer groups that haven’t been 
attracted by its current offer- 


ings. 

| re IV is positioned 
to attract singles, couples and 
young homemakers who want a 
more modern design. Its 4-pe. 
place setting features a mug, 
rather than the cup and saucer 
of Expressions and Corelle. Its 
design of a broad and a narrow 
stripe on rim-shaped plates and 
bowls will be offered in three 
colors, Cinnamon, Citrus and 
Almond, and its set of 16 pieces, 
rather than 20, puts its price 
under Corelle’s. 

The manufacturer’s concern 
with pricing the line as low as 
possible fits in with consumers’ 
attempts to hold down their ex- 
penses by purchasing lower- 
cost and value-oriented house- 
wares. 


Strength Examined 


Low cost was a factor in the 
cookware area, where Ekco’s 
broad assortment of Baker’s 
Secret bakeware captured nine 
of the 20 listings, including the 
top six places. 

The cookware that made the 
report either had a SilverStone 
or T-Fal nonstick finish, denot- 
ing the all-inclusive impact that 
these coatings have made on 
cookware. But even in cook- 
ware price was important. Bulk 
cookware in the Nos. 9, 18, 14 
and 18 places had greater unit 
and total dollar movement than 
the one set to make the listing, 
a Wear-Ever 9-pc. Premium 
with SilverStone offering. The 
latter was tagged at a $71.99 
average dollar retail, which is a 
top dollar price in a down econ- 
omy even though it’s a good val- 
ue compared to open-stock pur- 
chases of the same nine pieces.

Hoped-For UPC, OCR-A Compatibility Due Next Year 


Nationwide DSN Report 

The hoped-for compatibility 
of UPC and OCR-A will be- 
come a reality early next year, 
DSN has learned. 

Specifications that will, for 
the first time, enable manufac- 
turers to use both UPC and 
OCR-A as the marking systems 
for general merchandise are to 


be issued by the retailer/manu- 
facturer/equipment-maker 
group that developed OCR-A 
as a voluntary identification 
standard. 

OCR-A uses human and ma- 
chine-readable numbers while 
UPC uses a 10-digit number 
and a series of bars, the latter 
readable only by machine.

Other developments in the 
merchandise marking field. 
@ Wal-Mart this fall will test 
the use of UPC-marked mer- 
chandise in one store by install- 
ing slot scanner checkouts to 
read items UPC-marked by the 
discounter. The test will be ex- 
panded to another store in 1981. 
@ A DSN survey of the top 100 
discount store chains found that 
among the discounters re- 
sponding, 55.5% favored the 
adoption of OCR-A, 29.6% pre- 
ferred UPC and 14.8% were un- 
decided. 
e@ The National Mass Retailing 
Institute has formed an execu- 
tive committee that will meet in 
the fall to decide what, if any- 
thing, discounters as a group 
should do about merchandise 
marking. 

Development of OCR-A was 


spearheaded by the National 
Retail Merchants Association 
in conjunction with some gen- 
eral merchandise manufactur- 
ers and equipment producers. 

The voluntary group also de- 
veloped the technical standards 
that provides compatibility of 
OCR-A and UPC. 

UPC’s development was 
spurred by supermarkets and 
food producers. The UPC 
Council, however, didn’t sup- 
port development of compati- 
bility of the two systems. 

The UPC 10-digit number is 
the equivalent of an sku, but 
doesn’t include price or such 
specific information as size or 
color that discounters and other 
general merchandise retailers 
often incorporate in their mer- 
chandise identification.

Magazine Ad $$ by 40% 


TROY, Mich.—K mart is 
stepping up its national con- 
sumer magazine advertising in 
an effort to attract a more afflu- 
ent, better educated and big- 
ger-spending customer, and to 
improve its product credibility 
among its target groups. 

On at least some of the ads, 
K mart is sharing the cost with 
manufacturers. 

Sources estimate K mart’s 
gross magazine expenditures 
will climb to around $7 million

Discounters Invest Big Bucks 


In Energy-Saving Mechanisms & 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Discounters across the coun- 
try are insulating roofs, caulk- 
ing doors and installing a vari- 
ety of sophisticated electronic 
devices with the aim of stabiliz- 
ing skyrocketing utility bills 
this winter. 

For many the cost has been 
great. Computers that regulate 
electrical consumption and au- 
tomatically control lighting, 
heating and air-conditioning 


cost more than $13,000 per 
store to install. 

Even less sophisticated com- 
puters that only regulate a 
store’s electrical demand rate 
by cycling off heavy appliances 
during periods of peak usage 
cost from $8,000 to $10,000. 

Discounters who have reno- 
vated and installed as little as 
two inches of insulation in the 
roof of an 80,000-sq.-ft. store 
have found the single-store bill 


Hills, Glosser Bros. and Wal-Mart 
Run Ad Drive to Spark Coal Revival 


As most discounters try to cut their use of expensive im- 
ported oil and natural gas, three discount chains have begun 
campaigns advocating the replacement of foreign fuels with 
something that can be stamped “Made := the U.S.A.”: coal. 

Hills, Glosser Brothers and Wal-Mart bege:> their programs 
in the spring and summer, hitting consumers wi> a barrage of 
newspaper advertisements intended to gather yrass-roots 
support for the nation’s coal industry. Individual methods went 
even further than the newspaper campaign, including the air- 
ing of numerous television and radio spots, passing of peti- 
tions and mailing of almost one million letters to Congress- 
men and Senators urging a unified coal policy. 

“We’re in coal country and we see what the depression of 
that [coal] industry is doing to our economy,” explained Hills 
vice president Stephen A. Goldberger. “Too many of the peo- 
ple in our area are unemployed and it's hurting all of us.” 

Hills began its campaign in June, placing ads in 81 papers 
that reached an estimated 3.5 million persons. In addition, 30- 
second television spots and 60-second radio announce- 
ments were aired repeatedly during the month.

Howard’s 100th Store Is Due in Sept. 


MONROE, La.—Howard 
Bros. Discount Stores is her- 
alding its 100th unit, slated to 
open the first week of Septem- 
ber. 

The 48,500-square-footer 
(40,000 sq. ft. of selling space), 
will be in Slidell, La., and con- 
form to one of the chain’s three 
prototypes and its “BRANDis- 
count” marketing strategy. 

The strategy was devised 
two years ago (with the help of 
outside consultants) to unify all 
aspects of the chain’s visual pre- 
sentation, including signage, 
store packaging and layouts to 
focus customer attention on pri- 
mary competitive areas.

Romance Novels Hot But 
Cost Hikes Hurt Book Biz 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Increased selections of ro- 
mance novels, and strategic lo- 
cation of those and other paper- 
back books to encourage im- 
pulse buying may become 
trends of the future as increas- 
ing numbers of discount chains 
fight to maintain sales in view 
of increasing public resistance 
to publishers’ prices. 

Already, many chains report 
they are increasing their stocks 
of romance novels as well as a 
popular western series because 
the lower-priced publications 
appear to be immune to the re- 
sistance and are registering 
sales increases of up to 13%. 

Several chains—including 
FedMart—are also placing pa- 
perbacks at endcaps and check- 
outs as a means of perking up 


drooping sales. 

For many chains—such as 
K mart and West Virginia- 
based Heck’s—the resistance 
has not yet materialized and 
buyers report increased unit 
sales as well as profits. 

K mart, for example, said it 
will have “book corners” in more 
than 300 stores this year and 
that the number of stores add- 
ing them will continue to grow. 

But for chains such as Jeffer- 
son, Gold Circle, Woolco and 
others, it appears the paper- 
back boom reported as recently 
as last summer may be headed 
for trouble. 

Books that retailed for $1.95 
just two years ago are now $3 
and many chains report that 
customers are either being di-

Dayton Hudson 


Approves Grants 


MINNEAPOLIS—The 
Dayton Hudson Foundation has 
approved $3.5 million of its 1980 
$10.3 million budget for quar- 
terly grants to communities 
served by the Dayton Hudson 
Corporation, based here. 

Primary grants went to the 
Minneapolis YMCA ($1.2 mil- 
lion toward capital and inner- 
city programs); Macalester Col- 
lege in St. Paul ($1 million for 
the college’s capital fund drive), 
and the Boise Forte Indian Res- 
ervation Business Committee 
in Orr, Minn. ($166,650 to un- 
derwrite a three-year program 
for economic development, 
which includes a multiservice 
center for residents). 

The remainder was divided 
into 65 grants between $493 
and $12,000 and distributed in 
14 states.

Discounters’ Biz Up as Sears, Ward, Penney Slump 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Discounters are tightening 
their belts and becoming more 
promotional in response to 
tough economic times, and it 
appears the industry has so far 
been spared the heavy sales 
losses that have hit the big 
three mass merchandisers. 

A sampling of sales figures 
for six major discounters indi- 
cates that while sales have soft- 
ened somewhat, most are con- 


tinuing to rack up significant 
increases in volume. 

Wal-Mart led the list with 
June sales of $121,000,000—a 
25% increase over the volume 
recorded in June 1979. K mart’s 
sales rose 14% and Jamesway’s 
increased 23%. 

But the six chains surveyed 
averaged a 13.9% sales increase 
in June, down from the 15.4% 
increase recorded in May and 
the 19.2% in January. 


By comparison, a pte. 
three—Sears, J. C. Penney an 
Montgomery Ward—reported 
an average 0.7% decrease in 
volume. In January the three 
chains averaged 6.7% in sales 
growth. 

The steps being taken by the 
discount stores to combat 
slumping sales are routine. 
Costs are being cut wherever 
possible and in many cases mar- 
gins are being reduced on an

Bradlees President Frank Switches 
To A&S: Levin Takes Over His Duties 


BOSTON—Harold Frank, 
president of Bradlees, has re- 
signed and will be returning to 
the Abraham & Straus division 
of Federated (where he began 
his career) as executive vice 
president, merchandising and 
sales promotion. 

Robert F. Levin, senior vice 
president of Bradlees’ parent 
company, Stop & Shop, will as- 
sume Frank’s duties and the 
Bradlees executive committee 
will report to him. 


It’s a Throwback 


“There's a feeling of deja vu in 
this,” said Levin, who had 
served as Bradlees’ president 
prior to Frank’s selection, and 
who was chief executive officer 
vi the chain during the first 
year of Frank’s presidency. In 
fact, Levin hired Frank, who 
was at that time executive vice 


president and general mer- 
chandise manager at Feder- 
ated’s Gold Circle division. 

No other staff changes are 
planned at Bradlees, according 
to Levin. He said that “the best 
future management structure 
for the chain” would be studied 
during his interim manage- 
ment, but that the chain would 
probably stay with an arrange- 
ment similar to what has been 
in place, and that there will be a 
new chief executive officer 
named. No timetable has been 
established for finding Frank's 
replacement. “We’ll find some- 
one as soon as possible,” said 
Levin, “but we will not rush. 

“The six vice presidents that 
ran Bradlees with Hal Frank 
will continue to run the chain, 
reporting to me.” 

rank was on vacation out of 
the country when the news was 
released, and not available for

had extensive knowledge of 
A&S and its markets.

between April and July 1.

Fauber Visibly Pleased as He inspects 
K mart’s Upgraded Apparel Test Dept. 


LODI, N.J.—K mart chair- 
man and chief executive officer 
Bernard M. Fauber is a mer- 
chandiser, and he still enjoys 
merchandising. 

It was obvious in his anima- 
tion and enthusiasm as he ex- 
amined, for the first time, 
K mart’s upgraded apparel 
merchandising test here. His 
enthusiasm may prompt accel- 
eration of the test program. 

Fauber’s enormous satisfac- 
tion with the apparel test may 
also prompt him to advance 
scheduled hard lines merchan- 
dising tests, reportedly includ- 
ing an experimental racetrack 
configuration, at undisclosed 
sites. 

Fauber, executive vice presi- 
dent Robert E. Brewer, K mart 
Apparel’s Arnold Bachman and 
_many other K mart and K mart 
Apparel executives toured 
ladies’ apparel while Fauber 

ing from ear to ear) ex- 
plained the fashion presenta- 
tions and new fixtures, and 
introduced himself to shoppers 
and store personnel. 

“I hope you’ve been shopping 
here many times since the 
change in the apparel depart- 
ment,” Fauber said to one shop- 
per amid laughter. The woman 
seemed nonplussed to have met 
the chairman of the chain. 

“This fixture is five dollars 
less per unit than a plain one,” 
Fauber pointed out proudly, in- 
dicating a split round and com- 
paring it to a standard round 
rack. 

Fauber also pointed out a 


western-design blouse to the 
touring executives, citing the 
fact that the design was woven 
into the fabric, rather than 
printed. 

Fauber also made it a point to

25% of Korvettes’ future earn-

turing indicates that Korvettes 
would have to produce about 
$120 million in profits in the 
seven fiscal years through 1987 
for the four lenders to recover 
the approximately $31 million in

Trade observers said that 
while Korvettes could become 
profitable during the seven- 
year oiigre it was highly ques-

view of the chain’s past losses. 

A company executive said 
that the pending financial state- 
ment will show that Korvettes 
is “a totally different company” 
that is “financially viable and on 
its own.” 

This assertedly is the result 
of the financial arrangement 
reached with the major lenders 


and of a new relationship devel- _ 


oped with vendors during a se- 
ries of meetings held by chair-

of suppliers.

able response from vendors was 
evident from one apparel sup- 
ome who told DSN that “the 
ave made an agreement wit 
the banks . . . they seem to be 
making an effort to stay in busi- 
ness ... they are paying their 
bills, so we are shipping them.” 

The vendor acknowledged 
that there was a period when 
Korvettes wasn’t shipped 
goods. “Now it’s a credit ques- 
tion,” he said. “How much do 
we want to go for? As long as 
they pay, why not extend credit 
on our regular terms?” 

The arrangement with the 
lenders and the seemingly suc- 
cessful approach to vendors 
have raised questions among 
executives who deal with Kor- 
vettes, trade observers and fi- 
nanciers. 

An executive with one factor- 
ing firm said it was “unlike 
banks to be so magnanimous; 
there must be more to it [the 
agreement ].” 

The factor, as of the middle of 
July, had held off credit ap- 
proval for Korvettes. “I want to 
see the financial statement,” 
the executive said, noting that 
his action shouldn’t adversely 
affect the discounter.

geringly high, the statistics are 
relatively good. The survey,

In the 17 years of the survey, 
which samples suburban and 
urban stores, only one consis- 
tent factor has emerged. Shop- 
lifting, Griffin said, tends to 
change only gradually over the 
years. 


Many Boys Caught 


Discount merchants ap- 
prehend about 60% boys in the 
juvenile category, yet the dis- 
tribution between male and 
female tends to level off in 
adults with 538.7% females and 
45.8% males. There doesn’t 
seem to be any answer as to 
why boys are caught more often 
than girls and why those per- 
centages become more evenly 
matched in adult shoplifters, 
Griffin said. 

Discount stores also had a 
higher recovery of merchandise 
per apprehension (4.5%) than 
supermarkets (3.1%) and drug 
stores (2.6%). The average 
value of merchandise recovered 
per apprehension ran $25.44 in 
discount stores, compared to 
$7.87 in supermarkets and 
$9.07 in drug units. 


Thursday Is Bad News 


Discounters were hit hardest 
on Thursdays, with 17.4% of the 
cases recorded, and during the 
hours of noon and 3 p.m. and 3 
p.m. and 6 p.m. with 34.7%, re- 
spectively. 

During the 12 months, dis- 
count merchants apprehended 
the largest number of cases in 
March, November and Decem- 
ber, with 9.9% each month. 


Purses Hide Loot 


The survey also showed that 
shoplifters concealed stolen 
merchandise in discount stores 
more often in purses (29.6%), 
with shopping bags (15.9%) and 
“in pocket” (15.6%) of the time. 
“In purse” was highest for su- 
permarkets (30.6%), while 
drug store shoplifters more 
often put merchandise in 
pockets (29.5%).

Trade-up efforts were scat- 
tered among the other basic 
electrics. Producers showed 
new items that included elec- 
tronic controls for food pro-

compact irons, second-genera-

watts. 


Goal Is Refinement 


The total effort was toward 
refinement of basic electrics, 
rather than major innovations. 
Manufacturers are holding off 
the introduction of break- 
through small appliances until 
the economy improves, and dis- 
counters and other retailers are 
more receptive to making com- 
mitments for new items. 

The focus on staple small ap- 
pliances, particularly lower- 
priced products, was evident in 
the PMA. Categories such as 
curling wands and irons, in 
which lower-priced items domi- 
nated, had higher unit move- 
ment from more items than did 
categories such as food pro- 
cessors and stand mixers in 
which higher-priced models 
were the standard. 

Drip coffeemakers were the 
one exception as this category 
includes models that range to 
$40 as the average retail. Still, 
a $40 average retail is under the 
$60 average retail for food pro- 
cessors or the $75 average re- 
tail for a stand mixer with a 
dough hook.

the former while the latter's 
movement was sparked by the

K mart Will Issue 
$200M in Notes 


TROY, Mich.—K mart has 
filed a preliminary prospectus 
for the issuance of $200 million 
in K mart notes due July 15, 
1985. The New York invest- 
ment house Morgan Stanley & 
Co. is handling the public offer- 
ing. 

The proceeds will be added to 
the general funds of the com- 
pany to increase working capi- 
tal through a temporary reduc- 
tion of short-term borrowing, 
and will be used for acquisition 
and development of real estate, 
including distribution centers 
and stores. K mart plans the 
addition of five distribution 
centers by 1988, making it pos- 
sible to reach every K mart in 
one day from one of 11 distribu- 
tion centers nationwide. 

The notes will be issued in 
denominations of $1,000 or any 
multiple thereof, with the 
Chase Manhattan bank acting 


as trustee. Interest will be paid | 


twice annually.

Discount Directory 
For ’80 Published 


NEW YORK—the 1980 Di- 


rectory of Discount Depart- 
ment Stores, with more than 
1,400 pages, has been published 
by Business Guides Inc., a sub- 
sidiary of Lebhar-Friedman 
Ine. 

A separate section of the di- 
rectory this year includes a list- 


| ing of catalog showroom opera- 


tors and coordinators. A quick 
index of the top 50 discount de- 
partment store chains, ranked 
by volume, has also been add- 
ed. Other features include an 
industry profile that graphs a 
10-year pattern, a list of major 
trade shows (with hard lines 
and fashion events listed sepa- 
rately) and profiles of each ma- 
jor public chain—highlighting 
volume, total square footage, 
sales per square foot, store lo- 
cations and more. 

The directory contains infor- 
mation on 300 chains operating 
7,600 stores, 192 leased depart- 
ment operators, 28 catalog 
showroom coordinators and 379 
catalogers with some 1,500 
showrooms. 

To order a copy of the direc- 
tory, which costs $110, contact 
Business Guides Inc., 425 Park 
Ave., New York, N.Y. 10022, or 
call 212-371-9400.

Throughout the 70’s dis- 
counter hardware departments 
made substantial gains. 

Sales per square foot rose by 
more than 70% during the pe- 
riod while average sales per 
store jumped more than 150% 
to $426,644. 


Department size, after fluc- 
tuating over the course of the 
decade, seemed to settle at an 
average size of about 3,000 sq. 
ft.—a 50% increase over their 
size in the early 70's. 

More significantly, the sales 
gains occurred during a period 


when initial markups and gross 
margins remained fairly stable. 
This is evidence that both dis- 
counters and their customers 
are moving away from low-end 
product lines and toward bet- 
ter-quality, higher-priced 
goods.

Putting on Pressure 


“We're already hearing more 
requests for both — and 
rice breaks,” reported Bob 
arkwart, advertising man- 
er for the Chamberlain Man- 
ufacturing Corp. “Retailers are 
working on tighter budgets 
than they have in the past, and 
they are certainly avoiding 
stockpiling goods.” 
Accordingly, the company is 
devising new programs for the 
year that have been arrived at 
“strictly because of the econ- 
omy.” However, he pointed out: 
“We’re going to be careful about 
extending dating. When we of- 
fer our customers 90 days it 
costs us a lot more to carry it.” 
Other manufacturers are 
paying closer attention to the 
demands of the do-it-yourself 
(and the mass merchandise) 
marketplace and are repackag- 
ing lines to give retailers more 
of a hand on the sales floor. 
“We've repackaged our line 
to hone in on the DIY market,” 
said Joe Goloversic, advertising 
manager for Gibson-Holman, a 
manufacturer of caulks, seal- 
ants, and decorative products. 
The new packaging will be 
some of a the company is 
hoping will stimulate sales. 
“We’re getting better at it,” 
he said, referring to the com- 
pany’s industrial history. “We 
recognize the best way for any- 


| one to sell our product is for it 


to tell the whole story in a sin- 
gle glance.”

lrizarry Joins Mars 


NEW BEDFORD, Mass.— 
Julian Irizarry is the new buyer 
of ladies’ dresses, sportswear 
and coats at Mars Stores. 

A textile specialist, he has 
been with Anderson-Little, 
J. P. Stevens and United Mer- 
chants. The appointment is 
part of a long-range plan at the 
chain to improve personnel and 
sales performance. In 1979, 
sales increased 22%.

New Calif. Law 
May Up Biz in 
Smoke Alarms 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Sales of smoke alarms—at 
one time a red-hot hardware- 
department item—-have been 
cool for awhile. Even with 
steady retailer promotion and 
manufacturer rebate support, 
the item ceased to be an endcap 
star quite a while ago. 

New legislation in southern 
California, however, may recall 
the item from side-aisle obscu- 
rity—at least temporarily. 

“We’re running an ad now to 
capitalize on the new law,” re- 
ported Steve Moskowitz, buyer 
at The Treasury. Moskowitz an- 
ticipates that the new law, 
which requires Los Angeles 
landlords to install smoke de- 
tectors in multiple dwellings 
when they make more than 
$1,000 worth of improvements, 
will substantially boost sales 
from their current steady, but 
not exciting, levels. 

“Generally, we have to pro- 
mote smoke alarms to get them 
to move,” explained Ben Bow- 
en, a buyer with Rasco Stores, 
“even with the current rebate 
structure.” But Rasco expects 
the new law to make a dif- 
ference in the chain’s L.A. 
stores. 

Elsewhere in the country, 
however, business is flat. 

“Sales in that category have 
plateaued,” reported a Mur- 
phy’s Mart buyer. “One of our 
competitors recently offered a 
name-brand product at $11.88—

Outdoor Power 
Gear Shipments 
Go Up 4.1% 


WASHINGTON—Manufac- 
turers unit shipments of out- 
door power equipment in- 
creased 4.7% in the eight 
months ended April 30, 1980. 

However, that figure is not 
expected to change much by 
Aug. 31, according to a spokes- 
man for the Outdoor Power 
Equipment Institute, who 
pointed out that shipments 
peak in April and then are little 
more than a trickle in the final 
months of the year. (Years are 
measured according to manu- 
facturers’ shipping season: Sep- 
tember to September. ) 

A breakout of the data 
showed that walk-behind 
mower shipments were up 4.5% 
to about 4.5 million units com- 
pared to a 6.7% increase to 4.3 
million in 1978-79. 

Lawn tractor and riding 
mower shipments increased 
only 3.6% to 643,000. 

Front-engine mode! ship- 
ments increased 4.3% to 
386,000 from 370,500 units the 
previous year. 

Garden tractor movement, 
which increased moderately in 
recent years, decreased 3.3% to 
178,500 units from the previous 
year’s 184,600. 

Rotary tiller shipments ex- 
perienced the only substantial 
increase—up 11% to 530,000 
units. Last year the category 
showed a 0.6% decline with 
only 478,000 units shipped. 

The institute spokesman 
stressed the figures were esti- 
mates, but added: “The indus- 
try is in the middle of a severe 
recession that was helped along 
by last winter’s snow-blower di- 
saster.” He was referring to the 
virtually snow-less season

DIY Is a Rising Star at Gibson’ 


SEAGOVILLE, Tex.—The 
do-it-yourself trend has become 
a tidal wave at Gibson’s. 

Sales of electrical items now 
account for an average of 
$60,000 of each store’s annual 


sales—a figure that is rising 
25% each year, according to a 
chain buyer. 

Plumbing sales, which last 
year accounted for $25,000, are 
rising at the rate of 10% a year. 


Zr are water-resistan 
we 2 Sepicaings bot 


metals, tough-to-bond plastics 


_and nearly every other 


household material.

PRODUCT MOVEMENT AUDIT 


Stay-at-Homes 


(Continued from page 38) 

ft. extension cord outsold the 
50-ft. cord as the outdoor sea- 
son exerted its influence on 
movement. Sales of these items 
will be eclipsed later in the year 
by roof cables and heating 
tapes, historically strong fall 
sellers. 

Mailboxes also had a good 
month, holding five of eight top 
slots on the hardware PMA, ev- 
idence once again of springtime 
consumer interest in fixing up 
the House. 


Smoke Alarms 


(Continued from page 36) 
$6.88 after the rebate—and 
there was no real rush.” 

The same is true in Arkan- 
sas, Florida and downtown Chi- 
cago. 

Zeno Smith, a Magic Mart 
buyer, said the item had fallen 
from meteoric heights and be- 
come a department staple, 
while Larry Shapiro said the 
item had never done well in 
Florida. 

“There are few two-story 
homes or homes with base- 
ments here,” the Gold Triangle, 
divisional merchandise man- 
ager said. “We carry two or 
three sku’s, but business is just 
so-so. It hasn’t been a big item 
in years.” 


Fear Strikes Out 


Fear of fires in the home 
doesn’t seem to keep smoke 
alarm sales steady at Commu- 
nity Family Centers, in Chi- 
cago. 

“Sometimes, if the media re- 
ally play up a big fire we'll see 
sales start to move, but other- 
wise our customers have vir- 
tually no interest in the cate- 
gory,” reported Sam Falato, a 
buyer for the eight-store chain. 

“We've even tried selling 
them at prices below cost, and 
in combination deals with fire 
extinguishers,” said a per- 
plexed Falato, “but they just 
bomb.” 


‘Ellman’s Year: 


Biz Up, Net Flat 


ATLANTA—Ellman’s re- 
ported an 11.2% fiscal-year 
sales gain but flat earnings 
from its six catalog showrooms. 

Sales in the year ended May 3 
hit $56,432,000, up $5,681,000 
from the $50,750,757 reported 
for the previous fiscal year. 

Net income of $1,326,000 was 
down 0.9% or $13,000 from 
$1,338,828 produced in the 
prior fiscal year. 

The cataloger is due to open 
its seventh alli this fall. 
It will be its fifth in the Greater 
Atlanta market; other units are 


in Charlotte and Greensboro, 
N.C.

9-Mo. Pretax Loss 
Is Cut by FedMart 


SAN DIEGO—FedMart’s 
sales for the first three quar- 
ters of its fiscal year, ended 
May ll, 1980, totaled $733.8 
million, an increase of 9.6% 
over the $669.8 million reported 
in the comparable period a year 
earlier. 

The chain lost $2.1 million 
(pretax) and $1.6 million (after- 
tax) for the 36-week period. Its 
pretax loss was more than $23 
million the year before. 

Sales for the third quarter in- 
creased 3.1% to $237.7 million 
compared to $230.5 million in 
the third quarter of the pre- 
vious year. 

FedMart reported a small 
gain in soft lines sales, reaching 
10.3% of total volume for the 
first three quarters of the latest 
fiscal year, compared to 9.9% of 
sales in the previous fiscal year. 


Two Future Targets 


Include First in La. 


MINNEAPOLIS—Target 
has broken ground for two new 
stores—one in the Houston 
area and one in Lafayette, La. 

The latter will mark the 
chain’s Louisiana debut and is 
an example of a new expansion 
policy aimed at medium-sized 
markets. 

Each store will be 100,000 sq. 
ft. and is scheduled to open in 
the spring of 1981. 


K mart Plans Two 


TROY, Mich.—K mart will 
open, early in 1981, in an old 

larkins store (now closed) at 
Euclid Avenue and Richmond 
Road, Euclid, Ohio, and in a 
strip center now under con- 
struction at Garfield and 19 
Mile Road, Clinton Township, 
Mich. 

A Kroger superstore will co- 


anchor the shopping center.

Plastic Parts 
Elbow Further 
Into Plumbing 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Discounters are following an 
increasing number of consum- 
ers who are leaning away from 
metal and discovering the ad- 
vantages of plastic parts for use 
in plumbing. 

In the last year, major chains 
such as Zayre and Pamida have 
either introduced or substan- 
tially increased the percentage 
of plastic parts in their plumb- 
ing supplies mix. 

Woolco, for example, re- 
ported that the percentage of 
plastic parts is up to 65% and 
still growing. 


More Chains May Join Up 


Meanwhile, even major 
chains that have thus far stayed 
away from plastic parts—dis- 
counters such as Rose’s, Gibson 
and others—say they may 
change their mix in favor of 
plastic as early as next year if 
they are impressed with what 
they see at the hardware show. 

The only exception to the 
trend toward plastic, however, 
appears to be sink faucets, 
which are priced about 10% less 
than the metal ones. Many 
dealers say they are interested 
in stocking them; but buyers at 
Woolco, Gibson’s and Pamida 
say they are concerned about 
possible public resistance to 
oe that have traditionally 

een made of metal and are 
holding off for the time being. 

One of the chief advantages 
to the plastic pipes, elbows and 
other parts, buyers said, is 
their price. Chains have re-

Jefferson is one of many discounters that have responded to consumer demand for easier-to-handle 
plumbing parts with an assortment of plastic fittings, as in Fort Myers, Fla., store. 


(DSN photo) 


Plastic Parts 


(( ontinwed trom pretcfe 0) 
i 


ported plastic items to average 
about 10% to 15% less than their 
metal counterparts, and a Pam- 
ida spokesman said some plas- 
tic parts run as much as 50% 
less than metal. 

But more importantly, buy- 
ers say the ease of using plastic 
pipes has been attracting more 
do-it-yourselfers, who were 
previousiy frightened by the 
welding and fitting needed to 
install metal equipment. 

One Woolco buyer pointed 
out that many of the plastic 
pipes can easily be bent to fit 
around corners and then cut 
with a sharp knife to an exact 
length. In addition, he said, 
ends can either be snapped to- 
gether or glued, depending on 
the pipe 

Still, the ease of installation 
has not replaced all the initial 
consumer resistance to the 
product. 


Image Could Be Better 


Buyers at many chains re- 
ported customers continue to 
believe either that the plastic 
parts are weaker than the met- 
al ones or that the plastic will 
give water a poor taste. 

While most discounters sur- 
veyed agreed the lower cost of 
plastic was also helping to out- 
weigh some of the resistance, a 
Zayre buyer said that might not 
always be the case. 

Both plastic and metals are 
commodities that suffer fre- 
quent price fluctuation, he said, 
adding that as the cost of oil—a 
main ingredient of plastic— 
continues to increase, the mate- 
rial may no longer hold a price 
advantage over metal. 

Officials at Caldor, however, 
said they are not frightened at 
the possible future reverses in 
price, and the company will add 
its name to the list of those al- 
ready selling plastic plumbing 
items this fall. Caldor, however, 
will sell only small items and 
not the lengths of pipe stocked 
by other chains, a buyer said. 

“We feel we’ve been loosing 
business because we do not 
stock plastic parts,” explained 
a buyer for the chain. “People 
have been coming in our stores 
and leaving when they find out 
all we have is metal.”

Will Be Conversions to Jefferson Ward Format 


Ward Leaps In! Plans 115 More Discount Stores 


By Chris Haggerty 

Montgomery Ward is con- 
verting 115 of its stores in the 
East and Midwest to the dis- 
count format of the Jefferson 
Ward stores. The conversions 
will take place over the next 
three years. 

The announcement came in 
the wake of first-half losses re- 
ported at $82 million, and is one 
of a series of steps the chain will 
take to boost profits and 
streamline operations, accord- 
ing to E. S. Donnell, Ward 


chairman and ceo. 

These conversions, he noted, 
will occur in areas where the 
company feels its Jefferson 
stores have a better future than 
traditional Ward stores. 

A restructuring of Ward re- 
tail field operations was also an- 
nounced. Supervision of 310 
Ward retail stores, which are 
principally located in metro- 
politan areas, will be cen- 
tralized at the chain’s Chicago 
headquarters, and the staff 
functions of the three present

be established to supervise the

the Jefferson Ward format.

will be transferred to Jefferson 
Ward management under 
David H. Kenny, senior vice

in targeted Southwest and

to hand them up.

could have believed that their 
actions were justified and 
art sk and consequently 
wholly legal.

Woolworth/Woolco Spurs J. Brann 


Opens 15 Apparel Stores in One Day 


HOUSTON—Woolco took 
this town and two others by 
storm earlier this month open- 
ing arecord 15J. Brannam units 
in a single day—Aug. 13. 

The openings—10 here, one 
in Kansas City, Kan., and four 
in Kansas City, Mo.—com- 
pleted this year’s expansion 
plans, bringing the 27-unit 
chain a step closer to its pro- 
jected 45 units by 1981, and 100 
by 1984. 


Of the 15 stores just opened, 
nine conformed to the original 
mold and were “cut-downs’— 
25,000-sq.-ft. stores carved out 
of existing Woolco units, ac- 
cording to D. Rowlett, general 
manager for the chain. Five 
others, all of them in Houston, 
are newly built freestanding 
units also averaging 25,000 sq. 
ft. One of the Kansas City, Mo.., 
units was converted from a 
Woolworth store. 


FIC Confirms Investigation 
Of Satisfaction Guarantees 


WASHINGTON—The Fed- 
eral Trade Commission is in- 
vestigating to determine 
whether five mass merchandis- 
ers—including K mart, Wool- 
worth and Korvettes—have 
failed to make good on “satis- 
faction guaranteed” claims. 

FTC officials did not an- 
nounce the investigation, but 
confirmed that one was in prog- 
ress at presstime, after the 
three discounters and Sears 
and Montgomery Ward moved 
to legally block FTC subpoenas 
for information. 

A spokesman for the Wool- 
worth Co. said the investiga- 
tion is “without substance,” and 
motions filed with the FTC to 
block the subpoenas asked the 
Federal agency to disclose any 
complaints. 

Woolworth argued that over 
the past five years it has re- 
ceived few complaints about its 
money-back policy and that in 
1979 it made a total of seven 
million refunds totaling $89 mil- 
lion. 


A spokesman for K mart is- 
sued a brief statement sayin 
that it had supplied the FT 
with some documents but that 
it was seeking to quash addi- 
tional requests. 

The nation’s largest retailer, 
Sears, argued in its motion that 
to comply with the request for 
information “would require 
thousands of man hours and 
would significantly disrupt the 
normal operations of 3,500 
Sears units throughout the 
country.” 

It said the Government’s re- 
uest was “particularly bur- 
ensome at this time in view of 

the current adverse economic 
situation prevailing throughout 
the country.” 

At Ward, officials said they 
were told of the agency’s probe 
last August and formally 
called for an end to the probe 
several weeks ago. A spokes- 
man noted that its “satisfac- 
tion guaranteed” pledge has 
been carried in the company’s 
catalog since 1875. 


“That’s the way we chose to 
enter a market,” said Rowlett, 
reiterating what Woolworth 
chairman Edward F. Gibbons 
had told stock analysts earlier 
this year: “We have an ability to 
make an immediate impact on a 
market by opening several 
stores in a matter of days with 
relatively small capital, adver- 
tising and administrative costs 
per unit.” 

Put another way, Woolworth/ 
Woolco is using the J. Brannam 
units to make the adjoining 
Wooleo stores more profitable 
by forcing the discounter to 
make better use of the cube. 

Rowlett and other chain 
spokesmen said the trade-off 
stops there. “The Brannam 
stores have not taken away any 
of the Woolco apparel busi- 
ness,” Rowlett noted, “because 
they serve a different wearable 
customer.” Brannam customers 
tend to be department store 
shoppers looking for the more 
sharply priced—but branded— 
goods the chain is carrying, he 
said.

Waxes Shine 
Once More as 
Gas Cans Sink 


By Herb Rechter 
President, 

Allied Accessories and 

Auto Parts Company 
Waxes and polishes, along 
with most other traditional 
summer seasonals, were once 
again back to rr 
their leading 
positions in the 


Movement Au- 
dit, after hav- 
ing been par- 
tially displaced |; 
last year by af 
gas-hungry% 
public with its 

mind on other 

items. — 

The top seller on the chart in 
the summer of 1979—a 5-gal. 
gas can that sold 7,300 units— 
was No. 51 this time. The 1-, 2-, 
242 and even 6-gal. cans that 
made strong showings in ’79 
were also way down in move- 
ment in June of ’80. 

Waxes, spark plugs and auto- 
motive chemicals were the 
strong sellers this June, with a 
total of three polishes and 
waxes making it into the top 10. 

Many dealers were reporting 
that despite the current reces- 
sion, the increasing demand for 
fuel-saving items will be 
enough to make 1980 as strong a 
year for sales as 1979. 

Already, tune-up kits have 
become good sellers amid pre- 
dictions that air and oil filters 
will rise before the year is out to 
become leaders in sales. 

Even oil sales—thus far 
somewhat disappointing with 
significant sales drops com- 
pared to last year—are likely to 
make a comeback and add 
themselves to the list of sales 
leaders. 

Snowhite Lite ’n’ Easy was 
the top-selling polish in dollar 
volume this June, ranking sec- 
ond on the PMA with 2,992 
units moved. 

Blue Poly Sealant moved a 
greater number of units— 
3,671, but ranked third in the 
dollar figures, representing 
$36,673 at retail. 

The 14-0z. bottle of DuPont 
Rain Dance paste was also a 
strong seller, ranking sixth on 
the PMA in dollar volume with 
$29,281, but outdoing Lite ’n’ 
Easy and Blue Poly Sealant 
with unit sales of 5,988. 

The best seller in dollar vol- 
ume in the audit was a two-ton 
hydraulic floor jack, a sign that 
car Owners are investing more 
money in doing their own re- 
pairs. 

The jack was also a strong 
seller in a PMA conducted in 
May, when it ranked second. 

Automotive chemicals did 
somewhat better than last year, 
with Gunk aerosol and STP oil 
treatment both ranking among 
the 10 best sellers. 

Oil however, seemed to make 
a significantly better showing 
at this time last year. 

In the summer of 1979 a total 
of three oils made it into the top

Be Ready For Tough Questions 
From Floor at Annual Meeting 


NEW YORK—As share- 
holders become more knowl- 
edgeable about how corpora- 
tions work, retailers are finding 
themselves facing tougher 
questions from the floor at an- 


nual meetings and at other 
times. 


On Operations: 


Price Waterhouse, a large ac- 
counting firm headquartered 
here, recently compiled a list of 
questions retailers should be 
prepared to answer. On the op- 
erations side, the accounting 
firm suggested retailers be 
ready to field questions like the 
following: 

@ What was the company’s 
comparative revenue and net 
income this year and last, when 
stated in.dollars of similar pur- 
chasing power? 

° ind on comparable indus- 
try sales gains, is the company 
maintaining or improving mar- 
ket share? 

e@ Was the reduction in year- 
end inventories accomplished 
by a reduction or delay in or- 
ders for next season? If so, the 
effect is for inventory on hand 
to be relatively older than 
would otherwise be the case 
and would be less salable. 
Please comment. 

@ Recent news stories point 
out that certain retail execu- 
tives are in great demand and 
their contracts have reached 
limits often held by enter- 
tainers or sports personalities. 
Please describe the terms of 
Mr. X’s contract and why it is 
justified. 


@ Why don’t we have a divi- 
dend reinvestment plan? 


On Accounting: 


On the accounting side, the 
New York firm advises retail- 
= to prepare for questions 

e: 

@ Why hasn’t the company 
adopted LIFO? What would 
have been the reduction in net 
income and income tax expense 
if LIFO had been adopted this 
year? 

@ Way has the company 
adopted LIFO and what do you 
think has been the effect on 
market value of common stock 
due to reduction in our reported 
earnings offset by having more 
funds to invest? 

@ Are the company’s account- 
ing policies in areas like inven- 
tory valuation, store opening 
and closing costs, depreciation, 
employee benefit accruals, etc., 
consistent with the industry or 
preferred practices? 


On Fraud: 


As questions of fraud con- 
tinue to receive much publicity, 
the firm suggests retailers be 
prepared to answer consumer 
questions about the subject: 

@ How has the board satisfied 
itself that officers and employ- 
ees do not have a financial inter- 
est in merchandise vendor com- 
panies, real estate projects, 
etc? 

e@ Are controls designed to de- 
tect false data entered into the 
accounting system?

Fauber: K mart to Test 
Full Race-track Aisle 


INDIANAPOLIS—K mart will be yet another step closer to 
upscale discounting when it unveils a full race-track aisle in at 
least one of eight stores currently Seing remodeled here. 

Chairman and ceo Bernard M. Fauber told DSN the race- 
track aisle, which dead-ended inside the ladies apparel de- 
partment in the Lodi, N.J., store—scene of the chain's first 
major upscale effort, made earlier this year—will go fully 
around at least one of the Indianapolis stores. 

Fauber added: “Not every store will be exactiy the same.” 

As was true in apparel, the race track will generate a new 
hard lines presentation that will not be limited to refixturing, 
but will involve a “modest trade-up of goods,” Fauber told 


The showpiece of the Lodi remodeling was a ladies wea. 
department that replaced 30-fi. piperacks with fashion fix- 
tures—rounds, deltas, and waterfalls—and displayed them 
prominently along the entire front-left quadrant of the store. 

The hard lines upscaling was the next logical step for the 
giant chain which sees its market share siipping in favor of 
aggressive regionals that are going after consumer dollars 
with two-fisted fashion and value merchandising strategies.

Equities Ltd., sole owner of 
Barkers and Franklin Stores, 
was moving to consolidate its 
retail operations at presstime. 
The move would transfer own-

chain, neadquartered here, of 
which Cornwall owns a 12% 
controlling interest. 

The two management boards 
were expected to give the go- 
ahead on the King’s/Barker 
merger. 

The acquisition proposals 
being voted on were first pre- 
sented to the boards of direc- 
tors of King’s and Cornwall 
Equities approximately 90 days 
ago. 

Nathan Greenberg, King’s 
vice president and treasurer, 
and a member of the indepen- 
dent committee created last 
June to study the fine points of 
the acquisition, reported that if 
the proposal goes through as 
expected, Barkers’ United 
States stores will be consoli- 
dated into the King’s operation. 
Only in Puerto Rico and the 
Virgin Jslands, where 16 Bark- 
ers stores have successfully en- 
trenched themselves, will the 
name change not take place, he 
said. 

Greenberg viewed the possi- 
ble acquisition as a cost-effi- 
cient way for King’s to move 
into the Sunbelt. In addition to 
37 stores in Connecticut, New 
Jersey and New York (and the 
16 Puerto Rico and Virgin Is- 
land units), Barkers operates 11 
stores in Texas and Louisiana. 

The consolidation is also ex- 
_pected to allow King’s to main- 
tain a growth rate of 10% 


compounded annually in its ex- 
isting markets, according to 
Greenberg. 

“There’s very little dif- 
ferences between Barkers’ and 
King’s merchandise mix and 
presentation,” said Greenberg. 
“That’s why we’re so enthusias- 
tic about this move. The Bark- 
ers stores fit right into our 
existing markets in Connecti- 
cut and New York with little 
need for dramatic changes.”

Many Chains Spur Promos, Though 


Operations Costs Shaved as Nets Dip 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Many discounters are taking 
a sterner position on operations 
spending in the light of their 
sluggish profit performance for 
the first half of the fiscal year. 

Advertising and sales promo- 
tion will be spared surgery at 
many chains, however, aS many 
discounters choose to acceler- 
ate their promotional activities, 
as well as to shave margins, to 
remain competitive. 

“The temptation among some 
retailers is to battle for busi- 
ness at the expense of earnings, 
something that inevitably 
causes more problems than it 
solves,” said Fred Haddad, 
Heck’s chairman. The regional 
chain posted a 22% rise in in- 


come for the first half to $5.6 
million, or 87¢ per share, from 
last year’s first-half earnings of 
$4.6 million, or 72¢ a share. 

Heck’s will continue its policy 
to “maintain margins as vig- 
orously as possible,” Haddad 
said. 

Rink’s took a similar stance in 
its promotional policy. “We are 
not trying to buy sales,” said a 
spokesman. “Customers are 
cherrypicking items anyway, so 
you can’t force them to come 
into your stores. We’ve become 
more selective and productive 
in our advertising, but we will 
not be accelerating the pro- 
gram.” 

Rink’s parent, Gray Drug 
Co., will expand its H&BA pri- 


vate label brands in Rink’s 
stores and its drug store divi- 
sion. The company hopes to 
thus increase customer loyalty 
and to boost gross margins. 

Other plans for: bolstering 
profit margins at Rink’s include 
moving to a one-week reorder- 
ing cycle. “We will trade off 
higher delivery costs for better 
in-stock positions on staple 
merchandise, and lower inven- 
tory costs,” said the chain 
spokesman. The change in 
schedule is one part of a chain- 
wide costs study. 

Wal-Mart was one of the few 
discount chains reporting rec- 
ord earnings for the first half— 
up 32.4% to $20.6 million from

Ardan Will Add 9 Showrooms in Fall 


DES MOINES—Ardan 
plans a major expansion effort 
this fall that will see the cata- 
loger open at least nine show- 
rooms, go into a minimum of 
four new states and heighten its 
competition with Service Mer- 
chandise and H. J. Wilson while 
continuing to avoid competing 
with Modern Merchandising. 

Ardan, the fast-growing 
showroom arm of the Carlson 
Companies conglomerate, at 
presstime set seven openings to 
follow the two announced last 
month (See DSN, Aug. Hl, p. 
58. ) 

The latest openings will in- 
clude Ardan’s first thrust into 
Louisiana, home of H. J. Wil- 
son; Tennessee, Service Mer- 
chandise’s base, and Indiana. 
The openings announced ear- 
lier included the cataloger’s de- 
but in North Carolina in Wins- 


ton-Salem.

the Broadmoor Shopping Cen-

quarters city of H. J. Wilson. 

In Tennessee, Ardan’s show- 
rooms will be a 38,000-sq.-ft. 
unit in Knoxville near the West 
Town Mall, about two miles 
from a Service Merchandise; a 
40,000-sq.-ft. showroom in 
Chattanooga near the North- 
gate Mall about seven miles 
from a Service Merchandise,

ready has three showrooms. 

The Indiana Ardan will be a

anapolis in the Cherry Tree 
Shopping Center near the 
Washington Square Regional 


Mall. One of Service Merchan- 
dise’s three Indianapolis show- 
rooms is about a mile from the 
regional mall. 

The other two new Ardans 
will be a 42,000-sq.-ft. unit in 
Abilene, Tex., in an ex-Sears in 
Sayless Square, and a 40,000- 
sq.-ft. showroom in Lincoln, 
Neb., that will be connected to 
the East Park Plaza, anew mall 
opening this fall. Ardan will op- 
erate its smaller unit in down- 
town Lincoln through the end of 
the year. 

Ardan’s move into markets 
where other catalogers have 
showrooms reflects a growing 
trend of face-to-face competi- 
tion among showroom ope- 
rators. 

An Ardan source asserted 
that H. J. Wilson and Service 
Merchandise started the fight

King’s Is Expected to Acquire Barkers Hard 


(Continued from page 1) 

one to King’s. Greenberg esti- 
mated that 60%-70% of the 
chain’s past growth has come 
from acquisition. The most re- 
cent takeover was Mammoth 
Mart. In 1977, King’s paid $43 
million for the 57-unit chain. 

There is little direct market 
overlap between Barkers and 
King’s. While the two chains 
currently operate in several of 
the same Eastern States, it is in 
only one city—New Milford, 
Conn.—that they square off 
against each other. 

The acquisition of Franklin 
Stores, which would operate as 
a separate entity, would afford 
King’s “a wonderful way to get 
into the specialty apparel busi- 
ness,” according to Greenberg. 

The consolidation of Barkers 
and King’s, the executive 
pointed out, would demand a 
reduction of merchandising and 
financial staffs. In addition 
each Barkers store would be 
considered for layout changes. 
“The changes would not be 
made in one fell swoop,” said 
Greenberg. “We will be looking 
carefully at each situation. 

Greenberg's enthusiasm over 
the possible acquisition, how- 
ever, was not shared by some 
industry analysts, who sug- 
gested the merger could lead to 
litigation over what one viewed 
as a conflict of interest on Corn- 
wall’s part. 

“The chances of a lawsuit are 
very high,” said Fred Kopf, at 
Dean Witter Reynolds. “Both 


Barkers and Franklin are [fi- 


nancially] mediocre chains. It’s 
quite possible that share- 
holders will feel that King’s is 
dissipating their money to buy 
a poorly performing discount 
chain. They are going to won- 
der if the move was made with 
their best interests in mind.” 

Greenberg disagreed with 
this evaluation, countering: 

“If we weren’t trying to do 
this thing fairly, it wouldn’t 
have taken us so long to get to 
this point.” 

The toughest problem ahead 
for King’s under the proposed 
consolidation plan could be 
what some observers cite as the 
chain's lack of management tal- 
ent. 

The departures of King’s 
founders, Aaron O. Cohen and 
Murray Candib, after Cornwall 
bought out their interest, the 
resignation of William Kenney 
as chairman of the executive 
committee, as well as the 
abrupt departure of president 
Bernard Litwak this spring, 
have left the chain without the 
management team observers 
feel it would need to keep the 
operation on a steady course 
and to absorb the sudden ex- 
pansion. 

Litwak, who stepped in as 
president last summer, de- 
parted in March for FedMart, 
San Diego. Until his arrival, 
the top spot had been empty. 
The chain lost its only heir ap- 
parent, Paul Kwasnick, two 
years ago during another 


around cf merger talks, at that 


time with W. R. Grace. 


Observers now question 
whether Sol Kittay, Cornwall’s 
chairman, and the latest presi- 
dent of King’s will continue to 
head up the company or if he 
will turn the chain over to anew 
president. (Kittay is well 
known as an entrepreneur who 
runs his own show. Observers 
wonder if he has the team- 
mindedness necessary to guide 
the chain through this transi- 
tion. ) 

While King’s stores may not 
be as visually impressive as 
some discount operations, ob- 
servers give the chain credit for 
turning in an impressive finan- 
cial performance in past years. 
While DSN projections indicate 
flat sales for the current fiscal 
year, the chain has had a steady 
growth pattern over the years. 

King’s sales reached $576 
million in the most recently 
completed fiscai year, a gain of 
6.6% over the previous vear’s 
volume. The chain is expected 
to ring up $595 million this year. 
Last year, Barkers’ sales were 
estimated by DSN at nearly 
$300 million. 

“King’s was always an ugly 
duckling, but it is also a sur- 
vivor,” noted Dean Witter’s 
Kopf. “While many chains were 
spending money on expansion 
and losing their shirts, King’s 
management was always stick- 
ing their money in the bank, 
saving for a rainy day. It’s al- 
ways been run with a good deal 
of self-discipline, and always 


paid dividends. You’ve got to 


give them credit.”

Four other K mart stores—

the discounter still considers

pleased with the results so far,
