last year’s $15.6 million. A chain 
spokesman attributed the re- 
sults to first-half sales gains of 
nearly 30% and to the chain’s 
“diligent work” in tightening 
expenses and maintaining low 
price velocity. The chain’s pro- 
motional activity was kept to a 
level comparable with last 
year’s—a factor, the spokesman 
said, that helped the chain 
maintain margins. 

FedMart, a chain, which re- 
ported a $1.6 million loss in the 
year to date (down from the 
$13.8 million reported loss in 
the last fiseal year), is reaping 
some benefits from cost-cutting 
policies put into effect during 
the current fiscal year. 

The chain created the posi- 
tion of energy conservation 
manager whose responsibilities 
include developing ways to cut 
costs and to monitor energy 
usage at store level. Further 
help came from a computerized 
energy conservation system in- 
stalled in several test stores 
this year. 

At presstime, ALCO’s earn- 
ing figures were not yet in, but 
officials believed that profits 
would be down slightly. Sales to 
date are off by 5% on a store- 
for-store basis, they reported. 

In April, the chain started a 
profit protection plan, which 
led to cutbacks in administra- 
tive and travel expenses, and 
watching of fixed costs, such as 
insurance and rents. 

Officials are also using com- 
puters to monitor profits and 
sales on a per-store basis and 
have already cut hours where 
slow sales performance so indi- 
cated. 

T.G. & Y. adjusted its game 
plan this summer in response to 
tough competitive circum- 
stances. 

To draw traffic, the chain 
upped its advertising costs two- 
tenths of a per cent over this 
year’s budget allotment and ran 
two extra newspaper ads in 
June, July and August, accord- 
ing to Dan Kelly, the chain's se- 


nior vp, store operations. 

Kelly estimated that each ad 
cost the chain $350,000 in extra 
advertising expenditures. 

The chain is moving ahead 
with cost-cutting policies in en- 
ergy, maintenance, warehouse 
and store-level man-hour pro- 
ductivity, and hours schedul- 
ing, Kelly added. 

Target Stores was another 
discount chain that chose to go 
after traffic, at the expense of 
margins, according to a parent 
Dayton Hudson spokesman, 
who reported slight profit de- 
clines in the first half of Target's 
fiscal year. 

K mart too posted a substan- 
tial earnings decrease for the 
first half of 1980. Officials linked 
this performance to the con- 
tinued weakness in consumer 
demand, increased promotional 
activity, and inflationary pres- 

sures on expenses. For the sec- 
ond quarter, income fell 26.9% 
to $98.9 million from last year’s 
comparable-period earnings of 
$135.3 million.

ware Buyers Are Chipper 


(Continued from page 3) 


counter interest. Many chains 
with stores in the northern half 
of the country carried snow- 
blower inventory into this year 
because it failed to snow much 
last winter. 

Discounters were looking to 
manufacturers for new prod- 
ucts this year—as well as for 
greater co-op advertising al- 
lowances, better shipping 
terms and show deals. 

On show deals, some agreed 
with Fred Meyer’s Tripp who 
noted that few manufacturers 
had enough excess production 
this year to allow for show 
deals. 

Others, discounters, inter- 
ested in increasing their co-op 
allowances, found manufactur- 
ers much more willing to listen 
to their requests than in years 
past. The reason: Manufactur- 
ers were feeling the double 
pinch of depressed consumer 
sales and trimmed discounters’ 
inventories. 

For spring, discounters were 
still looking at string trimmers. 
Despite the category’s staple 
status, the product still gets 
plenty of discounter attention. 
This year buyers looked closest 
: the newer gas-powered mod- 
els. 

Gas grills and electronic bug 
killers continued to come on 
strong, and more manufactur- 
ers moved into the field. Lawn 
mowers also generated dis- 
counter interest, but buyers 
were still talking about the cost 
hikes that hit the category last 
year. 

A search for new products 
and more do-it-yourself related 
items took more discounters to 
McCormick Place West this 
year. By opening the show an- 
nex a day earlier than McCor- 
mick Place, and putting the 
new-product exhibition there, 
show promoters were able to 
draw more traffic to the build- 
ing materials exhibition. 

Buyers from chains not heav- 
ily into home improvement 
were looking at products there 
and making decisions for 1981 
mixes. For example, merchan- 
disers from Ann & Hope were 
among those looking at home 
improvement products, but 
they would not reveal their 
plans. 

Other chain representatives 
were out looking for new prod- 
ucts, and several new wrenches 
and an automatic nail feed ham- 
mer were getting a lot of atien- 
tion. 

“A new hand tool could turn 
out to be just right for Christ- 
mas. Even if it seems a little too 
gimmicky for a handyman, we 
know his family will probably 
buy it for him for Christmas,” 
reported a buyer for The Trea- 
sury. 


Anticipate Fuel Curbs 


(Continued from page 8s) 
shortage comparable to last 
summer’s supply crunch could 
prompt at least temporary re- 
strictions on weekend gas 
sales, odd-even-day purchase 
requirements and other regula- 
tions certain to affect consumer 
shopping patterns. 

There's little if anything that 
chains can do to prevent a sharp 
drop in traffic during the next 
major fuel shortage, but there 
are some precautions that mass 
merchandisers can take now to 
protect their supply lines in the 
event that Government conser- 
vation mandates are triggered: 

1—Convert to diesel- 
powered vehicles. Unlike gas- 
oline, diesel fuel will not be af- 
fected by the Federal coupon 
rationing plan, so chains and 
suppliers with a hefty propor- 
tion of diesel vehicles in their 
company fleets figure to be way 


ahead of the game. 

2—Develop statistics on com- 
pany-wide gasoline consump- 
tion. If rationing is ordered, 
chains will be entitled to special 
business supplements—but 
only after D.O.E. reviews each 
firm’s historic gas purchase pat- 
terns on a case-by-case basis. 
Companies supplying this doc- 
umentation at the last minute 
may have to wait months for 
their supplements, but chains 
furnishing information to 
D.O.E. in advance will get their 
extra allotments promptly. 

3—Work up standby emer- 
gency plans of your own. A 
number of large retail chains 
have already developed in- 
house “doomsday” contingency 
plans, including emergency van 
pooling systems to insure that 
each unit will be manned by a 
minimum number of employers 
at all times.

SEPTEMBER 22, 1980 


Discounters to Add 470 Stores, Hit $60.5B in ‘80 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Despite reports issued ear- 
lier in the year that some chains 
were curtailing their expansion 
plans in the face of a weakened 
economy and soaring construc- 
tion and interest costs, most 
discounters forged ahead and 
are opening 470 new stores in 
1980—25% more than they did 
last year—for a net gain of 32.8 
million sq. ft. of selling space. 

At the same time, with con- 
sumers under pressure to cut 
back on their spending, general 
merchandise sales volume is 
rising 11% industrywide to a 
record $55 billion—$60.5 billion 
including food. This, according 
to the 19th annual Discount 
Store News census. 

Along with their decision not 
to ak from their original 
expansion plans, discounters 
kept their resolve to build 
smaller stores, and to continue 
positioning themselves in the 
country’s smaller, more rural 
markets. 

The average store size of 
units built during the year is 
70,600 sq. ft., trimmer than the 
average (70, 646 sq. ft.) store 
built in 1979, and 1,470 sq. ft. 
smaller than the average store 
built five years ago. 

At the same time that this 
scaling down has helped dis- 
counters keep a lid on start-up 
and operating costs, it has also 
forced them to become more 
efficient operators. That this 
effort continues to pay off is evi- 
dent in increased sales per 
square foot productivity, which 


are projected to rise 8% this 
year to "3110. 79 (including food). 

Average sales per store are 
rising from $7.6 million to $7.8 
million this year. 

Further bolstering the bot- 
tom line are sales from spe- 
cialty and formerly leased de- 
partments. 

In 1980, discounters con- 
tinued to boost store sales by 
adding more service depart- 
ments to their mix and by tak- 
ing over operation of still more 
of the departments previously 
run by lessees. 


TBA centers, pharmacies, 
dental clinics and optometry 
services head the list of profit- 
able consumer services dis- 
counters are continuing to in- 
stall in their stores. 

Only in shoes do lessees con- 
tinue to retail significant con- 
trol—_48%-—of discounter busi- 
ness. But even here, their 
representation is diminishing, 
as discounters under pressure 
to improve sales productivity 
continue to find that their own 
organizations can successfully 
and profitably handle the cate- 


“ 1980, the Sunbelt con- 
tinued to lure discounters. This 
year for the first time, the (10) 
Southeastern States will have 
the greatest number of discount 
stores within their bound- 
aries—1,595 units by year's 
end—an 11% increase in unit 
growth over last year. This 
overturns the regional lead his- 
torically held by the East Cen- 
tral States. 

Conversely, major metro 
market new-store gains are 
dropping 35% from last year, 


with only 110 new stores (vs. 168 
last year) slated to open in the 
most densely populated sec- 
tions of the country in 1980. 
Texas, Alabama and Georgia 
are the states most often 
chosen by discounters as sites 
for new store growth. But here, 
too, only 15 of 88 stores to be 
opened in the three states were 
scheduled for metro markets— 
and of these, nine were tar- 
geted for the rapidly growing 
Dallas-Fort Worth area.

Rx Sections Mushroom From 35.3% 
To 40.8% of Nation’s Discount Stores 


The discount store industry 
appears on the verge of a pre- 
scription filling boom, as more 
chains than ever before dis- 
cover the drawing power and 
profitability of pharmacies. 

In the last year, the number 
of stores with pharmacies rose 
2.0 percentage points to a total 
of 40.8% of the industry’s units, 
according to DSN’s 19th annual 
census. 

K mart is one chain that has 
heavily moved into drug sales. 
Drug industry statistics list it 
among the country’s largest 
drug store chains in terms of 
prescription and nonprescrip- 
tion drug sales. 

Many discounters predicted 
that more and more chains will 
follow K mart’s lead as the lure 
of one-stop shopping increases 
the profits they can make not 
only on prescriptions, but also 
on over-the-counter products 
such as cough syrup, laxatives 
and nonprescription drugs. 


In addition, discounters said, 
there is a spillover effect that 
spurs sales increases in adja- 
cent departments. 

Most discounters questioned 
said they had not performed 
surveys to determine the over- 
all effects of pharmacies on 
sales in nearby departments. A 
spokesman for Ohio-based 
Harts said, though, that 
H&BA products sell about 
2.8% to 3.1% better in stores 
with pharmacies than in those 
without them. 

Murphy’s Mart leased phar- 
macy space in five of its Pitts- 
burgh area stores in 1975. A 
year later the chain took over 
its lessee’s operations and is 
now planning to open phar- 
macies in stores in more rural 
areas. 

Arizona-based Smitty’s has 
pharmacies in 15 of its 19 stores 
and plans to include them in 
each of three units scheduled to

{ DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, SEPTEMBER 22, 1980 


(_ Editorial 


Discounters Are Leading the Field 
Despite a Muddy Economic Track 


A turning point of major significance came for 
discounting in 1980. 

The industry proved again its ability to with- 
stand—and even prosper in—times of economic 
downturn, and discounting demonstrated its dy- 
namic nature by the frequency with which chains 
initiated new strategies, new store prototypes 
and new merchandise presentations. 

But this is old hat in discounting, just another 
year when of all major retail segments only dis- 
counting showed the vitality, flexibility and 
imagination necessary for continued growth. 

The most significant development of 1980 was 
the acceptance by all of retailing that there is a 
new leader for the 1980's: a new front-runner to 
set the pace and determine the direction of the 
race. We’re in a race, and we’re in the lead. 

In a footrace of sufficient length—a mile or 
more—a runner adjusts his pace to match that of 
the new leader, and plans to stay close enough to 
break the tape first with a last-minute burst of 
speed. 

In retailing, however, there is no tape and no 
end to the race. A strategy of winning at the last 
minute with a burst of energy is doomed to 
failure. The retail segment that attains the lead 
ean look forward to many years of leadership, 
assuming good execution. 

That’s where discounting has arrived—in front 
of the pack, setting the pace, determining the 
direction of the race. And the other runners are 
adjusting to our pace. 

Sears, Roebuck and Montgomery Ward, for 
example, are no longer looking over their shoul- 
ders at discounting, nor are they pooh-poohing 
its merchandising and marketing strategies. 

Instead, they are eating the dust of faster- 
growing, more innovative and more aggressive 
discount retailers who are leading the way in 
compound growth rates and market share gains. 


Where It's at In 


Sears and Ward have taken steps to match the 
pace set by the new discount leaders. Their strat- 
egy is to keep up, and it’s making them, step by 
step, more similar to our more successful form of 
retailing. 

Sears lost its price war with K mart, and has 
been forced to retreat to a pricing policy that 
simply meets opening price points at discount 
stores. Sears is also contemplating the addition 
of major brands to its merchandise mix. Sears 
wants to stay close to the leader. 

Ward has gone even further than Sears, with 
its rapid expansion of Jefferson Stores, and the 
adoption of many Jefferson marketing and mer- 
chandising techniques at a growing number of 
conventional Ward stores. 

J. C. Penney, with its lackluster discount arm 
trailing the pack but secure in its soft line domi- 
nance among the big three, has put distance 
between itself and the dogfight at the head of the 
pack. . 

But in a few years will Penney’s retreat be the 
right strategy? 

Trade-up merchandising by discounters—in- 
cluding K mart’s and Wal-Mart’s experiments 
this year—will increase the distance between 
discounters and Penney, making the discounters 
lead insurmountable. 

Newer retail segments are also emulating dis- 
counting with self-service, lower operating 
costs, fewer frills, more efficient use of space, 
lower gross margins and discount pricing pol- 
icies. 

The hard line discount specialists in toys, 
sporting goods, automotive and other markets 
have been joined by off-price apparel chains that 
are letting general merchandise discounters set 
the pace and direction, while staying close 
enough behind to follow in the path of least resis- 
tance. 


Making 
The Rounds 


with ae i <5 


Editor 


It’s difficult to know whether the off-price ap- 
parel market is here to stay or whether it will be 
swallowed up by discounting’s growing appeal to 
fashion- and value-conscious consumers. But 
while the opportunity lasts, the apparel specialty 
chains are simply following the leader. 

The merchandising battles must be fought on 
one front at a time, while a holding action main- 
tains gains already made on the other. 

Discounting’s hard line superiority must be 
maximized first, and solid defenses against antic- 
ipated competitive strategies (opening price 
point levels, brand name merchandise) put into 
place. Then the battle can be joined in earnest in 
the ladies’, children’s and domestics depart- 
ments. 

When that time comes—probably before the 
end of this decade—no other retail segment will 
be able to head the leader. 

What reason is there to shop a conventional 
department store, when (as seems inevitable) 
identical apparel and domestics merchandise be- 
come available in discount department stores at 
lower prices? 

What reason is there to shop Sears or Ward 
when discount stores offer broader selections 
and better values in hard lines, and soft line 
departments that match or exceed the selection, 
quality, and value found in those stores? 

A new age of retailing has dawned and our 
industry is the acknowledged leader. It is a time 
that will bring new hazards, new problems and 
new concepts to the forefront of American retail- 
ing. 

But it is also a time in which discounting will 
achieve its full potential, and it is a time of un- 
precedented opportunity for general merchan- 
dise discount chains of every description.

K mart’s Fauber 


Changes in the executive suite gave the industry more than a half dozen new chief 
officers this year. Veteran K mart executive Bernard M. Fauber was named ceo and 
chairman of the nation’s largest discount chain; Peter Harris stepped up to become 
president of Gemco/Memco, Lucky Stores discount division; George W. Nelson 
was made head of Woolworth/Wooico's United States division; Earl Holton, vice

Trade-up Merchandising Is Applied to Hard Lines 


Follows Chains’ Successful Upscaling of Apparel =~) 


_ Trade-up merchandising con- 
tinued to dominate the discount 
scene as the success of up- 
graded apparel presentations 
(and rising operating costs) 
prompted discounters to apply 
that technique in their hard 
lines departments as well. 

This search for ways to get 
better mileage out of store 
space also spurred an increased 
use of cubing. Discounters 
raised gondola heights in order 
to fit the same amount of mer- 
chandise into newer scaled- 
down stores, or to accommo- 
date additional goods in exist- 
ing units. 

mart will experiment with 
a trade-up hard line presenta- 
tion in eight Indianapolis 
stores, where a new race-track 
aisle layout will generate refix- 
turing and a “modest trade-up 
of goods” in hard line depart- 
ments, according to Bernard 
Fauber, chairman and ceo. 

This hard line test comes in 
the wake of K mart’s experi- 
ments with an upscaled apparel

T.G. & Y. is another chain 
planning a large-scale upgrad- 
ing of its hard line approach. 
The chain’s combined camera 
and consumer electronics de- 
partment and cosmetics dis- 
plays are being upscaled in new 
stores, and management hopes 
to add the new look to existing 
stores by mid-1981. 

“It’s like shining the toe of the 
shoe,” said Andrew Collins, di- 
vision vp, merchandising. “We 
plan to extend the upscaling 
over the entire store in the fu- 
ture, but for now we’re working 
on the departments that cus- 
tomers see when they first en- 
ter the store.” 

T.G. & Y.’s camera and elec- 
tronics merchandise will be 
highlighted with a carpeted 
background and segmented 
with smoked glass dividers. In- 
stallation costs of the display in 
existing stores will total $500,- 


000, according to Collins. 

In cosmetics, remerchandis- 
ing will introduce a black-and- 
white, mirrored display module 
in the store. Coinciding with 
the refixturing, the product 
mix will be expanded 60% to in- 
clude more of the higher-priced 
prestige cosmetics. 

Caldor took its cue from a 
successful move to upgrade its 
apparel section, and extended 
that concept to its housewares 
department this year. Ceramic 
brick floor tile and natural wood 
display units have been added 
to give the stores a “Bloom- 
ingdale’s” look. 

Already upscale Jefferson 
Stores got a facelift when the 
chain made its entry in the Phil- 
adeiphia market. A loop layout, 
wide-scaie use of focus walls 
and the inclusion of suspended 
fixtures were major features of 
the new layout, that focused on 
the chains’ hard line depart- 
ments.

Smaller regional and !ocal 
discounters—those with under 
$100 million in volume and with 
two dozen or fewer stores—are, 
on the whole, continuing to re- 
cord sales gains and add units 
despite the economy and 
stepped-up competition from 
such major chains as K mart, 
Target and T.G. & Y. 

e key to success, top ex- 
ecutives with a number of 
smaller discounters said, is 
doing your own thing, not just 
imitating the big discounters. 


The 42 discounters that meet 
both qualifications include 
chains that project sales gains 
ranging to as much as 33% 
(Grandpa Pidgeon’s) and are in- 
creasing the number of their 
stores up to 35% (Malone;’s). 

(A 48rd discounter that has 
sales of under $100 million is 
Bargain Town, which will have 
41 stores in Alabama at the end 
of the year that average 20,000 
sq. ft. in size. The small size 
accounts for the chain only gen- 
erating $32 million in volume or 


about $750,009 per store.) 

Doing your own thing, a Sin- 
gleton executive said, starts 
with being close to your stores 
so you can closely monitor 
what’s happening. 

“We are close to our [10] 
stores,” the executive said, “so 
that top management can be in 
each unit once a week for better 
control. We can get on a prob- 
lem at once and make a decision 
quickly, while a manager with a 
national chain has to go up the 

(Continued on page 32) 


These Chains 


Stores included in the 
statistical section of the 
census all meet DSN’s 
definition of a discount de- 
partment store; that is, 
they each have at least 
10,000 sq. ft., both hard 
and soft goods depart- 
ments, and an expense 
structure below that of a 
conventional department 
store.

Snowbelt States in unit growth with 16 new stores scheduled to be built within its 
boundaries by the end of the year. 

The one decrease posted was in the District of Columbia. 

A net gain ci 470 new stores comprising 29,975,000 sq. ft. is expected this year, 
a 25% increase over the 375 units added to the industry count last year. 

In space, the industry gained 32,779,000 sq. ft., a 31% increase over footage 
gains made during the previous year. The average space of additional units was 
69,742 sq. ft. This is consistent with the average store size reported in past census 


issues, and shows that discounters are sticking with their budgetary resolve to 
build smaller stores. 


The Sunbelt beckoned and top discounting chains continued to respond. 

Nearly 40% of the new discount stores slated to open this year will have their 
foundations in Southern soil. 

Texas heads the list of the Southern tier states most often targeted for chain 
expansion, with 35 new stores scheduled to open there by year’s end. Other states 
experiencing strong discount store growth are Arkansas, 28 units; Alabama, 25; 
— Carolina, 23; Floride, 20; South Carolina, 18, and Georgia and Louisiana 15 
each.

quartered there continued to fill in spaces in market strongholds. Ohio led the

Metro market store openings declined 35% in 1980 with only 110 new units 
scheduled to open in the nation’s top 50 market areas. Last year, nearly half of the 
industry’s new store growth—i68 units—were opened in the most densely popu- 
lated parts of the country. 

This growth pattern further underscores discounter commitments to small 
rural and exurban communities—many with populations of under 10,000. 

Two new metro markets made their way onto the top 50 list this year. 

Oklahoma City and Nashville bumped the three-city Albany-Schenectady- 
Troy, N.Y., market and Toledo, Ohio, markets to win 49th and 50th place on the 
list, respectively. Discount store count increases in these markets show that as 
population increases discounters respond with new store openings. 

Other shifts on the list include jumps in the listing by Houston to 10th place, 


***Sales are basea on total footage, including that of connecting supermarkets, expected to be in 
operation at end of calendar year, using industrywide average dollars per square foot. 


over Nassau-Suffolk Counties in New York; and similar place reversals between 
Riverside-San Bernardino-Ontario, Calif., and Milwaukee. Also Phoenix and 
Cincinnati; Rochester, N.Y., and Sacramento, Calif., and Portland, Ore., and 
Indianapolis, all switched rankings. 

The largest net store increase, for the second year in a row, was in the Dallas- 
Kort Worth area where T.G. & Y., Target, Woolco and K mart, among others 
continue to plot their growth. 

Phoenix ranked second in net unit gains with nine new stores slated to open 
there this year. Los Angeles placed third with seven new discount units coming on 
stream in 1980. 

Store gains in Philadelphia, however, slowed considerably from last year’s 10 
openings by Woolco, Clover and K mart to two this year.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, SEPTEMBER 22, 1980 


Chain-Run Depts. on Rise 


Discounters further tight- 
ened their grip on store profits 
this year by increasing the 
number of company-operated 
departments (vs. lessees) in 
nine out of 18 categories. 

(The nine categories showing 
no increase were all areas 
where discounters already op- 
erated more than 90% of the de- 
partments, industrywide.) 

The greatest gains this year 
were made in TBA (tires, bat- 
teries and accessories) service 
centers and apparel depart- 
ments. 

Auto service centers were 
long considered a traffic draw, 
and discounters who wanted 
the centers under roof pre- 
ferred to lease out the depart- 
ment rather than bankroll the 
considerable payroll and oper- 
ating costs. 

Now, that’s changing. In the 
past two years, the number of 
centers operated by discount- 
ers increased seven percentage 
points—five points in 1980 
alone—to 78%. 

Likewise in apparel, dis- 
counters are continuing to re- 
tire their lessees, recognizing 
that the category’s 30%-plus 
margins can easily boost 
sales—and profits 


In ladies apparel, discount- 
ers increased their takeover of 
departments by one percent- 
age point, giving them control 
and ROI from 94% of the indus- 
try’s women’s departments. 

Discounters also increased 
their operating hold by one 
point on infants and children’s 
wear, giving them control of 
86% of those departments. 

In men’s wear, the number of 
discounter-operated depart- 


ments rose by two percentage 
points to 89%. 

In shoes, where lessees still 
have the most significant 
amount of representation, dis- 
counters increased their con- 
trol by 2 points to 57%. 

Other discounter (takeover) 
gains were made in drugs, up 
one point to 96%; records, up 
one point to 92%, and in auto 
accessories, also up one point, 
to 93%.

learn from major discounters.

use of this format by a number 
of national discounters. The dis-

of sku numbers for every item 
so that “we can achieve a two- 
week turnover as have larger 
chains.”

and local discounters have sus-

few have run into problems.

after an expansion program re-

Average store size continues 
to shrink during 1980. 

While the largest per cent 
change vs. 1979 was recorded in 
the 140,000- to 149,000-sq.-ft. 
range—with nine new giant 
stores slated to open this year 
as compared to two last year— 
the real action was in the 
70,000- to 79,000-sq.-ft. and 
50,000- to 59,000-sq, -tt. stores. 

Growth in those two brack- 
ets—68 and 63 new units, re- 
spectively—account for 28% of 
this year’s new units. That de- 
velopment can be traced to fur- 
ther chain determination to fill 
in territories by exploring 
small exurban markets that de- 
mand scaled-down units and to 
increased operating costs. 

Caldor and Zayre, chains 
founded with 100,000-sq.-ft.- 
plus stores, opened smaller 
units this year—under 80,000 
sq. ft., and expansion plans for 
1981 call for new units of com- 
parable size. 

K mart continued to open its 
Group Nine stores this year, ac- 
counting for a considerable por- 
tion of the growth in the 50,000- 
to 59,000-sq.-ft. range. Like- 
wise, T.G. & Y. continued con- 
verting its small variety stores 
into Family Centers and Super 
Stores of 40,000 to 60,000 sq. ft. 

Wal-Mart's preference for a 
45,000-sq.-ft. prototype re- 
sulted in nearly 60% of the unit 
growth in this size range. 
Howard Bros., too, continued 
to base volume and store 
growth on a 40,000-sq.-ft. unit, 
with eight new stores in that 
size area opened this year, and 
20 more on line for 198i. That 
size accounts for nearly 12% of 
all discount stores currently in 
operation. 

Still, big stores are not on the 
verge of extinction—although 
the smallest percentage in- 
crease (2.7%) was in stores 
larger than 150,000 sq. ft. 

Target opened or seine to 
open by year’s end 17 new stores 
with an average size of 90,000 
sq. ft. Gemco/Memco and Gold 
Circle have plans to open units 
in excess of 100,000 sq. ft. 
sometime during 1981.

Discounters are continuing 
to build one-stop shopping ca- 
pabilities into their mix—and 

rofitability into their bottom 

ines—by adding and taking 
over specialty departments 
from lessees. 

In fact, of 18 (specialty) cate- 
gories reported on, advances in 
incidence were posted in 16. 

The only two departments to 
register declines in the inci- 
dence rate were sewing and 
millinary departments—two 
specialty departments excep- 
tionally susceptible to changing 
consumer tastes and habits. 
Sewing departments slipped 
1.6 points to 59.7%, evidence 
that, increasingly, some chains 
are closing ptm sewing de- 
partments. Millinery depart- 
ments, too, fell victim to chain 
demands that each square foot 
of sales space perform to max- 
imum capability. So while 50% 
of all chains now operate their 
own millinery departments— 
2% more than last year—the 
number of chains still putting 
millinery into their mix 
dropped to 39.1%. 

For the second year in a row, 
the largest advance in the rate 
of incidence was scored by 
candy departments. 

Other sizable gains—in both 
chain takeovers and in the rate 
of incidence—were made by 
snack bars, pharmacies and op- 
tometry departments. 

The number of chains now op- 
erating their own snack bars 
rose by 7.4 points to 54.6%. Of 
that number, more than two- 
thirds are operated by the 
chains themselves, rather than 
by lessees. Last year, DSN’s 

census of the industry showed 
that only 67% of the chains of- 
fering their shoppers this 
added convenience operated 
the departments themselves. 

Likewise, more discounters 
installed pharmacy and op- 
tometry services—for a total of 
40.8% and 30.3% of all chains 
respectively—under their roofs

banking on its heavy Sunbelt 
locations and its supermarket 
traffic to weather the present 
economy and to hoist the chain 
out of its profitability troubles. 

The chain has been plagued 
with losses in recent years— 
the most serious of which was 
an $11.1 million loss reported in 
fiscal 1979—although the cur- 
rent fiscal year’s results are 
somewhat improved. 

Net earnings of $2.8 million 
were recorded for the second 
quarter, ended Feb. 17, moving 
FedMart into the black by wip- 
ing out almost comparable 
losses reported during the first 
quarter. Net earnings for the 
first half were $225,000. 

Sales, however, slipped again 
during the third quarter, ended 
May 1], totaling $238 million— 
only 3% higher than the com- 
parable period a year ago—and 
net losses reached $1.8 million. 
This gives the discounter $734 
million in sales and a net loss of 
$1.6 million for the 36-week pe- 
riod ended May 11, compared to 
sales of $670 million and a net 
loss of $13.8 million for the same

Caldor to Invade R.1!., Vermont 


NORWALK, Conn.—Caldor 


will add two new states to its 
operating base with a store 
opening next month in Woon- 
socket, R.I., and another slated 
for Vermont in early 1981. 

This year’s expansion plans 
are part of a $10 million capital 
expenditure program aimed at 
boosting gross store space to 
500,000-700,000 sq. ft. 

Next vear, Caldor manage- 
ment expects to open six to 
eight new stores (with the pos- 
sible opening of another in 
Rhode Island and a couple in 
New Hampshire), all of which 
will conform to the conven- 
tional size of 85,000 sq. ft. and 
80% selling space. 

Caldor has opened five ne w 
stores this year, and by year's 
end will operate a total of 62 

(New Caldors were opene din 
March in Westfield, Mass., and 
Newburgh, N.Y. In May, the 
chain opened in Worcester, 
Mass., and in August, two 
stores were unveiled in Norwell 
and Chelmsford, Mass.) 

Refurbishing of Caldor’s 
120, 000-sq.-ft. two-level store 
in downtown Stamford, Conn, 
was completed in March. The 
store was given a new facade as 
well as a remodeled interior. 

For the fiscal year ended Jan. 


31, 1980, sales rose to $562.7 
million, a gain of 18.3%. Net 
earnings gains outpaced sales, 
rising 27.6% to $19.7 million 
from $15.5 million the year be- 
fore. The chain’s projections in- 
dicate that this year sales were 
on target for the annual goal 
with an 18.9% increase to 
$276.4 million from last year's 
$232.5 million. Caldor’s results 
are especially impressive con- 
sidering the softening economy 
and gasoline shortages. 

The new stores are receiving 
the upscale fashion apparel! em- 
phasis that was heightened in 
stores opened in 1979. This is 
part of an intensification of ap- 
pare! merchandise designed to 
bring soft lines volume from 
30% to 40% of total sales. 

The added emphasis on high- 
margin soft lines began with 
Caldor’s hiring of new merchan- 
dising personnel, and led to the 
inclusion of fashion fixtures, 
used most notably to highlight 
coordinates. Leonard Willner, 
the chain’s new general mer- 
chandise manager, is negotiat- 
ing with manufacturers of name 
brand apparel in an attempt to 
get their goods into the mix. 

This fashion orientation has 
filtered down to the presenta- 
tion of housewares, where re- 


modeled departments now use 
ceramic floor tiles and natural 
wood displays to give a “Bloom- 
ingdale’s” look to housewares 
items. Wicker, brass and cop- 
per products are sprinkled 
throughout the department. 


Cook Resumes Bows 


MAPLE HEIGHTS, N.J.— 
Though hard hit by the eco- 
nomic slowdown, Cook United 
is taking an aggressive stance. 
The chain is once again building 
new stores, opening two this 
vear, and is experimenting with 
such innovations as in-store 
snack bars and “no-frills” box 
stores. 

The chain has also launched a 
test of increased “home center” 
merchandising including lum- 
ber and paneling, hoping to at- 
tract the do-it-yourself market 
with discount pricing. 

With stores clustered in ma- 
jor metro markets in the 
Northeast, where family 
spending has been seriously 
limited by severe layoffs in the 
auto and construction indus- 
tries, sales have been flat and 
earnings have sagged. Soaring 
interest rates in the first quar- 
ter also adversely affected the 
chain. 

Kor the fiscal year ended 
Feb. 2, sales for the discount 
division totaled $353.7 million 


With Two Due in ‘80 


and earnings for the division 
were $5.9 million. The chain 
projects sales of $359 million. 

In addition to the two stores 
slated to open later this year, a 
remodeling program for exist- 
ing stores is also under way. 
Last year approximately 10% of 
the stores were facelifted, in- 
cluding an upgrading of fix 
tures. 

The chain is also tackling the 
strong competition it faces 
from other discounters in its 
market areas by relying in- 
creasingly on radio and TV ad- 
vertising. To raise traffic, the 
merchandise mix has been 
broadened and highly promot- 
able brand names are empha- 
sized, especially in hard lines. 

Parent Company Cook Uni- 
ted operates 81 discount 
stores—Cook’s, Clarks, Uncle 
3en’s, Ontario and Consoli- 
dated Sales Co.—whose aver- 
age store size Is over 60,000 sq. 
ft. Other corporate revenues 
are derived from six wholesal- 
ing companies. 


Target Acquisition of Ayr-Way Nears 


MINNEAPOLIS—Target is 
entering a period of dramatic 
growth, the keystone of which 
will be the pending acquisition 
of the 4l-unit Ayr-Way chain. 

Plans call for acquisition of 
the Indiana-based chain to be 
finalized around Oct. lat a price 
estimated to be between $25 
million and $30 million. 

If plans go as scheduled, the 
Ayr-Way signs will be replaced 
by the Target bull’s-eye by Jan. 
l. 

The resulting change in own- 
ership would give Target a par- 
ticularly strong base in Indi- 
ana, where 32 of the Ayr-Way 
stores are located. 

The takeover would also en- 


able Target to stretch without 
interruption across half of mid- 
dle America, hitting all of the 


major markets between its 
Minnesota headquarters and 
Memphis, its easternmost mar- 
ket. 

With the opening of new 
100,000-sq.-ft. stores last 
month, Target has also moved 
into Kansas and Tennessee for 
the first time. 


Adding It Up 


The new stores—three in 
Memphis and two in Wichita, 
Kan.—bring to 91 the number 
the chain operates currently in 
13 states. The chain plans to 
grow to 175 units by 1985. 

The expansion comes at the 
same time the chain is ae 
a large distribution center 
Little Rock, Ark. 

The center, which will have 


the capacity to serve a total of 
100 stores in the South and 
Southwest, is expected to be 
completed in 1981. It will fur- 
ther support the chain’s drive 
into new markets. 

With the marked growth, 
Target became one of only eight 
discount chains in the nation 
last year to reach sales in ex- 
cess of $1 billion. 

This year, despite an uncer- 
tain economy, prospects for the 
chain are even better, with com- 
pany officials predicting a 25% 
growth rate, to about $1.4 bil- 
lion in sales. 

The strong growth is good 
news for Dayton Hudson, Tar- 
get’s parent company, which 
had been investing heavily in 
the discount operation over the 
last few years.

Wal-Mart Roars Toward $1.6 Billion Sales

lion dollar mark in sales vol- 
ume, Wal-Mart is roaring along 
toward its current sales goal of 
$1.6 billion despite the reces- 
sion. 

The fast-growing regional 
chain started the year with 276 
stores, added 15 at midyear and 
plans to open another 35, for a 
year-end total of 326. Next 
year’s plans call for 55 to 60 
store openings. 

Besides continuing expan- 
sion within its ll-state South 
Central market area, the chain 
is experimenting with new mer- 
chandising approaches, to some 
extent targeted to stores serv- 
ing a more sophisticated subur- 
ban population than the chain's 
traditional small-town market. 
Two stores opened earlier this 
year in Pine Bluff, Ark., and 
Moore, Okla., on the outskirts 
of Oklahoma City, boast a race- 
track design and dramatically 
upgraded soft lines depart- 
ments. “So far we’re very 
pleased and we’re learning,” 
said soft lines vice president/ 
gmm Richard Jolosky. 


Although the upgraded soft 
lines tests are being conducted 
in stores close to large cities 
and the chain has been cluster- 
ing stores in the vicinity of Fort 
Worth, Jolosky insisted that 
the chain had no “urban strat- 
egy.” Most of the chain’s units 
are located in small towns 
within a 400-inile radius of 
headquarters with populations 
between 5,000 and 25,000. 

For the fiscal year ended Jan. 
31, the chain reported net in- 
come of $41.2 million on sales of 
$1.2 billion, an increase of 40% 
and 30%, respectively. For the 
six months ended July 31, the 
chain maintained the pace, re- 
co. earnings up 32% to 
$20.6 million on sales of $687.2 
million, an increase of 30% over 
the previous six-month period. 

The chain’s strong perfor- 
mance has attracted favorable 
comment from Wall Street ana- 
lysts who attribute the consis- 
tent growth to the chain’s small- 
town strategy, efficient dis- 
tribution network and an ag- 
gressive promotional posture. 
“We project a compound annual 
earnings growth rate of 20% 


during the next five years,” said 
Robert Roth, an analyst with 
Merrill Lynch, “predicated on 
continued rapid store expan- 
sion and market share gains as 
well as highly effective operat- 
ing controls.” Roth also noted 
that same-store sales have been 
unusually strong, scoring in the 
double-digit column for 20 con- 
secutive quarters. 

Wal-Mart reports good sales 
in its apparel division, despite 
reports that apparel sales na- 
tionwide have declined in the 
last 18 months. Apparel now ac- 
counts for about 30% of total 
revenues but is expected to in- 
crease to 35% of the mix. 

The upg aded apparel pre- 
sentation at the recently 
opened prototype stores in- 
clude the race-track layout, car- 
peted fashion areas and fashion 
fixtures. Merchandise, how- 
ever, is said to be the same as 
that offered by the rest of the 
stores. The increased cost of 
the upgraded departments— 
mainly fixture, lighting and 
signing costs—is expected to be 
offset by faster moving inven- 
tory.

More Ad $$ Go to Suburban Shoppers, Weeklies 


Nationwide DSN Report 

It’s not happening every- 
where, but as competition gets 
fiercer and ad costs keep climb- 
ing, discounters report that 
more of their ad budgets are 
being diverted to small subur- 
ban shoppers and weeklies and 
away from their traditional ad 
medium, city dailies. 

The reason: The suburban 
papers—both shoppers and 
paid-circulation weeklies— 
take better aim at target cus- 
tomers for a fraction of the cost. 

In the Denver market, for ex- 
ample, Woolco has begun shift- 
ing some of its ads from the dai- 
ly Rocky Mountain News and 
Denver Post to a group of 17 
weekly publications. 

A company spokesman said 
the results have been “impres- 
sive” and that it appears week- 


lies—if used properly—can 
provide the same sales results 


as dailies at a much lower cost. 


Ohio-based Rink’s is cur- 


rently doing about 2% of its ad- 
vertising in weeklies, and com- 
pany officials expect that per- 
centage to continue growing. 


Stronger Impact 


The greatest value of the 
weeklies, according to a Rink’s 
official, is that they are fre- 
quently better read and more 
widely circulated in rural areas 
than the dailies. 

Although no precise statis- 
tics are available, the most ad- 
vanced example of weeklies 
gaining strength in wooing dis- 
counters’ advertising may be in 
St. Louis, where a collection of 
34 suburban publications 
formed Suburban Pzepers of St. 
Louis to offer retailers a com- 
bined circulation greater than 
either of the two dailies. 

One of the reasons for the 
weeklies’ growing popularity, 
explained discounters, is their 
lower cost. A full-page ad in the 
Rocky Mountain News (cir- 
culation 300,000) runs about 
$1,000, according to a Woolco 
spokesman. The same ad in the 
Sentinel Papers-—a collection of 
17 dailies with a circulation of 
210,000—is only $400. The 
Woolco spokesman said the 
price advantage of the weeklies 
becomes even more apparent 
when circulation figures are ex- 
amined. Many of the News’ pa- 
pers are sold at newsstands far 


Barkers’ Phillips 
Joins FedMart 


SAN DIEGO—Jack Phillips, 
former vice president/general 
merchandise manager of New 
York-based Franklin Stores 
and Barkers, retail divisions of 
Cornwall Equities, is Fed- 
Mart’s new divisional merchan- 
dise manager—women’s ap- 
parel. He replaces Ellen Geiss 
who left the same company. 

Phillips is responsible for 
merchandising women’s 
dresses, coats, sportswear, 
loungewear and intimate ap- 
parel. 

Prior to his affiliation with 
Franklin, a specialty apparel 
chain, and Barkers, a dis- 
counter, Phillips was associated 
with Abraham & Straus in 
Brooklyn, N.Y., for 18 years. 
The last position held with A&S 
was divisional merchandise 
manager—ladies’ wear, home 
furnishings and shoes for the 
budget stores. 


outside the Denver market; all 
of the weeklies are distributed 
at home. 

Prices for tab inserts in 
weeklies vary, but discounters 
said the weeklies hold an ad- 
vantage there as well. Inser- 
tion rates range from $20 to $50 
eer thousand, but in any mar- 

et, average at least $10 below 
the dailies. 

The greatest value with 
weeklies, however, has been 
their operational flexibility. 

Many daily newspapers re- 
quire advertisers to go ROP 
with standard advertisements. 
Those that don’t require that 
ads run in entire regional edi- 
tions. 

Dailies are often equally as 
inflexible with tab inserts. Dis- 
counters said they can run any 
number they want, but have lit- 
tle control over where they are 
sent. 

With a chain of weeklies, 
however, a discounter can limit 


his ad to only one newspaper, 
which may have a circulation as 
small as 1,500. Likewise, with 
tabular inserts, a discounter 
can decide who gets his circu- 
lars on a block-by-block basis. 

In Denver, for example, 
Woolco originally de tabs in all 
210,000 copies of the papers, 
but now finds it can be just as 
effective by limiting its circula- 
tion to 110,000 by strategically 
determining where eack copy 
goes. 


Different Emphasis 


“We did couponing tests and 
found that the people in a Den- 
ver suburb weren't crossing a 
certain highway to get to one of 
our stores,” explained a Woolco 
executive. “So we said to our- 
selves, let’s just not advertise 
on that side of the highway any 
more.” 

Samuel Lee, Rink’s advertis- 
ing director, said weeklies have 


also proven valuable in promot- 
ing an item like carpeting, 
which only one store in a mar- 
ket may carry. 

“If one store needs an extra 
ush, we’ve found the weeklies 
elpful,” he said. 

Several chains surveyed said 
they were avoiding weekly pub- 
lications because there was un- 
certainty as to how many of the 
 patagprati: are actually read. 

any weeklies, discounters 
said, offer free subscriptions, 
which are generally not as ex- 
tensively read as a paid publica- 
tion. 

In addition, paid publications 
are more ieacuale taken to 
work, and may be read by more 
than one person on the train or 
bus. 

Spokesmen for Zayre and 
New Jersey-based Two Guys 
said their companies may be 
getting the best of both worlds 
by relying heavily on daily sub- 
urban-based publications. 


A Zayre spokesman said in 
many cases suburban dailies 
are even more extensively read 
than weeklies or other dailies 
from nearby big cities. 

To reach people in the Fram- 
ingham area, for example, the 
44 ,000-strong South Middlesex 
News is frequently a better me- 
dium than the Boston papers. 

A Two Guys official said be- 
cause there are few discounters 
in the urban areas it makes 
more sense to rely on suburban 
dailies. He said their coverage 
has given the chain “a phenome- 
nal umbrella.” 

The Woolco official cau- 
tioned, however, that many dis- 
counters may be underrating 
the weeklies. Coupon tests per- 
formed by the company in the 
Denver area over a six-week pe- 
riod last November and Decem- 
ber indicated that in many cas- 
es the drawing power of free 
weeklies was “surprisingly 
strong.”

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, SEPTEMBER 22, 1980

Good Omen: Compromise Marking System Test Due 


The OCR-A vs. UPC debate 
in recent years resembled the 
East and West of the old Kip- 
ling rhyme; it seemed retailers 
and vendors would never meet. 
But, one of next year’s promis- 
ing developments in operations 
will be trials of a compromise 
merchandise marking system. 

The move is significant. Pre- 
tax profits have increased a full 
2% at supermarkets which have 
introduced scanning equip- 
ment. A similar boost to the 
bottom line of any discounter 
(primarily from reduced labor 
costs) would give that chain an 
edge in competitive pricing of 
its merchandise. 


Caught in a Squeeze 


The controversy over which 
marking system to use has held 
up advances in tagging mer- 
chandise for some time. As an 
executive of Salt Lake City- 
based Grand Central put it: 


“The real need is standardiza- 
tion, be it OCR or UPC.” 

Discounters have been hold- 
ing back their commitment to 
either marking system, for the 
most part. Only 11% of dis- 
counters, ina DSN survey con- 
ducted this year, currently use 
OCR-A, vs. 4% using UPC. 

This does not mean there is 
no preference; 56% of chain ex- 
ecutives polled by DSN said 
they were in favor of OCR-A 
and only 30% preferred UPC. 
Almost one-quarter of the re- 
spondents expected to be using 
OCR-A within a one-year time 
frame, and another quarter ex- 
pected to be using it in the next 
two to three years. 

Despite this preference, the 
fact remains that almost half of 
the merchandise flowing 
through checkouts in an aver- 
age discount store is already 
marked with the familiar UPC 
black bars. Vendors using UPC 
have been reluctant to imple- 


ment another system when 
UPC has proven so effective 
already in one retail segment 
(supermarkets). 

Now that a compromise 
marking system has been 
worked out by a retailer- 
vendor-equipment-manufac- 
turer group, some in-store ex- 
perience should be available to 
the industry by the end of next 
year. This could be as impor- 
tant as the first tests of UPC 
after its development in 1970 by 
a joint retailer-vendor group. 
Field tests in a Kroger super- 
market in Cincinnati found by 
1972 that five automated check- 
outs could replace seven man- 
ual units. 

OCR-A was developed by a 
voluntary group in league with 
the National Retail Merchants 
Association, and this same 
group has now issued 
yuidelines for marking mer- 
chandise that will combine 
OCR-A and UPC elements. 


The compromise system 
could erase many of the stick- 
ing points in the OCR-A vs. 
UPC debate. One of the main 
complaints by discounters has 
been that OCR-A type is read- 
able to consumers, while the 
UPC bars are not. 

Another complaint by dis- 
counters, however, has been 
the ease of in-store marking 
with OCR-A. Printers already 
owned are more easily adapted 
to OCR-A type than to UPC 
marking. 


A Closer Look 


The wait-and-see attitude at 
many chains may bear fruit by 
the end of 1981. Wal-Mart is tak- 
ing the bull by the horns and 
running a test on UPC this fall 
and next spring, wnich will no 
doubt be watched closely by 
others in judging the cost-effec- 
tiveness of such a move.

the test this year, while a sec- 
ond Wal-Mart will be added to 
the test next year. A dozen cen- 
tral checkouts will use slot 
scanners and area checkouts in 
the stores will use wands. Soft 
goods will also be marked with 
a UPC ticket which can be 
passed across a slot scanner. 

The ability to sean—by what- 
e -r marking system—repre- 
sents a significant potential to 
cut operations costs. Not only 
can labor costs be cut at the 
front end of astore (as the early 
Kroger experiment showed), 
but labor in marking merchan- 
dise can be cut drastically. Ac- 
curacy of data capture is also 
increased. 

Labor is by far the most sig- 
nificant expense incurred by 
discounters, and a cost which is 
hard to control as minimum- 
wage levels climb. Latest fig- 
ures from the National Mass 
Retailing Institute show labor 
costs climbing from 11.9% of 
sales to 12.1% of sales as an in- 
dustry average. Most chains 
are within the 11%-13% of sales 
range for labor costs. 

Vendor marking of goods can 
reduce marking costs at chain 
level by 75%, some tests at de- 
partment stores show, while su- 
permarket scanning operations 
suggest that checkout labor can 
be cut more than 25%. 

Accuracy in scanning also 
contributes to the profit poten- 
tial. Estimates of wanding and 
slot-scanning accuracy by dis- 
counters range upward from 
Ga% to 99%, compared to an ac- 
curacy in data capture of 70% to 
87% when a cashier enters in- 
formation manually at the 
checkout. Additional savings 
can be accrued because auto- 
matic entry prevents cashiers 
from giving “sweetheart” pric- 
es on goods to a friend or rela- 
tive. 

It makes sense for discount- 
ers to purchase POS equipment 
compatible with wands or slot 
scanners. Payback on equip- 
ment costs now hovers around 
two years, according to one 
manufacturer estimate. The de- 
velopment of a compromise 
marking system, as well as ad- 
ditional tests on OCR-A and 
UPC in diseount stores will 
benefit the entire industry. 

Discounters as a whole are 
still moving into POS equip- 
ment; 39% of the industry re- 
ported they were fully POS- 
equipped in a DSN poll, 42% 
were partially equipped, and 
19% had no POS installations to 
date. 


Different Procedures 


There is great range in the 
industry at present. Chains 
such as Caldor, Target and 
Bradlees have all (or virtually 
all) stores equipped with POS 
terminals and are experiment- 
ing with advanced uses of their 
systems such as credit verifica- 
tion. Others (Zayre, FedMart, 
Two Guys, Barkers) have been 
beefing up their systems. Some 
(such as Murphy’s Mart) are ex- 
perimenting with small groups 
of stores before going chain- 
wide in a program. 

K mart has a smaller per- 
centage of its stores equipped 
than many chains, because of 
sheer size of the chain and the 
high cost of conversion. Per- 
store cost in the industry aver- 
ages $107,000 for the move to 
POS equipment.

parent SCOA Industries $880.2 
million in revenues, and 76% of 
SCOA’s $59.9 million pretax 
earnings. Operating earnings 
advanced 34% to $45.4 million, 
while sales increased 19% to an 
estimated $580 million. 

A similar performance is ex- 
pected for this current fiscal 
year. Hills officials projected a 
17.2% sales gain to $680 million.

While discounters reported 
sticking to the basics in home 
security—rather than stocking 
more expensive electronic sys- 
tems—the category has gained 
enough consumer interest in 
past years to prompt many 
chains like Zodys, Murphy's 
Mart, ALCO and Mr. Wiggs to 
create a separate department 
for home safety products. 

Security was one of the 
bright spots in hardware where 
across-the-board sales gains in 
the department were down 3% 
from last vear. 


Area of Reliance 


Most dealers found strength 
by staying in basics—locksets 
in the $9 to $12 range and pro- 
motional padlocks—and avoid- 
ing the higher-priced elec- 
tronics. 

The impasse regarding the 
high-end intrusion alarms was 
price. Mosi discounters said 
they were holding back on their 
buying until prices dropped. 
This, they said, would happen 
when technology becomes 
cheaper and more manufactur- 
ers enter the market. 

For now, only a small group of 
discounters—Target, Gold Tri- 
angle and Zodys among them— 
have venture into the upper 
price ranges with complete 
home or apartment electronic 
protection systems. 

There have beer. disappoint- 
ments. At Gold Triangle, one 
merchandiser noted that the re- 
ally expensive systems had 
been moved into the major ap- 


pliance department where they | 


could be sold by a trained sales- 
man. “It’s the type of item cus- 


tomers have to fiddle with be- | 


fore they'll buy,” he noted. 
Layout Changed 


Smoke-alarm stocking pat- 
terns also conform to dis- 
counter tendencies to stay with 
the basics. Once a red-hot sell- 
er, the now inexpensively 
priced items no longer capture 
endcap space. Rather, they are 
stocked in limited and greatly 
narrowed numbers in depart- 
ment side aisles. 

A bullish note: in California, 
new iegislation—mandating 
that landlords install the home 
safety devices when they make 
more than $1,000 in home im- 
provements in multiple dwell- 
ings—may stimulate sales in 
the state over the next few 
months.

A trend toward money-sav- 
ing vacations gave sporting 
goods a booster shot this year 
as consumers chose camping, 
hunting and fishing trips in lieu 
of more expensive forms of fam- 
ily entertainment. 

However, the department did 
not escape current economic 
conditions. Sales of high-ticket 
items were sluggish, buyers re- 
ported, indicating consumers’ 
decisions to postpone pur- 


chases of new sporting equip- 
ment this year. Instead they re- 
outfitted their existing equip- 
ment with accessory items— 
purchases that carried greater 
margins to discounters. 

This trend is changing buyer 
ordering patterns. For next 
year, buyers revealed they were 
trimming departments of 
fringe and high-ticket items, 
and banking on accessories, ap- 
parel, and a handful of growth 


categories such as exercise 
equipment and roller skates. 
The fishing category ex- 
emplifies what is happening 
throughout sporting goods. 
Sales of high-ticket rod and reel 
separates declined while sales 
of terminal gear and lures rose. 
Middle- and low-end combina- 
tion sets were popular this 
year, appeaiing to both the new, 
occasional fisherman and the 
avid sportsman seeking inex- 


pensive activities for family 
outings. 

Slow demand for high-ticket 
rod and reels were offset by dis- 
counter’s promotional efforts. 
Wisconsin-based Prange-Way 
noted that rod, reel and elec- 
tronic item sales soared during 
promotions, then dropped dra- 
matically as the ad finished. 

Stem Distributors’ Jim Syl- 
vester reported that 35% of 
total fishing category sales 


came out of promotional ac- 
tivity, and 50% of combo sets 
were so!d on promotion. 
Keeping in tune with the 
need for promotional efforts in 
fishing, one Zayre store in Con- 
necticut drew customers to its 
fishing section with a two bin 
display filled with terminal 
gear, all priced at $1. The dis- 
play included two X-racks 
showing fishing rods in a verti-

(DSN photo) 


Discounters say consumable 
sales will continue to skyrocket 
as increasing numbers of shop- 
pers—many armed with regu- 
lar and double coupons—turn 
to them for added savings. 

In the last two years alone 
some discounters have re- 
ported sales gains as high as 
60% to 100%. Most of the major 
chains surveyed said the com- 
ing year could bring sales in- 
creases as high as 40%. 

Most of the items being add- 
ed to houseware and snack sec- 
tions—detergents, cleansers, 
tuna fish and pickles—are not 
big moneymakers because of 
the low markups. 

Those items do succeed, how- 
ever, in increasing traffic in dis- 
count stores and result in sig- 
nificant increases in sales of 
related items. 


Promising Area 


A buyer for Ohio-based Gold- 
man’s, for example, reported 
sales of household chemicals in- 
creasing by 20% to 25% this 
year. But the real profit was in 
the 18% increase in the sale of 
mops and brooms—items with 
a higher markup. 

Still, despite the traffic 
boost, most discounters sur- 
veyed said they had mixed feel- 
ings about accepting consum- 
able coupons. 

While couponing increases 
traffic at a time when the only 
new business a chain can ac- 
quire is that which can be 
“swiped” from a competitor, 
chains pay for them dearly out 
of profits. 

The loss in profits can be- 
come even more substantial, 
discounters said, when a chain 
begins double couponing, fore- 
ing his competitors to do like- 
wise. 


Over the years, U.S. BORAX products have built a very impressive track record of saiiahineiteinens 


attracting and holding loyal customers. By displaying and promoting these products, 
you can attract them too. 

The products of U.S. BORAX have successfully built traffic and sales wherever 
they’ve been sold. So why not stock them. Properly displayed and premoted, the U.S. 
BORAX product line can give you the kind of following that pays. 


Double couponing—and in 
some cases even triple coupon- 
ing—can bring other problems 
as well. Discounters said such 
coupon specials are frequently 
accompanied by irate custom- 
ers, large out-of-stocks and op- 
erational problems.

Escalating costs coupled 
with the tight economy have 
stationery buyers turning to 
basics and predicting tough 
times ahead. They’ve taken a 
number of steps to deal with 
sluggish sales. 

Some buyers expected that 
economic conditions will dis- 
courage customers from high- 
priced merchandise. For this 
reason, Gene O’Donnell, mer- 
chandise manager at Hills, de- 
cided to build a better in-stock 
position of price basics and to 
cut back on his assortment of 
more fashion-oriented mer- 
chandise in preparation for fall 
back-to-school. 

Supply shortages and an ex- 
pected 8%-12% cost increase in 
paper products have many dis- 
counters planning to buy short- 
er counts or raise retail prices, 
or possibly do both, within this 
category. 

Others reacted to their cus- 
tomers’ increased price/value 
concerns by increasing sku’s in 
multipack paper products. 
Adding higher-count typing pa- 
per, erasable bond, or steno 
notebooks with 2% times as 
many pages were popular 
moves. 

Soaring petrochemical costs 
have pushed pen prices up 22% 
although most buyers said sales 
are unaffected by these in- 
creases on low-ticket writing 
instruments. 

Still, buyers noticed an up- 
surge in popularity of multi- 
pack pens, which they said cus- 
tomers viewed as a good value. 

“We sell Bic medium-point 
crystal pens for 26¢ in a single 
pack,” said Bob Braunstein, di- 
visional merchandise manager 
at Bradlees. “That same pen is 
sold in a 10-pack for $1.69. That 
represents a 91¢ savings to the 
customer who buys the multi- 
pack.” 

Multipack items have also be- 
come popular promotional 
tools. “When we run a writing 
instrument other than the Pa- 
per Mate retractable, we run a 
multipack,” said Braunstein. 
Multipack pens are given 4 ft. of 
pegboard, and are segregated 
from single pens to improve vis- 
ibility. 

Some buyers chose to offset 
cost hikes on the major brands 
by infiltrating stationery sec- 
tions with private label brands. 
Gold Circle for instance has pri- 
vate label crayons and cel- 
lophane tape, and might ex-

Discount stores are one of the 
major retailers of electric 
housewares, and this fact has 
resulted in discounters more 
than holding their own in sell- 
ing traffic appliances despite 
the vicissitudes of the economy. 

Manufacturers have esti- 
mated that discounters account 
for about one-third of vendor 
sales to retailers. DSN projects 
discounters’ electric house- 
wares volume this year will hit 
$1.3 billion, up 8.8% from last 
year’s $1.2 billion. 

Discounters’ electric house- 
wares strength in the past has 
been merchandising of staple 
items with quick thrusts into 
and out of hot fad items—and 
it’s the same basic approach 
that is seen as maintaining vol- 
ume small-appliance sales 
throughout this year and the 
key holiday fourth quarter. 

A Target merchandiser 
summed it up best when he de- 
clared: “It’s a very basic vear in 
traffic appliances and [| think it 
will stay that way.” 

Two divergent factors are be- 
hind this. 

One is the lack of any hot fad 
electric that discounters can 
sharply promote to boost traf- 
fic. Discounters across-the- 
board at the housewares show 
in Chicago cited the absence of 
any fad item or any small appli- 
ance that seemed like a candi- 
date for a hot Christmas gift 
item. 

The second factor is the econ- 
omy, which has caused shop- 
pers to focus on low- and mid- 
priced goods, the core mer- 
chandise carried by discount- 
ers, rather than the high-end 
items that are selectively used 
as step-ups by a number of dis- 
counters. 

A Matco merchandiser as- 
serted: “Low-end basics are 
doing well, but basically the 
middle price range in most cat- 
egories is the strongest. I think 
the strength will be in the mid- 
dle prices during the rest of the 
year.” 

The reason for this, a Cook 
United executive noted, is that 
shoppers “are looking for value, 
not just price, and they are will- 
ing to buy a better quality basic 
electric that will last longer.” 

The limited appeal of higher- 
priced small appliances is re- 
flected in the items discounters 
report are selling well, the 
price points being hit in promo- 
tions and the greater reliance 


on ads and manufacturer re-

Hardware department sales 
grew by 16% over the last 12- 
month period—a three-per- 
centage-point decline from the 
gain reported in DSN’s 1979/80 
census. 

Sales on a per-store basis 
grew 8% to $460,827, only 
slightly ahead of inflation. Sales 
per square foot increased com- 
mensurately as the average 
hardware department grew by 
only five additional square feet 
during the period. 

The report from discounters 
shopping the Hardware Show 
in Chicago last month was that 
sales were expected to remain 
flat in the second half of the 
year. 

Still, the departmental fore- 
cast was not all doom and 
gloom. There have been several 
bright spots already this year— 
home security and lawn and 
garden—and energy conserva- 
tion purchases were expected 
to keep sales afloat during the 
remainder of the year. 

Consumers interest in doing 
home repair projects them- 
selves continued to prove a 
boon to department sales. 

Jamesway, K mart, Woolco, 
T.G. & Y., and Rink’s—to 
name just a few—all upped 
their commitment to serve DIY 
customers by expanding their 
product mix and increasing the 
number of building materials 
departments in their chains. 

Plastic plumbing, for exam- 
ple, which finds its way into 
most discounter departments 
in the form of basic repair kits 
(toilet and sink) garnered more 
consumer interest in home im- 
provement oriented chains. 

At S. E. Nichols, sales of 
CPVC and PVC pipe and fit- 
tings rose on a par with conven- 
tional copper plumbing, pro- 
ducing a 25% overall sales 
advance last year. 

Zayre and Pamida introduced 
plastic parts into their plumb- 
ing departments this year and 
Woolco reported that plastic 
supplies now account for up to 
65% of its mix. 

In electricals, most discount- 
ers reported deriving consider- 
able profitability from exten- 
sion cords but added that the 
bulk of sales came in spring and 
summer months when custom- 
ers shopped for cables to aid 

them in outdoor maintenance 
and repair projects. 

Bulbs, including fluores- 
cents, switchplates, fuses, TV

Ladies’ Apparel Enjoys Upgrade 


(Continued from page SO) 

Another traditional dis- 
counter, Wal-Mart, upgraded 
presentation but stopped short 
of trading up on merchandise in 
its new prototype stores. Im- 
provements echo those of 
K mart and other chains seek- 
ing a department store-like im- 
age for their budget-minded 
shoppers. 

Front quadrant location, 
race-track layout, carpeting, 
upscale features, hanging signs 
and department store decor are 
hallmarks of the Arkansas- 
based chain’s prototype. The 
absence of an upgraded mix, 
however, evidences the con- 
trast between Wal-Mart and its 
role model, Target. 

Caldor is taking steps to in- 
crease soft goods profits to 40% 
of the chain’s volume from the 
current 30%. 

Since that decision was 
made, more fashionable mer- 
chandise, displayed in modern 
Plexiglas fixtures and on styl- 
ized mannequins, has appeared 
in women’s rtw. By accessoriz- 
ing and coordinating display 
items, the chain hopes to build 
both multiple sales and a 
higher-fashion image. For in- 
stance, a mannequin on a Plex- 
iglas platform displays fashion- 
able coordinates, available on 
surrounding deltas, and shoes, 
hat and handbag available in 
nearby departments. 

Zayre’s recent remodeling 
elaborates on the “Take An- 
other Look at Zayre” promo- 
tion to attract new customers 
and spotlight soft lines at the 
traditional discounter. Here, 
too, merchandise presentation 
and a mix of up-to-date styles 
keynote the program. 

Other chains seeking to boost 
women's wear profits through 
changes in presentation and by 
keying more on high-end fash- 
ion items are: 


@ S. E. Nichols, which is about 
to complete a program moving 
women’s rtw departments up 
front from the middle of the 
store. 

® Gold Circle, where the pro- 
totype was remodeled and the 
presentation for wearables up- 
graded. 

@ TSS, which has taken over its 
previously leased women’s 
wear departments and added 
brand name merchandise. 

@ Maxway, the new discount 
offspring of Mack’s Variety 
stores, emphasizing soft lines 
including the Levi's brand. 

@ Bradlees, where branded 
goods, though usually not spe- 
cial purchases, are emphasized. 

Thanks in part to the de- 
signer jeans boom and consum- 
ers’ heightened quality con- 
sciousness now that they have 
less spending clout, branded 
goods have become important 
to buyers. In fact, in women’s 
rtw, as in domestics and other 
soft lines categories, buyers say 
that higher-ticket fashion items 
have become basics. 

The new emphasis on fashion 
has opened doors to increased 
profits in women’s wear catego- 
ries besides the traditional 
“missy” departments. 

Half-size categories, a bur- 
geoning fashion area for up- 
stairs stores, are getting more 
space and sometimes separate 
departments at discount 
stores. Junior departments, 
where many fashion trends in- 
cluding disco, western wear 
and activewear looks began, 
have been expanded to capture 
sales from younger and more 
liberal-spending shoppers. 

Lingerie, often rack-jobber 
territory in the past, is getting 
attention on merchandise and 
presentation counts. Cottons 
and other high-quality content 
items are being artfully dis- 
played on mannequins.

FABRIC S/HOME SEWING Discount Store Census ’80/’81 


Quilting Revived to Counter Stagnant Sales 


a ee ee 


Fabrics/Sewing Shop 


@ Discount Store Sales .. $1.0 billion 
@ Sales per Store ........ $129,266 
e@ Department Size .... 1,400 sq. ft. 
e@ Annual Sales per Sq. Ft. ..... $92 
@ Annual Turns ............... 28 


@ Initial Markup..............42% 


e Gross Margin oe i ee rn Fabric buyers are expanding into quilteds after recent retreats to basic items. Higher margins of the 


craft fabric equal higher volume for stores like Oklahoma City T.G. & Y. (DSN photo) 


Fabric department buyers 
are reviving the old-fashioned 
art of quilting to counter stale 
sales in the high investment 
category. 

Discounters are using quilted 
fabrics to introduce the higher 
profit margins of soft craft 
goods into the slow-growing 
home-sewing category. 

Buyer Henry Curran at 
Woolco described quilteds as 
“one of the few bright spots’ in 
his fall buying program. From 
testing the category in selected 
stores last year, he has devel- 
oped a year-round craft-quilt 
program as part of the 15% to 
20% of his mix annually as- 
signed to craft and home decor 
fabrics. 

“We’re hoping to develop the 
whole fabrics category by excit- 
ing sewers with quilteds, which 
I see as a breakthrough in sew- 
ing marketing,” he said. 

Quilted sales are so be- 
tween craft and appare! uses at 
Woolco. Manufacturers’ promo- 
tions, including pattern give- 
aways, have spurred sales for 
novelty/gift and do-it-yourself 
items like duffel bags, purses 
and placemats. 

Placemat quilteds, with six 
cut-and-sew outlines to the 
yard, have been especially pop- 
ular because of the compara- 
tively wide assortment of fabric 
patterns and prints available to 
the sewer, Curran said. At six 
mats per yard, their $1.00 retail 
is slightly higher than that of 
ready-made counterparts, but 
this has not tempered sales, he 
added. 

With a minimum of sewing 
expertise, a nonsewer can 
make a gift or home-decor 
item, and thus potentially be- 
come a regular fabrics cus- 
tomer. Home sewers also buy 

rofitable craft supplies before 
eaving the department, Cur- 
ran pointed out. 

Already, fiberfill garment 
quilteds have performed well, 
in response to energy costs. 

Overall, the category is still a 
cold-weather one. 

T.G. & Y. fabric buyer Wes 
Phillips reported good dollar 
volume, but he was also leery 
about the category’s relatively 
new burst of popularity. 

“We’ve put tremendous em- 
phasis on it from a resource 
standpoint,” commiting to the 
category for a third season, he 
said.

Stay-at-home consumers 
spread plenty of green at dis- 
counters’ lawn and garden de- 
partments this year, although 
increased movement of promo- 
tional models in string trim- 
mers and cost increases in 
mowers clipped volume dollars 
down before they could reach 
the bottom line. 

New items such as bug kill- 
ers, less promotional gas- 
powered string trimmers, 
trade-up models in gas grills, 
and larger live plant nurseries 
were used to bolster the bottom 
line. 

In string trimmers, a depart- 
mental favorite for the last 
three seasons, chains continued 
to stock a half-dozen sku’ in an 
effort to move consumers up to 
high-ticket trimmers. Al- 
though a replacement market is 
developing, raising hopes for 
gas-powered models next year, 
action continued to be hottest 


at the low end. 

Bradlees, Hills and ALCO 
were among those reporting 
the greatest activity in sharply 
priced, low-end models, and 
more than one buyer com- 
plained that the category has 
now “shaken down prices, and 
price fighting among chains has 
made it harder to make money.” 

There is no question that the 
initial sales market—before re- 
placement or trade-up goods— 
is still a growth area. Manufac- 
turers looked to finish the sea- 
son with a 5% to 10% unit 
growth in the category, as only 
about 20% of households in the 
country own a string trimmer, 
according to one manufac- 
turer's estimate. 

However, with increasing 
competition forcing more 
chains to run near cost on the 
promotional models, profit dol- 
lars must be made elsewhere 
despite the very high sales vol- 


ume. 

Ames has experienced a 20% 
real growth in the category this 
season, but primarily from the 
promotional models. One pro- 
motional model at Bradlees ac- 
counted for almost half the total 
sales in the category at that 
chain, according to a buyer 
there. Two promotional models 
at ALCO accounted for 90% of 
sales volume in the category. 

The problem with these rosy 
increases in sales volume is the 
thin margins. As a Hills buyer 
put it, “the bottom has fallen 
out” of the market. This ac- 
counts for the interest in gas- 
powered models, which were 
stocked heavily this year by 
chains ranging from K mart to 
Caldor. 

K mart’s program this sea- 
son contained three sku’s in 
gas-powered trimmers ($129 
everyday price, $99.99 on sale). 
Rose’s carried three gas models 


in most stores. Woolco carried 
two gas models in its assort- 
ment of seven sku’s in trim- 
mers. Heck’s added two sku’s in 
gas-powered trimmers for the 
season. 

Chains that did stock gas 
models this year found sales 
volume rewarding. Lasting 
power and lack of a cord, advan- 
tages over battery-operated 
and corded models, spurred 
consumer response. A Caldor 
spokesman praised gas- 
powered trimmers as ideal 
items in a developing replace- 
ment market. 

“The same customers who 
bought their first string trim- 
mer at a promotional price now 
come into our stores looking for 
items with deluxe features,” he 
said. 

A buyer at Rose’s attributed 
much of his chain’s 40% volume 
increases in string trimmers 
this season to the gas models. A 


Hills buyer said the models 


were “the health and future of 


string trimmers.” 
The other major power tools 
in lawn and garden, the 
mowers, are the subject of con- 
cern once again because of price 
increases. After being hit with 
cost increases of 10% to 12% this 
season, similar cost increases 
were announced for next year 
by lawn mower manufacturers. 
In addition to cost increases 
on mowers at present, after 
next season the “deadman 
clutch” law will be in effect, re- 
quiring mower blades to stop 
automatically once the handle 
is released. The safety require- 
ment will add 8% to 10% toa 
mower’s cost, in manufacturers’ 
estimates, and $20 at retail 
(minimum) in estimates by 
chain buyers. 

At least one chain has beaten 
the regulators to the punch.

Discounters are predicting 
that the skyrocketing prices on 
new cars and continued increas- 
es In auto repair costs will 
translate into substantial sales 
increases in the auto after- 
market during the coming year, 
as more motorists than ever do 
their own repairs. 

Most discounters surveyed 
were reluctant to say exactly 
how much sales should rise. But 
many said that a good winter- 
ization program this fall and 
strong promotions throughout 
| the year could generate an in- 
crease of at least 10%; probably 
closer to 20%. 
| Car beautification items will 

do well, discounters said, as in- 
creasing numbers of people put 
| off new car purchases and try to 
| better maintain the cars they 
have. 
| 


DIY Stars 


| The real stars, though, are 

|going to be the traditional fa- 
PHILLIPS vorites of do-it-vourselfers— 

oll, spark plugs, filters and 

other maintenance items. 

Officials of chains such as 
Wooleo, Gold Circle and King’s ; 
have noticed that do-it-vour- 
selfers have been getting more 
adventuresome and taking on 
increasingly complicated repair 
tasks. 

In the coming year, many 
predict, hard parts now stocked 
by only a few chains will grow in 

importance. Those items in- 
'clude fuel pumps, alternators 
| and electric radiator fans. 
| Figures supplied in several 
| recent product movement au- 
i dits by the Allied Accessories 
and Auto Parts Company, 
!' which deals with more than 
1,700 discount stores, tend to 
support the trend. 

Spark plugs, as well as tune- ; 
up kits, chemicals and oils, 
were the strongest performers 
in 1979, and preliminary statis- 
tics indicate they are doing even 
better in 1980. 

Creeping up to more domi- 
nant positions on the list are 
items that allow car owners to 
do more complicated repairs 
and heavy duty jacks that allow 
them to get under their vehicles 
with greater ease. 

Two makes of mufflers made 
it onto the list of top 100 best 
sellers this summer and a 
$69.96 two-ton hydraulic floor 
jack continued to make impres- 
sive showings.

Despite the vicissitudes of 
the economy, housewares has 
turned into a stellar depart- 
ment for discounters, with 
sales not only holding up but 
actually growing and capturing 
a greater share of total store 
volume. 

This situation reflects the 
fact that the nonelectric house- 
wares category offers discount- 
ers the twin opportunities of 
merchandising basic, fast-turn- 
ing goods such as gadgets and 
chemicals, and step-up, fash- 
ion-oriented home decor items 
such as modular furniture, pic- 
tures and mirrors. 

The shining outlook for 
housewares can be seen in the 
statistical profile of the depart- 
ment which shows that total 
discount store housewares 
sales will hit $4.2 billion this 

ear, up 23.5% from $3.4 bil- 
ion. Volume per store will 
jump 16% to $542,916 from 
$467 ,933. 

A 12.4% increase in depart- 
ment size to 5,734 sq. ft. will lift 
sales per square foot 3.5% to 
$95 from $91.75. The low sales- 
per-square foot figure is decep- 
tive. At first glance it auld 
seem to make housewares a 
low-profit department, among 
the lowest for hard lines. 

Housewares, however, has a 
4.2 annual turn, which, com- 
bined with a 38% initial marku 
and a 34% gross anie-oboth 
higher than last year—makes 
the department a strong gener- 
ator of gross profit dollars. 

The production of bottom- 

line dollars, and the total 
sales—No. 3 among all catego- 
ries—explain why discounters 
are strengthening their com- 
mitment to housewares. Ob- 
jects of these efforts include: 
@ Gourmet cookware. Zayre 
and Jefferson are among a 
growing number of chains that 
have developed gourmet cook- 
ware sections that combine 
stepped-up cookware with spe- 
cialty items such as steamers 
and spinners to dry vegetables. 
The upscale fixturing uses nat- 
ural wood units to mass-display 
the merchandise. 

Jefferson plans to have the 
section in all its stores, having 
put it in units opened this sum- 
mer in Philadelphia and in re- 
modelings of older stores in 
Florida. Zayre has the section 
in almost two dozen stores that 
have been remodeled and is set 
to put it in another 15 to 20
