Skyrocketing gold prices 
changed the character of many 
discounters’ jewelry depart- |i 
ments this year. Buyers for |@ 
chains in smaller or non- 
metropolitan markets saw 
themselves being priced out of 
the 14-karat gold business, and 
consequently placed greater 
emphasis on gold-filled items, 
based metal watches and cos- 
tume jewelry. 

At the same time, the change 
in jewelry prices opened the 
door for many upscaled chains 
that capitalized on their depart- 
ment store images and lower 
prices to win sales. These dis- 
counters upscaled their presen- 
tations and introduced dia- 
monds and gemstones into

periment with glue. Bi-Mart of- 
fered private label pencils, and 
will expand its private label in 
stationery in the future. Buyer 
Larry Polen noted that in cate- 
gories where brand names 
were well established, the 
chain would stay with those 
names. 

The home/office category 
continued to pump new life into 
the department this year. Buy- 
ers added high-ticket items, 
and learned to stretch the cate- 
gory’s already high profit po- 
tential with year-round promo- 
tional activity. 

Caldor established its home/ 
office section two years ago 
with just a “smattering” of 
items and ina handful of stores, 
according to buyer Al Pius. To- 
day, all stores carry a section. 
Size of the section depends on 
the strength of the business 
community surrounding the 
store, although the average size 
is 8 running ft. Assortment in- 
cludes home safes, globes and 
desk accessories.

CORNING 


Domestics buyers over the 
past year have been influenced 
by revived consumer interest in 
home-decor departments and 
the ongoing concern about the 
high cost of energy. 

Summer'’s-end sales and fall 
buying witness this year's ap- 
proach to curtains and drap- 
eries. 

Curtains, in particular, re- 
flect home decor trends with 
new fashion touches. New sty]- 
ings include smocking and vari- 
ous ruffle treatments; and 
prints are making a more im- 
portant statement here, just as 
they are in piece goods, apparel 
and other fashion categories. 

The expense of staying warm 
and keeping cool is one major 
selling point in energy conser- 
vation pitches emphasizing 
draperies that insulate. 

The energy story is of prime 
importance at Caldor, where 
curtain, drapery and f Mase 
buyer Gale Egan said self-lined 
drapes will be emphasized in 
POS and print advertisements. 
With draperies comprising 42% 
of the mix in her department, a 
new energy-conserving self- 
lined Malimo was added to 
spark fall sales. 

In curtains, which dominate 
the mix, the smock tier con- 
tinues as a strong performer. 
New print and eyelet trims 
have been added to tiers, while 
embroidered panels and lace 
dress up tailored and cape cur- 
tain categories. 

Continued success in those 
styles is seen at Gibson's, too, 
where new smock and ruffle de- 
tail entries were added for fall. 

But, like at Caldor, the big 
story is in energy promotions. 
Gibson's buyer also added a 
self-lined drape this season and 
said he was “looking for sub- 
stantial sales increases as a re- 
sult.” 

He expects turns to be three 
times better for those he pro- 
motes as energy savers. 

“We are looking for a low- to 
middle- price point to promote 
at $9.99,” he said. “Our cus- 
tomer wants the most current 
drapery fashion at moderate 
prices.” 

Fashion in drapes translates 
to traditional earth tones, new 
prints, jacquards and satins in 
draperies. 

Basic items with new styl- 
ings are the rule at Heck’s, 
which has experienced a con- 
servative year, compared to 
Caldor.

Toy buyers are fine tuning 
their basic assortments and se- 
lecting items for dependable 
turns at decent margins. They 
hope that strong basic assort- 
ments will help stretch both toy 
sales and profits over the entire 
year, weakening their de- 
pendence on the highly promo- 
tional Christmas season. 


Back to Basics 


The move toward basics 
comes in response to consumer 
demand for greater play value, 
durability and family entertain- 
ment, buyers said. Last Christ- 
mas, consumers showed in- 
creased interest in getting 
mileage out of their dollars as 
evidenced by the strong sales 
performances turned in by pre- 
school, board games, non-TV 
dolls, and miniature wheel 
goods categories. 

This trend also led buyers to 
scrutinize their TV toy selec- 
tion, where high-tickets con- 
tinued to meet consumer resis- 
tance. Yet buyers did not lose 
sight of the importance of car- : 
rying an adequate selection of 
these traffic drawing items. 
They cherry-picked TV toys 
based on such factors as manu- 
facturers’ advertising support 
and price points. For instance, 
at Hecks, buyer Bob Kuhns 
avoided TV toys priced over $15 
because of customer resistance 
to prices beyond that point last 
Christmas. 


Ad Support 


hee 


T.G. & Y. buyers were also 
among those who chose not to 
be as aggressive this year with 
TV toys, according to buyer 
Nick Jung. They are backing 
up the major TV toy com- 
panies, but are not going as 
deep as in previous years. TV 
toys must also be supported by 
at least $700,000 of network 
television advertising before 
they are considered for the 
T.G. & Y. toy lineup, he said.

Electronic Games Hurt by Supply Problems 


Buyers hope to draw year-round toy sales with high-quality basics 
that have family appeal. This Caldor, in Middletown, N.Y., devotes 
backwall space to model sets and accessories. 


DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, SEPTEMBER 22, 1980 


TOYS 


(DSN photo) 


Electronic games continued 
their runaway sales growth this 
year, but price hikes (up 
10%-20%, according to manu- 
facturer estimates) and linger- 
ing supply problems had buyers 
proceeding with caution as they 
selected their toy lineups for 
the coming season. 

“This could be the year when 
a lot of people get burned on 
electronics,’ warned Gary 
Jackson at Magic Mart. He and 
other buyers saw price points 
as the critical factor in stocking 
patterns this coming year, as a 
flood of new low-end knockoffs 
vie with step-up newcomers for 
consumer dollars. 

Buyers added that the con- 
sumer shift away from expen- 
sive TV toys would sharply 
effect electronic game sales. 

In response, many buyers— 
including those from Hecks, 
ALCO, Caldor and T.G. & Y.— 
have honed down their elec- 
tronic toy selection to better 


prepare toy departments for 
this shift in attitude. 

Supply shortages which 
dampened electronic sales last 
Christmas are predicted again 
for this season. Toy manufac- 
turers reported continued diffi- 
culty in getting supplies of vital 
computer chips. 

A spokesman at Texas In- 
struments, a major chip sup- 
plier pointed to an “explosion in 
demand” as one reason this 
company couldn’t keep up. 

“We can’t respond to the 
problem as rapidly as we’d like 
to,” said the spokesman. “Our 
supply of chips will hold steady 
in 1980. We hope that things 
will be under control late this 
year or in early 1981.” 

Many buyers have chosen to 
support the nationally adver- 
tised name brands this season. 
Bob Binder at Jefferson Stores 
spurned off-brand products in 
favor of running with Bradley, 
Mattel and Coleco.

Fashion continues to be the 
major selling factor in glass- 
ware, with colors and styles re- 
flecting trends in tabletop mer- 
chandise and in the tones that 
have become important in other 
housewares categories. 

Pressures from the economy, 
however, have cracked fashion’s 
domination—price and promo- 
tion are now coming to the fore. 

A Danner’s 3-D merchan- 
diser summed up the situation 
by noting the discounter will 
rely heavily on 4-packs around 
$5 as featured merchandise to 
draw shoppers. 

The importance of price as an 
indicator of value was noted by 
a Times Square Stores mer- 
chandiser who pointed to 24-pc. 
sets at $10-$12 as strong sellers 
all year, with sharp sales peaks 
evident in June just before the 
summer vacation and outdoor 
entertainment period and in 
October-November for Christ- 
mas partying. 

The fashion interest remains 
strong, a Nichols executive 
added. Sales of higher priced 
bulk glasses and sets are only 
possible, he explained, using 
traded up domestic or imported 
merchandise in which clean 
lines and the newest colors are 
evident. 

A Zodys merchandiser as- 
serted that merchandising 
glassware as fashion ties in 
with consumers interest in get- 
ting away from the sterile basic 
housewares look. It’s part of the 
same trend that has boosted 
sales of all types of home decor 
merchandise, the merchan- 
diser added. 

Merchandising glassware as 
part of the lifestyle area that 
includes tabletop goods and 
other home decor merchandise 
has helped to boost glassware 
sales in the face of the weak 
economy, a Hills merchandiser 
said. 

The Danner’s 3-D merchan- 
diser added that playing up 
fashion was an important ele- 
ment in promoting glassware. 
He explained that ads and dis- 
plays have to make customers 
aware of how glassware relates 
to the total look a consumer 
wants in his or her home; price 
without this fashion factor 
won't generate the maximum 
response to a promotion. 

Discounters upbeat outlook 
for glassware in spite of the 
economy is reflected in indus- 
try sales, which should hit $385 
million, a 10% increase.

Scheduling Affects Detectives’ Performance 


By S. J. (Bob) Curtis 
(Another in a regular series of articles on the pre- 
vention of pilferage by the former head of security of 
Lord & Taylor and J. L. Hudson. Mr. Curtis 1s a 
lecturer, consultant and author.) 


Supervising Detectives: Part V (Conclusion) 

Scheduling detectives is an art in itself. Some 
stores mistakenly think that July and August are such 
slow months of the year that it is best to give detec- 
tives their vacations in those two months. Asa result, 
many discounters have thin floor coverage during two 
of the hardest-hit shoplifting 
months of the year. 

Common sense doesn’t always 
work in the field of store security. 
People don’t seem to act the wav 
we assume they'll act. We think, 
because we take our vacations in 


traffic is slower during those two 
months, that shoplifting will be 
down. Not so. 

After several years of careful 
study of shoplifting activity and 
case production we have found that July and August 
are top months for shoplifting thefts. Those are not 
the months to give detectives their vacations. It 
would be better if they took vacations in the spring or 
fall. 

Why should July and August (particularly August) 


DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, SEPTEMBER 22, 1980 


. 


(Pilferage Prevention 
aan 


be periods of heavy shoplifting? We can’t be sure of 
the reason but it is likely that the generation of posi- 
tive ions in the air as a result of the city’s heat is a 
major cause. 

Crimes of violence, such as assault and murder, 
peak in August. Researchers have long associated the 
crime wave that hits public law enforcement people 
during the hottest months can be attributed to the 
generation of excessive positive ions in the air. The 
beneficial negative ions come around in the spring and 
early fall. They also follow gentle rains and cooler 
weather. The hot pavements and buildings of the city 
hold their heat after sunset during the summer and 
the cities never recover from this onslaught of heat 
which kills off the negative ions and leaves the air 
heavily ionized with harmful positive ions, day and 
night. 

European scientists have for many years found a 
direct correlation between a high level of positive ions 
and high levels of crime. But, whatever the causes of 
increased shoplifting during July and August, the fact 
remains this 7s a critical period for store security. 

Another critical period is the week following 
Christmas. Studies we did at the J. L. Hudson Com- 
pany in Detroit showed consistently that more shop- 
lifting apprehensions are made during the week 
following Christmas than in any other single week of 
the year. Yet some stores who add temporary detec- 
tives to their staff for the Christmas season often 
dismiss them shortly after Christmas. This is unwise. 
Hold them until after the first of the year. You'll have 


the case production to justify the added expense. 

Store security directors are constantly seeking 
ways to increase the productivity of their floor detec- 
tives and one of the A oie overlooked ways to do so has 
to do with scheduling. 

It is well recognized today that as a nation we are 
divided into two types of people in terms of our sleep- 
ing habits. Some of us are awake at the crack of dawn. 
At 6 in the morning we are eager to leap out of bed. 

On the other hand many of us are as sluggish as a 
tired hound dog in the early morning hours. If we had 
our way we’d sleep until noon every day. 

Now that first group, the early risers, are called 
“morning workers” and they are at their peak within a 
few minutes of waking up. Their energy and drive 
make them fireballs in the morning and early after- 
noon hours. By 3 inthe afternoon, however, they start 
to run out of steam and by early evening they are 
yawning a bit and soon will be ready to hit the hay. 

By contrast, those sluggards who love to cuddle in 
the soft warmth of their beds until noon are slow to 
get their juices running and don’t know their own 
name much before ll a.m. By 2:00 in the afternoon 
they are just beginning to hit their stride and by early 
evening ‘hey are reaching their peak of energy and 
drive that sustains them until midnight or long after. 
These are called “night workers” and when the morn- 
ing workers are ready to hit the hay those night 
workers are just getting their second wind and are 
ready for partying, cleaning the house, or just plain 
hell raising. 

Detective supervisors should 


Dor’t hire a thief. 


Studies show that one out of every three job applicants 
is a bad apple—a potential thief with access to 

your money or valuables. The trick is 

to spot this bad apple before you hire him. NOT after 
he’s stolen. Because for every thief you fire, you could 
hire another potential thief. 


Traditional methods of screening people are outdated. 
Police checks, credit checks, etc., often 
don’t tell the whole story. 


But now there is a method that goes right to 

the heart of the matter—the Reid Report. 

An easy to administer, psychologically validated 

written test that determines the honesty and integrity 
of prospective employees. Acting on 

its results, companies have reduced their internal theft. 


Isn’t it time you took off the blindfold? 


Write for more information.

talk with each floor detective 
about his or her sleeping hab- 
its, find out how much sleep the 
individual needs and whether 
the person is an early or late 
riser. Establish whether each 
detective is a “morning worker” 
or a “night worker.” You can 
then effectively increase your 
shoplifting apprehensions by 
scheduling the early risers on 
your earlier work shifts and 
your late risers on the late-hour 
shifts. 

At Hudson's we successfully 
increased detective case pro- 
duction by 38% with a simple 
scheduling change whereby we 
put early workers on the morn- 
ing and afternoon shift and 
night workers on the noon to 
closing hour shift. You can 
make a similar improvement in 
your case production. A detec- 
tive who is rested and energetic 
has the maximum ability to con- 
centrate, and that’s what detec- 
tive production is all about. 

It goes without saying that 
detective lunch and relief peri- 
ods should be staggered so you 
have proper floor coverage at all 
times the store is open. When 
court appearances thin your 
staff, try to shift people so you 
have at least some floor se- 
curity on hand. 

When you can, try to sched- 
ule at least one detective to 
roam the selling floor a half 
hour before store opening and 
another one to remain on the 
selling floor for a half hour after 
closing. It is surprising how 
many shoplifting cases can be 
made during those periods. 
Customers leaving the store 
after closing are often tempted 
to shoplift because some of the 
overhead lights are off, casting 
shadows on the racks and 
counters. The floors are also 
fast being deserted by employ- 
ees eager to get home. The po- 
tential thief feels safe and as- 
sumes the detectives (if any) 
have probably also left. 

A similar situation exists 
shortly before store opening 
but in this instance it isn’t cus- 
tomers who are a risk but the 
early working employees.

As Net Income %, Margins Drop 
Smaller Chains Record 


Substantial Sales Gains 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Increasing promotion has re- 
duced the average gross margin 
for small chains—those with 
volume under $100 million—by 
almost one-fifth from 29.6% to 
24.1%, ad brought downside 
pressure on their net income as 
a percentage of sales, down 
from 2.27% of sales to 1.9%. 

But the tactic was successful 
in bringing substantial sales 
gains for the smaller chains, 
which last year had an average 
store volume of $4.3 million, up 
more than 50% from the pre- 
vious year’s $2.7 million. 

In contrast to the smaller 
chains, those with volume in ex- 
cess of $260 million have gained 
19.2% in average sales volume 

er store (to $4,554,000 from 
3,821,000), and midsized 


chains—those with volume be- 
tween $100 million and $260 
million—reported a 9.7% de- 
cline in the average, to $4,134,- 
000 from $4,576,000 the pre- 
vious year. 

These are some of the find- 
ings in the National Mass Re- 
tailing Institute’s 1979-80 study 
of 38 participating chains (2,376 
stores) doing $10.1 billion in 
sales. The bulk of the informa- 
tion comes from 30 chains 
which have participated for two 
or more consecutive years, and 
which operate 2,019 stores. The 
same-store group generated 
85% of the total sales of $10.1 
billion. 

The NMRI’s 16th annual 
study, conducted by Cornell 
University, showed the overall 
net earnings to be 1.94% of 


sales, up slightly from the 
1.92% secured in the previous 
year. It was the fifth consecu- 
tive year in which the net per- 
centage had increased since the 
0.99% average reported in the 
1974-75 study. 

Continued improvement of 
the 38-chain group was evident 
in other operations areas as 
well. 

Average store sales in 1979- 
80 rose to $4,432,000, from 
$3,968,000 reported for the pre- 
vious fiscal period. 

Average sales per square foot 
of selling space hit $96.83, com- 
pared with $84.21 in the 1978-79 
period.

with $100 million to $260 million 
in volume) and large chains

noted that consumers seeking

Macks Opens Second 


Maxway’s Unit in Virginia 


BEDFORD, Va.—Macks, 
the variety store parent chain 
headquartered in Sanford, 
N.C., opened its second Max- 
way discount unit here last 
month. 

Sales projections call for the 
unit to generate $4 million— 
$100 per square foot—during 
the first year of operation. 
These are the same first-year 
figures chain executives project 
for each the six discount stores 
they plan to open by the end of 
1981. 

In the case of the Bedford 
store, the figures may be a bit 
conservative for two reasons: 
First, the unit—a former W. T. 
Grant—is bigger, and second, it 
is located in a larger population 
center than is planned for fu- 
ture Maxways, said R. C. Dod- 
son, Macks’ director of adver- 
tising. 

“The new store is basically 
the same as the first one, and 
we will continue to make all our 
stores look alike,” he explained. 

One slight departure from 
the prototype unit, built this 
spring in Sandersville, Ga.,isa 
slightly larger sales floor: 
41,000 sq. ft. in Bedford vs. 
40,000 sq. ft. in Sandersville. 

The extra space in the new 
store accommodates expanded 


soft lines—especially domes- 
tics—and H&BA categories. 

With the Bedford store’s size 
and location in mind, Dodson 
explained: “We expect sales to 
be greater at the Bedford store, 
but we aren’t making any other 
projections. We think perhaps 
the Bedford store has more po- 
tential than the others.” 

He called the Grant takeover 
a unique opportunity for the 
chain, which will locate its dis- 
count stores in rural areas 
where each can be “the only 
store in town” of its kind. 

“We think the Grant store 
was one of the stores K mart 
overlooked in their W. T. Grant 
buying sweep,” Dodson said, 
adding that the Bedford site is 
roughly equidistant between 
two Virginia population cen- 
ters, Lynchburg and Roanoke. 

Five other sites, in 
Wadesboro, Warrenton and 
Hillsborough, N.C., and Chase 
City and Pearisburg, Va., have 
been signed already, and each 
will get a new store built from 
the ground up to prototype 
specifications. 

A third discount store, in 
Wytheville, Va., was occupied 
Sept. 15 in preparation for a 
grand opening later this month.

Downgraded Image Draws Mexican shoppers 


JUAREZ, Mexico—When 
Futurama (SAISA) opened its 
doors in this border city abut- 
ting El Paso, Mexican shoppers 
were put off by the neat, up- 
graded appearance. 

Customers were suspicious 
that the store’s prices were in- 
flated to reflect the physical im- 
age of the stcres, according to 
Jorge Mares, general merchan- 
dise manager. 

Consequently, the chain 
made some physical adjust- 
ments, such as replacing pro- 
fessionally made signs with the 
dozens of ceiling-hung, hand- 
lettered banners that now clut- 
ter the store, and deliberately 
taking gondolas out of their 
neat, straight runs. 

As a result, business in the 
eight Futurama stores, ranging 
in size from 40,000 sq. ft. to 
100,000 sq. ft. of selling space, 
rang up more than $60 million 
last year, Mares said. Approx- 
imately 6.5% of the sales trans- 
lated into profit dollars, he 
indicated. The same eight units 
are expected to increase sales 
35% for the current fiscal year 
ending in January. 

Unlike its major competitor, 
FedMart, which has an E] Paso 
unit, Futurama officials see 
their in-store supermarkets as 
adjuncts to their main line of

Toddler Wear 


Babies clothes have come a long way. Zip front jeans are taking 
space from pull-on pants, paving the way for more upgraded items 


as buyers examine the fashion potential of toddler and infant wear. 


Fred Meyer Playclothes 


BE ' 


Ae 


Pursues 


Fashion Upgrade Trend 


By Laura Mulcahy 
Nationwide DSN Report 

Like maternity and plus-size 
fashions, toddler wear is be- 
coming more than a pull-on 
pants category for discount 
chains. 

Spring 1981 may be the indus- 
try’s turning point as buyers ac- 
customed to stocking all-basics 
assortments are now shopping 
vendors for more fashionable 
items. 

New will be brighter colors, 
more sophisticated fabrications 
and detailed stylings, as buyers 
move away from primary colors 
and conventional piece goods. 

“Last year, jewel tones, 
fuschia, teal and jade hit the 
children’s market. We’re trying 
to pull that influence down to 
the toddler department,” Mar- 
cy Zell, assistant buyer at Alex- 
ander’s, the metropolitan New 
York chain, said. Upgradings 
that began last spring in the 
then predominantly basics tod- 
dler wear category have 
brought the fashion-to-basic 
item ratio up to 50%. 

“A few years ago, no one 
heard of dressing a toddler in 
jeans. Now it’s just a matter of 
the category catching up with 
the fashion movement,” Zell 
said. 

Catching up includes an in- 
dustrywide effort to scale down 
older-age-group fashion trends. 
Coordinates and active-wear 
looks in better quality fabrics 
and new wovens, all in bright 
tones, offer toddler customers 
the same value and fashion ap- 
peal long available in childrens, 
men’s and women’s categories. 

Increases in the United 


States birthrate—slow but 
steady in the last several 
years—have buoyed buyers’ in- 
novativeness and spurred fash- 
ion commitments, along with 
sales and traffic, in their de- 
partments. The National Cen- 
ter for Health Statistics charts 
a 3%-and-rising increase for the 
first four months of this year, 
compared to the same period in 
1979, when the birthrate for the

Chains Focus Shoplifting Security 
On Deterring, Rather Than Catching 


By Bernard Cullen 

Nationwide DSN Report 

A wave of shoplifting, 
spurred in part by high infla- 
tion, is causing discounters to 
intensify their security opera- 
tions and in the process to 
change the focus from catching 
shoplifters to merely deterring 
them. 

In some cases security men 
are donning their badges for 
the first time to let customers 
know who they are. In many 
cases, loss-prevention person- 
nel are training clerks and cash- 
iers to spot the potential shop- 
lifter and prevent the crime 
before it occurs. 

In addition, many discount- 
ers are reporting big rises in the 
less costly problems of price-tag 
switching and fraudulent re- 
turns, and are beginning train- 
ing programs to help clerks and 
cashiers combat these as well. 

“The answer is to be pre- 
ventive,” explained a Woolco 
spokesman. “You don’t want to 
catch someone and have to ac- 
cuse.” 

Most discounters surveyed 
said the recent wave of shoplift- 
ing appears to have begun from 
eight to 10 months ago, with the 
problem worsening as the year 
progressed and the economy 
deteriorated. 

Zayre, for example, reported 
15,000 shoplifting incidents 
through August—an 18% in- 
crease over the identical period 
in 1979. For Nebraska-based 
Pamida, the increase has been 
25% to 30%. 

Ironically, the shoplifting 
boom seems to come after four 


years of industry gains in com- 
bating the problem. 

According to a recent Na- 
tional Mass Retailing Institute 
study of 38 chains, stock short- 
age as a percentage of sales de- 
clined from 2.61 in the 1975-76 
fiscal year to 2.09 in the 1979-80 
year. 

Although chains with sales 
ranging from $100 million to 
$260 million reported their 
stock shortage went from 
2.49% to 2.79% of sales in the 
sampling. 

One of the larger discount 
chains to begin a major pro- 
gram aimed at deterrence is 
Hills. 

Starting last October two- 
hour training programs were 
begun that will be given to all 
employees three times per 
year. 

The purpose of the programs, 
explained David Baldwin, Hills’ 
director of loss prevention, is to 
explain the value of merchan- 
dise to cashiers so they will be 


more likely to spot items with 
switched price tags. 

The program was begun after 
cashiers failed to question the 
unusually low prices that were 
appearing on an increasing 
number of items. In two in- 
stances, Baldwin said chain 
saws were sold for $7.97 and 
$9.87. 

In addition, he noted Cole- 
man coolers and bathroom ham- 
pers were becoming a favorite 
vehicle for shoplifters who 
filled them with high-ticket 
items and hoped that cashiers 
didn’t check inside before ring- 
ing them up. 

Apparently the program is 
working, with a rising number 
of misticketed items being dis- 
covered. Last month one such 
theft was averted when a newly 
trained cashier questioned the 
$7.28 price on an $89.98 electric 
sander. 

Zayre has also begun a train- 
ing program for its 22,000 em-

FIC Decision Could Untie Discounters From Warranty Bind 


NEW YORK—The Federal 
Trade Commission is consider- 
ing an NMRI request that 
manufacturers be required to 
print their warranties on prod- 
uct boxes—a move that would 
free discounters from having to 
maintain a warranty file in each 
store. } 

A favorable decision by the 
FTC would take more than a 
year to implement, but dis- 
eounters said shifting the re- 
sponsibility to manufacturers 
would save them thousands of 
dollars each year in wasted cler- 
ical time. 

The request to change the 
procedure by which the public 
is given access to warranty in- 


formation before the purchase 
of a product was made in late 
July by the NMRI, acting with 
the support of 17 major dis- 
counters who supplied state- 
ments from store managers 
attesting to the inadequacy of 
the present system. 

Discounters have been re- 
quired to keep warranty infor- 
mation, on all the products they 
carry, on display in each store 
since 1977 as a result of the pas- 
sage of the Magnuson-Moss 
Warranty Act in 1975. 

Kevin Shein, NMRI govern- 
mental affairs director, said the 
act was passed by Congress in 
an attempt to increase con- 
sumer awareness, but that it 


has failed to do so. 

Shein and spokesmen for 
chains such as Zayre, Cook 
United and others said rela- 
tively few customers have 
asked to see the file before pur- 
chasing a product. 

A spokesman for Cook 
United, for example, said the 
chain maintains a collection of 
guarantees and warranties in a 
binder in each of its 82 stores. A 
survey of managers indicated, 
however, that in 95% of the 
stores no one has ever looked at 
the binder. 

For Zayre, which has more 
than 12,000 hard line products, 
maintaining the binder has also 
been difficult. A spokesman for 


the chain said binders must be 
maintained in each of the 
chain’s 256 stores. 

In addition, discounters said 
many of the binders in stores 
throughout the nation may be 
inaccurate because manufac- 
turers seldom send them noti- 
fication of changes in various 
products’ warranties. 

Rachael Miller, an FTC staff 
attorney, declined to comment 
on the possibility that the rules 
will be changed. 

She said it is possible the 
NMRI petition will be dis- 
missed, but that the FTC could 
also devise a plan to share the 
burden between retailers and 
manufacturers more fairly. 


open two stores in Phoenix, 
Ariz.—the chain’s first venture 
into that market. 

The chain also recently com- 
pleted the remodeling and 
20,000-sq.-ft. expansion of its 
Hollywood flagship. 


New Moves 


Arnold Suval, Zodys presi- 
dent, said the chain expects to 
make its first move out of Cal- 
ifornia and into the Phoenix 
market with at least two stores, 
each 80,000 sq. ft., inthe spring 
of 1981. A third Phoenix unit 
may be added before the end of 
next year. 

Zodys, which reported sales 
of $305 million in the last com- 
pleted fiscal year, is also ex- 
pected to remodel five to six 
units in 1981, Suval said, noting 
that the chain’s expansive re- 
modeling program will be com- 
pleted within the next 2 to 2% 
years. 

Hartfield-Zodys’ officials 
yroject sales to reach about 
$440 million for the current fis- 
cal year, with the Zodys divi- 
sion contributing an estimated 
$340 million. 


Sales Estimated 


Approximately 75% of the 
total corporate general mer- 
chandise sales are generated by 
the Zodys division. Within Zo- 
dys, 75.6%, or sales of $230.3 
million during the last fiscal 
year, came from company-oper- 
ated departments. Suval point- 
ed out that this didn’t include 
sales of the Karl’s Shoe depart- 
ments, which are owned by 
Hartfield-Zodys, and operated 
in the Zodys units. 

Presently, Hartfield-Zodys 
has 450,000 sq. ft. of warehouse 
and distribution facilities, of 
which 300,000 is devoted to the 
Zodys units. However, “within 
the next couple of years,” Ed 
Solomon, Hartfield-Zodys 
chairman and ceo, said, “the 
company will need more dis- 
tribution facilities.” 

Preliminary estimates of 
earnings for the second quar- 
ter, which ended Aug. 1, were 
not “relatively good,” Solomon 
said, but the numbers in the 
quarter are usually “relatively 
low.” He pointed out that 85% of 
the company’s earnings are re- 
alized in the last six months of 
the fiscal year.

Dewar to Address Annual NRMA Conference 


LOS ANGELES—Robert 
Dewar, chairman of K mart’s 
executive and finance commit- 
tees, will make the keynote ad- 
dress at the 22nd annual data 
processing and retail systems 
conference held by the National 
Retail Merchants Association 
Oct. 19-22 at the Marriott Hotel 
in Los Angeles. 

The 60 different sessions in- 
clude case studies involving a 


number of discounters. 

Zayre’s efforts to improve re- 
lations with uses of its data pro- 
cessing system will be the topic 
of a session Oct. 22 from 1:45 
p.m. to 3 p.m. Zayre executives 
participating are Mervyn 
Weich, senior vice president of 
systems and technical services: 
William Harmon, manager of 
business systems interface; 
Arthur Loewy, senior vp, fi- 


nance, and Stepher Wener, vice 
president merchandising. 

Woolworth’s use of computer 
graphics and communications 
technology to distribute store 
forms and other communica- 
tions will be detailed by a com- 
pany executive on Oct. 20 from 
3:45 p.m. to 5 p.m. 

Procession of fashion apparei 
through a distribution center 
will be discussed by Lee Paul- 


son, vp management informa- 
tion systems for Lucky Stores, 
parent of Gemco/Memco, on 
Oct. 21 from 10:45 a.m. to noon. 

Delegates to the conference 
can register through NRMA’s 
information systems division at 
100 West 31st St., New York, 
N.Y. 10001. Fees for NRMA 
members range from $i35 for 
one day to $265 for the full con- 
ference.

discounters once again opened 


up the pipeline and began to 
rebuild their depleted invento- 
ries. 

True, retail-dollar movement 
and unit movement totals were 
off substantially from what 
they were last year at this time. 
For example, only one listed 
item produced more than 
$10,000 in retail sales, while 
last year there were four. 

Coleman’s gallon can of 
Champion camping fuel sold 
5,267 units, generating retail 
sales estimated at $20,018. 

Nevertheless, there was a 
sales burst during the closing 
end of the period that included 
heavy movement of camping 
equipment, basketballs and 
items like the Hoppe shotgun 
cleaning kit, in addition to fish- 
ing and hunting equipment. 

The rod and reel making the 
biggest gain was the Zebco 33 
reel with the 3366 rod, with a 
total of 162 units moved. A year 
ago only 90 of the units were 
sold into discount stores. 

Smaller gains were reported 
with both the top of the line— 
Zebco’s 808 reel with the 8965 
rod—and with the less expen- 
sive Zebco rods and reels. 

The reluctance of discounters 
to maintain normal inventory 
levels and to advertise as much 
as they had last year began to 
make itself felt in April and was 
a major factor in the slowdown. 

One previously popular prod- 
uct that was hard hit by the 
advertising decline was Rem- 
ington’s .22 cal. Thunderbolt 
ammunition. 

Last year, during a similar 
period, the item moved 6,300 
units. This year, though, only 
2,200 units were sold. 

Substantial price increases in 
Coleman equipment over the 
last two years—and in the last 
year in particular—also hurt 
sales. 

A Coleman two-burner 
stove, for example, carrying an 
average retail price of $24.40, 
reflected a 29% increase over 
last year’s price, which trans- 
lated into a drop in unit sales. 

Propane fuel came in second 
on the list of Coleman best-sell- 
ers, with a total of 1,740 units 
moved. 

Fire extinguishers also per- 
formed reasonably well. The 
best retail dollar producer was 
a Kidde Fireaway extinguisher, 
carrying an average price 
ticket of $22, although it was 
Kidde’s low-end $8.64 model 
that produced the greatest unit 
volume.

If promotions come to you as a surprise, look into Ashflash 
Lighting promotions. Our 12-month promotions calendar offers 
you everything from key-chain lights to camping lanterns. 
Ashflash Lighting promotions include the right products to build 
traffic and sales—at the right price and the right time. 


THE RIGHT PRICE POINTS 


Ashflash Lighting promotions include disposable lights for 
under a dollar, functional flashlights for the car in the two-dollar- 
and-up range and lamps and lanterns for the right gift 
item — products that give you the right price points at the right 
time. 


THE RIGHT TIME OF YEAR 


Our 12-month promotions calendar lets you plan promotions 
for Dad-days, Grad-days, Dollar-days or Holidays. That means 
the right product, at the right price, for stocking stuffers at 


Christmas or camping in the summer. 

Our 12-month promotions calendar replaces the surprise 
packages that other suppliers use to reduce their inventories, 
with the right products, at the right price and at the right time to 
build traffic and sales.

with their sales.

NMRI Weighs 
Marking Codes 


CHICAGO—The nine-mem- 
ber National Mass Retailing In- 
stitute Marking Standards 
Committee was set to meet 
Oct. 15 and 16 at the Marriott 
Hotel here to decide on a rec- 
ommendation for its board of di- 
rectors on which tack the dis- 
count industry should take to 
modernize its marking code 
system. 

The choices are to give a vote 
of confidence to one of four sys- 
tems, to decide that no system 
should be endorsed, or (and 
NMRi chairman Richard 
Hersh said this is most likely) 
to recommend further study of 
the issue. 

The UPC (Universal Product 
Code), OCR-A and/or -B (Opti- 
cal Character Recognition), a 
system that combines both of 
these codes, or the continental 
version of the UPC, the Euro- 
pean Article Number code, are 
the four code choices. 

While NMRI president Da- 
vid Godfrey said one of his ob- 
jectives in office would be to 
develop a consensus on the is- 
sue, members of the committee 
said their objective was to 
create a forum of ideas, and in

Chapter XI Petition a Surprise 


DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, OCTOBER 20, 1980 


Sam Solomon’s Fiscal Woes Laid to Banks’ Harsher Loan Terms 


CHARLESTON, S.C.— 
Why did Sam Solomon, in a 
move that surprised other 
showroom operators and sup- 
pliers, file a Chapter XI peti- 
tion? 

The move, made in Federal 
Bankruptcy Court in Colum- 
bia, S.C., startled the industry 
on two counts: first, the cata- 
loger wasn’t insolvent and, sec- 
ond, it reported more than $12 
million in net worth in fiscal 
1980. 

The losses on sales gains for 
the quarter and half-year, both 
of which ended before the bank- 


FIC Is Expected 


ruptcy filing late last month, 
aren’t seen as enough of a rea- 
son for the Chapter XI move. 

The half-year loss went up 
60% to $1,458,000 on an 11.5% 
sales gain to $33,000,000. In 
the quarter, loss jumped by 
more than 900% to $634,000 on 
a 10.3% sales increase to $17,- 
200,000. 

Company executives, assert- 
ing that all debts will be paid in 
full, and other sources point to 
the cataloger’s three lender 
banks as cause for the filing.

and president, said the banks 


to Ease Guide 


Covering Warranty Advertising 


WASHINGTON—Within 
the next six months, the 
Federal Trade Commission is 
expected to loosen its 
guidelines regarding warrant 
advertising. When the FT 
completes its present — the 
proposed changes should, for 
the first time in 20 years, make 
it simpler for retailers and 
manufacturers to advertise 
warranty products. 

The public comment period 
on recommendations for 
changes was scheduled to end 
in early October, but a staff 
member of the FTC said an ex- 
tension was likely. 

At issue is how much dis- 
closure is necessary for a war- 
ranty advertisement to avoid 
deception. The present guides 
require that advertising men- 
tioning a warranty must dis- 
close all the terms, conditions 
and limitations of the warranty. 

But, as the commission offi- 
cial noted, these requirements 
have added substantial costs 
and have served as deterrents 
to advertising warranties. At 
the time the requirements were 
issued—in 1960—warranty ad- 
vertisements generally were 
the only way warranty informa- 
tion was available to consumers 
before an item was purchased. 


The Magnuson-Moss War- 
ranty Act, however, which be- 
came effective in 1975, required 
that the terms of written war- 
ranties be available prior to 
sale. Among other provisions, 
Magnuson-Moss required that 
warranty information be avail- 
able at point-of-sale. 

The alternative presently 
being considered by the com- 
mission for warranty advertis- 
—— the following: 

e@ Warranty advertising would 
be treated like most other 
forms of advertising, and the 
commission would rely on exist- 
ing advertising laws to deter- 
mine which warranty advertis- 
ing is deceptive. 

9 hibited on a rule or case- 
by-case basis would be specific 
language in warranty advertis- 
ing which is found to be decep- 
tive. For example, if the phrase 
“X-year limited warranty” was 
determined to be deceptive, 
use of that phrase would be pro- 
hibited. 

@ Required by rule or on a 
case-by-case basis would be dis- 
closures to remedy deceptive 
warranty advertising so that 
customers would not 5 misled 
by partial information. For ex- 
ample, if a warranty advertise-

Aerial Display Lends 
Bike-Store Flavor 


Increased productivity 
frequently means more 
merchandise in the 
Same—or less—floor 
space. One way to get 
more into less is to use the 
air space above normal 
floor displays. 

The Treasury, Granada 
Hills, Calif., packs its air 
space with bicycles hung 
from a steel frame sus- 
pended above the typical 
bike display. 

The aerial display also 
provides an unmistakable 
signature for the depart- 
ment, and helps create a 
massive ‘“we’re-in-the- 
business’ look for the de- 
partment. The slightly 
raised platform adds to the 
look. 

These preassembled 
bikes are hung by the front 
rim on large hooks, easily 
lifted down for close ex- 
amination or sale, if nec- 
essary. 

The sale table in the 
middle of the display adds 
to a sense of complete- 
ness, and brings tie-in 
Sales of accessories with 
each bike sale. (DSNphoto)

Payroll Costs Are Spiraling as Per Cent of Sales 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Spiraling wages have put se- 
vere upward pressure on 
payro!l costs as a percentage of 
sales in discount department 
store chains. 

According to the 1979-80 Na- 
tional Mass Retailing Institute 
study of the industry's operat- 
ing results—its annual Cornell 
University survey—the num- 
ber of chains that keep payroll 
under 11% of sales has dropped 
sharply. 

The NMRI study of 38 dis- 
count chains includes 30 chains 
that have participated for at 
least two consecutive years. Of 
those 30 identical firms, only 
six reported payrolls under 
11%, with an average of 10.19%. 
The preceding year, 11 of the 
same group of companies had 


song 


reported payroll percentages 
under 11%. 

More than half of the 30 iden- 
tical firms—16—reported 
payrolls between 11% and 13% 
of sales, averaging 12.11%. The 
year before, = 12 had been in 
that range. 

Eight firms from the group of 
30 reported payrolls in excess of 
13%—averaging 14.31%—an in- 
crease from the 1978-79 NMRI 
study, which had shown 7 
chains with payrolls in excess of 
13%. 

Net income as a percentage 
of sales fell sharply, from 2.5% 
to 1.6%, among those six chains 
that maintained payroll ratios 
under 11%. A causal relation- 
ship between the two facts is 
unlikely, however, and that in- 
come decline is the probable re- 
sult of other pressures on earn- 
ing power. 

The net income percentage 
for chains with higher payroll 
ratios rose. Among the 16 
chains with payrolls between 
11% and 13%, the net income 
rose to 2.29% of sales from 
1.82% the year before. 

A lower net percentage ac- 
companies the highest payroll 
ratios, with those chains with 
payrolls in excess of 13% net-

Solomon’s Woes Laid to Banks’ Terms 


(Continued from page 2) 
ange on the cataloger’s fil- 

A NCNB executive said 
the bank’s policy didn’t allow 
him to comment on loan terms. 
Neither the banks nor Sam Sol- 
omon executives would detail 
what the harsher lending terms 
were. 

Factors behind the banks’ ac- 
tion reportedly include inven- 
tory problems and poor earn- 
ings in the fiscal year ended 
Jan. 28, 1980. Also contributing 
to the crackdown was $4,250, - 
000 in seasonal loans outstand- 
ing at the end of the fiscal year. 
The company’s lending slate 
had been wiped clean at the 
close of previous fiscal years. 

“The banks seemed to feel 
that prudent lending policies 
required a change in the 
terms,” one source said. 

Without explaining why the 
banks imposed new require- 
ments, Reese said the banks 
first agreed to “essentially the 
same type of unsecured sea- 
sonal borrowing as in the past 
and the company had begun to 
take down these funds. We got 
only a portion when the banks 
imposed the new require- 
ments.” 

The cataloger’s sales went up 
in the past fiscal year by 26.7% 
to $88,034,300 from $69,461,- 
400. But net income plunged 
from $1,665,600 to only $124,- 
600.

Reese cited the cataloger’s 
shift to a LIFO accounting 
method during the year and a 
68.8% jump in interest ex- 
penses—or $1,138,500—due to 
increased short-term borrow- 
ing, higher interest rates and 
interest on capitalized equip- 
ment leases as contributing to 
the cataloger’s situation. 

The two accounting changes 
were a switch to LIFO that de- 
creased net income by $397,000 
and expensing store openings 
as they occurred, rather than 
over a two-year period, which 
reduced net income by $362,- 
400. 

Besides the accounting 
changes, Sam Solomon in fiscal 
1980 had to write off about $1 
million in inventory and take 
down cumulative start-up costs 
of about $1.4 million, some for 
the past year and the rest for 
the opening of its Pembroke 
Pines, Fla., unit in late Novem- 
ber, just before the close of the 
fiscal year. 

The cataloger’s concern 
about its inventory was evident 
in a report by Melvin Solomon 
earlier this year that the com- 
pany had “instituted additional 
inventory planning and con- 
trols which resulted in in- 
creased inventory turn.” He 
added he “plans to increase em- 
phasis on data processing to 
provide the latest and most ac- 
curate information on inven- 
tory, including calculations on 
return on investment.” 

These moves, he said, “will 
allow the company to better 
evaluate the performance of its 
operations and merchandising 
strategies.” 

Sam Solomon is currently ne- 


gotiating for interim financing 
with one lender, a company ex- 
ecutive said, to go along with » 
the support offered by its major 
suppliers. 

At a creditors committee 
meeting called at presstime, 
the company’s vendors infor- 
mally agreed to continue to 
supply the cataloger, with most 
of the manufacturers shipping 
merchandise to allow the com- 
pany to back the Merchandis- 
ers Association Inc. catalog it 
distributes for its 11 showrooms 
in four Southeast states. 

Reese said there would be 
only a minor cutback in the 
number of books distributed 
and that no changes were 
planned in the cataloger’s ex- 
tensive fourth-quarter ro- 
togravure program—two fliers 
a month in the period before 
Christmas. 

While backing the catalog is 
vital for showroom operators, 
it’s slightly less important for 
Sam Solomon, whose units 
mass display most categories. 

All of Sam Solomon’s show- 
rooms are reportedly profitable 
except for the Pembroke Pines 
unit which hasn’t completed a 
full year of operation. 

Reese said the company had 
no plans to close any show- 
rooms or make any extensive 
changes in its operations. 

Sam Solomon is due to pre- 
sent its financial plan to its 
creditors just after Christmas. 
The nine-member creditors 
committee is composed of the 
three banks and the six largest 
vendors: General Electric first, 
followed by Texas Instruments, 
Panasonic, Mattel, and Milton 
Bradley.

Among Basics

By Harold Rubin 
President 

HalMar Inc., Distributors 

Discounters seem to have 
successfully adjusted house- 
wares merchandising to cope 
with the fluc- : 
tuating econ- 
omy by sharp- 
ly focusing on 
traditional 
fast-turning 
staples such as 
cookware with 
nonstick fin- 
ishes and 
eight-piece 
glassware 98 
sets. ee. 

The Product Movement Au- 
dit report for the Jan. 1 through 
Aug. 6 period, covering the 
months with the widest shifts 
in the economy, denotes this re- 
sponsive merchandising—the 
top items in all 10 categories 
were old reliable products such 
as 20-pe. Corelle sets in table- 
top, Ekeo Baker’s Secret 
Elowaen in cookware, large- 
size wastebaskets and laundry 
baskets in Rubbermaid and 
Menu-ette sets and small por- 
tion microwave cookware in 
Corning Ware. 

That discounters and other 
retailers have been relying 
heavily on housewares basics is 
evident from the 100 items that 
made the PMA, 86 of which 
were among the top 100 best 
sellers in the previous report. 

Of the 14 items not on the last 
report, 13 were housewares 
that appeared on earlier PMAs. 
Only one item is new to the 
chart—a 24%-qt. Corning Ware 
casserole in the French White

It's Christmas as Usual in Well-to-do Houston 


Tale of 2 Cities: a Contrast in Economies, Sales 


By Chris Haggerty 

“Christmas is Christmas,” 
said one woman who had just 
been shopping at a Target in 
Houston. “I’ll probably be 
spending a little more than last 
year.” 

This answer reflects the atti- 
tudes shared by most custom- 
ers polled by DSN in Houston 
about their Christmas plans. 
These consumers weren't feel- 
ing the economic pinch as were 
shoppers polled in recession- 
worn Cleveland—where most 
plan to chop Christmas spend- 
ing by half or more. 


Whether they live in Houston 
or Cleveland, however, discount 
store customers are shopping 
the ads and becoming more 
price-selective today than ever 
before. What makes “business 
as usual” more difficult in 
Cleveland is consumer cutbacks 
on impulse purchases. 

In Houston, shoppers were 
leaving the stores with both un- 
planned as well as planned pur- 
chases, while most customers 
in Cleveland had stuck to shop- 
ping lists composed before they 
entered the store. 

This fallout in impulse shop- 


ping has virtually destroyed 
the primary benefit and pur- 
pose of promotional activity— 
to draw traffic to higher-gross- 
ing departments. In Cleveland, 
this fallout has led to declines in 
store sales and profits and a 
succession of cost-cutting mea- 
sures at store level. 

Those were some of the find- 
ings of a DSN study of the 
Cleveland and Houston mar- 
kets, representing the Indus- 
trial Belt and Sunbelt, respec- 
tively, to determine how the 
economic climate of each mar- 
ket has affected consumer buy- 


ing patterns and store opera- 
tions. 

Houston, with its low unem- 
ployment rate of 4.6% (August 
figure) and average after-tax 
household income of $25,520, 
continues to be a fast-paced 
growth market for many dis- 
counters including Target, 
Woolco, and T.G. & Y. 

Cleveland cannot boast of 
similar economic health. The 
city has suffered along with the 
auto, rubber and steel indus- 
tries that account for a large 
part of its citizens’ employ- 
ment. Unemployment rates 


dynamics of each market. 

The most striking contrast 
between the areas was in 1m- 
pulse sales activity. One 
mother of three had driven out 
of her way to pick up specific 
items on sale at the Zayre store 
in Brook Park, a suburb of 
Cleveland. “I only buy ad 
items,” she explained. “I sit 
back and wait until an item I 
need is on sale. I usually shop at 
the K mart near my home but 
Zayre’s sale on paper products 
this week made it worth the 
trip.” 

Most consumers surveyed in 


the Cleveland market spoke of 
considerable cutbacks in im- 
pulse purchases, and store 
managers there were well 


have hovered around 8% in re- 
cent months, and reductions in 
work hours hurt those still em- 
ployed. 


Patrons Cut Gift Plans in Depressed Cleveland 


CLEVELAND—tThe lack of 
confidence in the economy that 
has put a crimp in impulse sales 
activity in the Cleveland mar- 
ket is also reflected in consum- 
ers’ conservative plans for 
Christmas there. 

Discounters in the area have 
responded by predicting stable 
or minimal sales increases this 
coming holiday season, and 
have adjusted inventories ac- 
cordingly. 

A majority of disccutit store 
shoppers surveyed by DSN in 
Cleveland said they would be 
paring down Christmas expen- 
ditures by half or more. 

“We’ve already bought our 
two boys their ‘big’ Christmas 
present,” said one customer 
shopping a K mart with his 
family. “In years past, we usu- 
ally spent about $100 on each 


kid. But this year we didn’t 
spend more than $25 on each of 
them—and that includes 
clothes and toys.” 

Uncle Bill’s, one chain that 
has been hard-hit by the sales 
slowdown, will be a little more 
selective on electronic toys, 
more prudent in its buying of 
trim-a-tree items (to eliminate 
excess markdowns), and will 
concentrate on the age-old 
basics in toys and clothing, ac- 
cording to one store manager. 

Inventory quantities have 
been cut in traffic appliances, 
he added. The chain is project- 
ing slightly lower sales than 
last year’s, and no increases in 
promotional dollars for sea- 
sonal advertising. 

A K mart manager projected 
single-digit increases over last 
year’s Christmas sales for his 


store. “No one is going to drop a 
lot of money on kids this Christ- 
mas,” he explained. “They’ll be 
doing what they did for back-to- 
school—shopping every ad that 
came out. The competition is 
going to be fierce.” 

Zayre stores in the market 
will benefit from a slightly ac- 
celerated advertising program 
this Christmas, according to 
Malcolm Sherman, executive 
vice president and general 
manager. “We're really excited 
by what we’re coming out with 
in our circulars, radio and TV 
advertising for the season,” he 
added. 

Zayre’s headquarters man- 
agement is predicting only 
slight sales increases over last 
year’s Christmas performance 
for the 10 Cleveland metro 
stores, Sherman said.

Quilted Place Mats Sew Up 
Rising-Star Role in Domestics 


By Laura Mulcahy 
Domestics Market Outlook 
Quilted place mats have the 

jump on the spring 1981 kitchen 
domestics market, thanks to 
last season’s coordinate empha- 
sis and manufacturers’ new pro- 
lificness, both springboards to 
heated activity in the category. 

Buyers emphasized enthusi- 
astically for spring (and, for 
those buying closer to season, 
Christmas) heavy mat pro- 
grams in quilted cloths and 
stepped-up commitments to 
natural fibers. 

De-emphasized were viny] 
place mats, in response to grow- 
ing consumer disinterest in sta- 
ples, and tablecloths in all 
fabrications, to beef up high 
unit-volume place mat busi- 
ness. 

“The unit volume is abso- 
lutely incredible. I don’t see an 


end to it,” said Dan Ryan, a 
Target buyer. 

Ryan anticipates place mats 
will do $1 million to $2 million in 
the spring, more than doubling 
the classification’s sales contri- 
bution to kitchen domestics. 

“We’ve been developing 
kitchen domestics and expand- 
ing place mats for the last year 
and one half, and we bought ac- 
cordingly for spring,” said 
Ryan, who pared basics from 
50% to 30% of the mix and in- 
creased quilteds and straws. 
With 6-10 solid and 8-20 print 
offerings, he expects sales to in-

They Up Traffic, Lose $$, Housewares Panel Told 


The outlook for housewares and small appliances in the face of the weak economy was the 
topic of a recent DSN panel. Retailer participants included Angelo Bianco, assistant vice 
president, Jamesway; Alan Long, vice president, merchandise manager, hard lines, Magic 
Mart; Ron McDiarmid, dmm, hard lines, Zodys; Jim Peters, dmm, Hills, and Dean Stokes, 
dmm, Cook United. Manufacturer participants included Ed Donaldson, vp, marketing, 


Rubbermaid; Bill Foley, manager, marketing services, Anchor Hocking; Dick Gonzalez, vp, 
advertising, Norelco; John J. Higgins, vp, product marketing, Moulinex; Paul Miltenberger, 
national marketing manager, and Terry Nauslar, marketing manager, Reynolds Metal; Jack 
O’Dea, retail sales development manager, Corning Glass, and David Weger, national sales 


manager, Panasonic. 


Stu Horton: Thank you 
for coming. We want to get 
down to basics, so let’s find 
out from the discounters 
what the prognostication is 
as to housewares for the rest 
of the year in this economy. 
Then we can have some give- 
and-take on how we are 
going to make housewares a 
better category in the re- 
mainder of 1980. 


Angelo Bianco: Well, I 
think packaging will play a 
very important part as far as 
telling the consumer why 
they need that product, and 
why it is a necessity rather 
than a luxury. That’s the key. 
I think we all have to realize 
that we can’t continually 
mark our merchandise up 
and up, because eventually 
we are going to get out of 
price range. 

There is just so much 
money that can be spent. De- 
duct the utility bills and en- 


ergy-related products and 
there is just so much that is 
left. It is going to be spent on 
a consumer product that is 
needed, that is a must for 
their household. If you can’t 
get that across, then we are 
not going to sell the product. 
As far as an edge is con- 
cerned, it is a twofold thing. 
The item has to be in de- 
mand, and it has to be ex- 
plained to the consumer. 
Then it’s our job to make 
sure that we have it on our 
shelves at the right price. 


David Weger: I am curi- 
ous. In a soft marketplace 
such as ours, do you see the 
retailer forming and putting 
together price reductions, 
using top name brands as op- 
posed to brand X products? 
Will you be staying with 
name brands as opposed to 
the off-shoot items, and will 
you be running more ads at 
an intensified level for con- 


sumer appeal with price? 
Does that seem to be the 
trend for a soft marketplace? 


Jim Peters: I would like to 
respond to that. National 
brands are a double-edged 
sword. Most of us will agree 
that we are working on lower 
markups with a lot of the na- 
tional brands. That makes it 
more difficult to come across 
to the customer with a value 
image because your every- 
day price is based on a lower 
margin. 

It becomes difficult to 
build traffic using national 
brands unless you are willing 
to lose money. I think that 
might be the danger for the 
rest of the year—to fall into 
the trap of losing money on 
promotional items. We have 
dangerously low markups up 
front, so where do you go 
from there?

Frank and Hays 


Resume Chain 
Prexy Positions 


Special DSN Report 

Hal Frank and Thomas Hays 
have resumed their previous 
positions as president of Brad- 
lees and Venture, respectively, 
causing some industry tongues 
to wag. 

Frank, who left Bradlees a 
few months ago to “go home to 
Abraham & Straus,” resumed 
his still-open position at Brad- 
lees for “family consider- 
ations,” according to a spokes- 
man. 

In St. Louis, Hays returned 
as president and chief executive 
officer of The May Co.’s Ven- 
ture, replacing Ira ¢ es who 
had headed the chain for only 16 
months. 

The official explanation of 
Quint’s departure cited his in- 
terest in pursuing “other busi- 
ness interests.” 

But speculation on the 
change centers on Venture’s 
still lackluster performance 
years after the chain bit off a 
big part of Chicago with its ac- 
quisition of Turn-Style. 

Quint had been expected, be- 
cause of his merchandising 
background, to perk up Ven- 
ture’s sales performance 
through merchandising strat- 
egems. His department store 
background was considered a 
plus in that area. 

Hays, who is familiar with 
Venture from his previous term 
as president, is a financial man. 

“There may have been some 
conflict, or confusion on the op- 
erations side,” explained one 
Venture insider. “The feeling in 
the company is that Hays is ex- 
pected to coordinate, with his 
discounting background, the 
operations and financial sides 
more effectively than Quint.” 

Quint’s experience at Sears, 
Roebuck also worked against 
him at Venture. While insiders 


; ; 


Venture'’s Hays 


Bradlees Frank 


cited his energy (a “ball of fire”), 
they also said he “locked him- 
self in his office and expected 
his staff to execute,” as it had at 
Sears. 

“But in this industry, where 
if you don’t do it it doesn’t get 
done, that’s the wrong move,” 
said a Venture executive. 

“You can’t bring in a depart- 
ment store guy and expect him 
to do the job,” said another 
Venture executive. “Hays has 
the background to understand 
and improve our operations.” 


Commentator Levine Urges More Worker Productivity 


MBS Show Shoppers to Focus on Basics 


MIAMI BEACH—Discount- 
ers attending the Merchants 
Buying Syndicate MultiMart 
‘80 show here last month re- 
ported that sales so far hadn’t 
reflected any major economic 
upturn, and that staple goods 
were the only merchandise sell- 
ing consistently. 

Fourth-quarter plans, they 
said, are to sharply focus on 
basics to guard against further 
sales erosion. 

One merchandiser explained: 
“We want to maintain our base, 
even though we may miss out on 
any possible big fourth-quarter 
jump in the economy.” 

While discounters shopping 
the show were eying the imme- 
diate economic situation, the 
long-range outlook was dis- 
cussed by NBC News economic 
affairs correspondent Irving R. 
Levine, the featured speaker at 
the 3lst semiannual exhibition. 

Levine's prescription to solve 
the nation’s long-term economic 
problems was to increase work- 
ers productivity and encourage 
business investments in plants 
and equipment. 

Productivity in the United 
States, he reported, “has been 
declining while it is increasing 
in the major competitor na- 
tions.” The decline in produc- 
tivity, he added, “has made the 
inflation problem worse... 
and the current high level of in- 
flation will make our recovery 
slower and more difficult.” 

Levine, however, pointed to 
some hopeful signs for the fu- 
ture. 

“There is a clearer under- 
standing in Congress and 
among the Presidential candi- 
dates that any long-range solu- 
tion to inflation depends on 
increasing and improving pro- 
ductivity,” he said. 

There is also the realization 
that the nation “needs a more 
favorable tax climate for indus- 
try to make investments to in- 
crease productivity through 


new technology and other 
methods. . . and a need to re- 
duce Government regulations 
that result in higher costs.” 

Energy is the other major 
economic problem facing the 
nation. “We need to be self-suf- 
ficient to overcome the whims 
of OPEC,” Levine declared. 
“The Congress and the Admin- 
istration now realize that this is 
feasible only when there are 
price incentives to support en- 
ergy development.” 

The long-range answers to 
solving the problem of inflation 
aren’t seen as having the same 
adverse impact on the country 
as the immediate short-range 
solution. Levine said that this is 
“the current painful recession.” 

The newscaster asserted that 
political efforts have resulted in 
the major candidates “outdoing

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, NOVEMBER 3, 1980 


Discounters’ Margins, 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Discounters boosted their 
gross margins by 3.6% and 
their pretax income by 1.2% but 
saw sales per square foot fall by 
60¢ in the 1979-80 fiscal period. 

Conventional department 
stores, in these key fiscal mea- 
surements, showed markedly 
different results: Gross mar- 
gins remained flat and pretax 
income dropped 8.2% but sales 
per square foot jumped 6.5% or 
$6.92. 

The figures for discounters 
cover chains that had sales in 
the $100 million-$260 million 
range. The figures for conven- 
tional department stores cover 
chains with volume over $100 
million. 

The discounter statistics 


Pretax Net Rise; Sales/Ft. Dip | 


Conventional Stores’ Sales/Ft. Jump But Pretax Net Drops 


came from the National Mass 
Retailing Institute’s Operating 
Results of Self-Service Dis- 
count Department Stores 
1979-80, and cover about 15 
firms, most of which reported 
results for the 1978-79 and 
1979-80 fiscal periods. 
Conventional department 
stores’ information came from 
the National Retail Merchants 
Association’s Financial and Op- 
erating Results (FOR) report, 
with 28 firms generating a total 
of just over $6 billion in sales 
reporting for the 1979-80 pe- 
riod, and 29 companies produc- 
ing $6.2 billion in volume re- 
porting for the 1978-79 period. 


Discounters’ gross margins 
hit 30.73% from 29.65% while 
conventional department 
stores had a much smaller in- 
crease, going from 42.32% to 
42.61%. The big jump in dis- 
counters’ margins reflects the 
continuing effort to trade up 
lines. 

The discounters’ improved 
gross margins helped to boost 
pretax income from 4.14% to 
4.19%. 

The flat gross margin for con- 
ventional department stores, 
coupled with higher expenses, 
helped reduce their pretax in- 
come to 5.45% from 5.94%.

Promos, Discounts Help Restore 


DSN Nationwide Report 

Discounters are experienc- 
ing revived book sales as buyers 
go heavier into promotions, fic- 
tion titles and, in some cases, 
children’s books. 

Discounting basics—mer- 
chandising the 20% of product 
that does 80% of the business— 
and aggressive promotions 
have played a large part in 
keeping sales hot at discount 
stores, while the retail book in- 
dustry is generally stagnant. 

Increased sales at most 
chains, compared to last year, 
are also being generated by re- 
fining mixes. 

“It’s a fashion business. You 
have to be flexible enough to 
change quarterly,” said as- 
sistant Target buyer Marshall 
Hanson. 

Book sales increased across 
the board for spring, with hard- 
covers up 31%%, paperbacks 
27%%, children’s 482%, and 
magazines 132% at the chain. 

The newest addition is a 
top-10 selection of paperbacks, 
whieh has been excellent, 
Hanson said. He has empha- 


sized a promotional push in the 
chain’s 80-ft. departments, 
which have three tables and 
four endcaps. Those tables now 
display one-time buys of re- 
maindered hardcovers, and 
seasonal promotions of cook- 
books or Bibles, for instance. 

Children’s books are slated as 
a growth category. 

“I want to expand sku’s. The 
potential is in more sku'’s per 
square foot,” Hanson said. 

At Venture, children’s books 
have been the “single fastest- 
growing category” for the last 
18 months, buyer Mike Martin 
said, noting that sales are way 
up from last year’s flat volume. 

“We’re showing an increase, 
and we’re discounting books for 
the first time,” Martin said. 
This year, the chain revised its 

ricing policy, discounting all 
ooks 10%. 

Explained Martin: “There's 
more profit to be made that 
way, because the department is 
rack-jobbed with safe, stan- 
dard margins. When we lower 
prices, although we are taking a 
bigger risk, we get better turns 


Agreement Is Reached on $o1M Sale 
Of 16 Jewelcor Showrooms to Wilson 


WILKES-BARRE, Pa.— 
Jewelcor and H. J. Wilson at 
presstime reached agreement 
on Jewelcor’s sale of 16 show- 
rooms and a warehouse to Wil- 
son for approximately $51 mil- 
lion, $40 million of en Fs is for 
inventory. 

Jewelcor this month plans to 
hold eee tat 
sales in its Plantation and West 
Hollywood, Fla., showrooms, 
two of the three units in the 
Sunshine State that aren’t 
being sold to Wilson. The West 
Palm Beach, Fla., showroom, 
so far, is scheduled to remain in 
operation. 

The sale of the 16 showrooms 
in five Sunbelt States is part of 
Jewelcor’s plan to restructure 
its —— to focus on the 
Northeast, where it will have 10 
of its remaining 11 on-going 
showrooms and where the com- 


pany plans to build an ethanol 
ame plant. (See DSN, Sept. 
22, P. 3.) 

A Jewelcor executive added 
that the sale of the showrooms 
would also reduce the firm’s di- 
rect competition with other 
showroom operations so that 
the company would be in a bet- 
ter position to interest other 
catalogers in using the book 
published by the Jewelcor Mer- 
chandising catalog coordinating 
division. 

Wilson’s purchase of the 
showrooms would tie in with 
the company’s efforts to expand 
in the Sunbelt where it has 
most of its 47 units. The acquisi- 
tion would put Wilson into two 
new states, California and Ari- 
zona, while expanding its eq- 
uity in Texas, Alabama and 
Florida.

Target Completes Ayr-Way Buy 
After Exhaustive Site Inspections 


MINNEAPOLIS—Target 
has completed its purchase of 
the Indianapolis-based Ayr- 
Way chain for an undisclosed 
amount of cash. 

An agreement in principle 
between Dayton Hudson, Tar- 
get’s parent, and Stephens Inc., 
the Arkansas-based invest- 
ment firm which owned 71% of 
Ayr-Way’s stock, was first an- 
nounced July 15. At that time, 
industry sources put the pur- 
chase price at between $25 mil- 
lion and $30 million. 

Target attributed the delay 
in consummation of the deal to 
an exhaustive on-site inspec- 


tion of the Ayr-Way stores. A 
rumored FTC investigation of 


the takeover never mate- 
rialized, “as far as we know,” a 
chain spokesman told DSN. 
With the addition of the Ayr- 
Way stores, which will operate 
under the Target/Ayr-Way ban- 
ner for the next year and a half, 
Target will increase its opera- 


that use minimum footage. 
Their hard lines effort is 
focused on higher-priced items 
such as console TVs. 

While discounters and con- 
ventional department stores 
went different ways in these 
three financial areas, the two 
types of retailers followed simi- 
lar trends in four other areas— 
turns, out of stock, leased de- 
partment sales percentage, 
and sales-to-assets ratio—and 
showed markedly distinct re- 
sults in eash sales as a percent- 
age of total volume. 

Both types of retailers im- 
proved turns slightly, discount- 
ers by 1.2% to 3.46 and conven- 
tional department stores by 
2.1% to 3.34.

Thirty-one of the Ayr-Way 
stores are in Indiana; the oth-

Ohio. 
Industry watchers point out 
that the takeover, coinciding as 
it does with the massive remod- 
eling and upgrading efforts of 
K mart’s nine stores in that 
market, sets the stage for an 
interesting merchandise battle 
in the coming months. 
Current plans call for the 
Ayr-Way staff to remain intact 
and for president Ronald G. 
Mayer to continue mending the 
chain, which has now become 
an operating region of Target 
Stores. 

Fred Schmid, formerly direc- 
tor of store operations for Tar- 
get, has been named vice presi- 
dent and regional manager of 
the Ayr-Way operating region. 
He will be responsible for store 
operations activities and will 
report to Mayer.

Zodys Remodels Flagship Store, Adds 20,000 Ft. 


LOS ANGELES—With an 
80,000-sq.-ft. sales floor, Zodys 
Hollywood flagship had been 
operating in “cramped quar- 
ters,” according to chain presl- 
dent Arnold Suval. A 20,000- 
sq.-ft. addition and a total re- 
modeling—both highlighted at 
a grand reopening last month— 
should have changed all that. 

Apparel and The Home Store 
benefited most from the addi- 
tional floor space, garnering 
75% of it. The remainder was 
used to widen aisles and com- 
mon areas and to provide room 
for increased merchandise pre- 
sentation. (The chain did not 
add to the mix or change the 

rice points at the store, which 
is its largest volume producer,
